text:
At least six Chinese universities blacklisted by the US government have reported purchasing restricted Nvidia computer chips in recent years, a CNN review of business records found—highlighting Washington’s struggle to control access to the in-demand technology.

Two of those universities, known for close ties to China’s military establishment, reported buying the high-powered chips within just the last few months, revealing a previously unreported scope of institutional purchases.

While the deals—made through obscure Chinese sellers—involved relatively small quantities of older processors rather than industrial-scale, cutting-edge systems, they show how widely available restricted Nvidia chips remain inside China even to high-risk buyers.

“Once these chips are in China, it’s very hard for anyone to be able to stop their sale,” said Kate Koren, a former US export control official now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

The findings are likely to feature in this week’s high-stakes meeting between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, coming days after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following revelations of an affair with a woman whose former firm is suspected of smuggling chips into China.

Speaking last week, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning rejected US national security arguments, stating Beijing firmly opposes Washington “overstretching the concept of national security and formulating various types of discriminatory lists to go after Chinese institutions.”

CNN’s review examined nearly 300 public procurement notices collected in a commercial database—excluding overseas data-center rentals—and found most involved export-controlled Nvidia chips such as the A100, A800, H100, H200, and H800, with universities accounting for nearly 80% of the 90 buyers reviewed and research institutes nearly 14%.

Most notably, records show Harbin Institute of Technology bought an A100 chip in September for about $7,000, while Northwestern Polytechnical University bought four H200 chips in September and October for roughly $240,000 total.

Both schools belong to the “Seven Sons of National Defense,” a group of universities closely linked to the People’s Liberation Army where Decision Tree Research CEO Gregory Allen noted much of China’s military AI investment begins.

The notices offered scant supply-chain details beyond showing both schools bought from little-known domestic firms rather than Nvidia—even though US officials are highly unlikely to approve case-by-case H200 sales to blacklisted entities, and banned A100 chips may have come from pre-2022 stockpiles, according to Koren.

A third “Seven Sons” school, Beihang University—blacklisted since 2001—also reported more than a dozen purchases between 2022 and 2024, mostly of A100 and A800 chips, alongside three other Entity List universities that reported high-end Nvidia purchases in recent years.

Because Chinese institutions often post procurement notices locally or remove them quickly, the records are likely incomplete, and CNN could not verify whether the hardware was delivered in every case.

While US rules require chipmakers to verify end users, Koren noted smuggling networks rely on shell companies, multi-country hops, currency shifts, and falsified documents—leaving officials in a constant struggle where “despite your best efforts, some will get through.”

text:
THE HEDGE FUND THAT CRIED CHINA: A REBUTTAL TO HUNTERBROOK

Hunterbrook is not a newsroom. It is a hedge fund that bought itself a newsroom, and the distinction matters more today than on any day since this outfit started publishing, because this morning the fund and the newsroom worked the same trade from both ends. At 10:27 AM Eastern, Hunterbrook Media published a lengthy piece titled "AMD Has Its Own China Problem." At the top of that piece, in the disclosure language the authors clearly hoped would be skimmed past on the way to the scary headline, sits the only sentence in the entire article that is beyond dispute: based on Hunterbrook Media's reporting, Hunterbrook Capital, the investment fund under common control with the publication, is short Advanced Micro Devices, and long a basket of the securities of AMD's competitors. The newsroom wrote the fear. The fund was positioned to collect on it. The stock obliged within minutes, swinging from an intraday high of $555.01 to a low of $470.56, a range of more than eighty-four dollars in a single session, erasing tens of billions of dollars of shareholder value before lunch. Nothing about that sequence is journalism. It is a trade with a bibliography.

Begin where Hunterbrook itself ends, because the most honest sentence in the piece is the one its authors buried in the middle of it, surrounded by enough ominous scaffolding that a hurried reader might never notice the building has no floor. "Hunterbrook does not know how IEIT obtained AMD's code, or whether AMD or anyone else held a license to supply it." Sit with that sentence for a moment, because it dissolves everything around it. The investigation does not know how the allegedly sensitive material changed hands. It does not know whether the transfer was licensed, and licenses in this area are confidential by design, a fact Hunterbrook's own quoted expert, former Commerce Department undersecretary William Reinsch, states plainly in the piece itself when he cautions that the existence of a license requirement does not mean a license was denied, and that companies do in fact obtain them. It does not establish a single export violation, a single illegal shipment, a single controlled chip delivered to a single blacklisted buyer. Reuters, summarizing the affair for the wire, included the clause that should have been every headline: it could not independently verify the report. What Hunterbrook published was not a finding of wrongdoing. It was an arrangement of true, mostly old, mostly publicly available facts, assembled in the order most likely to frighten a momentum crowd, released at the hour of maximum fragility, by authors who profit directly and immediately if the fright works. That is not an investigation. That is a short and distort campaign with unusually good footnotes.

Consider the supposed smoking gun, because once it is described accurately the entire piece deflates. The gun is firmware. AMD designs processors, and for a processor to wake up inside a server it needs initialization code, the low-level instructions that bring the chip and the board to life before any operating system loads. AMD's version of this code for its current EPYC server processors is called TurinPI, and server manufacturers incorporate it into their BIOS, the firmware they ship and maintain for their machines. Hunterbrook's discovery is that IEIT Systems, a Chinese server maker placed on the Commerce Department's Entity List in March 2025, has continued to publish BIOS updates containing newer versions of this code, and that three other server companies with historical ties to IEIT publish nearly identical firmware. Now consider what the piece works very hard to keep you from understanding. EPYC processors are not controlled items under United States export law. AMD sells them into China legally, today, openly, and lists China among the markets for its flagship EPYC 9965 in its own product materials. The code at issue exists to boot a product the United States government permits to be sold in the country where IEIT operates. The piece never alleges, because it cannot, that a single controlled AI accelerator was shipped to IEIT or to anyone else on the Entity List. The entire firmware narrative is about support software for a legal product line, and the sinister framing depends entirely on the reader never learning that distinction.

Consider also how this supposedly clandestine material was obtained by the investigators. They downloaded it from IEIT's public support website, where it sits with release notes and version histories, available to any system administrator, competitor, journalist or short seller with an internet connection. Technology that is being smuggled does not get posted on a public download page. Every major server maker on earth, from Dell to Supermicro to Lenovo, publishes firmware updates in exactly this way, because that is how the installed base of machines gets security patches and stability fixes. IEIT sold AMD-based servers legally for years before its listing. Those machines exist, they are running, and the updates Hunterbrook catalogs, several of which contain security fixes, are the ordinary maintenance traffic of an installed fleet. The piece even notes, without absorbing its own observation, that one IEIT build contained a fix for a flaw AMD had not yet publicly disclosed, and invites the reader to find that sinister, when the mundane explanation is the one the entire industry runs on: AMD distributes its reference code to the manufacturers who build on its platform, on AMD's schedule, because that is the only way the platform functions. A leak theory requires evidence of a leak. Hunterbrook has a download page.

The pattern repeats through every supporting allegation, each of which turns out on inspection to be a disclosure AMD made itself, years ago, in documents filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission and read by every analyst who covers the stock. The piece reports, as though it were a discovery, that AMD booked $67 million of licensing income in 2025 traced to two Chinese chip ventures blacklisted in 2019. Those ventures are the Hygon arrangement, a joint venture structure AMD entered in 2016 to license first-generation Zen technology into the Chinese server market, a deal announced publicly at the time, dissected in the financial press for years, and described in AMD's own filings ever since. The licensing income is the tail of a decade-old, fully disclosed agreement covering technology generations behind anything AMD sells today, an agreement that predates the 2019 listings it is now being used to imply something about. Likewise the Tongfu Microelectronics material, presented with Lisa Su photographed at a factory launch as though attendance were evidence, describes assembly and test joint ventures formed in 2016, in which AMD holds a 15 percent stake, whose operations in Suzhou and Penang appear in every annual report AMD has filed for a decade, including the $100 million loan Hunterbrook cites, which is sitting in AMD's financial statements where AMD put it. A reporter who finds a fact in a company's 10-K has not uncovered anything. He has read the same document the company's shareholders were given, and the decision to narrate old disclosures in the tone of revelation is an editorial choice with a position attached to it.

The revenue numbers receive the same treatment. Yes, AMD billed $7.75 billion to customers in China and Hong Kong in fiscal 2025, 22.4 percent of revenue, a figure from, once again, AMD's own annual report. What the piece buries is the composition. That figure is a billing address, not a product category, and it is overwhelmingly made up of processors and client chips that face no export restrictions whatsoever, the same categories AMD and Intel have sold into China through every administration of the last thirty years. The one product line that is controlled, the China-specific MI308 AI accelerator, tells the real story, and it is the opposite of the one Hunterbrook is selling. When Washington imposed a license requirement on the MI308 in April 2025, AMD immediately took roughly $800 million in inventory charges and told shareholders exactly what happened. When licenses were subsequently granted, AMD shipped approximately $390 million of the product in the fourth quarter of 2025, under the United States government's own licensing process and under the administration's publicly reported expectation of a 15 percent revenue share on those licensed sales. That is what compliance looks like from the inside: a charge taken in the open, a license obtained, a shipment made under the government's terms. The growth story Hunterbrook claims rests on restricted chips is in fact the most American demand story in the market, the multi-year capacity commitments of Meta, OpenAI, Microsoft and Oracle, hyperscalers building in the United States, whose orders fill AMD's data center segment and whose names are on the earnings calls anyone can read. Singapore gets the same billing-address fallacy, $4.28 billion of invoices routed through the region's standard commercial hub presented as though it were $4.28 billion of hardware evaporating into the mainland, followed by a new licensing rule that is described in the language of a blockade when it is, on its face, a licensing requirement of the kind AMD already operates under across its business.

Then there is the timing, and the timing is where the piece stops being merely misleading and starts being a legitimate subject for regulators. AMD had risen roughly 45 percent in the five sessions through November 12, carried by the collapse of confidence in Nvidia, whose chief executive resigned on November 12 amid a scandal that has drawn a Senate inquiry and genuine, specific, evidenced allegations about diverted hardware. Anthropic's initial public offering priced today, guaranteeing the full attention of every technology investor alive. Into that exact moment, maximum altitude, maximum attention, maximum ambient fear about China and chips, Hunterbrook released a piece whose own text concedes it cannot establish wrongdoing, and released a companion attack the same morning through The Bear Cave, a newsletter Hunterbrook owns, authored in part by one of the same writers, pressing a second front about circular financing. One fund. Two publications. One disclosed short position, and an undisclosed amount of money made or lost on the day depending on how the position was traded around publication. The article even pauses to sneer that Nvidia's reported China revenue share is probably understated, an evidence-free aside aimed at the competitor its fund is long a basket of, which tells you everything about the editorial standards being applied when the position runs the other way. This is the architecture the securities laws exist to examine. Short selling is lawful and useful. Short selling coordinated with captive media, timed for maximum panic, built from decade-old disclosures and publicly posted firmware, and wrapped around an admission that the authors do not know whether any law was broken, is the fact pattern the phrase short and distort was coined for.

AMD's response deserves to be quoted in full because its brevity is the sound of a company that knows what its compliance record contains. The claims, AMD said, "misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships. AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity." Against that, Hunterbrook offers the fact that AMD asked for more than a day to answer a sprawling set of questions from a publication owned by a fund short its stock, and treats the missed deadline as an implication. Any investor who has watched this genre of report knows that implication is doing the work evidence declined to do.

So here is the call, made plainly and for the record. The Securities and Exchange Commission should open an investigation into Hunterbrook, into the coordination between Hunterbrook Capital and Hunterbrook Media, into when the short position was established and at what size, into how it was traded in the sessions before and after publication, into the decision to publish on the morning of a major sector IPO at the peak of a five-session run, and into whether a publication that concedes it cannot establish a violation, issued by an entity positioned to profit from the resulting decline, complies with the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws. If Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security believes an export violation exists anywhere in this record, it has subpoena power, licensing records and enforcement staff, and it should use them, and if it finds a violation the market should hear it from the government, in a filing, with evidence. What the market should not accept is a regime in which any fund can rent the credibility of journalism, aim it at a company whose real offense is winning share from a wounded competitor, and be paid by the panic before a single regulator has read a single document.

I hold AMD shares, and I am disclosing that the way Hunterbrook disclosed its short, at the top rather than the bottom, because the reader is entitled to weigh every argument in this essay against the interest of the person making it. Mine is long, patient and based on the filings. I have read the same 10-K Hunterbrook read, and I found in it a company that discloses its China billing, its licensing tail, its packaging ventures and its export charges in plain sight, which is an odd way to run a smuggling operation. If a regulator produces evidence of an actual violation, I will change my mind in public, because that is how evidence is supposed to work. Until then, the only established facts in this story are a fund, a position, a publication timed like a weapon, and a sentence in the middle of it that gives the whole thing away. They do not know. They published anyway. They got paid. Investigate that.

The Sell report is barely two days old, yet its most revealing opportunities come from opposite corners of the market. $UNH, $HUM and $CNC fell sharply following Tuesday's Sells as Washington proposed recovering Medicare Advantage overpayments going back years. Meanwhile, Sells in $OKTA and $CRWD ran into a cybersecurity rally sparked by $PANW's stronger outlook. Insurers faced the possibility of paying for the past; cybersecurity companies were being rewarded for protecting the future.
Palo Alto's November 16 Buy tells the other side of that story. Three days later, it was reaching new highs even as much of the market fell. The new Sell signals in its industry struggled precisely where a fresh Buy was finding strength.
$APP offers an especially revealing example of how both directions create opportunities. Its October 29 Buy arrived before record earnings, and the advance continued for 18 days before peaking November 16. Much of that gain remains, while a November 17 Sell caught part of the subsequent retreat. Two signals, different directions, both finding opportunities as the story changed.
$U's late-October Buy followed another path. Strong earnings and takeover speculation carried shares to their November 9 high, 11 days after the signal. Ten days have passed since that peak. The stock has surrendered some excitement but remains above its Buy price, probably because improving operations offer support even without a completed acquisition.
The AI infrastructure Buys expose a less forgiving pattern. $AXTI, $NBIS and $CRDO reached their highs quickly, only to fall below their original Buy prices. AXT faced China export uncertainty despite rising demand for optical components. Nebius faced growing concern over the enormous cost and delays of building AI computing capacity. Their early highs didn't survive the market's reassessment.
Yet $ANET and $COHR retained gains from their Buys despite the broader technology selloff. Even within AI infrastructure, strong demand wasn't enough to protect every stock equally.
The Buy table has weeks of history; the Sell table has only two days. That difference matters. The most fascinating comparisons are between the signals that found quick opportunities, the highs that endured, and the gains that vanished. text:
⚠️ Palmer Luckey says Washington has the Nvidia-China debate backwards. Beijing doesn't want Chinese AI companies buying American chips, he argues. It wants them dependent on Chinese technology.

“China doesn't want Nvidia to sell GPUs to Chinese companies,” the Anduril founder says, pointing to approximately 600,000 Nvidia H200 processors reportedly stranded in Hong Kong because Beijing has withheld import permits.

His argument exposes a distinction often overlooked in Washington: Chinese technology companies want access to the most advanced American processors, while Beijing is trying to build a domestic semiconductor industry that can eventually operate independently of US suppliers.

That tension now intersects with a major congressional disclosure.

On Thursday, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast released confidential Commerce Department records showing that Washington had approved exports of 879,868 Nvidia and AMD AI chips to Chinese companies as of May 11, 2026.

The approvals included 150,000 chips for Tencent, 75,000 for Alibaba, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD. All four appear on the Pentagon's list of Chinese military companies.

The scale is considerably larger than the approved total. Companies had applied for licenses covering 3,444,160 chips, including Nvidia H200 and AMD MI325X processors.

Crucially, every approved entry in the May records was marked “approved, not shipped.” The documents establish what Washington authorized, not how many processors ultimately reached China.

The disclosures also raise questions about intermediaries. Nvidia applications identified companies including Maginfra, Beijing New Matrix Information Technologies and ZTE Kangxun Telecom as potential participants in installations inside China. Congressional investigators cited concerns that some intermediaries could facilitate chip diversion, while the applications assessed diversion risks as low.

Luckey's argument offers a different interpretation of the controversy surrounding former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Selling American processors to Chinese companies could strengthen those firms in the short term while simultaneously undermining Beijing's longer-term goal of semiconductor independence.

That does not resolve Washington's national security concerns. Access to advanced American computing power can accelerate Chinese AI development regardless of whether Beijing ultimately wants to eliminate that dependence.

The contradiction runs through both countries' policies. Washington approved exports of hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips while warning about China's military technology ambitions. Beijing restricted access to processors that its own leading technology companies wanted to purchase.

With Nvidia under congressional scrutiny and lawmakers pushing for tighter export controls, the dispute now reaches beyond Jensen Huang's leadership and the company's commercial interests.

It goes to the central strategic question in the US-China technology competition: whether selling advanced American chips to Chinese companies preserves US technological leverage or accelerates the development of a rival capable of challenging it. https://t.co/RfX7KmbU0U

🚶🏾‍➡️ 
                   “Winston Stunner Samuel”

In the wake of an acquittal that shook the islands, a searing indictment of the Police Service rose like smoke from the ruins of justice. Winston “Stunners” Samuel, once a celebrated national footballer whose feet danced with the ball as if possessed by destiny itself, stood free of the murder charge that had stained his name. ⚽ Yet freedom proved a crueler sentence, for the streets had already seized him whole, wrapping their comfort around his talent until escape became a myth whispered only in quieter hours.

He and Junior Estick had been brothers of the pitch, sharing laughter and late-night stories of goals that felt like kingdoms won. 👂 Even after Junior fled to SVG,🇻🇨 their bond endured across the miles; they spoke of uniting again, of reclaiming the joy the game had once given them. Then 2006 arrived and the bars closed around Stunners, shattering every plan. Two years later, on October 10, 2008, while those same bars still held him, Junior’s life was stolen. The family that remained reached across the sea with an offer of vengeance, a ticket home so Stunners might settle the debt. He refused. Loyalty, once simple, became a wound.

By the summer of 2011 the refusal had cost him every remaining shield. Crooked officers who counted Junior’s people as friends arranged the trap. They seized him, delivered him into the hands of his enemies, and cleared the road that led into the mountains. There the officers themselves ended him with their bullets; his body was then cast over the cliff like discarded refuse. His enemies descended, plucked out his eyes, and set them upon the rails above so that, in death, Stunners appeared to watch his own ruin. 😔

From the glory of the national jersey he had become a sharpshooter for the G-Unit gang, a man whose name now trailed both trophies and graves. To the family of Emmanuel Holder, and to every household whose loved one fell by his hand, these words carry only condolences. 💐 No triumph lives in the recounting of such loss.

Father God, these memories press upon me until breath itself feels borrowed. I failed You; I failed them. So many of my people were taken by violence and I could save none. My heart lies broken before You, and still I ask: how can this be, even after they crucified me? Is this the life of the resurrection? I want out, Father. I cannot keep watching lives stolen. I do not abandon the missions You set before me, yet I must ask when this world will finally choose peace. ☮️

Winston “Stunners” Samuel became a warning carved into the mountainside, a tale of talent surrendered to the streets, of loyalty punished by those sworn to uphold law, and of eyes left staring at a body that once ran free. His story demands we refuse the comfort of silence, that we name the crooked paths and the graves they dig, until the islands learn that no jersey, no gun, and no badge can outrun the cost of blood. In the quiet after the cliff, only the question remains: how many more must watch their own ending before we choose a different road.

#TruthOverSilence #JusticeForTheFallen #ChoosePeaceNow  #Washington #Him

text:
MIT Technology Review’s How To series helps you get things done.

Hundreds of Chinese large language models have been released since the government started permitting AI companies to open up their models for the general public to play around with in the summer of 2023. 

For users in the West, finding these Chinese models and trying them out can feel challenging, owing to language barriers and registration requirements. And indeed, there are still hoops to jump through if you don’t have a valid Chinese phone number.

But in fact, a lot of the chatbots support conversations in English and are surprisingly easy to access. Whether you’re just curious to find out how well they perform or want to conduct more serious experiments for work, there are lots of ways to access Chinese LLM-powered chatbots. 

Here’s how anyone can try one out in minutes. 

If you have a Chinese phone number

First of all, if you have a Chinese phone number, there’s little trouble accessing any of the models we describe. In China, a domestic phone number is often a proxy for identity verification, and with it, you can basically access any online service, including AI chatbots. You just go to the model’s website and use the number to register an account. 

In our tests, we found that while some LLMs are accessible for users outside China, a few major ones, including models developed by Huawei, the cybersecurity firm 360, and the Chinese Academy of Sciences, can only be accessed with a Chinese phone number. Unfortunately, if you are outside China, getting a local phone number can be close to impossible. Luckily, there are other ways.

Accessible without a Chinese number

A small number of Chinese AI platforms allow users outside China to access their chatbots directly. All you need to do is sign up, enter your phone number, and then enter the verification code you’ll get in a text message.

These chatbots include Doubao, an AI made by ByteDance that can generate text and images, search the internet, and make a summary of the documents you upload. ChatGLM, a multimodal tool developed by the newly emerged Chinese AI unicorn Zhipu, offers a similar set of features and is also available to non-Chinese numbers. 

Finally, DeepSeek, an AI company that’s barely a year old, is known in the industry for how cheap its model is. (It’s free for casual users but costs $0.14 per million tokens for business users. OpenAI’s similar model, GPT4-Turbo, costs $10 per million tokens.) You can easily test out its text chatbot and coding chatbot on its website by registering with an email address.

Hugging Face

Hugging Face is probably the largest global AI community right now, and it acts as a sort of GitHub for AI. Many open-source LLMs have put their code and applications on Hugging Face’s website. 

Chinese companies are no exception. A few have shared their code on Hugging Face for AI developers to use. Some have also set up a demo on the website so that less tech-savvy people can get instant access to the model without having to write any code of their own. Since Hugging Face doesn’t require a Chinese number to register, it becomes a workaround for testing out many Chinese models.

Most notably, there’s Qwen, an LLM made by Alibaba that recently topped Hugging Face’s Open LLM Leaderboard, a ranking that compares the results of different LLMs and assesses their qualities. Qwen surpassed models made by Meta, Microsoft, and other Chinese peers. You can easily have a text-based conversation with Qwen’s 2.0 version here.

Another Chinese tech giant, Tencent, also uploaded an AI model to Hugging Face; called Hunyuan-DiT, it can generate images based on text prompts. Other models based on the Hunyuan foundation, however, are not accessible on this website.

Yi, also called https://t.co/1rK3HJaqq4, was founded by the famous Taiwanese AI investor Kai-Fu Lee. Yi put a chatbot version of its model (which seems to be down at the moment) and another AI tool that can analyze and understand images on Hugging Face. DeepSeek, the aforementioned startup, put a similar visual analyzing tool on the company’s platform.

ModelScope

In November 2022, Alibaba released a platform called ModelScope. It’s sort of a domestic version of Hugging Face, where the Chinese AI community can congregate, access open-source models, and discuss trade. 

And because ModelScope allows users to register with a non-Chinese number, it acts as another useful workaround for accessing Chinese LLMs. A few Chinese companies—like Baichuan, another buzzy AI startup with Alibaba’s backing—have made their models available on ModelScope for anyone to test.

But what’s most useful on the platform is an “LLM Arena” application put together by Open Compass, an AI lab in Shanghai that works on evaluating different models. The arena, as its name suggests, lets users pit two models against each other and directly compare how they respond to the same prompt. Conveniently, since this application has integrated 11 Chinese models, it offers easy access to several AI tools that are otherwise off limits for non-Chinese users.

Beyond the Chinese models mentioned above, the Arena can generate answers from Baidu’s Ernie Bot and iFlytek’s Spark, as well as Minimax, Moonshot, and InternLM, all of which are heavyweights in the Chinese industry. Right now, you can’t generate photos or upload photos to the models this way, even if the models themselves support these multimodal capabilities. But for comparing text generated by Chinese models, as well as a few Western models like Llama 3 and Cohere’s Command R+, this seems like a very handy tool.

To celebrate the 35th anniversary of HKUST, the University will host the "HKUST 35th Anniversary Impact Fiesta: Explore. Experience. Enjoy" on November 27 and 28 at the AIA Vitality Park on the Central Harbourfront. Bringing HKUST's achievements in innovation and entrepreneurship from its Clear Water Bay campus into the heart of the city, the event invites members of the public to get up close with cutting-edge research. Through a series of interactive exhibitions, STEM workshops, and public lectures, visitors can experience firsthand how HKUST's innovations drive social and economic development, while exploring unlimited possibilities for the future. All proceeds from the event will be donated to the Children’s Cancer Foundation to spread care and support throughout the community.

Upholding its “Can-do” spirit, HKUST has long been committed to advancing frontier technologies and accelerating the translation of research breakthroughs from the laboratory into real-world impact. Beyond offering the public a close-up experience of innovation and technology, this event aims to inspire the younger generation to embrace an innovative mindset. Visitors will witness how HKUST leverages its spirit of exploration, bold creativity, and entrepreneurial culture to contribute to the well-being of Hong Kong, the nation, and the world.

The event features themed areas including the Innovation Showcase, Space Zone, and AI & Robotics Zone, allowing members of the public to experience pioneering technologies spanning aerospace, the low-altitude economy, robotics, AI in healthcare, and sustainability.

The fusion of art and technology promises visitors a truly immersive sensory experience. Returning after its acclaimed debut, "SURREALITY," the world's first large-scale cross-regional Mixed Reality (MR) × AI Art Exhibition, invites visitors into a realm where the virtual and the real converge. Movie enthusiasts can look forward to AI Cinema, which features a curated selection of AI-generated films. Spanning futuristic sci-fi comedies and poignant reflections on family, memory, and the passage of time, the screenings offer insight into how AI is opening up new possibilities in filmmaking.

text:
I am fucking appalled by the audacity of some people.

The past few weeks have been hell. My identity was stolen, my bank accounts compromised, my trading account blew up, and my jewelry business is having its slowest holiday season in 15 years.

I’m doing a TENTH of my normal holiday sales. Last weekend I didn’t even make my booth fee back. In NOVEMBER.

I’ve been surviving on cash in my wallet, $1 in my X account, and $7 in Venmo that I spent on PARKING at the neurologist today while fighting to resolve this nightmare with my bank.

I’m homeschooling two children, making jewelry, running deliveries, helping women move out of difficult situations, and taking whatever work I can find.

My husband spent 20 years in tech, once earning $180,000 a year. After 350+ job applications and two interviews that went nowhere, he’s driving Uber at night.

And I’m DAMN proud of him. There is no shame in honest work.

Something is wrong when two hardworking adults do everything in their power and still barely stay afloat.

Anyway, I digress.

Months ago, I befriended someone on Twitter. We exchanged numbers and talked about trading and life. What I thought was a genuine friendship.

After my trading account blew up, he offered to help me restart. He believed in my abilities and said he’d be overjoyed to help.

I told him trading was the LAST thing on my mind. I’m trying to survive and feed my children.

Tonight, he offered me $5,000.

I was floored and told him I’d be grateful.

Then suddenly he needed to consult his attorney.

“What do you have for collateral?”

Excuse me?

He started asking whether I owned diamonds, Rolex watches, or expensive jewelry.

BRO. WHO THE FUCK DO YOU THINK I AM?

I live below the poverty line supporting a family of four. Almost everything in my house came from estate sales, thrift stores, or the side of the road.

I don’t have a fucking Rolex.

And more importantly, I NEVER ASKED YOU FOR A LOAN.

YOU approached ME.

You offered to help someone struggling, and when I swallowed my pride enough to accept, you treated me like I was taking advantage of you.

He actually told me, “I’m not a sucker.”

Neither am I.

I can’t know his intentions, but the interaction left me sick.

Do you understand how difficult it is for me to admit I need help?

I’ve spent years figuring it out. Working harder. Sleeping less. Making another necklace. Booking another show. Pulling another rabbit out of my ass.

But I’m tired. I’m so fucking tired.

There is a difference between being desperate and dishonest. Between needing help and being a leech. Between offering kindness and using desperation as leverage.

Most of us are closer to homelessness than becoming millionaires.

One layoff. One diagnosis. One fraudulent transaction. One catastrophic expense.

That’s all it takes for life to unravel. And it snowballs FAST.

I’m living it.

My husband works nights. I work days. We’re raising our babies, keeping the lights on, and by the grace of God, we’re still here.

My jewelry business and the boutiques supporting me for 15 years are keeping a roof over our heads and food on our table.

It isn’t glamorous. But it’s a life filled with love.

I have two beautiful children, a hardworking husband, and hands that create beauty from rocks and beads.

I’m still incredibly wealthy where it counts.

So yes, I need help. REAL help. Admitting that publicly is incredibly difficult.

But I don’t need someone dangling money like a carrot. I don’t need another trading account or a lecture about wealth.

I need breathing room.

And if you’re pretending to be someone’s friend to exploit their vulnerability, you’re a special kind of piece of shit.

Stop mistaking desperation for stupidity.

Some of us are just trying to survive.

To everyone working three jobs, raising children, stretching their last $20, wondering how they’ll make it through Christmas…

I see you. I AM you.

And I hope we all find a little breathing room soon. ❤️

text:
When a 200-pound man tried to carjack a 5-foot-5, 130-pound driver in 1946, he expected an easy mark. He had no idea his victim had personally killed 240 enemy soldiers.
The baby-faced driver was Audie Murphy, one of the most decorated American combat soldiers of World War II.
To understand why this encounter went poorly for the larger man, it helps to look at Murphy's recent history. Over the previous three years, Murphy had been wounded three times and earned every military combat award for valor available from the U.S. Army, including the Medal of Honor. He earned that highest honor by jumping onto a burning tank destroyer and using its .50-caliber machine gun to hold off a German infantry company for an hour while taking fire from three sides.
He was accustomed to surviving close-quarters combat against armed, trained soldiers.
When the carjacker tried to violently pull him from his vehicle, Murphy did not freeze or yell. According to accounts of the incident, Murphy went into combat mode. He did not fight like a participant in a chaotic street brawl; he fought with the precision of a soldier neutralizing a threat. Using his military hand-to-hand combat training, Murphy systematically dismantled the attacker.
Despite giving up nearly a foot in height and 80 pounds in weight, Murphy beat the larger man severely, leaving the would-be carjacker battered.
The giant had to be informed exactly who he had tried to victimize. He had picked a physical fight with a veteran who had survived the most intense infantry combat the European theater had to offer.

text:
Every day across Hollywood, scores of film school graduates and production assistants work as script readers. Their job is to find the diamonds in the rough from the 50,000 or so screenplays pitched each year and flag any worth pursuing further. Each script runs anywhere from 100 to 150 pages, and it can take half a day to read one and write up a “coverage,” or summary of the strengths and weaknesses. With only about 50 of these scripts selling in a given year, readers are trained to be ruthless. 

Now the film-focused tech company Cinelytic, which works with major studios like Warner Bros. and Sony Pictures to analyze film budgets and box office potential, aims to offer script feedback with generative AI. 

Today it launched a new tool called Callaia, which amateur writers and professional script readers alike can use to analyze scripts at $79 each. Using AI, it takes Callaia less than a minute to write its own coverage, which includes a synopsis, a list of comparable films, grades for areas like dialogue and originality, and actor recommendations. It also makes a recommendation on whether or not the film should be financed, giving it a rating of “pass,” “consider,” “recommend,” or “strongly recommend.” Though the foundation of the tool is built with ChatGPT’s API, the team had to coach the model on script-specific tasks like evaluating genres and writing a movie’s logline, which summarize the story in a sentence. 

“It helps people understand the script very quickly,” says Tobias Queisser, Cinelytic’s cofounder and CEO, who also had a career as a film producer. “You can look at more stories and more scripts, and not eliminate them based on factors that are detrimental to the business of finding great content.”

The idea is that Callaia will give studios a more analytical way to predict how a script may perform on the screen before spending on marketing or production. But, the company says, it’s also meant to ease the bottleneck that script readers create in the filmmaking process. With such a deluge to sort through, many scripts can make it to decision-makers only if they have a recognizable name attached. An AI-driven tool would democratize the script selection process and allow better scripts and writers to be discovered, Queisser says.

The tool’s introduction may further fuel the ongoing Hollywood debate about whether AI will help or harm its creatives. Since the public launch of ChatGPT in late 2022, the technology has drawn concern everywhere from writers’ rooms to special effects departments, where people worry that it will cheapen, augment, or replace human talent.  

In this case, Callaia’s success will depend on whether it can provide critical feedback as well as a human script reader can. 

That’s a challenge because of what GPT and other AI models are built to do, according to Tuhin Chakrabarty, a researcher who studied how well AI can analyze creative works during his PhD in computer science at Columbia University. In one of his studies, Chakrabarty and his coauthors had various AI models and a group of human experts—including professors of creative writing and a screenwriter—analyze the quality of 48 stories, 12 that appeared in the New Yorker and the rest of which were AI-generated. His team found that the two groups virtually never agreed on the quality of the works. 

“Whenever you ask an AI model about the creativity of your work, it is never going to say bad things,” Chakrabarty says. “It is always going to say good things, because it’s trained to be a helpful, polite assistant.”

Cinelytic CTO Dev Sen says this trait did present a hurdle in the design of Callaia, and that the initial output of the model was overly positive. That improved with time and tweaking. “We don’t necessarily want to be overly critical, but aim for a more balanced analysis that points out both strengths and weaknesses in the script,” he says. 

Vir Srinivas, an independent filmmaker whose film Orders from Above won Best Historical Film at Cannes in 2021, agreed to look at an example of Callaia’s output to see how well the AI model can analyze a script. I showed him what the model made of a 100-page script about a jazz trumpeter on a journey of self-discovery in San Francisco, which Cinelytic provided. Srinivas says that the coverage generated by the model didn’t go deep enough to present genuinely helpful feedback to a screenwriter.

“It’s approaching the script in too literal a sense and not a metaphorical one—something which human audiences do intuitively and unconsciously,” he says. “It’s as if it’s being forced to be diplomatic and not make any waves.”

There were other flaws, too. For example, Callaia predicted that the film would need a budget of just $5 to $10 million but also suggested that expensive A-listers like Paul Rudd would have been well suited for the lead role.

Cinelytic says it’s currently at work improving the actor recommendation component, and though the company did not provide data on how well its model analyzes a given script, Sen says feedback from 100 script readers who beta-tested the model was overwhelmingly positive. “Most of them were pretty much blown away, because they said that the coverages were on the order of, if not better than, the coverages they’re used to,” he says. 

Overall, Cinelytic is pitching Callaia as a tool meant to quickly provide feedback on lots of scripts, not to replace human script readers, who will still read and adjust the tool’s findings. Queisser, who is cognizant that whether AI can effectively write or edit creatively is hotly contested in Hollywood, is hopeful the tool will allow script readers to more quickly identify standout scripts while also providing an efficient source of feedback for writers.

“Writers that embrace our tool will have something that can help them refine their scripts and find more opportunities,” he says. “It’s positive for both sides.”

And look you should still read it at least once, that's where you learn the principles. But a book explains a principle like "intensify the pain" and you can understand it in your head and still not really know how hard to push it or how it's supposed to feel to the person reading it

These promos are those same principles pushed to the extreme, and that's why they teach you more, because on top of understanding the concept you can actually see the copy and feel it. The safe way to write pain on a weight loss offer is something like "carrying extra weight can affect your confidence", and a degenerate promo would write her sucking her stomach in for every picture at her own kid's birthday party and her husband banging 18 year olds cuz he's disgusted with her body. You read that and you can picture it so clearly you kinda cringe for her, which is exactly what the principle is supposed to do to the prospect

Once you've felt the extreme version it's easy to dial it back to whatever your market can handle, but if all you've got is the principle you'll write the safe version every time because you have no idea how far you're even allowed to push

Plus the books were written for print and direct mail way before anybody was scrolling a feed. People today are drowning in content and offers, so their brain literally doesn't register most of what it sees unless it's brutal and sharp enough to shove their pain right in their face and point and laugh at it. That's exactly how the aggressive advertorials are written, which is why they're the better thing to study if you want your copy to actually land with somebody today

A joint pain advertorial or a stock newsletter promo that's been running for months is basically a live case study, because these guys kill anything that isn't printing

Here's what you actually pick up from them

Visceral mechanisms

They make the UMP something you can literally picture happening inside your body. There's a joint supplement advertorial that calls the enzymes chewing up your cartilage an army of microscopic termites eating it like swiss cheese, so every cream and pill you already tried suddenly feels pointless because the termites are still in there eating

Nicknaming the mechanism

They give the thing a name that's vague enough you need to know what it is but physical enough you can picture it, then they keep repeating that name so all the emotion sticks to it. A rodent repellent ad opens on doctors using "these strange pouches" to get rid of disease-spreading rodents, and now you kinda have to find out what's in the pouches

A common enemy

When you're selling to a low emotional state avatar, people who are broke and embarrassed about it, you give them someone else to blame so the shame comes off them. A fin pub promo will tell a guy in his 60s who's way behind on retirement that the reason his savings never got him anywhere is the Fed printing money and quietly eating away at what it's worth, then the newsletter is how regular people are fighting back

Selling the big idea before the product

They sell you the big idea way before they ever show you the product. The long fin pub promos can go pages without mentioning the newsletter because the whole front half is selling you on something like an event coming that's about to wreck people's retirement, so by the time they pitch the subscription it feels like the obvious next move

Why now

Pretty much every fin pub promo gives you a reason this has to happen right now, usually some date coming up like a Fed meeting or a new law kicking in, so waiting even a week feels like losing money

Staying in character

An advertorial is an ad dressed up as an article, and the aggressive ones pick one kind of article and never break character, whether it's a breaking news story, a doctor's warning, a whistleblower or somebody's "I tested them all" review. Picture a gut supplement advertorial written as "I tried 7 gut supplements so you don't have to". The whole page reads like an honest review and rips the other 6 for reasons that sound legit until theirs just happens to come out on top, so the reader never feels sold because the whole time they think they're reading a review

Here's how I'd actually study them

Open the Meta ad library, set the category to all ads and the country to the US, and search the words these guys live on like "doctors" "warning" "strange" or "breakthrough", or just type in a niche like joint pain, gut health, credit score or retirement

Skip anything that just launched. You want ads that started running months ago and are still active, especially the ones where it says a bunch of ads use this creative, because that means they're scaling it

Click the ad and go through everything after it, the advertorial, the VSL or sales page and the order form, and screenshot every step. If you wanna see the upsells you have to buy something, so just grab the cheapest package lol

For fin pub, sign up for a few of the free investing e-letters with a burner email and your inbox turns into a swipe file

Then for every promo write down the same things

The hook

What they call the mechanism

Who they blame

Every "without X" and "even if Y" they throw in, like a credit ad saying "even if you're stuck in the 500s"

What kind of article it's pretending to be

Why it has to be right now

Honestly do that for like 10 promos and you'll start seeing the same handful of moves show up over and over, and those are the ones worth stealing. Steal the moves and leave the claims, because a lot of what's in a joint pain advertorial would get your ad account restricted if you ran it word for word

Then take a couple of those moves and put them on your own offer. Say you sell fitness coaching to dads over 40. Stop calling it "my 12 week program" and give the method a name they can picture, like "the kitchen counter routine", then blame the 6 day bro splits every fitness influencer sells that a guy with a job and kids was never gonna stick to

The ad library is free bro, go start tearing these promos apart

text:
SANOFI IS SAID TO WEIGH A BID. INSMED $INSM ROSE 21%:

Insmed (INSM) at $144.46, +$24.66 / +20.58% on Thursday.

Insmed is still on the Hypergrowth Len5 and on no other Len5 we weigh, and Thursday's close cleared the price we named on November 10 as the first step toward the Momentum Len5. Sanofi (SNY) at $46.06, -$1.06 / -2.25% on Thursday. The Paris drugmaker is weighing a purchase of Insmed, the New Jersey maker of the lung-disease pill Brinsupri, Bloomberg News reported that morning, and no price has been reported. Nasdaq paused trading in Insmed for ten minutes, and the shares ended with their largest one-day gain since August 6. Our post said nothing about a buyer, and all but 31 cents of the gain since it came on Thursday. Belen Garijo, Sanofi's chief executive, wrote three weeks ago that buying companies will be critical to Sanofi. Nicole Schaeffer, Insmed's chief people strategy officer, gave notice of a share sale the same day, and Insmed still has no finance chief.

Insmed is #8 on the Hypergrowth Len5, from #9 in our post. Hypergrowth wants sales multiplying, and Insmed's September-quarter sales of $524.4M were 268% above a year earlier; Thursday's report changed no sales figure. What would knock it off the Hypergrowth Len5 is unchanged: Brinsupri sales under $433M in the December quarter, the low end of Insmed's own forecast. Momentum wants gains over one, three and six months and a price near its high; at $144.46 Insmed is 51.6%, 10.6% and 34.5% above its closes of October 19, August 19 and May 19. It is 31.7% under $211.41, its highest close of the past year, set last December 1. What would put it on the Momentum Len5 is the test in our post, a close above $134.75 that holds through the January 28 FDA decision on Arikayce, its inhaled antibiotic. Thursday's close is $9.71 above that line, with ten weeks left to hold it. Deep-Value and Special-Situations wants an event the market has mispriced, and a report with no offer gives no price to set $144.46 against. What would put Insmed on the Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5 is still the test in our November 2 post, an Arikayce approval the shares fail to move on. Insmed is on neither the Quality-Value nor the Income Len5, and its loss keeps it off the Quality Len5 until a full year ends in profit.

Bloomberg cited people it did not name. Reuters, relaying the report by 10:25am ET, wrote that Sanofi is "speaking with advisers as it studies a potential deal for Insmed" and that "any deal could still be weeks away." Neither company immediately answered Reuters's requests for comment, and Insmed has put out no release on it. Graig Suvannavejh, an analyst at Mizuho, told clients he does not believe Insmed is ready to sell itself, The Fly reported.

Thursday by the clock, each against Wednesday's $119.80 close:
- 10:03am ET: $121.59, 1.5% above.
- 10:05am ET: $128.03, 6.9% above, when Nasdaq's automatic pause for fast-moving stocks began.
- 10:15am ET: trading resumed at $145.00 and reached $148.94 within the minute, the day's high.
- About 10:35am ET: $136.30, the low after the pause, 13.8% above.
- 4:00pm ET: $144.46, the highest close since April 22.
About 14.4M shares traded, six times the daily average of the past two weeks. The gain added about $5.4B to Insmed's market value.

Thursday's close is $24.97 a share, or 20.9%, above the $119.49 in our post. SPDR S&P Biotech ETF (XBI) at $144.12, -$0.92 / -0.63% on Thursday. The biotech fund lost 6.5% from our post through Wednesday while Insmed held its price. Buyers now pay about 17 times this year's forecast sales, from 14 in our post.

Dupixent, Sanofi's drug for eczema and asthma, brought in 5.7B euros in the September quarter, about two-fifths of Sanofi's sales. Garijo wrote in the October 30 results release that Sanofi's priority is protecting profit once copies of Dupixent can be sold. "Business development and M&A will be critical," she wrote; M&A is the buying of other companies. Insmed's market value at Thursday's close, about $31.7B, is more than a quarter of Sanofi's. Sanofi's Paris shares were already 2.6% lower at 10:00am ET, before Insmed jumped, and closed 2.9% lower. Sanofi is on none of the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es; Hypergrowth wants sales multiplying, and Sanofi's rose 14.3% last quarter, currency swings left out.

Schaeffer's notice to securities regulators covers 101,100 shares she received on Thursday through Insmed's employee stock program. It dates her selling plan to May 11, about six months before the report. The notice gives no sale price, and the sale may already be done. Insmed has named no finance chief in the 20 days since Sara Bonstein left on October 30.

A report with no offer behind it added $24.66 a share, and no sales figure changed. Insmed's managers next present on December 1 at 9:10am ET, at an investor conference in Coral Gables, Florida. The FDA decides on Arikayce by January 28, and the December quarter, tentatively reported February 18, has to show at least $433M of Brinsupri sales to stay inside Insmed's forecast. Neither company has set a date to speak about the report, and the last close before it was $119.80.

Not investment advice.

That was the clear boundary I set the day she got engaged, knowing how badly she wanted a huge celebration.

It sounded completely fair to me, until the demands started rolling in:

Her fiancé's parents offered $8,000, and the couple said they would cover whatever was left.

The original wedding plan was for 120 guests. The venue, catering, decorations, and photography were arranged within the budget they had discussed.

Then, three weeks before the wedding, my daughter sent me a revised guest list.

She had added 45 people.

Some were distant relatives, former classmates, her fiancé's coworkers, and people I had never heard her mention before.

I reminded her that the venue charged per guest and the extra invitations would increase the catering bill considerably.

She said she had already promised those people invitations and wasn't going to embarrass herself by uninviting them.

The additional catering cost came to $4,950. There were also extra tables, chairs, drinks, and transportation arrangements.

I told her I wasn't adding another dollar to my contribution.

text:
The following morning, I discovered that Patricia had contacted the grain storage manager directly. She instructed him to release the 15,000 bushels to her friends and told him that her husband had approved the sale.

The grain was loaded onto trucks before I even knew what was happening.

When I confronted the owner, he admitted that he had allowed his wife to arrange the transaction.

He told me the farm could afford the difference and accused me of embarrassing his family by challenging her authority.

I showed him the original buyer's offer and the financial calculation. He glanced at the paperwork and pushed it back across the desk.

His response was, "Not every business decision needs to be about squeezing every dollar out of people."

I was speechless.

A few days later, Patricia arrived at the farm with one of her friends. They walked around the equipment yard, took photographs beside our new combine harvester, and joked about how cheap the soybeans had been.

One of them even said the farm was lucky to have generous owners.

At the end of the month, I was informed that my position was being eliminated because the company wanted to reduce management expenses.

My replacement was the owner's nephew, who had recently graduated from college and had never managed a commercial farming operation.

Six months later, I heard that the farm had taken out a $175,000 operating loan to cover expenses after a difficult sales season.

Patricia's friends had already purchased their soybeans at the discounted price.

The owner still attended agricultural business events, proudly describing the farm as a family enterprise.

And the people who worked through planting season, repaired machinery, managed the harvest, and kept the operation running were left out of the family's little business arrangement.

authorBio: Digital Content Creator • Entertainment • Daily posts | Every post is a scene.

text:
Running a large commercial farm in the United States leaves zero room for error.

I managed operations across massive acres of corn, soybeans, and wheat with 24 full time workers and a wave of seasonal hands every planting and harvest.

Everything depends on timing, weather, and trust, until one season tested all three.

My salary was $86,000 a year, and I was responsible for purchasing seed, organizing equipment, supervising field operations, monitoring storage, and negotiating crop sales.

The farm had been profitable for several years. We had invested heavily in modern harvesting equipment, grain storage facilities, and irrigation systems.

Then the owner's wife, Patricia, decided she wanted to become involved in the business.

She had never managed a farm, but she suddenly started attending management meetings and contacting our grain buyers.

At first, I didn't mind. The owner had every right to involve his family in the company.

The problem began after our autumn harvest.

We had approximately 42,000 bushels of soybeans ready for sale. Based on the market prices and the quality of the crop, I had negotiated a deal with a commercial buyer willing to pay around $12.40 per bushel.

That would have brought the farm approximately $520,800.

Before I finalized the agreement, Patricia called me into the office.

She explained that three of her friends wanted to purchase some of the soybeans for their own agricultural businesses. She instructed me to sell them 15,000 bushels at $6.50 per bushel.

I thought she was joking.

The market price was nearly twice that amount.

I explained that selling such a large quantity below market value would cost the farm almost $90,000 compared with the offer I had already negotiated.

She told me her friends were important people and that the farm should support their businesses.

I refused to approve the transaction.

text:
We often take the internet for granted. It’s an ocean of information at our fingertips—and it simply works. But this system relies on swarms of “crawlers”—bots that roam the web, visit millions of websites every day, and report what they see. This is how Google powers its search engines, how Amazon sets competitive prices, and how Kayak aggregates travel listings. Beyond the world of commerce, crawlers are essential for monitoring web security, enabling accessibility tools, and preserving historical archives. Academics, journalists, and civil societies also rely on them to conduct crucial investigative research.  

Crawlers are endemic. Now representing half of all internet traffic, they will soon outpace human traffic. This unseen subway of the web ferries information from site to site, day and night. And as of late, they serve one more purpose: Companies such as OpenAI use web-crawled data to train their artificial intelligence systems, like ChatGPT. 

Understandably, websites are now fighting back for fear that this invasive species—AI crawlers—will help displace them. But there’s a problem: This pushback is also threatening the transparency and open borders of the web, that allow non-AI applications to flourish. Unless we are thoughtful about how we fix this, the web will increasingly be fortified with logins, paywalls, and access tolls that inhibit not just AI but the biodiversity of real users and useful crawlers.

A system in turmoil 

To grasp the problem, it’s important to understand how the web worked until recently, when crawlers and websites operated together in relative symbiosis. Crawlers were largely undisruptive and could even be beneficial, bringing people to websites from search engines like Google or Bing in exchange for their data. In turn, websites imposed few restrictions on crawlers, even helping them navigate their sites. Websites then and now use machine-readable files, called robots.txt files, to specify what content they wanted crawlers to leave alone. But there were few efforts to enforce these rules or identify crawlers that ignored them. The stakes seemed low, so sites didn’t invest in obstructing those crawlers.

But now the popularity of AI has thrown the crawler ecosystem into disarray.

As with an invasive species, crawlers for AI have an insatiable and undiscerning appetite for data, hoovering up Wikipedia articles, academic papers, and posts on Reddit, review websites, and blogs. All forms of data are on the menu—text, tables, images, audio, and video. And the AI systems that result can (but not always will) be used in ways that compete directly with their sources of data. News sites fear AI chatbots will lure away their readers; artists and designers fear that AI image generators will seduce their clients; and coding forums fear that AI code generators will supplant their contributors. 

In response, websites are starting to turn crawlers away at the door. The motivator is largely the same: AI systems, and the crawlers that power them, may undercut the economic interests of anyone who publishes content to the web—by using the websites’ own data. This realization has ignited a series of crawler wars rippling beneath the surface.

The fightback

Web publishers have responded to AI with a trifecta of lawsuits, legislation, and computer science. What began with a litany of copyright infringement suits, including one from the New York Times, has turned into a wave of restrictions on use of websites’ data, as well as legislation such as the EU AI Act to protect copyright holders’ ability to opt out of AI training. 

However, legal and legislative verdicts could take years, while the consequences of AI adoption are immediate. So in the meantime, data creators have focused on tightening the data faucet at the source: web crawlers. Since mid-2023, websites have erected crawler restrictions to over 25% of the highest-quality data. Yet many of these restrictions can be simply ignored, and while major AI developers like OpenAI and Anthropic do claim to respect websites’ restrictions, they’ve been accused of ignoring them or aggressively overwhelming websites (the major technical support forum iFixit is among those making such allegations).

Now websites are turning to their last alternative: anti-crawling technologies. A plethora of new startups (TollBit, ScalePost, etc), and web infrastructure companies like Cloudflare (estimated to support 20% of global web traffic), have begun to offer tools to detect, block, and charge nonhuman traffic. These tools erect obstacles that make sites harder to navigate or require crawlers to register.

These measures still offer immediate protection. After all, AI companies can’t use what they can’t obtain, regardless of how courts rule on copyright and fair use. But the effect is that large web publishers, forums, and sites are often raising the drawbridge to all crawlers—even those that pose no threat. This is even the case once they ink lucrative deals with AI companies that want to preserve exclusivity over that data. Ultimately, the web is being subdivided into territories where fewer crawlers are welcome.

How we stand to lose out

As this cat-and-mouse game accelerates, big players tend to outlast little ones.  Large websites and publishers will defend their content in court or negotiate contracts. And massive tech companies can afford to license large data sets or create powerful crawlers to circumvent restrictions. But small creators, such as visual artists, YouTube educators, or bloggers, may feel they have only two options: hide their content behind logins and paywalls, or take it offline entirely. For real users, this is making it harder to access news articles, see content from their favorite creators, and navigate the web without hitting logins, subscription demands, and captchas each step of the way.

Perhaps more concerning is the way large, exclusive contracts with AI companies are subdividing the web. Each deal raises the website’s incentive to remain exclusive and block anyone else from accessing the data—competitor or not. This will likely lead to further concentration of power in the hands of fewer AI developers and data publishers. A future where only large companies can license or crawl critical web data would suppress competition and fail to serve real users or many of the copyright holders.

Put simply, following this path will shrink the biodiversity of the web. Crawlers from academic researchers, journalists, and non-AI applications may increasingly be denied open access. Unless we can nurture an ecosystem with different rules for different data uses, we may end up with strict borders across the web, exacting a price on openness and transparency. 

While this path is not easily avoided, defenders of the open internet can insist on laws, policies, and technical infrastructure that explicitly protect noncompeting uses of web data from exclusive contracts while still protecting data creators and publishers. These rights are not at odds. We have so much to lose or gain from the fight to get data access right across the internet. As websites look for ways to adapt, we mustn’t sacrifice the open web on the altar of commercial AI.

Shayne Longpre is a PhD Candidate at MIT, where his research focuses on the intersection of AI and policy. He leads the Data Provenance Initiative.

text:
Anyone who crammed for exams in college knows that an impressive ability to regurgitate information is not synonymous with critical thinking.

The large language models (LLMs) first publicly released in 2022 were impressive but limited—like talented students who excel at multiple-choice exams but stumble when asked to defend their logic. Today’s advanced reasoning models are more akin to seasoned graduate students who can navigate ambiguity and backtrack when necessary, carefully working through problems with a methodical approach.

As AI systems that learn by mimicking the mechanisms of the human brain continue to advance, we’re witnessing an evolution in models from rote regurgitation to genuine reasoning. This capability marks a new chapter in the evolution of AI—and what enterprises can gain from it. But in order to tap into this enormous potential, organizations will need to ensure they have the right infrastructure and computational resources to support the advancing technology.

The reasoning revolution

“Reasoning models are qualitatively different than earlier LLMs,” says Prabhat Ram, partner AI/HPC architect at Microsoft, noting that these models can explore different hypotheses, assess if answers are consistently correct, and adjust their approach accordingly. “They essentially create an internal representation of a decision tree based on the training data they’ve been exposed to, and explore which solution might be the best.”

This adaptive approach to problem-solving isn’t without trade-offs. Earlier LLMs delivered outputs in milliseconds based on statistical pattern-matching and probabilistic analysis. This was—and still is—efficient for many applications, but it doesn’t allow the AI sufficient time to thoroughly evaluate multiple solution paths.

In newer models, extended computation time during inference—seconds, minutes, or even longer—allows the AI to employ more sophisticated internal reinforcement learning. This opens the door for multi-step problem-solving and more nuanced decision-making.

To illustrate future use cases for reasoning-capable AI, Ram offers the example of a NASA rover sent to explore the surface of Mars. “Decisions need to be made at every moment around which path to take, what to explore, and there has to be a risk-reward trade-off. The AI has to be able to assess, ‘Am I about to jump off a cliff? Or, if I study this rock and I have a limited amount of time and budget, is this really the one that’s scientifically more worthwhile?'” Making these assessments successfully could result in groundbreaking scientific discoveries at previously unthinkable speed and scale.

Reasoning capabilities are also a milestone in the proliferation of agentic AI systems: autonomous applications that perform tasks on behalf of users, such as scheduling appointments or booking travel itineraries. “Whether you’re asking AI to make a reservation, provide a literature summary, fold a towel, or pick up a piece of rock, it needs to first be able to understand the environment—what we call perception—comprehend the instructions and then move into a planning and decision-making phase,” Ram explains.

Enterprise applications of reasoning-capable AI systems

The enterprise applications for reasoning-capable AI are far-reaching. In health care, reasoning AI systems could analyze patient data, medical literature, and treatment protocols to support diagnostic or treatment decisions. In scientific research, reasoning models could formulate hypotheses, design experimental protocols, and interpret complex results—potentially accelerating discoveries across fields from materials science to pharmaceuticals. In financial analysis, reasoning AI could help evaluate investment opportunities or market expansion strategies, as well as develop risk profiles or economic forecasts.

Armed with these insights, their own experience, and emotional intelligence, human doctors, researchers, and financial analysts could make more informed decisions, faster. But before setting these systems loose in the wild, safeguards and governance frameworks will need to be ironclad, particularly in high-stakes contexts like health care or autonomous vehicles.

“For a self-driving car, there are real-time decisions that need to be made vis-a-vis whether it turns the steering wheel to the left or the right, whether it hits the gas pedal or the brake—you absolutely do not want to hit a pedestrian or get into an accident,” says Ram. “Being able to reason through situations and make an ‘optimal’ decision is something that reasoning models will have to do going forward.”

The infrastructure underpinning AI reasoning

To operate optimally, reasoning models require significantly more computational resources for inference. This creates distinct scaling challenges. Specifically, because the inference durations of reasoning models can vary widely—from just a few seconds to many minutes—load balancing across these diverse tasks can be challenging.

Overcoming these hurdles requires tight collaboration between infrastructure providers and hardware manufacturers, says Ram, speaking of Microsoft’s collaboration with NVIDIA, which brings its accelerated computing platform to Microsoft products, including Azure AI.

“When we think about Azure, and when we think about deploying systems for AI training and inference, we really have to think about the entire system as a whole,” Ram explains. “What are you going to do differently in the data center? What are you going to do about multiple data centers? How are you going to connect them?” These considerations extend into reliability challenges at all scales: from memory errors at the silicon level, to transmission errors within and across servers, thermal anomalies, and even data center-level issues like power fluctuations—all of which require sophisticated monitoring and rapid response systems.

By creating a holistic system architecture designed to handle fluctuating AI demands, Microsoft and NVIDIA’s collaboration allows companies to harness the power of reasoning models without needing to manage the underlying complexity. In addition to performance benefits, these types of collaborations allow companies to keep pace with a tech landscape evolving at breakneck speed. “Velocity is a unique challenge in this space,” says Ram. “Every three months, there is a new foundation model. The hardware is also evolving very fast—in the last four years, we’ve deployed each generation of NVIDIA GPUs and now NVIDIA GB200NVL72. Leading the field really does require a very close collaboration between Microsoft and NVIDIA to share roadmaps, timelines, and designs on the hardware engineering side, qualifications and validation suites, issues that arise in production, and so on.”

Advancements in AI infrastructure designed specifically for reasoning and agentic models are critical for bringing reasoning-capable AI to a broader range of organizations. Without robust, accessible infrastructure, the benefits of reasoning models will remain relegated to companies with massive computing resources.

Looking ahead, the evolution of reasoning-capable AI systems and the infrastructure that supports them promises even greater gains. For Ram, the frontier extends beyond enterprise applications to scientific discovery and breakthroughs that propel humanity forward: “The day when these agentic systems can power scientific research and propose new hypotheses that can lead to a Nobel Prize, I think that’s the day when we can say that this evolution is complete.”
