Oh dear. Three paragraphs, three elementary misunderstandings, and not a single argument worth the name.

Firstly, pointing out someone's ignorance of a subject isn't necessarily an ad hominem fallacy. It becomes fallacious when their character is offered as a substitute for addressing their argument. You might wish to learn the distinction before announcing that anyone has lost.

Secondly, most modern Satanists, particularly those associated with the Satanic Temple, don't believe Satan exists, much less worship him. They employ Satan as a literary symbol of rebellion against arbitrary authority and religious dogmatism. Your insistence that they must secretly worship a supernatural being they explicitly reject is merely your theology masquerading as a description of someone else's beliefs.

Thirdly, your assertion that anyone who doesn't worship your particular deity must therefore serve Satan is a splendid example of circular reasoning. It only follows if we first accept the very religious framework whose truth is in dispute.

I'm an atheist. I don't believe in your God, Satan, or the supernatural machinery of your religion. You don't get to assign me an imaginary allegiance simply because your theology struggles to accommodate people who don't share its assumptions.

And perhaps the most amusing part is that you've managed to demonstrate precisely the sort of intellectual carelessness you began by accusing me of exhibiting.

Now, would you care to establish that either of these supernatural beings actually exists, or are we expected to take your theological assertions as evidence of themselves?

This is more than an immigration proposal. It offers an early indication of how Democrats intend to use their newly won congressional power.

The political contrast is striking:

Trump has made tougher immigration enforcement a central priority.

But winning Congress is not the same as controlling Washington.

Democrats won't take control of both chambers until January 2027. Trump will remain president, with the power to veto legislation.

The midterms changed the balance of power. The next question is how much they will change American law.

text:
Silicon Valley begins to change its tune! Musk distances himself from MAGA as tech giants begin reaching out to Democrats
Musk, who once spent more than $400 million supporting Republican candidates, is now reflecting on his political donations and says he is not MAGA. Other technology companies are also adjusting their relationships with Democrats.

Following the U.S. midterm elections, billionaire Elon Musk has begun adjusting his public statements about the Republican Party. He has not only extended goodwill toward Democratic Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, but also expressed regret over spending more than $400 million on Republican candidates, saying that if he could do it again, he would spend less.

Speaking at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, November 18, Musk said he had spent large sums on elections without seeing a corresponding return, adding, “That makes me feel rather stupid.” However, he also added that without that funding, the outcome might have been worse.

Reflecting on huge political donations, Musk emphasizes checks and balances

Musk said one of his goals in supporting Republican candidates was to maintain a balance of power in Washington, rather than have the presidency, Senate and House of Representatives all controlled by the same party.

He explained that he wanted at least one of the presidency, House or Senate to be held by another party. Musk believes U.S. elections are not determined solely by money, and that even large expenditures may have a relatively limited effect on election outcomes.

Musk’s remarks marked a departure from his previous support for the “Make America Great Again” (MAGA) movement. At the summit, he described himself as quite moderate ideologically and said, “I am not MAGA.” He also said he did not fully agree with the Republican Party’s policy positions and believed both parties had positive and negative aspects.

Responding in an interview with NBC News on Thursday, November 19, Trump said Musk was his friend and had “very good intentions.” However, Trump also stressed that MAGA has a clear meaning and that those who stray from that vision would not achieve good results.

Musk extends goodwill toward Texas’ new Democratic governor as the technology industry adjusts its political relationships

Musk also offered a relatively positive assessment of the Democrats’ victory in the Texas gubernatorial election. Markets had previously worried that a Democratic victory in Texas could affect data center construction and the development of artificial intelligence-related companies.

As a Texas resident, Musk said he believed Hinojosa would be a fairly moderate governor, rather than a member of the far left, and expected affairs in the state to continue proceeding normally after she took office.

Other technology industry executives have also begun sending similar signals. Palantir CEO Alex Karp previously told Politico in an interview that he had been a Democrat his entire life, had grown up in a left-leaning environment and believed Palantir’s products were inherently progressive.

This shift in political positioning is also related to the regulatory environment facing technology companies. Democrat-controlled congressional committees are expected to launch investigations and hearings into the technology industry, and the companies concerned are preparing for changes in the balance of political power in Washington.

Meta Platforms (META.O) has also recently been adjusting its political lobbying team. Joel Kaplan, who previously worked in Republican circles and later became Meta’s head of global affairs, has announced his departure. Axios previously reported that Meta had hired former Democratic staffers to strengthen its influence in Washington, while continuing to bring in former Trump administration officials to maintain ties with the White House.

Musk’s latest remarks, along with technology companies’ realignment of their relationships with both parties, show that the midterm election results are prompting Silicon Valley to reassess its political spending and policy relationships.

This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get it in your inbox first, sign up here.

It can be tricky for reporters to get past certain doors, and the door to the International Association of Chiefs of Police conference is one that’s almost perpetually shut to the media. Thus, I was pleasantly surprised when I was able to attend for a day in Boston last month. 

It bills itself as the largest gathering of police chiefs in the United States, where leaders from many of the country’s 18,000 police departments and even some from abroad convene for product demos, discussions, parties, and awards. 

I went along to see how artificial intelligence was being discussed, and the message to police chiefs seemed crystal clear: If your department is slow to adopt AI, fix that now. The future of policing will rely on it in all its forms.

In the event’s expo hall, the vendors (of which there were more than 600) offered a glimpse into the ballooning industry of police-tech suppliers. Some had little to do with AI—booths showcased body armor, rifles, and prototypes of police-branded Cybertrucks, and others displayed new types of gloves promising to protect officers from needles during searches. But one needed only to look to where the largest crowds gathered to understand that AI was the major draw. 

The hype focused on three uses of AI in policing. The flashiest was virtual reality, exemplified by the booth from V-Armed, which sells VR systems for officer training. On the expo floor, V-Armed built an arena complete with VR goggles, cameras, and sensors, not unlike the one the company recently installed at the headquarters of the Los Angeles Police Department. Attendees could don goggles and go through training exercises on responding to active shooter situations. Many competitors of V-Armed were also at the expo, selling systems they said were cheaper, more effective, or simpler to maintain. 

The pitch on VR training is that in the long run, it can be cheaper and more engaging to use than training with actors or in a classroom. “If you’re enjoying what you’re doing, you’re more focused and you remember more than when looking at a PDF and nodding your head,” V-Armed CEO Ezra Kraus told me. 

The effectiveness of VR training systems has yet to be fully studied, and they can’t completely replicate the nuanced interactions police have in the real world. AI is not yet great at the soft skills required for interactions with the public. At a different company’s booth, I tried out a VR system focused on deescalation training, in which officers were tasked with calming down an AI character in distress. It suffered from lag and was generally quite awkward—the character’s answers felt overly scripted and programmatic. 

The second focus was on the changing way police departments are collecting and interpreting data. Rather than buying a gunshot detection tool from one company and a license plate reader or drone from another, police departments are increasingly using expanding suites of sensors, cameras, and so on from a handful of leading companies that promise to integrate the data collected and make it useful. 

Police chiefs attended classes on how to build these systems, like one taught by Microsoft and the NYPD about the Domain Awareness System, a web of license plate readers, cameras, and other data sources used to track and monitor crime in New York City. Crowds gathered at massive, high-tech booths from Axon and Flock, both sponsors of the conference. Flock sells a suite of cameras, license plate readers, and drones, offering AI to analyze the data coming in and trigger alerts. These sorts of tools have come in for heavy criticism from civil liberties groups, which see them as an assault on privacy that does little to help the public. 

Finally, as in other industries, AI is also coming for the drudgery of administrative tasks and reporting. Many companies at the expo, including Axon, offer generative AI products to help police officers write their reports. Axon’s offering, called Draft One, ingests footage from body cameras, transcribes it, and creates a first draft of a report for officers. 

“We’ve got this thing on an officer’s body, and it’s recording all sorts of great stuff about the incident,” Bryan Wheeler, a senior vice president at Axon, told me at the expo. “Can we use it to give the officer a head start?”

On the surface, it’s a writing task well suited for AI, which can quickly summarize information and write in a formulaic way. It could also save lots of time officers currently spend on writing reports. But given that AI is prone to “hallucination,” there’s an unavoidable truth: Even if officers are the final authors of their reports, departments adopting these sorts of tools risk injecting errors into some of the most critical documents in the justice system. 

“Police reports are sometimes the only memorialized account of an incident,” wrote Andrew Ferguson, a professor of law at American University, in July in the first law review article about the serious challenges posed by police reports written with AI. “Because criminal cases can take months or years to get to trial, the accuracy of these reports are critically important.” Whether certain details were included or left out can affect the outcomes of everything from bail amounts to verdicts. 

By showing an officer a generated version of a police report, the tools also expose officers to details from their body camera recordings before they complete their report, a document intended to capture the officer’s memory of the incident. That poses a problem. 

“The police certainly would never show video to a bystander eyewitness before they ask the eyewitness about what took place, as that would just be investigatory malpractice,” says Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst with the ACLU Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project, who will soon publish work on the subject. 

A spokesperson for Axon says this concern “isn’t reflective of how the tool is intended to work,” and that Draft One has robust features to make sure officers read the reports closely, add their own information, and edit the reports for accuracy before submitting them.

My biggest takeaway from the conference was simply that the way US police are adopting AI is inherently chaotic. There is no one agency governing how they use the technology, and the roughly 18,000 police departments in the United States—the precise figure is not even known—have remarkably high levels of autonomy to decide which AI tools they’ll buy and deploy. The police-tech companies that serve them will build the tools police departments find attractive, and it’s unclear if anyone will draw proper boundaries for ethics, privacy, and accuracy. 

That will only be made more apparent in an upcoming Trump administration. In a policing agenda released last year during his campaign, Trump encouraged more aggressive tactics like “stop and frisk,” deeper cooperation with immigration agencies, and increased liability protection for officers accused of wrongdoing. The Biden administration is now reportedly attempting to lock in some of its proposed policing reforms before January. 

Without federal regulation on how police departments can and cannot use AI, the lines will be drawn by departments and police-tech companies themselves.

“Ultimately, these are for-profit companies, and their customers are law enforcement,” says Stanley. “They do what their customers want, in the absence of some very large countervailing threat to their business model.”

Now read the rest of The Algorithm

Deeper Learning

The AI lab waging a guerrilla war over exploitative AI

When generative AI tools landed on the scene, artists were immediately concerned, seeing them as a new kind of theft. Computer security researcher Ben Zhao jumped into action in response, and his lab at the University of Chicago started building tools like Nightshade and Glaze to help artists keep their work from being scraped up by AI models. My colleague Melissa Heikkilä spent time with Zhao and his team to look at the ongoing effort to make these tools strong enough to stop AI’s relentless hunger for more images, art, and data to train on.  

Why this matters: The current paradigm in AI is to build bigger and bigger models, and these require vast data sets to train on. Tech companies argue that anything on the public internet is fair game, while artists demand compensation or the right to refuse. Settling this fight in the courts or through regulation could take years, so tools like Nightshade and Glaze are what artists have for now. If the tools disrupt AI companies’ efforts to make better models, that could push them to the negotiating table to bargain over licensing and fair compensation. But it’s a big “if.” Read more from Melissa Heikkilä.

Bits and Bytes

Tech elites are lobbying Elon Musk for jobs in Trump’s administration

Elon Musk is the tech leader who most has Trump’s ear. As such, he’s reportedly the conduit through which AI and tech insiders are pushing to have an influence in the incoming administration. (The New York Times)

OpenAI is getting closer to launching an AI agent to automate your tasks

AI agents—models that can do tasks for you on your behalf—are all the rage. OpenAI is reportedly closer to releasing one, news that comes a few weeks after Anthropic announced its own. (Bloomberg)

How this grassroots effort could make AI voices more diverse

A massive volunteer-led effort to collect training data in more languages, from people of more ages and genders, could help make the next generation of voice AI more inclusive and less exploitative. (MIT Technology Review) 

Google DeepMind has a new way to look inside an AI’s “mind”

Autoencoders let us peer into the black box of artificial intelligence. They could help us create AI that is better understood and more easily controlled. (MIT Technology Review)

Musk has expanded his legal assault on OpenAI to target Microsoft

Musk has expanded his federal lawsuit against OpenAI, which alleges that the company has abandoned its nonprofit roots and obligations. He’s now going after Microsoft too, accusing it of antitrust violations in its work with OpenAI. (The Washington Post)

text:
What if America's restrictions on China end up creating the very technological competitor they were designed to contain?

History offers an interesting lesson.

Intel once dominated the processor industry. Its technological and commercial position seemed extraordinarily difficult to challenge.

Then AMD fought back.

Through architectural innovation, engineering, and competitive execution, AMD regained market share and demonstrated that technological dominance is never necessarily permanent.

Now consider Nvidia, Huawei, and the global race for artificial intelligence.

The United States has imposed restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips and semiconductor technologies, partly to preserve strategic and national security advantages.

The immediate objective is understandable: limit access to computing capabilities considered critical.

But what happens when a technologically capable competitor encounters a restriction it cannot simply overcome by purchasing existing products?

It has two possibilities.

Accept the limitation.

Or find another way.

And this is where human intelligence becomes the most unpredictable variable in the equation.

Restrictions create constraints.

Constraints can generate frustration.

And frustration, when combined with scientific knowledge, engineering capabilities, resources, and determination, can become a powerful incentive to innovate.

Enter Huawei.

Huawei is already developing its own AI accelerators through the Ascend ecosystem.

But imagine something more ambitious.

What if Huawei eventually concludes that competing directly with Nvidia's GPU architecture is not the most effective strategy?

What if the real opportunity lies in designing an entirely different computing architecture?

Not simply another GPU.

Not merely an improved accelerator.

But a different computational engine, optimized around another way of organizing operations, memory, data movement, and energy consumption.

Such a breakthrough would still need to demonstrate measurable advantages, reliable manufacturing, competitive software, and the ability to scale commercially.

There is no evidence that Huawei has already achieved this hypothetical transformation.

But the possibility raises an important strategic question.

Why must the next generation of artificial intelligence computing follow the architecture that dominates the current generation?

Scientific progress does not require every competitor to follow the same technological path.

Sometimes, the most significant innovation emerges when established solutions can no longer satisfy new constraints.

And here lies the potential paradox of American export restrictions.

By limiting China's access to advanced US technologies, Washington may also strengthen the economic incentives for Chinese companies to develop independent alternatives.

Huawei could invest more aggressively in architectures that reduce dependence on restricted technologies.

If one of those architectures eventually delivers superior performance, efficiency, and scalability, the competitive landscape could change dramatically.

Perhaps Huawei would not need to defeat Nvidia by building a better version of Nvidia's technology.

Perhaps it would need to make the dominant architecture less relevant.

That is the distinction.

A restriction can delay technological development.

But it can also redirect research toward alternatives that might otherwise receive less investment.

Neither outcome is guaranteed.

Innovation requires more than frustration, and independent architectures still face enormous scientific, industrial, and economic obstacles.

Nevertheless, history repeatedly reminds us that technological leadership is not permanent.

Intel's dominance did not prevent AMD's resurgence.

Nvidia's current position does not guarantee that GPUs will remain the preferred architecture for every future AI workload.

And Huawei's present limitations do not determine the boundaries of its future research.

Which brings us to a question worth considering.

Could the United States, by restricting China's access to today's most advanced AI processors, unintentionally accelerate the search for a computing architecture that challenges tomorrow's technological order?

The greatest strategic surprise would not necessarily be Huawei catching up with Nvidia.

It would be Huawei discovering that catching up was never the only possible move.

In chess, the strongest move is not always the one that confronts your opponent's position directly. Sometimes, it is the move that changes the entire position.

text:
It’s not easy being one of Silicon Valley’s favorite benchmarks. 

SWE-Bench (pronounced “swee bench”) launched in November 2024 to evaluate an AI model’s coding skill, using more than 2,000 real-world programming problems pulled from the public GitHub repositories of 12 different Python-based projects. 

In the months since then, it’s quickly become one of the most popular tests in AI. A SWE-Bench score has become a mainstay of major model releases from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google—and outside of foundation models, the fine-tuners at AI firms are in constant competition to see who can rise above the pack. The top of the leaderboard is a pileup between three different fine tunings of Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet model and Amazon’s Q developer agent. Auto Code Rover—one of the Claude modifications—nabbed the number two spot in November, and was acquired just three months later.

Despite all the fervor, this isn’t exactly a truthful assessment of which model is “better.” As the benchmark has gained prominence, “you start to see that people really want that top spot,” says John Yang, a researcher on the team that developed SWE-Bench at Princeton University. As a result, entrants have begun to game the system—which is pushing many others to wonder whether there’s a better way to actually measure AI achievement.

Developers of these coding agents aren’t necessarily doing anything as straightforward cheating, but they’re crafting approaches that are too neatly tailored to the specifics of the benchmark. The initial SWE-Bench test set was limited to programs written in Python, which meant developers could gain an advantage by training their models exclusively on Python code. Soon, Yang noticed that high-scoring models would fail completely when tested on different programming languages—revealing an approach to the test that he describes as “gilded.”

“It looks nice and shiny at first glance, but then you try to run it on a different language and the whole thing just kind of falls apart,” Yang says. “At that point, you’re not designing a software engineering agent. You’re designing to make a SWE-Bench agent, which is much less interesting.”

The SWE-Bench issue is a symptom of a more sweeping—and complicated—problem in AI evaluation, and one that’s increasingly sparking heated debate: The benchmarks the industry uses to guide development are drifting further and further away from evaluating actual capabilities, calling their basic value into question. Making the situation worse, several benchmarks, most notably FrontierMath and Chatbot Arena, have recently come under heat for an alleged lack of transparency. Nevertheless, benchmarks still play a central role in model development, even if few experts are willing to take their results at face value. OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently described the situation as “an evaluation crisis”: the industry has fewer trusted methods for measuring capabilities and no clear path to better ones. 

“Historically, benchmarks were the way we evaluated AI systems,” says Vanessa Parli, director of research at Stanford University’s Institute for Human-Centered AI. “Is that the way we want to evaluate systems going forward? And if it’s not, what is the way?”

A growing group of academics and AI researchers are making the case that the answer is to go smaller, trading sweeping ambition for an approach inspired by the social sciences. Specifically, they want to focus more on testing validity, which for quantitative social scientists refers to how well a given questionnaire measures what it’s claiming to measure—and, more fundamentally, whether what it is measuring has a coherent definition. That could cause trouble for benchmarks assessing hazily defined concepts like “reasoning” or “scientific knowledge”—and for developers aiming to reach the much–hyped goal of artificial general intelligence—but it would put the industry on firmer ground as it looks to prove the worth of individual models.

“Taking validity seriously means asking folks in academia, industry, or wherever to show that their system does what they say it does,” says Abigail Jacobs, a University of Michigan professor who is a central figure in the new push for validity. “I think it points to a weakness in the AI world if they want to back off from showing that they can support their claim.”

The limits of traditional testing

If AI companies have been slow to respond to the growing failure of benchmarks, it’s partially because the test-scoring approach has been so effective for so long. 

One of the biggest early successes of contemporary AI was the ImageNet challenge, a kind of antecedent to contemporary benchmarks. Released in 2010 as an open challenge to researchers, the database held more than 3 million images for AI systems to categorize into 1,000 different classes.

Crucially, the test was completely agnostic to methods, and any successful algorithm quickly gained credibility regardless of how it worked. When an algorithm called AlexNet broke through in 2012, with a then unconventional form of GPU training, it became one of the foundational results of modern AI. Few would have guessed in advance that AlexNet’s convolutional neural nets would be the secret to unlocking image recognition—but after it scored well, no one dared dispute it. (One of AlexNet’s developers, Ilya Sutskever, would go on to cofound OpenAI.)

A large part of what made this challenge so effective was that there was little practical difference between ImageNet’s object classification challenge and the actual process of asking a computer to recognize an image. Even if there were disputes about methods, no one doubted that the highest-scoring model would have an advantage when deployed in an actual image recognition system.

But in the 12 years since, AI researchers have applied that same method-agnostic approach to increasingly general tasks. SWE-Bench is commonly used as a proxy for broader coding ability, while other exam-style benchmarks often stand in for reasoning ability. That broad scope makes it difficult to be rigorous about what a specific benchmark measures—which, in turn, makes it hard to use the findings responsibly. 

Where things break down

Anka Reuel, a PhD student who has been focusing on the benchmark problem as part of her research at Stanford, has become convinced the evaluation problem is the result of this push toward generality. “We’ve moved from task-specific models to general-purpose models,” Reuel says. “It’s not about a single task anymore but a whole bunch of tasks, so evaluation becomes harder.”

Like the University of Michigan’s Jacobs, Reuel thinks “the main issue with benchmarks is validity, even more than the practical implementation,” noting: “That’s where a lot of things break down.” For a task as complicated as coding, for instance, it’s nearly impossible to incorporate every possible scenario into your problem set. As a result, it’s hard to gauge whether a model is scoring better because it’s more skilled at coding or because it has more effectively manipulated the problem set. And with so much pressure on developers to achieve record scores, shortcuts are hard to resist.

For developers, the hope is that success on lots of specific benchmarks will add up to a generally capable model. But the techniques of agentic AI mean a single AI system can encompass a complex array of different models, making it hard to evaluate whether improvement on a specific task will lead to generalization. “There’s just many more knobs you can turn,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist at Princeton and a prominent critic of sloppy practices in the AI industry. “When it comes to agents, they have sort of given up on the best practices for evaluation.”

In a paper from last July, Kapoor called out specific issues in how AI models were approaching the WebArena benchmark, designed by Carnegie Mellon University researchers in 2024 as a test of an AI agent’s ability to traverse the web. The benchmark consists of more than 800 tasks to be performed on a set of cloned websites mimicking Reddit, Wikipedia, and others. Kapoor and his team identified an apparent hack in the winning model, called STeP. STeP included specific instructions about how Reddit structures URLs, allowing STeP models to jump directly to a given user’s profile page (a frequent element of WebArena tasks).

This shortcut wasn’t exactly cheating, but Kapoor sees it as “a serious misrepresentation of how well the agent would work had it seen the tasks in WebArena for the first time.” Because the technique was successful, though, a similar policy has since been adopted by OpenAI’s web agent Operator. (“Our evaluation setting is designed to assess how well an agent can solve tasks given some instruction about website structures and task execution,” an OpenAI representative said when reached for comment. “This approach is consistent with how others have used and reported results with WebArena.” STeP did not respond to a request for comment.)

Further highlighting the problem with AI benchmarks, late last month Kapoor and a team of researchers wrote a paper that revealed significant problems in Chatbot Arena, the popular crowdsourced evaluation system. According to the paper, the leaderboard was being manipulated; many top foundation models were conducting undisclosed private testing and releasing their scores selectively.

Today, even ImageNet itself, the mother of all benchmarks, has started to fall victim to validity problems. A 2023 study from researchers at the University of Washington and Google Research found that when ImageNet-winning algorithms were pitted against six real-world data sets, the architecture improvement “resulted in little to no progress,” suggesting that the external validity of the test had reached its limit.

Going smaller

For those who believe the main problem is validity, the best fix is reconnecting benchmarks to specific tasks. As Reuel puts it, AI developers “have to resort to these high-level benchmarks that are almost meaningless for downstream consumers, because the benchmark developers can’t anticipate the downstream task anymore.” So what if there was a way to help the downstream consumers identify this gap?

In November 2024, Reuel launched a public ranking project called BetterBench, which rates benchmarks on dozens of different criteria, such as whether the code has been publicly documented. But validity is a central theme, with particular criteria challenging designers to spell out what capability their benchmark is testing and how it relates to the tasks that make up the benchmark.

“You need to have a structural breakdown of the capabilities,” Reuel says. “What are the actual skills you care about, and how do you operationalize them into something we can measure?”

The results are surprising. One of the highest-scoring benchmarks is also the oldest: the Arcade Learning Environment (ALE), established in 2013 as a way to test models’ ability to learn how to play a library of Atari 2600 games. One of the lowest-scoring is the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark, a widely used test for general language skills; by the standards of BetterBench, the connection between the questions and the underlying skill was too poorly defined.

BetterBench hasn’t meant much for the reputations of specific benchmarks, at least not yet; MMLU is still widely used, and ALE is still marginal. But the project has succeeded in pushing validity into the broader conversation about how to fix benchmarks. In April, Reuel quietly joined a new research group hosted by Hugging Face, the University of Edinburgh, and EleutherAI, where she’ll develop her ideas on validity and AI model evaluation with other figures in the field. (An official announcement is expected later this month.) 

Irene Solaiman, Hugging Face’s head of global policy, says the group will focus on building valid benchmarks that go beyond measuring straightforward capabilities. “There’s just so much hunger for a good benchmark off the shelf that already works,” Solaiman says. “A lot of evaluations are trying to do too much.”

Increasingly, the rest of the industry seems to agree. In a paper in March, researchers from Google, Microsoft, Anthropic, and others laid out a new framework for improving evaluations—with validity as the first step. 

“AI evaluation science must,” the researchers argue, “move beyond coarse grained claims of ‘general intelligence’ towards more task-specific and real-world relevant measures of progress.” 

Measuring the “squishy” things

To help make this shift, some researchers are looking to the tools of social science. A February position paper argued that “evaluating GenAI systems is a social science measurement challenge,” specifically unpacking how the validity systems used in social measurements can be applied to AI benchmarking. 

The authors, largely employed by Microsoft’s research branch but joined by academics from Stanford and the University of Michigan, point to the standards that social scientists use to measure contested concepts like ideology, democracy, and media bias. Applied to AI benchmarks, those same procedures could offer a way to measure concepts like “reasoning” and “math proficiency” without slipping into hazy generalizations.

In the social science literature, it’s particularly important that metrics begin with a rigorous definition of the concept measured by the test. For instance, if the test is to measure how democratic a society is, it first needs to establish a definition for a “democratic society” and then establish questions that are relevant to that definition. 

To apply this to a benchmark like SWE-Bench, designers would need to set aside the classic machine learning approach, which is to collect programming problems from GitHub and create a scheme to validate answers as true or false. Instead, they’d first need to define what the benchmark aims to measure (“ability to resolve flagged issues in software,” for instance), break that into subskills (different types of problems or types of program that the AI model can successfully process), and then finally assemble questions that accurately cover the different subskills.

It’s a profound change from how AI researchers typically approach benchmarking—but for researchers like Jacobs, a coauthor on the February paper, that’s the whole point. “There’s a mismatch between what’s happening in the tech industry and these tools from social science,” she says. “We have decades and decades of thinking about how we want to measure these squishy things about humans.”

Even though the idea has made a real impact in the research world, it’s been slow to influence the way AI companies are actually using benchmarks. 

The last two months have seen new model releases from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta, and all of them lean heavily on multiple-choice knowledge benchmarks like MMLU—the exact approach that validity researchers are trying to move past. After all, model releases are, for the most part, still about showing increases in general intelligence, and broad benchmarks continue to be used to back up those claims. 

For some observers, that’s good enough. Benchmarks, Wharton professor Ethan Mollick says, are “bad measures of things, but also they’re what we’ve got.” He adds: “At the same time, the models are getting better. A lot of sins are forgiven by fast progress.”

For now, the industry’s long-standing focus on artificial general intelligence seems to be crowding out a more focused validity-based approach. As long as AI models can keep growing in general intelligence, then specific applications don’t seem as compelling—even if that leaves practitioners relying on tools they no longer fully trust. 

“This is the tightrope we’re walking,” says Hugging Face’s Solaiman. “It’s too easy to throw the system out, but evaluations are really helpful in understanding our models, even with these limitations.”

Russell Brandom is a freelance writer covering artificial intelligence. He lives in Brooklyn with his wife and two cats.

The India–U.S. trade deal is “almost done.” What, exactly, is Washington offering?

Donald Trump, Marco Rubio and Sergei Gor have all signalled that a deal is close. 

So have Nirmala Sitharaman, S. Jaishankar and Piyush Goyal.

Then came a revealing caveat.

On November 18, Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said India was waiting for clarity on U.S. tariff policy and pending Section 301 investigations. The outcome could determine whether Indian exporters gain an edge over their competitors or fall behind.

But waiting for today’s investigations to end offers no protection against tomorrow’s. 

Washington can open fresh Section 301 investigations even after a deal is signed.

It could also threaten tariffs under the Graham Act over India’s purchases of Russian oil.

The real question goes back to February 20. When the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the reciprocal tariffs imposed under IEEPA, Washington lost its main bargaining chip.

Since then, no country signed trade deal with the US as it has nothing to offer.

India remains the sole nation still negotiating along those pre-ruling lines—leaving its sweeping concessions on the table while Washington’s replacement tariff offer remains undefined and unknown.

The half-day event, which attracts various advocacy groups, offered a glimpse of progressive policy objectives ahead of the state legislative session that will begin in January.

THE INMATES ARE RUNNING THE ASYLUM 

As budget gap looms, Washington progressives say state isn’t spending enough

Nov. 19, 2026

TACOMA — As state lawmakers and agencies brace for budget cuts amid a projected $4 billion shortfall, some members of Washington’s progressive community think the state should actually be spending, and taxing, more.

Business groups and Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson have indicated they don’t want to see new taxes on the table for next year. But progressives insist that this month’s decisive election win for the state’s new “millionaires tax” shows that voters are on board with increased spending and shifting the tax burden from the poor to the wealthy. 

“There is a mandate to continue to fix our upside-down tax code and have enough revenue to support the programs that people clearly want more investment in, like education (and) healthcare,” said Eli Taylor Goss, executive director of the left-leaning Washington State Budget and Policy Center, during the group’s annual policy summit at Tacoma’s Asia Pacific Cultural Center on Tuesday.

The half-day event, which attracts various advocacy groups, offered a glimpse of progressive policy objectives ahead of the state legislative session that will begin in January. 

At last year’s summit, state Sen. Noel Frame, D-Seattle, previewed a proposal for the new tax on high-earner income. This year’s lineup didn’t feature lawmakers or lay out specific legislation. And it’s far from clear what appetite state legislators may have for additional revenue.

State Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen recently floated the idea of a state corporate income tax to replace Washington’s archaic business and occupation tax. However, the Seattle Democrat made clear he wants a “neutral” change that doesn’t raise additional tax revenue for the state. He also said a bill calling for the switch is not likely before 2028.

On Monday, Ferguson directed state agencies to propose cuts to deal with a $4 billion projected shortfall in the state’s next fiscal year, and his top budget official insisted that “we’re not considering new revenue as part of our solution for the budget problem.”

Another major uncertainty for progressives is whether a state income tax, which is central to many of their tax plans, will be upheld by the courts.

Those uncertainties didn’t dampen the mood at the summit or keep advocates from touting ideas for new revenue — including a corporate income tax and a wealth tax — along with new strategies to turn those concepts into viable legislation.

“Transforming our tax code requires us to transform how we win, who we work with, and how we work together in coalition,” said Taylor Goss. 

One big focus is winning over voters who might not have backed progressive causes in the past, advocates said Tuesday. 

That includes residents in Central and Eastern Washington, where there is often little trust in the Democratic Party and skepticism toward state government generally, said Elana Mainer, executive director of Rural People’s Voice, an advocacy organization based in north-central Washington.

Mainer said her group’s approach is to focus on shared goals around economic class — such as taxing billionaires, or protections for working-class families — rather than trying to get conservative voters to change parties or embrace government. 

“There’s no way I can win on that conversation,” Mainer said. When she knocks on doors, she added, “I am really clear that I’m not there to go to bat for the Democratic Party.”

Progressives also think they need to stop letting tax opponents control the narrative about the budget crisis.

Many business leaders and Republicans, for example, have argued that the state’s current budget shortfall results not from inadequate revenue, but from decades of overspending. 

That has also been the message of former Govs. Christine Gregoire and Gary Locke, both Democrats.

text:
This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get it in your inbox first, sign up here.

Generative AI models have become remarkably good at conversing with us, and creating images, videos, and music for us, but they’re not all that good at doing things for us. 

AI agents promise to change that. Think of them as AI models with a script and a purpose. They tend to come in one of two flavors. 

The first, called tool-based agents, can be coached using natural human language (rather than coding) to complete digital tasks for us. Anthropic released one such agent in October—the first from a major AI model-maker—that can translate instructions (“Fill in this form for me”) into actions on someone’s computer, moving the cursor to open a web browser, navigating to find data on relevant pages, and filling in a form using that data. Salesforce has released its own agent too, and OpenAI reportedly plans to release one in January. 

The other type of agent is called a simulation agent, and you can think of these as AI models designed to behave like human beings. The first people to work on creating these agents were social science researchers. They wanted to conduct studies that would be expensive, impractical, or unethical to do with real human subjects, so they used AI to simulate subjects instead. This trend particularly picked up with the publication of an oft-cited 2023 paper by Joon Sung Park, a PhD candidate at Stanford, and colleagues called “Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior.” 

Last week Park and his team published a new paper on arXiv called “Generative Agent Simulations of 1,000 People.” In this work, researchers had 1,000 people participate in two-hour interviews with an AI. Shortly after, the team was able to create simulation agents that replicated each participant’s values and preferences with stunning accuracy.

There are two really important developments here. First, it’s clear that leading AI companies think it’s no longer good enough to build dazzling generative AI tools; they now have to build agents that can accomplish things for people. Second, it’s getting easier than ever to get such AI agents to mimic the behaviors, attitudes, and personalities of real people. What were once two distinct types of agents—simulation agents and tool-based agents—could soon become one thing: AI models that can not only mimic your personality but go out and act on your behalf. 

Research on this is underway. Companies like Tavus are hard at work helping users create “digital twins” of themselves. But the company’s CEO, Hassaan Raza, envisions going further, creating AI agents that can take the form of therapists, doctors, and teachers. 

If such tools become cheap and easy to build, it will raise lots of new ethical concerns, but two in particular stand out. The first is that these agents could create even more personal, and even more harmful, deepfakes. Image generation tools have already made it simple to create nonconsensual pornography using a single image of a person, but this crisis will only deepen if it’s easy to replicate someone’s voice, preferences, and personality as well. (Park told me he and his team spent more than a year wrestling with ethical issues like this in their latest research project, engaging in many conversations with Stanford’s ethics board and drafting policies on how the participants could withdraw their data and contributions.) 

The second is the fundamental question of whether we deserve to know whether we’re talking to an agent or a human. If you complete an interview with an AI and submit samples of your voice to create an agent that sounds and responds like you, are your friends or coworkers entitled to know when they’re talking to it and not to you? On the other side, if you ring your cell service provider or doctor’s office and a cheery customer service agent answers the line, are you entitled to know whether you’re talking to an AI?

This future feels far off, but it isn’t. There’s a chance that when we get there, there will be even more pressing and pertinent ethical questions to ask. In the meantime, read more from my piece on AI agents here, and ponder how well you think an AI interviewer could get to know you in two hours.

Deeper Learning

Inside Clear’s ambitions to manage your identity beyond the airport

Clear is the most visible biometrics company around, and one you’ve likely interacted with already, whether passing security checkpoints at airports and stadiums or verifying your identity on LinkedIn. Along the way, it’s built one of the largest private repositories of identity data on the planet, including scans of fingerprints, irises, and faces. A confluence of factors is now accelerating the adoption of identity verification technologies—including AI, of course, as well as the lingering effects of the pandemic’s push toward “contactless” experiences—and Clear aims to be the ubiquitous provider of these services. In the near future, countless situations where you might need an ID or credit card might require no more than showing your face. 

Why this matters: Now that biometrics have gone mainstream, what—and who—bears the cost? Because this convenience, even if chosen by only some of us, leaves all of us wrestling with the effects. If Clear gains ground in its vision, it will move us toward a world where we’re increasingly obligated to give up our biometric data to a system that’s vulnerable to data leaks.  Read more from Eileen Guo.

text:
Imagine sitting down with an AI model for a spoken two-hour interview. A friendly voice guides you through a conversation that ranges from your childhood, your formative memories, and your career to your thoughts on immigration policy. Not long after, a virtual replica of you is able to embody your values and preferences with stunning accuracy.

That’s now possible, according to a new paper from a team including researchers from Stanford and Google DeepMind, which has been published on arXiv and has not yet been peer-reviewed. 

Led by Joon Sung Park, a Stanford PhD student in computer science, the team recruited 1,000 people who varied by age, gender, race, region, education, and political ideology. They were paid up to $100 for their participation. From interviews with them, the team created agent replicas of those individuals. As a test of how well the agents mimicked their human counterparts, participants did a series of personality tests, social surveys, and logic games, twice each, two weeks apart; then the agents completed the same exercises. The results were 85% similar. 

“If you can have a bunch of small ‘yous’ running around and actually making the decisions that you would have made—that, I think, is ultimately the future,” Park says. 

In the paper the replicas are called simulation agents, and the impetus for creating them is to make it easier for researchers in social sciences and other fields to conduct studies that would be expensive, impractical, or unethical to do with real human subjects. If you can create AI models that behave like real people, the thinking goes, you can use them to test everything from how well interventions on social media combat misinformation to what behaviors cause traffic jams. 

Such simulation agents are slightly different from the agents that are dominating the work of leading AI companies today. Called tool-based agents, those are models built to do things for you, not converse with you. For example, they might enter data, retrieve information you have stored somewhere, or—someday—book travel for you and schedule appointments. Salesforce announced its own tool-based agents in September, followed by Anthropic in October, and OpenAI is planning to release some in January, according to Bloomberg. 

The two types of agents are different but share common ground. Research on simulation agents, like the ones in this paper, is likely to lead to stronger AI agents overall, says John Horton, an associate professor of information technologies at the MIT Sloan School of Management, who founded a company to conduct research using AI-simulated participants. 

“This paper is showing how you can do a kind of hybrid: use real humans to generate personas which can then be used programmatically/in-simulation in ways you could not with real humans,” he told MIT Technology Review in an email. 

The research comes with caveats, not the least of which is the danger that it points to. Just as image generation technology has made it easy to create harmful deepfakes of people without their consent, any agent generation technology raises questions about the ease with which people can build tools to personify others online, saying or authorizing things they didn’t intend to say. 

The evaluation methods the team used to test how well the AI agents replicated their corresponding humans were also fairly basic. These included the General Social Survey—which collects information on one’s demographics, happiness, behaviors, and more—and assessments of the Big Five personality traits: openness to experience, conscientiousness, extroversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism. Such tests are commonly used in social science research but don’t pretend to capture all the unique details that make us ourselves. The AI agents were also worse at replicating the humans in behavioral tests like the “dictator game,” which is meant to illuminate how participants consider values such as fairness. 

To build an AI agent that replicates people well, the researchers needed ways to distill our uniqueness into language AI models can understand. They chose qualitative interviews to do just that, Park says. He says he was convinced that interviews are the most efficient way to learn about someone after he appeared on countless podcasts following a 2023 paper that he wrote on generative agents, which sparked a huge amount of interest in the field. “I would go on maybe a two-hour podcast podcast interview, and after the interview, I felt like, wow, people know a lot about me now,” he says. “Two hours can be very powerful.”

These interviews can also reveal idiosyncrasies that are less likely to show up on a survey. “Imagine somebody just had cancer but was finally cured last year. That’s very unique information about you that says a lot about how you might behave and think about things,” he says. It would be difficult to craft survey questions that elicit these sorts of memories and responses. 

Interviews aren’t the only option, though. Companies that offer to make “digital twins” of users, like Tavus, can have their AI models ingest customer emails or other data. It tends to take a pretty large data set to replicate someone’s personality that way, Tavus CEO Hassaan Raza told me, but this new paper suggests a more efficient route. 

“What was really cool here is that they show you might not need that much information,” Raza says, adding that his company will experiment with the approach. “How about you just talk to an AI interviewer for 30 minutes today, 30 minutes tomorrow? And then we use that to construct this digital twin of you.”

I’ve spent my whole life saying yes. Even at this age, I still struggle to put myself first.”
She asked to see the terms in writing.

Someone else took the compensated offer.

She flew that day.

Later, passengers who had been complaining started questioning why a woman her age had to demand basic information that should have been offered from the start.

One of them said:

I don’t know what’s worse a company expecting someone to sacrifice for free, or the rest of us treating it as normal.”

Helping others is good. Automatically abandoning yourself is not.

When did you last say yes before checking what you were actually agreeing to?

Market Open | AI Selloff Deepens Despite Anthropic's Record Debut

Global markets are under heavy pressure this morning. The selloff in AI stocks spread across Asia overnight, and Anthropic's record stock market debut did little to slow it.

On Wall Street, the S&P 500 fell 2%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 2.2% and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.3%. Anthropic opened 34% higher but faded to close its first day of trade up 17%, and its rally failed to lift other AI stocks.

Economic data added to the gloom. The Philadelphia Fed manufacturing index fell sharply to 6.3 in November, well below the consensus estimate of 20.1 and its weakest reading in six months.

Asia is following Wall Street lower, with regional shares on track for their worst week since 2020. The dollar is holding steady on safe haven flows after reaching its strongest level since April 2025 earlier this week.

Commodities offer little relief. Gold is down 0.6% on the day and heading for a 7.3% weekly loss. Brent crude settled flat and is on track for a third consecutive weekly decline, as expectations of ample supply outweigh the threat of new US strikes on Iran.

Locally, the Reserve Bank left the repo rate unchanged yesterday after two increases this year. Four members of the Monetary Policy Committee favoured a hold and three favoured a 25bps hike. Governor Lesetja Kganyago said the committee would not hesitate to raise rates if needed. The rand weakened 1.06% to its weakest close in over a year, weighed down by a stronger dollar, rising global yields and uncertainty over the Gauteng coalitions. The ANC is negotiating with ActionSA, the EFF and the MK Party to govern Johannesburg and Tshwane, and the councils sit next week.

With Asian tech stocks under heavy selling, gold still falling and the rand at its weakest level in over a year, the All Share is expected to open sharply lower this morning.

text:
The Philippines could become a future launch site for @SpaceX, the aerospace company led by the world's richest man, @elonmusk, as President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. revealed plans to explore opportunities in the global commercial space launch industry.

Speaking during a press briefing in Shenzhen, China, on Friday, Nov. 20, Marcos said the country could leverage its strategic geographical location to attract investments in rocket launch infrastructure.

“Maybe the Philippines can look into it. We are not trying to be @NASA. We are not trying to send a man to the moon or to Mars,” Marcos said. “What we are trying to do is to get into the business of launch sites.”

The proposal could open opportunities for aerospace investments, satellite deployment, engineering and high-skilled employment. The Philippines' proximity to the equator offers potential advantages for certain rocket launches, including reduced fuel requirements.

The development comes after Philippine Ambassador to the United States Jose Manuel “Babes” Romualdez revealed that Musk frequently visits the Philippines and is reportedly developing one or two islands in the country.

“From what I'm told, Elon Musk comes here quietly very often because he has one or two islands, I'm told, that he's developing,” Romualdez said in an interview with ANC.

“Again, that's a big sign. The richest man in the world is actually very interested in the Philippines,” the ambassador added.

Musk landed in Manila aboard his private aircraft on Nov. 18 before boarding Air Force One to accompany U.S. President @realDonaldTrump to China.

Interest in establishing a SpaceX facility in the Philippines dates back to February 2025, when Romualdez disclosed that the company was considering a rocket launchpad in Mindanao, citing the region's proximity to the equator.

SpaceX already maintains a presence in the Philippines through @Starlink, its satellite internet service, which officially became available on Feb. 22, 2023. Musk's electric vehicle company Tesla also entered the Philippine market on Nov. 8, 2024, opening its first showroom and service center in Bonifacio Global City, Taguig.

text:
Disability is a benefit offered on enlistment as an assurance, not a job specific bonus like hazard pay which is temporary and tied to specific duties. 

Think of it like a qualified pension less than “disability” and also consider that “office” jobs often do qualify for danger pay depending on duty location (the key for those incentive pays is the “incentive”)

Another thing to consider is while person A gets less incentives working CONUS, their job directly impacts the ability for person B to do theirs safely or at all and come home. Is there incentive for the “more dangerous” job? Yes, and that’s the incentive pay you receive, but all members are equals in the fight and no soldier is going to complain about another outside of the banter. 

The razzing civilians witness looks a lot like animus between branches/jobs, names like nonners for non flying jobs or chair force for the Air Force, there is a smaller portion of earnest no different than a lineman envying the AC of the contractor or the contractor resenting the straight forward and lower pressure of hands on “just doing the job” but that’s normal in all aspects of careers, but the boogeyman of military “dark humor” is that we take that inter-departmental beef to a level civilians would see as unprofessional at best and nearly abusive. To us it’s almost always funny and done in a brotherly love way, tough love, whatever you wanna call it. 

Is a cook in the Air Force living the good life? Sure, easy predictable work indoors without something aimed at them 9/10 times, but you think me taking the piss means I resent them? Absolutely not. I wouldn’t trade what I did for it, and I also deeply respect security forces and ground troops and cooks and hell, the most hated group, finance! Because without them the job doesn’t get done. Without a cook, I’m stuck with local hire AFES shit that has a 50% chance of some horrible disease or spit or just being cooked in some foreign way which sucks. A mil cook has my back and makes living in a tent in the desert feel a little more like home, less stress about how I’ll feel in the morning or if I am fit to fly or if I’m bringing some communicable disease into a tin can with a bunch of other dudes who need to be in their best shape to operate or we could all die. 

But maybe that won’t make sense, it’s something that is developed not taught.

text:
February 1977. 

Kampala. 

Idi Amin insisted Archbishop Luwum and two ministers died in a car crash. 

The world didn't buy it. 

So Amin staged a press conference with the alleged driver, Major Moses Okello. 

But the desperate theatrical maneuver only exposed the regime's macabre panic.

The official version of events was as grotesque as it was unbelievable. 

Amin insisted that Archbishop Janani Luwum, alongside Ministers Charles Oboth-Ofumbi and Erinayo Oryema, had died after trying to overpower their driver to escape. 

But President Jimmy Carter publicly called the incident "horrible murders that have disgusted the whole world," and eyewitnesses who viewed the Archbishop’s body reported no crash damage, only three distinct bullet holes. 

As the chorus of disbelief mounted globally, a desperate Amin resorted to a bizarre maneuver: he allowed the press to meet the alleged driver in a frantic attempt to sell his crumbling lie.

The man paraded before the cameras was Major Moses Okello, an army intelligence officer. 

Six days after the supposed high-speed crash, Okello appeared in considerable pain, his voice weak, claiming he lacked the strength to even eat properly. 

He stumbled through a rambling testimony, alleging he was "ambushed" by Oryema grabbing the steering wheel and that he blacked out after losing control. 

He claimed he didn't know where the car crashed or how he survived when three others perished. 

"I'm talking from the bottom of my heart," he insisted. 

Yet, his performance was undermined by foreign journalists who quietly noted that the supposedly bedridden Major had been seen walking around the barracks completely unhurt just days earlier.

To patch the gaping holes in this absurd narrative, the regime trotted out Captain Christopher Ntalo, the military doctor who had treated Okello. 

Ntalo dutifully testified that the Major had arrived covered in blood and glass, suffering from a closed head injury. 

But under pointed questioning, the doctor’s story collapsed. 

He admitted that despite the blood, Okello had no cuts at all, only a bruise on his knee and shoulder. 

When pressed on where the blood came from, the doctor offered a chilling deduction: the blood covering the Major’s shirt and chest must have come from the severely injured men who had been riding with him.

This comical, deeply macabre double interview marked the moment the mask of the "lovable big daddy" was completely stripped away. 

The world, which had once laughed at Amin's cowboy hats and bullet belts, now saw only the panicked flailing of a tyrant butchering his own inner circle and staging a farce to cover it up. 

The driver and the doctor had been offered up as proof of innocence, but their contradictory testimonies only cemented the global conviction of Amin's absolute ruthlessness. 

The official story of the motor accident had been exposed as a grotesque joke, and the world’s eyes were now fully open to the horror of Uganda.

The blood on Major Okello's shirt was supposed to prove he had been in a crash. 

Instead, it proved he had been sitting next to dying men. 

The world watched the rambling, contradictory testimony and saw the truth Amin was trying so desperately to hide. 

The laughing stopped. 

The horror began.

text:
November 20, 1917, 6:30 a.m. For six hours the British broke through everything Germany had built to stop them — with a weapon that had never been used in anger before. By December 7, almost all of it was gone again.

**THE SETUP:**

Cambrai was a quiet sector. The town in France's Nord department was an important supply centre for the Hindenburg Line; take it and Bourlon Ridge to its north, and you threaten the rear of the German line. But the Germans had built an elaborate defence in depth, and no one expected anything here. Major General Henry Tudor, commander of the 9th Division's artillery, had an idea: move guns into position at night under cover of darkness, register them by sound ranging without firing a single shot — "silent registration" — then open fire at dawn with instant suppression and total surprise. His tanks would cut paths through the deep wire obstacles, supported by a new No. 106 fuze that detonated high explosive without cratering the ground. Brigadier Hugh Elles of the Tank Corps wanted to use tanks on this quiet front; General Julian Byng of the Third Army combined both plans into one operation. Two weeks before H-hour, the Royal Flying Corps began training in ground attack: trenches, supply points, enemy airfields.

**DAWN:**

6:30 a.m., November 20. 1,003 guns fire without prior registration — smoke and a creeping barrage 300 yards ahead of the infantry. Nine battalions of the Tank Corps roll out with six infantry divisions of III and IV Corps — over 400 Mark IV tanks (the Imperial War Museum counts 476 deployed in total, 378 in combat roles).

The Germans had intelligence: an attack at Havrincourt was anticipated, as was the use of tanks. But the barrage caught them off guard. The Hindenburg Line, with its deep wire fields that German commanders supposed impregnable, gave way. In six hours the British advanced up to 5 miles (8 km) — more ground than they had taken in three months at Passchendaele, at half the casualty rate.

On the right the 12th Division pushed as far as Lateau Wood before being ordered to dig in; the 6th took Ribécourt and Marcoing, but when the cavalry finally came through it was repulsed from Noyelles. West of Flesquières the 62nd Division swept all the way through Havrincourt and Graincourt to within reach of the woods on Bourlon Ridge — the deepest advance of the day. The 20th forced its way through La Vacquerie and captured a bridge across the Canal de Saint-Quentin at Masnières — then the bridge collapsed under the weight of a tank, killing the crossing. In the centre the 51st (Highland) Division was stopped dead at Flesquières, one of the most fortified points in the line: its defenders knocked out almost forty tanks with field guns, and a myth grew up around a lone gunner credited with most of the kills — in reality it was a specialist anti-tank unit. The Germans abandoned Flesquières during the night.

By nightfall 180 of the roughly 437 tanks were out of action — only 65 destroyed; 71 broke down and 43 ditched in shell holes and mud. The British lost about 4,000 men on day one and took 4,200 prisoners.

**THE RIDGE:**

Haig wanted Bourlon Ridge. From November 21 the advance slowed to a crawl: Flesquières and Cantaing were retaken before dawn, but Moeuvres was lost that day and Fontaine the next; Anneux fell, yet the road into Bourlon Wood stayed blocked. The exhausted 62nd Division was replaced by the 40th; on November 23 it attacked the woods with almost 100 tanks and 430 guns — reached the crest, held there, over 4,000 casualties in three days. A final effort on November 27 (the 62nd again, with 30 tanks) was reversed by a German counter-attack. The offensive stopped on November 28: the British sat in an 11 km by 9.5 km salient with its front along the crest of the ridge, digging in under fire — more than 16,000 shells fell into Bourlon Wood that day alone.

**GERMANY ANSWERS:**

Twenty German divisions assembled around Cambrai. Their answer was a new tactic: a short intense shelling followed by a rapid assault — Hutier infiltration tactics, leading elements attacking in groups rather than waves and bypassing strong opposition, methods developed against the Russians. Three divisions of Gruppe Arras were to take Bourlon; Gruppe Caudry would drive from Bantouzelle toward Marcoing on the salient's eastern flank; Gruppe Busigny advanced from Banteux — seven infantry divisions in all. British VII Corps, holding to the south, warned III Corps that something was coming.

At 7:00 a.m. on November 30 the counter-attack began. In the south it came in unexpectedly fast: the commanders of two British divisions were almost captured; Brigadier Berkeley Vincent had to fight his way out of his own headquarters and grab men from retreating units to try to stop the Germans. The advance spread across 13 km and came within a few miles of cutting off Bourlon.

On the ridge itself the British held with reckless determination — one group of eight machine guns fired over 70,000 rounds into the German assault. Only counter-attacks by the Guards Division, the arrival of British tanks, and the fall of night saved the day. By December 3 Haig ordered a partial retreat from the north salient; the Germans took La Vacquerie and pushed the British back to the east bank of the St Quentin canal, and their capture of Bonavis ridge made the hold on Bourlon precarious. By December 7 the gains were abandoned except for a sliver around Havrincourt, Ribécourt and Flesquières.

**WHAT IT LEFT BEHIND:**

Church bells rang across Britain on news of the first day — press enthusiasm was unprecedented. The lesson cut both ways: even the most elaborate field fortifications could be broken by surprise and combined arms; but a breakthrough without reserves is not a victory. Germany had to divert resources into anti-tank defences it could ill afford, and its own staff wrote that wherever the ground offered suitable going for tanks, such attacks must now be expected — "there can be no more mention of quiet fronts." The Germans learned their own lessons too: supply beyond railheads, and a machine gun (the MG 08) built for trenches but clumsy in rapid movement.

Cambrai was the dress rehearsal for 1918: predicted fire, sound ranging, infiltration tactics, close air support, combined arms. The young officer Ernst Jünger, who would write Storm of Steel, served on this sector.

The official British historian put Third Army, Tank Corps and RFC losses from November 20 to December 8 at 44,207 men — about 40,000 of them in the main battle; German medical reports put their own casualties at 54,720. The British took 11,105 prisoners and captured 98 field guns and howitzers, forty heavy pieces, 456 machine-guns and 74 trench mortars.

Today the Royal Tank Regiment commemorates Cambrai Day every year; the Cambrai Memorial to the Missing lists 7,048 names of men with no known grave.

Conflict Chronicles — Where history is told in the language of those who lived it.

*November 20, 1917*

Six hours of breakthrough. Three weeks of giving it back. Was Cambrai a victory or a lesson? Reply below.

text:
Saint Edmund (c. 841–870), often called Edmund the Martyr, was the last native king of East Anglia, one of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms in eastern England. Born around 841 A.D., probably in Nuremberg (according to later medieval tradition), he was of uncertain but likely royal East Anglian or continental Germanic descent. He succeeded to the throne in 855 at the age of fourteen and ruled for about fifteen years during a turbulent period when Viking invasions were intensifying.  

Edmund is remembered almost entirely through the lens of his dramatic death rather than his reign, about which almost nothing reliable is known. In 869–870, a large Danish “Great Heathen Army” led by brothers Ivar the Boneless and Ubba invaded East Anglia. According to the earliest accounts (written a century or more later by Abbo of Fleury and Ælfric of Eynsham), Edmund fought bravely but was defeated at a battle whose location is unknown (traditions place it variously at Bradfield St Clare, Hoxne, or Maldon).  

Captured rather than killed on the battlefield, Edmund was offered his life and kingdom if he would submit to the Viking leaders, accept their overlordship, and renounce or subordinate Christianity. He refused, declaring (in the classic hagiographic telling) that he would not betray his faith or his people. The Vikings then tortured him: he was beaten, shot full of arrows (making him an English parallel to Saint Sebastian), and finally beheaded on 20 November 870. His severed head was thrown into thick brambles in a forest, but (miraculously) was later found protected by a wolf that called out “Here, here, here” to guide searchers.  

Edmund’s body was at first buried in a simple shrine at Hoxne (or nearby Sutton), but in 902–905 it was translated to Beodricsworth (modern Bury St Edmunds), where a major abbey grew up around his cult. By the late 10th century, under the patronage of King Æthelstan and later kings, Edmund had become one of the most popular saints in England. His banner (a golden crown pierced by arrows on blue) was carried into battle, notably at Agincourt in 1415.  

Politically, his cult served as a symbol of English Christian resistance against pagan invaders. After the Norman Conquest, the powerful Abbey of St Edmundsbury kept his memory alive, and he remained England’s patron saint until displaced by St George under Edward III in the 14th century.

text:
I got a lot of overwhelming responses and DMs on the back of this post. Thank you brothers and sisters, who are all in various stages of your own journey. I’d like to clarify a few things at the outset to the many comments on the post .thought I’ll address it as one big write up. 

- i am very clear that my journey started when i was 22, back in 2011 . 
- I am not comparing this to someone who is the same age in 2026, 
- i am aware of the many difficulties your generation faces like the entry level job market , the US doors being shut due to Trump administration, agentic AI stealing jobs , cost of living.

Now to the specifics of my journey 

- at 22, I had a BTech in IT. I did not land a campus job, though many of my peers did. So I had to crack an off campus grid and I got a Tech Mahindra offer after 4 rounds in one day. 

- many of peers post training phase there went into development. Wanting to relocate to my hometown chennai I took up a support project opportunity , it was application support, which was looked down upon by many. It also was rotational shifts so wasn’t easy on the body either. 

- many nights I’ve been the only one in office doing maintenance, woken up weekend mornings and festival days doing oncall. Wasn’t easy but first 3.5 years learnt the ropes of corporate IT , customer client support, projects. Picked up SQL ,App support, Linux skills , soft skills that would aid me for rest of my life.

- whole of 2014 while working this job, I studied for MBA exams on the side and ran the gauntlet - CMAT, CAT, XAT, SNAP, IIFT. Got a few high 90s but due to caste wasn’t enough to land any college I actually wanted. No IIMs 

- in 2015 I switched to TCS after 3 years in TechM. Worked a year there with added responsibility but wasn’t considered for an onsite opportunity I had worked hard for, office politics .

- so decided to write GRE and target a masters degree in USA, which I did in 2015, got a score of 319. Had no arrears in BTech, applied to 5 colleges, got University of Florida., MS in CS.

- my dad had purchased lands with his savings, used this as collateral to get a student loan to go to USA. I acknowledge this is a privilege many don’t have. 

- August 2016 I went there , had a rough time in my masters, scraped thru with a GPA 3.4 , homesick, hated cooking all the time. But I made good friends for life too there. Graduated in December 2018 cause I had to do an extra sem caused I failed a subject and had to repeat it. But December 2018 I also landed a startup company in Atlanta as a Cloud operations engineer. 

- Jan 2019- July 2019 worked in the startup learnt the ropes of Cloud and distributed systems, Devops and SRE.

- August 2019 saw a Microsoft job posting for Azure cloud , applied, cracked it and worked there for roughly 4 years till June 2023. Experienced Layoff with Microsoft

- worked a interim job posting layoff in a consulting company in USA, till I applied to AWS in December 2023 and cracked it.

- worked with AWS till July 2026. 

- after about 10 years in USA, I took a personal call to return to India, now I know I’ll get a lot of opinions on this, I did so for my parents, both of who are hard of hearing and mute, they made an enormous sacrifice to get me so far, so I made this call that I’m tired of living away from them for long lengths of time and that’s why I am back in india now.

- I’ll share my LinkedIn definitely when I feel safe enough, but most of time here is a political handle opposing the DMK, so revealing my identity isn’t without significant risk . 

- that’s all I felt like sharing at this moment. Thank you all for your support. Stay blessed. Never give up, never quit, the night is always darkest before it’s dawn.
