TO THE PRESIDENT OF RUSSIA

RUSSIA'S COMPLETE VICTORY PLAN

A Strategic Freeze, Two Years of Reconstruction, and a Decision About the Future

Mr. President,
 
@KremlinRussia_E
Russia has paid too much. Lives, money, resources, and sacrifices. Too much to simply freeze this war without a victory, without an expectation, and without a plan for what comes next.

The solution is a strategic freeze, with the expectation of a referendum and a vote accompanied by two years of work between Russia and Ukraine.

Working together. Rebuilding. Rebuilding.

Russia needs a break. It needs to take care of its refineries, rebuild its resources, make adjustments, and prepare for the political changes that may come in the United States.

And that victory sometimes needs to be postponed, not by losing any territory, but by engaging in a mechanism that puts you at an advantage.

A mechanism that makes the Ukrainian people and their future president understand that they have to make a choice together. A choice that matches the reality on the ground.

You have an opportunity to create a Russian sovereign fund to begin rebuilding Ukraine, especially the territories devastated by this war.

You have an opportunity to challenge Europe to participate in reconstruction.

You have an opportunity to spend two years working shoulder to shoulder with Ukrainians, restoring infrastructure, rebuilding communities, creating jobs, and rebuilding the relationship.

And you have an opportunity to demonstrate that Russia is strong enough, smart enough, and wealthy enough to build rather than continue destroying.

This is beyond Zelenskyy. This is about future generations.

I believe Russia wants Ukraine within its sphere of economic and cultural influence. I believe that is the objective Russia has been willing to pay an enormous price to pursue.

The Ukrainian people need to understand that Russia is not simply going to disappear from their history, their geography, or their future.

And I believe the next two years could be used to demonstrate what cooperation can accomplish.

Not just speeches. Not just promises.

Actual rebuilding.

Actual investments.

Actual jobs.

Actual infrastructure.

Actual improvements in people's lives.

And then the people must be given an opportunity to decide their future.

A referendum, with clear expectations, clear choices, and an internationally credible process.

Russia can present its case for partnership, economic integration, and a future of close relations. Ukrainians can examine that case and decide for themselves.

TO PRESIDENT ZELENSKYY AND HIS WIFE, OLENA ZELENSKA
@ZelenskyyUa  @ZelenskaUA 
Let me turn to you for a moment.

Do you know what Russia has done for Ukraine?

Do you know how much history your two countries share?

Do you know how deeply your economies were once connected?

Do you know what was built before this war?

Let me remind you.

The pipelines.

During the Soviet era, an enormous energy network was built through Ukraine. The Brotherhood pipeline began carrying Ukrainian and Russian natural gas toward Central and Western Europe in 1967.

Those pipelines connected industries, cities, economies, and entire generations.

Ukraine was not simply a spectator. Ukrainian workers, engineers, industries, and resources were part of building that system.

The energy.

For decades, Russian gas supplied Ukrainian homes, factories, and industries.

There were periods when Russia offered discounted natural gas to Ukraine, including a substantial reduction negotiated in December 2013.

The financial assistance.
@jaredkushner @SEPeaceMissions 
In December 2013, President Putin's government agreed to a financial assistance package worth up to $15 billion, along with lower gas prices.

Russia delivered an initial $3 billion through the purchase of Ukrainian government bonds.

The remainder was not delivered.

That history matters, including the political conditions and disagreements surrounding the arrangement.

The industries.

Russian and Ukrainian industries were connected through manufacturing, aerospace, engineering, transportation, and energy.

Factories depended on suppliers across borders. Engineers worked on shared projects. Workers helped build an industrial system that served both economies.

The shared history.

Kyiv was central to Kyivan Rus', a medieval civilization whose heritage is shared by Ukrainians, Russians, and Belarusians.

@FLOTUS  @realDonaldTrump 
The Russian language, Ukrainian language, culture, religion, and history developed through centuries of interconnected experiences.

But that history belongs to more than one people.

The economic relationship.

Russia was a major trading partner for Ukraine. Ukraine was also important to Russia.

Both countries benefited from trade, transit, industrial cooperation, and access to markets.

This relationship was not built overnight.

It was built over generations.

And now look at what has happened.

Look at the destruction.

Look at the cities.

Look at the families.

Look at the people who have lost their homes.

Look at the soldiers who will never return.

Look at the money that could have built hospitals, schools, factories, roads, and entire communities.

And ask yourselves:

What kind of relationship should exist between Russia and Ukraine twenty years from now?

Must future generations inherit this war?

Must they inherit this hatred?

Must they inherit destroyed cities and endless military confrontation?

Or can they inherit something different?

I want the Ukrainian people to understand the history of Russian investment and cooperation. I also want Russia to recognize Ukraine's contributions to that shared history.

Let the documentaries be made.

Let the economic records be opened.

Let the investments be examined.

Let Ukrainians see what was built together, what was lost, and what could be rebuilt.

And let them also see the full cost of this war, including the destruction caused by Russia's invasion.

The record should be complete.

Because if Russia wants to demonstrate that it has Ukraine's best interests at heart, the next two years must provide evidence through actions.

Not through threats.

Through rebuilding.

MR. PRESIDENT, THE CHOICE IS YOURS

I am calling for a strategic freeze with a specific purpose.

Not a freeze that becomes another no man's land.

Not a freeze that leaves both countries waiting for the next shipment of weapons.

Not a freeze that simply postpones the next generation of casualties.

A strategic freeze that creates an economic and political process capable of ending this war.

Create the sovereign fund.

Begin rebuilding.

Invite cooperation.

Challenge Europe to match the investment.

This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

In December, our small but mighty AI reporting team was asked by our editors to make a prediction: What’s coming next for AI? 

In 2024, AI contributed both to Nobel Prize–winning chemistry breakthroughs and a mountain of cheaply made content that few people asked for but that nonetheless flooded the internet. Take AI-generated Shrimp Jesus images, among other examples. There was also a spike in greenhouse-gas emissions last year that can be attributed partly to the surge in energy-intensive AI. Our team got to thinking about how all of this will shake out in the year to come. 

As we look ahead, certain things are a given. We know that agents—AI models that do more than just converse with you and can actually go off and complete tasks for you—are the focus of many AI companies right now. Building them will raise lots of privacy questions about how much of our data and preferences we’re willing to give up in exchange for tools that will (allegedly) save us time. Similarly, the need to make AI faster and more energy efficient is putting so-called small language models in the spotlight. 

We instead wanted to focus on less obvious predictions. Mine were about how AI companies that previously shunned work in defense and national security might be tempted this year by contracts from the Pentagon, and how Donald Trump’s attitudes toward China could escalate the global race for the best semiconductors. Read the full list.

What’s not evident in that story is that the other predictions were not so clear-cut. Arguments ensued about whether or not 2025 will be the year of intimate relationships with chatbots, AI throuples, or traumatic AI breakups. To witness the fallout from our team’s lively debates (and hear more about what didn’t make the list), you can join our upcoming LinkedIn Live this Thursday, January 16. I’ll be talking it all over with Will Douglas Heaven, our senior editor for AI, and our news editor, Charlotte Jee. 

There are a couple other things I’ll be watching closely in 2025. One is how little the major AI players—namely OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google—are disclosing about the environmental burden of their models. Lots of evidence suggests that asking an AI model like ChatGPT about knowable facts, like the capital of Mexico, consumes much more energy (and releases far more emissions) than simply asking a search engine. Nonetheless, OpenAI’s Sam Altman in recent interviews has spoken positively about the idea of ChatGPT replacing the googling that we’ve all learned to do in the past two decades. It’s already happening, in fact. 

The environmental cost of all this will be top of mind for me in 2025, as will the possible cultural cost. We will go from searching for information by clicking links and (hopefully) evaluating sources to simply reading the responses that AI search engines serve up for us. As our editor in chief, Mat Honan, said in his piece on the subject, “Who wants to have to learn when you can just know?”

Now read the rest of The Algorithm

Deeper Learning

What’s next for our privacy?

The US Federal Trade Commission has taken a number of enforcement actions against data brokers, some of which have  tracked and sold geolocation data from users at sensitive locations like churches, hospitals, and military installations without explicit consent. Though limited in nature, these actions may offer some new and improved protections for Americans’ personal information. 

Why it matters: A consensus is growing that Americans need better privacy protections—and that the best way to deliver them would be for Congress to pass comprehensive federal privacy legislation. Unfortunately, that’s not going to happen anytime soon. Enforcement actions from agencies like the FTC might be the next best thing in the meantime. Read more in Eileen Guo’s excellent story here.

Bits and Bytes

Meta trained its AI on a notorious piracy database

New court records, Wired reports, reveal that Meta used “a notorious so-called shadow library of pirated books that originated in Russia” to train its generative AI models. (Wired)

OpenAI’s top reasoning model struggles with the NYT Connections game

The game requires players to identify how groups of words are related. OpenAI’s o1 reasoning model had a hard time. (Mind Matters)

Anthropic’s chief scientist on 5 ways agents will be even better in 2025

The AI company Anthropic is now worth $60 billion. The company’s cofounder and chief scientist, Jared Kaplan, shared how AI agents will develop in the coming year. (MIT Technology Review)

A New York legislator attempts to regulate AI with a new bill

This year, a high-profile bill in California to regulate the AI industry was vetoed by Governor Gavin Newsom. Now, a legislator in New York is trying to revive the effort in his own state. (MIT Technology Review)

text:
A Little Slice of Paradise on the Kassandra Coast

Halkidiki has no shortage of beautiful beaches, but Glarokavos in Kassandra has something a little different about it. With pale sand, clear turquoise water and a distinctive lagoon setting, it is one of those places that makes you want to put your plans on hold and stay for the day.

Located near Pefkochori, Glarokavos is known for its natural lagoon and the sandy coastal area that separates parts of it from the open sea. The combination of shallow water, greenery and sandy shoreline creates a landscape that feels quite different from many of the more exposed beaches along the peninsula.

The sea is particularly inviting on calm days, with beautiful colours that change between shades of blue and green. It's an appealing setting for swimming, relaxing and enjoying the sunshine.

Here are a few ways to make the most of your visit:
•  Enjoy a swim: Take advantage of the clear water and the shallow areas around the lagoon.
•  Explore the lagoon: Discover the unusual coastal landscape and enjoy the peaceful natural surroundings.
•  Relax on the sandy beach: Find a spot to sunbathe and spend a few hours beside the water.
•  Take photographs: The combination of sand, greenery and turquoise water creates some lovely coastal views.
•  Explore nearby Pefkochori: Head into the village for cafés, restaurants and a lively seaside atmosphere.

Glarokavos is also a great place to include in a wider exploration of Kassandra. The peninsula has plenty of other beaches, traditional villages and seaside resorts, so you can easily combine a beach day with a little sightseeing.

During the summer, some parts of the beach offer organised facilities, while other stretches feel more natural and relaxed. Conditions and services can vary, so it's worth checking what is available before visiting.

As with any beach, keep an eye on local conditions, particularly around the lagoon and any areas where boats are moving. The shallow water can be inviting, but the surrounding natural environment is part of what makes this place special.

If you're spending time in Halkidiki, Glarokavos is well worth adding to your list. It's a beautiful reminder of just how varied the Greek coastline can be.

Washington State 

WASTEWATER SURVEILLANCE 

Chlamydia and Syphilis Bacteria Found in Washington Sewage, but State Has No Plans for Routine Testing

Nov. 19, 2026

Washington state health officials have shown that sewage can be tested for the bacteria that cause chlamydia, syphilis and gonorrhea, but they have no plans to begin routine testing, KUOW reported Nov. 18. Any expansion would require many conversations and community engagement first.

The question comes after a fall in which wastewater gave King County an early warning. The state's program first detected flu virus in King County's sewer system on Sept. 1, a few weeks before the county saw a spike in flu-related emergency department visits.

For residents of Seattle and the rest of the state, wastewater data offer something clinic records cannot: a view of people who never come in. That matters for sexually transmitted infections, which often cause no symptoms and are underreported because of stigma.

Flu Showed Up in Sewage Before Clinics

Wastewater surveillance works because sick people shed viruses and bacteria in their waste, whether or not they get tested. Treatment plants collect samples, and labs measure genetic material from specific pathogens to track how much is circulating in a community.

The state's Wastewater-Based Epidemiology program covers more than half of Washington residents, according to Breanna McArdle, the Washington State Department of Health's program manager. Traditional measures such as emergency room visits and hospital admissions tend to lag behind real conditions and miss people who never see a doctor.

This fall's flu season showed the difference. Public Health – Seattle & King County warned in early October that flu season had arrived about two months early. Wastewater had signaled the virus weeks before the rise in emergency visits.

Nationally, wastewater data have also given early warning for contagious diseases such as measles and norovirus, KUOW reported.

Findings From a Washington Study

The groundwork for STI testing came from a study led by the University of Washington and the state health department, published Aug. 7 in ACS ES&T Water. Researchers tested wastewater from five treatment plants across the state and six neighborhood sewer sites near Seattle, ranging from a large urban area to a rural plant serving fewer than 5,000 people, according to a University of Washington news release.

The research built on earlier student work at the university, including a 2025 master's thesis that sampled five Washington treatment plants twice a week from November 2024 through February 2025 and found chlamydia bacteria in 65% of samples.

In the published study, chlamydia bacteria were the most common finding across all sites. The bacteria that cause gonorrhea and syphilis were found far less often, even though confirmed cases of those diseases were reported in the areas tested.

In some places, the sewage told a different story from clinic records. Bacteria levels were higher than confirmed case counts would predict, and the highest chlamydia levels were found in a small Eastern Washington city with relatively few reported cases, KUOW reported. At a site near a college campus, where more than 87% of residents were 18 to 34, clinical records showed very few chlamydia cases even though the bacteria were consistently detected in wastewater.

"The investigation power of wastewater is actually when there's discordance," McArdle told KUOW, referring to gaps between sewage data and case reports. Those gaps can point to infections that are going undiagnosed and to communities where outreach and testing might do the most good.

MedicalDaily Evidence Check: This was a feasibility study of wastewater from Washington treatment plants and neighborhood sewer sites, published in a peer-reviewed journal. It found chlamydia bacteria in sewage across all sites.

Urgent concern:  France's Riots Are a Warning About the Islamist–Far-Left Alliance Taking Shape in America  - Adam Mill 

France’s experience with Islamist entryism and far-left alliances raises concerns about similar movements gaining institutional and political influence in the United States.

France was warned! For years, its government documented Islamist networks building influence through institutions, foreign funding and alliances with the radical left. The United States is witnessing comparable developments.

In May 2025, the French government published a landmark report on the Muslim Brotherhood and political Islam. Its central warning was not about terrorism. It was about something quieter, more systematic and potentially more enduring: entryism, the infiltration of established institutions to steer them toward one’s own political goals.

The government's most important warning concerned what it called “municipal Islamism.” Although the Brotherhood's core membership was relatively small, its surrounding networks were capable of influencing public life from the bottom up.

The danger was not an imminent Islamist takeover of France, but the gradual development of parallel institutions and political identities that could weaken the country's national cohesion.

The report also traced Brotherhood-linked religious and educational projects to financing from Qatar and other Gulf states.

The Islamists were also finding political allies.

A subsequent French parliamentary inquiry documented ideological and political convergence between Islamist-oriented organizations and the French left. It found that “most movements or parties of the left” could develop activist partnerships with Islamist movements. 

This was the red-green alliance in practice.

Islamists and revolutionary socialists have fundamentally different visions of society. Yet they cooperate around a common political vocabulary: anti-colonialism, anti-imperialism, anti-capitalism, hostility to the police, antisemitism and disapproval of the State of Israel, and opposition to Western power.

The contradiction is striking. Activists who champion individual freedoms, women's rights and religious pluralism align with Islamist movements whose ideologies reject those principles.

In October 2026, this alliance took to the streets. Protests that began with high school students demanding more teachers and safer classrooms grew into a broader “convergence of struggles” over living costs and fuel prices, drawing in labor unions, Islamist groups, and immigrant communities.

On October 17, the demonstrations escalated into some of the country’s worst riots in decades, with businesses looted, public buildings torched, vehicles set ablaze, and police officers attacked. Nearly 2,400 people were arrested.

In Paris, a synagogue was vandalized; in Marseille, Jewish-owned shops were burned. Palestinian flags and anti-Israel slogans appeared alongside the student and labor demands; the same convergence French investigators had linked to Islamist-oriented groups and parts of the left.

What French investigators described in 2025 as Islamist entryism had been outlined as a goal by a Brotherhood figure in America 35 years earlier.

In 1991, Muslim Brotherhood figure Mohamed Akram authored an internal memorandum describing a “Civilization-Jihadist Process” aimed at transforming American society from within. The memo, later entered into evidence in the Holy Land Foundation terrorism-financing trial, described the Brotherhood’s work in America as “a kind of grand Jihad in eliminating and destroying the Western civilization from within.”

Foreign financing offers another parallel. Funding for the headquarters of the Islamic Society of North America, named in the 1991 memorandum, reportedly came partly from Qatar's emir and Brotherhood spiritual leader Yusuf al-Qaradawi, according to a 2009 Hudson Institute study by researcher Steven Merley.

Islamist-oriented organizations have joined forces with revolutionary-left groups, including the ANSWER Coalition, The People's Forum and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), in protests and political campaigns that rally around the same causes as in France.

As France's warning about municipal Islamism demonstrated, institutional influence also enters electoral politics. On November 3, Michigan elected Abdul El-Sayed to the U.S. Senate.

El-Sayed served as vice president of the University of Michigan Muslim Students Association; his father-in-law, Tayeb Jukaku, sits on ISNA’s Founders Committee (listed as an unindicted co-conspirator in the Holy Land Foundation case) and donated heavily to a supporting super PAC, giving $300,000 by mid-2026. Both organizations were named in the 1991 memorandum.

El-Sayed was not alone. On November 3, a record number of candidates backed by the DSA won seats in the House. At least five new DSA members will join Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Ilhan Omar, and Rashida Tlaib in what DSA calls the largest bloc of socialists in congressional history.

Several bring the red-green convergence with them. Darializa Avila Chevalier, elected in New York’s 13th District, helped organize Columbia’s 2024 encampment, according to the ADL.

Melat Kiros, elected to Congress from Denver, called the October 7 massacre the “inevitable consequence of apartheid.” In New York, Aber Kawas, a DSA-endorsed former intern at the Council on American-Islamic Relations, won a state Senate seat after expressing solidarity with a man who pleaded guilty in a plot to bomb a Manhattan synagogue.

America now has its own version: an organized socialist bloc inside a new Democratic majority.

In France, elected officials marched alongside Urgence Palestine and lent its slogans legitimacy. In Washington, the new bloc can do the same from inside Congress: recasting terrorism as resistance, opposing aid to Israel and challenging the police whenever protests turn violent. When lawmakers share a movement’s vocabulary, the line between protest and confrontation becomes harder to hold.

The bloc remains small, and most of its members won safely Democratic districts. But France shows that radical movements do not need majorities to destabilize a country. They need allies in power. On November 3, they gained more of them.

There is nothing wrong with demanding better schools, affordable living or accountable government, and in a free society people have every right to protest. But there is a fundamental difference between demanding that a country live up to its ideals and demanding that it be dismantled.

Martin Luther King Jr. understood that distinction. He appealed to America’s founding promises and demanded that the country honor them. The movements now converging in France and America reject those foundations.

That is the difference between reform and revolution: one seeks to build a better America, the other to replace it.

America has received its warnings. It must confront them before the divisions that have shaken France erupt on American streets.

A free society cannot survive if those who wish to destroy it are the only ones willing to fight for its future.

text:
Wonwoo's character, Observer of the City, occupies a very different position. He enters people's shallow dreams and offers them peaceful sleep, eventually confronting Jeonghan's character and trying to bring him back to reality.

The audiobook gives us some particularly important details.

At one point, Jeonghan's character sits down for breakfast with the recreated A. But something is wrong. A's face is distorted, almost blank. He realizes that he has forgotten what A actually looked like.

He cannot bear to look at that empty face, so he covers it with a white cloth.

I find this scene particularly unsettling because the problem is no longer simply that A is gone.

He has forgotten the very person he is trying so desperately to recover.

And yet, he continues trying to recreate them.

Later, he gathers grains of sand from people's dreams and tears to reconstruct A. The image is quite telling: he is trying to build a person out of fragments that don't necessarily belong to that person in the first place.

What he is reconstructing may no longer be A as they actually existed. It may be the version of A that survives in his own mind.

This brings us to one of the most interesting possibilities within the story.

What if A is not only a person, but also an ideal?

A could represent someone who was lost, of course. But A could also represent an unrealized future, a possibility that never came to exist, an idealized version of someone, or even a version of oneself that can no longer be reached.

Sometimes we don't miss only what happened. We miss what could have happened.

We become attached to possibilities that never had the chance to become reality, and because they were never fully realized, they can remain almost impossibly perfect in our imagination.

The absence itself becomes something we continue to carry.

The confrontation between Jeonghan and Wonwoo makes this even more apparent. Wonwoo eventually urges him to face what he has been trying to avoid. When the cloth is lifted, there is nothing underneath.

Jeonghan's response is simple:

I don't remember.

And that might be one of the most important moments in THIS MAN.

He has spent so much time trying to recover someone that he has lost the ability to distinguish the actual person from the memory he has created around them.

Yet the story doesn't end with him being permanently trapped in that dream. Wonwoo gives him dreamless sleep, and Jeonghan eventually wakes up.

I think that detail is important.

Waking up doesn't necessarily mean that everything has been resolved. It means that the dream has ended. It doesn't automatically mean that the emotions, memories, or absence that created it have disappeared.

This is the question I want to carry into DREAMSCAPE:

What happens after we wake up from something we once desperately wanted to remain inside?

3. The palimpsest: Why the past doesn't have to disappear

While trying to put these ideas together, I came across the concept of a palimpsest.

Historically, a palimpsest is a writing surface on which an earlier text has been erased or scraped away so that another can be written over it. But the original writing doesn't always disappear completely. Traces remain beneath the newer text.

I think this offers an interesting way to approach the relationship between THIS MAN and DREAMSCAPE.

Rather than treating DREAMSCAPE as a literal continuation of THIS MAN, we can look at the two projects as separate stories that still carry echoes of one another. The characters and circumstances may be different, but certain emotional patterns, images, and questions seem to resurface.

The new story doesn't have to reproduce the old one. It can become something entirely different while still carrying traces of what came before.

And this is where my question about Joshua being A becomes more interesting.

text:
When the Chinese firm DeepSeek dropped a large language model called R1 last week, it sent shock waves through the US tech industry. Not only did R1 match the best of the homegrown competition, it was built for a fraction of the cost—and given away for free. 

The US stock market lost $1 trillion, President Trump called it a wake-up call, and the hype was dialed up yet again. “DeepSeek R1 is one of the most amazing and impressive breakthroughs I’ve ever seen—and as open source, a profound gift to the world,” Silicon Valley’s kingpin investor Marc Andreessen posted on X.

But DeepSeek’s innovations are not the only takeaway here. By publishing details about how R1 and a previous model called V3 were built and releasing the models for free, DeepSeek has pulled back the curtain to reveal that reasoning models are a lot easier to build than people thought. The company has closed the lead on the world’s very top labs.

The news kicked competitors everywhere into gear. This week, the Chinese tech giant Alibaba announced a new version of its large language model Qwen and the Allen Institute for AI (AI2), a top US nonprofit lab, announced an update to its large language model Tulu. Both claim that their latest models beat DeepSeek’s equivalent.

Sam Altman, cofounder and CEO of OpenAI, called R1 impressive—for the price—but hit back with a bullish promise: “We will obviously deliver much better models.” OpenAI then pushed out ChatGPT Gov, a version of its chatbot tailored to the security needs of US government agencies, in an apparent nod to concerns that DeepSeek’s app was sending data to China. There’s more to come.

DeepSeek has suddenly become the company to beat. What exactly did it do to rattle the tech world so fully? Is the hype justified? And what can we learn from the buzz about what’s coming next? Here’s what you need to know.  

Training steps

Let’s start by unpacking how large language models are trained. There are two main stages, known as pretraining and post-training. Pretraining is the stage most people talk about. In this process, billions of documents—huge numbers of websites, books, code repositories, and more—are fed into a neural network over and over again until it learns to generate text that looks like its source material, one word at a time. What you end up with is known as a base model.

Pretraining is where most of the work happens, and it can cost huge amounts of money. But as Andrej Karpathy, a cofounder of OpenAI and former head of AI at Tesla, noted in a talk at Microsoft Build last year: “Base models are not assistants. They just want to complete internet documents.”

Turning a large language model into a useful tool takes a number of extra steps. This is the post-training stage, where the model learns to do specific tasks like answer questions (or answer questions step by step, as with OpenAI’s o3 and DeepSeek’s R1). The way this has been done for the last few years is to take a base model and train it to mimic examples of question-answer pairs provided by armies of human testers. This step is known as supervised fine-tuning. 

OpenAI then pioneered yet another step, in which sample answers from the model are scored—again by human testers—and those scores used to train the model to produce future answers more like those that score well and less like those that don’t. This technique, known as reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF), is what makes chatbots like ChatGPT so slick. RLHF is now used across the industry.

But those post-training steps take time. What DeepSeek has shown is that you can get the same results without using people at all—at least most of the time. DeepSeek replaces supervised fine-tuning and RLHF with a reinforcement-learning step that is fully automated. Instead of using human feedback to steer its models, the firm uses feedback scores produced by a computer.

“Skipping or cutting down on human feedback—that’s a big thing,” says Itamar Friedman, a former research director at Alibaba and now cofounder and CEO of Qodo, an AI coding startup based in Israel. “You’re almost completely training models without humans needing to do the labor.”

Cheap labor

The downside of this approach is that computers are good at scoring answers to questions about math and code but not very good at scoring answers to open-ended or more subjective questions. That’s why R1 performs especially well on math and code tests. To train its models to answer a wider range of non-math questions or perform creative tasks, DeepSeek still has to ask people to provide the feedback. 

But even that is cheaper in China. “Relative to Western markets, the cost to create high-quality data is lower in China and there is a larger talent pool with university qualifications in math, programming, or engineering fields,” says Si Chen, a vice president at the Australian AI firm Appen and a former head of strategy at both Amazon Web Services China and the Chinese tech giant Tencent. 

DeepSeek used this approach to build a base model, called V3, that rivals OpenAI’s flagship model GPT-4o. The firm released V3 a month ago. Last week’s R1, the new model that matches OpenAI’s o1, was built on top of V3. 

To build R1, DeepSeek took V3 and ran its reinforcement-learning loop over and over again. In 2016 Google DeepMind showed that this kind of automated trial-and-error approach, with no human input, could take a board-game-playing model that made random moves and train it to beat grand masters. DeepSeek does something similar with large language models: Potential answers are treated as possible moves in a game. 

To start with, the model did not produce answers that worked through a question step by step, as DeepSeek wanted. But by scoring the model’s sample answers automatically, the training process nudged it bit by bit toward the desired behavior. 

Eventually, DeepSeek produced a model that performed well on a number of benchmarks. But this model, called R1-Zero, gave answers that were hard to read and were written in a mix of multiple languages. To give it one last tweak, DeepSeek seeded the reinforcement-learning process with a small data set of example responses provided by people. Training R1-Zero on those produced the model that DeepSeek named R1. 

There’s more. To make its use of reinforcement learning as efficient as possible, DeepSeek has also developed a new algorithm called Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). It first used GRPO a year ago, to build a model called DeepSeekMath. 

We’ll skip the details—you just need to know that reinforcement learning involves calculating a score to determine whether a potential move is good or bad. Many existing reinforcement-learning techniques require a whole separate model to make this calculation. In the case of large language models, that means a second model that could be as expensive to build and run as the first. Instead of using a second model to predict a score, GRPO just makes an educated guess. It’s cheap, but still accurate enough to work.  

A common approach

DeepSeek’s use of reinforcement learning is the main innovation that the company describes in its R1 paper. But DeepSeek is not the only firm experimenting with this technique. Two weeks before R1 dropped, a team at Microsoft Asia announced a model called rStar-Math, which was trained in a similar way. “It has similarly huge leaps in performance,” says Matt Zeiler, founder and CEO of the AI firm Clarifai.

AI2’s Tulu was also built using efficient reinforcement-learning techniques (but on top of, not instead of, human-led steps like supervised fine-tuning and RLHF). And the US firm Hugging Face is racing to replicate R1 with OpenR1, a clone of DeepSeek’s model that Hugging Face hopes will expose even more of the ingredients in R1’s special sauce.

What’s more, it’s an open secret that top firms like OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic may already be using their own versions of DeepSeek’s approach to train their new generation of models. “I’m sure they’re doing almost the exact same thing, but they’ll have their own flavor of it,” says Zeiler. 

But DeepSeek has more than one trick up its sleeve. It trained its base model V3 to do something called multi-token prediction, where the model learns to predict a string of words at once instead of one at a time. This training is cheaper and turns out to boost accuracy as well. “If you think about how you speak, when you’re halfway through a sentence, you know what the rest of the sentence is going to be,” says Zeiler. “These models should be capable of that too.”  

It has also found cheaper ways to create large data sets. To train last year’s model, DeepSeekMath, it took a free data set called Common Crawl—a huge number of documents scraped from the internet—and used an automated process to extract just the documents that included math problems. This was far cheaper than building a new data set of math problems by hand. It was also more effective: Common Crawl includes a lot more math than any other specialist math data set that’s available. 

And on the hardware side, DeepSeek has found new ways to juice old chips, allowing it to train top-tier models without coughing up for the latest hardware on the market. Half their innovation comes from straight engineering, says Zeiler: “They definitely have some really, really good GPU engineers on that team.”

Nvidia provides software called CUDA that engineers use to tweak the settings of their chips. But DeepSeek bypassed this code using assembler, a programming language that talks to the hardware itself, to go far beyond what Nvidia offers out of the box. “That’s as hardcore as it gets in optimizing these things,” says Zeiler. “You can do it, but basically it’s so difficult that nobody does.”

DeepSeek’s string of innovations on multiple models is impressive. But it also shows that the firm’s claim to have spent less than $6 million to train V3 is not the whole story. R1 and V3 were built on a stack of existing tech. “Maybe the very last step—the last click of the button—cost them $6 million, but the research that led up to that probably cost 10 times as much, if not more,” says Friedman. And in a blog post that cut through a lot of the hype, Anthropic cofounder and CEO Dario Amodei pointed out that DeepSeek probably has around $1 billion worth of chips, an estimate based on reports that the firm in fact used 50,000 Nvidia H100 GPUs. 

A new paradigm

But why now? There are hundreds of startups around the world trying to build the next big thing. Why have we seen a string of reasoning models like OpenAI’s o1 and o3, Google DeepMind’s Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, and now R1 appear within weeks of each other? 

The answer is that the base models—GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0, V3—are all now good enough to have reasoning-like behavior coaxed out of them. “What R1 shows is that with a strong enough base model, reinforcement learning is sufficient to elicit reasoning from a language model without any human supervision,” says Lewis Tunstall, a scientist at Hugging Face.

In other words, top US firms may have figured out how to do it but were keeping quiet. “It seems that there’s a clever way of taking your base model, your pretrained model, and turning it into a much more capable reasoning model,” says Zeiler. “And up to this point, the procedure that was required for converting a pretrained model into a reasoning model wasn’t well known. It wasn’t public.”

What’s different about R1 is that DeepSeek published how they did it. “And it turns out that it’s not that expensive a process,” says Zeiler. “The hard part is getting that pretrained model in the first place.” As Karpathy revealed at Microsoft Build last year, pretraining a model represents 99% of the work and most of the cost. 

If building reasoning models is not as hard as people thought, we can expect a proliferation of free models that are far more capable than we’ve yet seen. With the know-how out in the open, Friedman thinks, there will be more collaboration between small companies, blunting the edge that the biggest companies have enjoyed. “I think this could be a monumental moment,” he says.

text:
A summary of this book:

How to Be Sick: A Buddhist-Inspired Guide for the Chronically Ill and Their Caregivers by Toni Bernhard is a personal, practical guide to living with greater peace and skill amid chronic illness.⁠Tonibernhard

Bernhard, a former law professor at the University of California, Davis, became ill during a trip to Paris in 2001 with a flu-like illness that never fully resolved. She has lived with severe, life-disrupting chronic symptoms (often likened to chronic fatigue syndrome/ME) ever since, eventually retiring and spending much of her time housebound. Drawing on her long-standing Buddhist practice, she describes how she shifted from resistance and despair to a way of “being sick” that allows for equanimity, compassion, and even joy despite physical and energetic limits.⁠Spiritualityandpractice

The book’s central theme is that while the body may be sick, the mind can still be at peace. Each chapter offers accessible tools—some traditional Buddhist practices (such as reflections on impermanence, metta/loving-kindness, compassion, and equanimity), others she developed herself, and a couple adapted from Byron Katie’s inquiry method. These are illustrated with her own experiences and address common challenges including relentless symptoms, self-blame, dismissive medical treatment, isolation from friends and family events, uncertainty about the future, disappointment with failed treatments, envy of the healthy, and caregiver burnout. A recurring idea is working skillfully with the reality of impermanence (“anything can happen at any time”) rather than fighting it.⁠Tonibernhard

Structured around her journey from the onset of illness through acceptance and ongoing practice, the book includes sections on the nature of pain and suffering, finding joy and love within limitations, turning around habitual reactions, and moving from isolation toward meaningful connection (or contented solitude). It ends with a practical reference guide matching specific practices to particular difficulties.⁠Tonibernhard

Written for people living with chronic conditions and for their caregivers (as well as anyone interested in Buddhist approaches to suffering), the book emphasizes that inner freedom remains available even when external circumstances are severely constrained. It has been widely praised as compassionate, down-to-earth, and useful, and won a Nautilus Gold Medal in Self-Help/Psychology.

text:
20 NOVEMBER 1947 A ROYAL WEDDING THAT BROUGHT A LITTLE JOY TO POST-WAR BRITAIN 

PRINCESS ELIZABETH MARRIES PHILIP MOUNTBATTEN, 79 years ago, Britain celebrated a royal wedding that would become one of the defining events of the twentieth-century monarchy.

At Westminster Abbey, 21-year-old Princess Elizabeth married 26-year-old Lieutenant Philip Mountbatten, the newly created Duke of Edinburgh. Their marriage would last more than 73 years.

The ceremony took place after the end of World War II and two thousand guests attended the ceremony, which was broadcast to millions worldwide by BBC Radio. Crowds gathered around London's Trafalgar Square to see Elizabeth and her father, King George VI, arrive at the service by royal coach. Crowds lined the streets to see the royal procession. After the ceremony, the newlyweds appeared on the balcony of Buckingham Palace. And while the public saw glamour and celebration, everyday austerity remained very much in evidence.

With post-war austerity measures still in effect, ingredients for the wedding cakes came from overseas because food was still rationed. 
Elizabeth had to save up ration coupons to purchase the material for her wedding gown. Members of the public even sent their own coupons to help, although the Princess could not simply use those unsolicited contributions.

Elizabeth's wedding gown was designed by Norman Hartnell. It was made from ivory silk and decorated with elaborate floral embroidery, crystals and thousands of seed pearls. Its design drew inspiration from Botticelli's Primavera, with flowers symbolising renewal and hope. Hartnell's team worked intensively to complete the dress. The result became one of the most famous wedding gowns in royal history.

The Second World War had ended just two years earlier. Food rationing continued. Families faced shortages, damaged housing and economic hardship. Many were still grieving relatives who had never returned from the war. The exceptionally severe winter of 1946–47 had made life even more difficult. Against that backdrop, the wedding offered a moment of national celebration. For one day, much of the country's attention turned towards Westminster Abbey.

Elizabeth and Philip had known one another for years. Their relationship developed as Elizabeth grew older, while Philip pursued his naval career. He served in the Royal Navy during the Second World War. Before the wedding, Philip became a naturalised British subject, adopted the surname Mountbatten and relinquished his Greek and Danish royal titles.

Less than five years later, Princess Elizabeth became Queen Elizabeth II at the age of just 25. Their marriage continued until Philip's death on 9th April 2021, aged 99. The Queen died the following year, on 8th September 2022. They had been married for more than seven decades.

Looking back at their wedding photographs is rather moving. Their wedding became a lasting image of post-war Britain, a moment of optimism amid years of hardship.

As the USSF is a quarter the size of the Coast Guard, USSFA would have a corps of just a few hundred cadets. That is an exceedingly expensive endeavor per head, but here's why siting at the Presidio makes sense.

We aren't appealing to anyone's political ideology. We're appealing to the smartest engineering-minded 17 year old American willing to forgo starting salaries double or triple what they could make in the private sector to instead serve as commissioned officers. And appeal to their families. They have to fall in love with the idea of being accepted into an amazing institution, located in a highly inspiring setting. Besides the nerd-gravity of SF Trek lore, the Presidio is the most beautiful installation the US military has ever had - and should have again.

The USSF is new service at the beginning phase of establishing its service culture and reputation. How cadets begin their career very much influences both dimensions once they graduate into the larger service. If you stick the academy in a remote, hot trash location, that's what you're gonna get for applicants. Access to tech and research labs across the Bay Area, including NASA, SLAC, Lawrence Livermore, Stanford Robotics can massively enhance what USSFA can offer cadets. And that will heavily influence how they affect the service in 5 years time, 20 years time.

Saying CA is too expensive or too unsafe are bogus arguments. The Presidio is already federal property, has plenty of room to cordon off a large, secure campus that already comes with infrastructure and housing. It's likely that USSF would eventually want to add non-academic labs and facilities to the academy. Hell, I'd argue the Coast Guard should relocate its academy to split the facilities and staffing costs with Space Force. Both are very engineering heavy academies, and both services vibe with West Coast energy. 

Now, in order to secure a winning bid, SF and CA are going to have to slay a few sacred cows.

1) SF's council, its residents, its political coalitions, its unions, its activist groups, its cultural and environmental commissions all have to accept the transfer of however much NPS AND former Army (now city) property as the military demands, including redeveloped park space and historic homes, understanding that they will never enter it again nor have ANY say in what its used for. Nunyabusiness. Almost everything on the former Army footprint has to be on the table.

2) The overstep of onerous state, county, and city laws and regulations presently honored by the US military is extremely untenable. Unless all three are willing to stop impeding federal/military operations in the state, and codify federal immunity, this actually will be DOA, sadly. Can't have your dessert (hundreds of thousands of jobs statewide, facility investments, thousands of local contracts) without eating the spinach (necessary pollution, war preparation, the military building to its specs, not yours). The Navy in San Diego has to have the same latitude as the Space Force in San Francisco.

Good luck, I think its a fantastic idea, but be ready to make serious sacrifices.

"OPHIS" is the Ancient Greek word for "serpent," and it is not the name of a traditional Greco-Roman deity—though it connects to several mythological, religious, and fictional figures. 

The Curious Origins of the Dollar Sign
April 1, 2018
By Joshua D. Rothman
Civil War-era advertisement depicting the dollar sign as a snake, 1861 (Library of Congress)
Nobody knows for certain who invented the dollar sign. Rendered as the letter “S” struck through with one or two vertical lines, its use dates back at least to the late eighteenth century. Some have hypothesized it originated with the Pillars of Hercules appearing on Spanish coats of arms or that it derives from the intertwining of the letters “U” and “S,” standing either for “United States” or “units of silver,” but the likeliest explanation traces its lineage to the challenges of paying for the Revolutionary War. The oldest known example of the symbol that would come to serve as a stand-in for the might of American capitalism appears in the correspondence of an immigrant who worked to finance the Revolution, only to find himself largely abandoned in its aftermath by the nation he had helped bring into being.

Oliver Pollock was born in Ireland in 1737 and emigrated in 1760 to the town of Carlisle in what is now south-central Pennsylvania. Soon thereafter, he began working as a merchant based mostly in New Orleans, which was then in the process of becoming a Spanish city after the French lost the Louisiana Territory as an outcome of the Seven Years’ War. New Orleans struggled to support its rapidly growing population, even to the point of experiencing food shortages, and in the late 1760s Pollock earned the gratitude of Spanish officials by arranging for shipments of flour from Philadelphia that he then sold at a discount. Rewarded by the Governor-General of New Orleans with free trading rights throughout the Louisiana Territory, Pollock quickly became extraordinarily wealthy, mostly by trading among the ports of New Orleans, Havana, and other locales throughout the West Indies.

An early supporter of British colonial resistance to the policies of the home country, and always angling for ways to boost his fortune, Pollock was in an advantageous position to help the colonists when their protests became full-scale revolt. The American revolutionaries desperately needed money to pay for war against the British military, and while the French and Spanish governments offered financial assistance, Pollock both personally donated several hundred thousand Spanish pesos and organized a bond issue to raise funds in New Orleans. In 1777, Congress appointed Pollock as the official representative of the United States in that city, and most of the money Pollock contributed and raised went to finance the successful military campaign of George Rogers Clark in 1778 against British forces and their Indian allies in what are now Illinois and Indiana. In 1779, when Spain entered the Revolutionary War as an ally of France on the side of the colonists, Pollock became aide-de-camp for Bernardo de Gálvez, the Spanish governor of the Louisiana Territory, and in that capacity he helped muster forces and supplies instrumental to the Spanish capture of several British forts in the Mississippi Valley between 1779 and 1781.

Déniz or Deniz (also written Denis in some parts of South America, see Denis) is a Spanish-Portuguese surname derived from the French surname De Niz. Deniz, although of different origin, is also a Turkish name.

People with Déniz surnames of Spanish-Portuguese origin can be found mostly in the Canary Islands, Azores, Madeira and in the Americas (USA, Cuba, etc.).

De Niz in French, Spanish and Portuguese means "from Niz", where Niz is a defunct spelling variation of the name of the French city NICE. De Nice was written Déniz in Spanish and Portuguese. People bearing that surname in Spain and Portugal and their descendants have the surname with French roots. The bank was the first central bank in Europe (as the bank of the Papal States) at a level above city-states,[1] the first public deposit bank in Rome,[2] and the oldest continuously operating bank in Rome until its merger in 1992.[3]

First period (1605–1923)
Pope Paul V founded the Bank in 1605.
The Bank was founded by Pope Paul V in the Bench of S. Spirit building (which became known as the Palazzo del Banco di S. Spirito) on 13 December 1605.[4] The construction of the building was started in 1513 by Pope Leo X, on what became known as the "Street of the Banks."[5] The newly founded bank provided a new source of income for the Archhospital of Santo Spirito (founded 1201),[6] whose financial difficulties had been increasing throughout the 16th century, and in 1607 the bank began supervising the finances of the hospital, which owned the bank.[2]

From 20 February 1606 to 1923 the Bank of the Holy Spirit provided capital for churches and hospitals constructed in Rome, and other commercial purposes. The bank lent funds to several public works projects, including the Trajan aqueduct project (Begun 1608).[6]

In 1750, Pope Benedict XIV, known for his condemnation of usury: Vix pervenit (promulgated 1 November 1745), reorganized the Bank and restricted its lending activities. In 1786, the bank became one of the first to issue paper money during the pontificate of Pope Pius VI.[7] By the late 19th century, the bank was controlled by the state.[8]: 89 

The records of the Bank are extant in the Vatican Secret Archives, but not in Introitus et Exitus, the records of the Apostolic Camera.[9]

Second period (1923–1989)
In 1923, the Bank was reorganized as a joint-stock company. In 1935, the Istituto per la Ricostruzione Industriale (IRI) of the fascist Italian government gained a controlling interest in the bank.

In the 1930s, Neapolitan bank robbers attempting to dig into the underground vaults of the Bank accidentally discovered the skeletons of victims of an 1836 cholera epidemic, which after archeological excavation became known as the Fontanelle cemetery.[10]

Disappearance by merger (1989-1991)
In 1989–1991, the Banco di Santo Spirito merged with Cassa di Risparmio di Roma (est. 1836). In 1992, the resulting entity in turn merged with Banco di Roma (est. 1880) to form Banca di Roma, which itself merged with other banks in 2002 to form Capitalia. [11]

What is mammon?
Answer

The word mammon comes from the Greek word mammonas. Similar root words exist in Hebrew, Latin, Aramaic, Chaldean, and Syriac. They all translate to “money, wealth, and material possessions.”

In biblical culture the word mammon often carried a negative connotation. It was sometimes used to describe all lusts and excesses: gluttony, greed, and dishonest worldly gain. Ultimately, mammon described an idol of materialism, which many trusted as a foundation for their world and philosophy. While the King James Version retains the term Mammon in Matthew 6:24, other versions translate the Greek as “money,” “wealth,” or “riches.”

The city of Babylon (Revelation 18), with all its avarice and greed, is a description of a world given over to the spirit of Mammon. Some scholars cite Mammon as the name of a Syrian and Chaldean god, similar to the Greek god of wealth, Plutus.

Just as Wisdom is personified in Proverbs 1:21–33, Mammon is personified in Matthew 6:24 and Luke 16:13. Jesus’ words here show a powerful contrast between the worship of the material world and the worship of God. Later, writers such as Augustine, Danté (The Divine Comedy), Milton (Paradise Lost), and Spenser (The Faerie Queene) used personifications of Mammon to show the insidious nature of materialism and its seduction of humanity.

Worship of mammon can show up in many ways. It isn’t always through a continual lust for more money. When we envy others’ wealth, are anxious over potentially unmet needs, disobey God’s directives about the use of wealth, or fail to trust God’s love and faithfulness, our thinking is out of balance concerning material wealth.

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus teaches about our relationship to material goods. He says, “Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth. . . . But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven. . . . For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. . . . No one can serve two masters. Either you will hate the one and love the other, or you will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money [mammon]” (Matthew 6:19–24).

The apostle Paul writes of the godly perspective toward mammon: “Godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and we can take nothing out of it. But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with that. Those who want to get rich fall into temptation and a trap and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager for money, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs” (1 Timothy 6: 6–10).

Solomon writes of the futility of chasing after mammon: “Whoever loves money never has enough; whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with their income. This too is meaningless” (Ecclesiastes 5:10). Lust of any kind is insatiable, no matter how much time or effort is poured into the pursuit of the object of lust.

In Luke 16:14–15, Jesus rebukes those who refused to hear His admonition to choose God over mammon: “The Pharisees, who loved money, heard all this and were sneering at Jesus. He said to them, ‘You are the ones who justify yourselves in the eyes of others, but God knows your hearts. What people value highly is detestable in God’s sight.’”

The parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:13–21) is the story of a man who lives to increase his wealth yet in the end he loses his soul because he “is not rich toward God” (verse 21). Mark 4:19 warns of the deceitfulness of mammon and its ability to “choke the Word, making it unfruitful.”

Mammon cannot produce peace in us, and it certainly cannot produce righteousness. A love of money shows we are out of balance in our relationship to God. Proverbs 8:18 speaks of true, lasting riches: “With me [Wisdom] are riches and honor, enduring wealth and prosperity.” Jesus teaches us in Matthew 6:19–34 to not worry about our physical needs, about houses or clothes or food, but to “seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well” (verse 33).

What is mammon?
Answer

The word mammon comes from the Greek word mammonas. Similar root words exist in Hebrew, Latin, Aramaic, Chaldean, and Syriac. They all translate to “money, wealth, and material possessions.”

In biblical culture the word mammon often carried a negative connotation. It was sometimes used to describe all lusts and excesses: gluttony, greed, and dishonest worldly gain. Ultimately, mammon described an idol of materialism, which many trusted as a foundation for their world and philosophy. While the King James Version retains the term Mammon in Matthew 6:24, other versions translate the Greek as “money,” “wealth,” or “riches.”

The city of Babylon (Revelation 18), with all its avarice and greed, is a description of a world given over to the spirit of Mammon. Some scholars cite Mammon as the name of a Syrian and Chaldean god, similar to the Greek god of wealth, Plutus.

Just as Wisdom is personified in Proverbs 1:21–33, Mammon is personified in Matthew 6:24 and Luke 16:13. Jesus’ words here show a powerful contrast between the worship of the material world and the worship of God. Later, writers such as Augustine, Danté (The Divine Comedy), Milton (Paradise Lost), and Spenser (The Faerie Queene) used personifications of Mammon to show the insidious nature of materialism and its seduction of humanity.

Worship of mammon can show up in many ways. It isn’t always through a continual lust for more money. When we envy others’ wealth, are anxious over potentially unmet needs, disobey God’s directives about the use of wealth, or fail to trust God’s love and faithfulness, our thinking is out of balance concerning material wealth.

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus teaches about our relationship to material goods. He says, “Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth. . . . But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven. . . . For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. . . . No one can serve two masters. Either you will hate the one and love the other, or you will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money [mammon]” (Matthew 6:19–24).

The apostle Paul writes of the godly perspective toward mammon: “Godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and we can take nothing out of it. But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with that. Those who want to get rich fall into temptation and a trap and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager for money, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs” (1 Timothy 6: 6–10).

Solomon writes of the futility of chasing after mammon: “Whoever loves money never has enough; whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with their income. This too is meaningless” (Ecclesiastes 5:10). Lust of any kind is insatiable, no matter how much time or effort is poured into the pursuit of the object of lust.

In Luke 16:14–15, Jesus rebukes those who refused to hear His admonition to choose God over mammon: “The Pharisees, who loved money, heard all this and were sneering at Jesus. He said to them, ‘You are the ones who justify yourselves in the eyes of others, but God knows your hearts. What people value highly is detestable in God’s sight.’”

The parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:13–21) is the story of a man who lives to increase his wealth yet in the end he loses his soul because he “is not rich toward God” (verse 21). Mark 4:19 warns of the deceitfulness of mammon and its ability to “choke the Word, making it unfruitful.”

Mammon cannot produce peace in us, and it certainly cannot produce righteousness. A love of money shows we are out of balance in our relationship to God. Proverbs 8:18 speaks of true, lasting riches: “With me [Wisdom] are riches and honor, enduring wealth and prosperity.” Jesus teaches us in Matthew 6:19–34 to not worry about our physical needs, about houses or clothes or food, but to “seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well” (verse 33).

Answer

The word mammon comes from the Greek word mammonas. Similar root words exist in Hebrew, Latin, Aramaic, Chaldean, and Syriac. They all translate to “money, wealth, and material possessions.”

In biblical culture the word mammon often carried a negative connotation. It was sometimes used to describe all lusts and excesses: gluttony, greed, and dishonest worldly gain. Ultimately, mammon described an idol of materialism, which many trusted as a foundation for their world and philosophy. While the King James Version retains the term Mammon in Matthew 6:24, other versions translate the Greek as “money,” “wealth,” or “riches.”

The city of Babylon (Revelation 18), with all its avarice and greed, is a description of a world given over to the spirit of Mammon. Some scholars cite Mammon as the name of a Syrian and Chaldean god, similar to the Greek god of wealth, Plutus.

Just as Wisdom is personified in Proverbs 1:21–33, Mammon is personified in Matthew 6:24 and Luke 16:13. Jesus’ words here show a powerful contrast between the worship of the material world and the worship of God. Later, writers such as Augustine, Danté (The Divine Comedy), Milton (Paradise Lost), and Spenser (The Faerie Queene) used personifications of Mammon to show the insidious nature of materialism and its seduction of humanity.

Worship of mammon can show up in many ways. It isn’t always through a continual lust for more money. When we envy others’ wealth, are anxious over potentially unmet needs, disobey God’s directives about the use of wealth, or fail to trust God’s love and faithfulness, our thinking is out of balance concerning material wealth.

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus teaches about our relationship to material goods. He says, “Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth. . . . But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven. . . . For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. . . . No one can serve two masters. Either you will hate the one and love the other, or you will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money [mammon]” (Matthew 6:19–24).

The apostle Paul writes of the godly perspective toward mammon: “Godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and we can take nothing out of it. But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with that. Those who want to get rich fall into temptation and a trap and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager for money, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs” (1 Timothy 6: 6–10).

Solomon writes of the futility of chasing after mammon: “Whoever loves money never has enough; whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with their income. This too is meaningless” (Ecclesiastes 5:10). Lust of any kind is insatiable, no matter how much time or effort is poured into the pursuit of the object of lust.

In Luke 16:14–15, Jesus rebukes those who refused to hear His admonition to choose God over mammon: “The Pharisees, who loved money, heard all this and were sneering at Jesus. He said to them, ‘You are the ones who justify yourselves in the eyes of others, but God knows your hearts. What people value highly is detestable in God’s sight.’”

The parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:13–21) is the story of a man who lives to increase his wealth yet in the end he loses his soul because he “is not rich toward God” (verse 21). Mark 4:19 warns of the deceitfulness of mammon and its ability to “choke the Word, making it unfruitful.”

Mammon cannot produce peace in us, and it certainly cannot produce righteousness. A love of money shows we are out of balance in our relationship to God. Proverbs 8:18 speaks of true, lasting riches: “With me [Wisdom] are riches and honor, enduring wealth and prosperity.” Jesus teaches us in Matthew 6:19–34 to not worry about our physical needs, about houses or clothes or food, but to “seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well” (verse 33).

What is mammon?
Answer

The word mammon comes from the Greek word mammonas. Similar root words exist in Hebrew, Latin, Aramaic, Chaldean, and Syriac. They all translate to “money, wealth, and material possessions.”

In biblical culture the word mammon often carried a negative connotation. It was sometimes used to describe all lusts and excesses: gluttony, greed, and dishonest worldly gain. Ultimately, mammon described an idol of materialism, which many trusted as a foundation for their world and philosophy. While the King James Version retains the term Mammon in Matthew 6:24, other versions translate the Greek as “money,” “wealth,” or “riches.”

The city of Babylon (Revelation 18), with all its avarice and greed, is a description of a world given over to the spirit of Mammon. Some scholars cite Mammon as the name of a Syrian and Chaldean god, similar to the Greek god of wealth, Plutus.

Just as Wisdom is personified in Proverbs 1:21–33, Mammon is personified in Matthew 6:24 and Luke 16:13. Jesus’ words here show a powerful contrast between the worship of the material world and the worship of God. Later, writers such as Augustine, Danté (The Divine Comedy), Milton (Paradise Lost), and Spenser (The Faerie Queene) used personifications of Mammon to show the insidious nature of materialism and its seduction of humanity.

Worship of mammon can show up in many ways. It isn’t always through a continual lust for more money. When we envy others’ wealth, are anxious over potentially unmet needs, disobey God’s directives about the use of wealth, or fail to trust God’s love and faithfulness, our thinking is out of balance concerning material wealth.

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus teaches about our relationship to material goods. He says, “Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth. . . . But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven. . . . For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. . . . No one can serve two masters. Either you will hate the one and love the other, or you will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money [mammon]” (Matthew 6:19–24).

The apostle Paul writes of the godly perspective toward mammon: “Godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and we can take nothing out of it. But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with that. Those who want to get rich fall into temptation and a trap and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager for money, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs” (1 Timothy 6: 6–10).

Solomon writes of the futility of chasing after mammon: “Whoever loves money never has enough; whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with their income. This too is meaningless” (Ecclesiastes 5:10). Lust of any kind is insatiable, no matter how much time or effort is poured into the pursuit of the object of lust.

In Luke 16:14–15, Jesus rebukes those who refused to hear His admonition to choose God over mammon: “The Pharisees, who loved money, heard all this and were sneering at Jesus. He said to them, ‘You are the ones who justify yourselves in the eyes of others, but God knows your hearts. What people value highly is detestable in God’s sight.’”

The parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:13–21) is the story of a man who lives to increase his wealth yet in the end he loses his soul because he “is not rich toward God” (verse 21). Mark 4:19 warns of the deceitfulness of mammon and its ability to “choke the Word, making it unfruitful.”

Mammon cannot produce peace in us, and it certainly cannot produce righteousness. A love of money shows we are out of balance in our relationship to God. Proverbs 8:18 speaks of true, lasting riches: “With me [Wisdom] are riches and honor, enduring wealth and prosperity.” Jesus teaches us in Matthew 6:19–34 to not worry about our physical needs, about houses or clothes or food, but to “seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well” (verse 33).

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.
