# **THE CHESS BOARD – #Africa : THE GREAT LAKES – #Kenya**
# **THE DREADED CALL FROM WASHINGTON,#USA : WHY MOI OBEYED AND LEFT POWER IN 2002**

**"Why #African Democracy Is a Farce Tied to Western Interests — And The Three Kings Who Shaped Modern Kenya"**

Why do unpopular African presidents fear a call from Washington? Because Moi received one in 2002. And when Washington calls, even a lion becomes a lamb.

 **PROLOGUE: THE PHONE THAT ENDED A PRESIDENCY**

State House, Nairobi. 2002. Midnight. The phone rings. Not a normal phone. The red phone, that  rings for orders & urgency.

On one end: Daniel arap Moi, president for 24 years. The Lion. The Professor.

On the other: Washington. The Real King. The message was calm and clear: *Daniel. Don't rig. Don't impose Uhuru. We are comfortable with Kibaki. Our man. Leave peacefully.*

Moi listened. The Lion became a Lamb.

Why would a man who jailed opponents, tortured dissidents  and presided over disputed elections & had all the state machinery & resources suddenly obey and leave? Because Moi understood the chessboard. When the King calls, the Rook must move. Otherwise, the Rook is removed.

Museveni understands this too. That is why he sleeps with one eye open. If Moi obeyed, Museveni can also be called.

Interesting Fact:Kenya's intelligence, then led by Brigadier Wilson Boinnet, informed Moi that Washington opposed a rigged victory for Uhuru and favoured Kibaki. Moi, who trusted intelligence more than almost anyone, understood that #USA was serious.

 **CHAPTER 1: MOI — THE PROFESSOR WHO READ THE TIMES**

Moi was no amateur. He was a grandmaster. He became president in 1978 after Jomo Kenyatta's death and ruled until 2002: 24 years.

In the 1980s, Africa was coups and instability. Uganda, Ethiopia, Somalia, Sudan, Nigeria, Ghana, Liberia, Chad — all in turmoil. Moi concluded that opening space could expose Kenya to similar instability. So he closed it. He jailed, tortured and killed dissidents, banned opposition and made Kenya a one-party state.

Was it right? No. Torture is never right. But critics argue Moi prioritised stability through fear over freedom.

Then the 1990s arrived. Cold War ended. Washington demanded multiparty democracy. Meanwhile, Goldenberg devastated the economy. Moi could no longer rule as brutally as in the 80s. Washington could cut aid. Kenyans could revolt.

So the Professor adapted. He allowed multiparty in 1991. But he ensured opposition did not stay united. FORD split into FORD-Kenya under Oginga Odinga and FORD-Asili under Kenneth Matiba. Two camps, divided by politics and ethnicity. Moi won 1992 with only 36%. He repeated it in 1997.

Critics say Moi was not a democrat. He was a divider who exploited tribal divisions. And Washington watched and said, "Moi is still our man."

**The Final Calculation: 2002**

Why did Moi appear to prefer Kibaki? Kibaki was quiet in opposition. He rarely organised mass protests or confronted Moi aggressively.

By 2002, critics also alleged Moi and his family had substantial offshore wealth, in Switzerland, London and Dubai. Moi had wealth, family, and a retirement home in Kabarak. Rigging for Uhuru could bring sanctions, isolation, and losing everything. Leaving peacefully offered a safer retirement.

So the Professor made his final calculation. He obeyed. He left. Not because he loved democracy. Because he loved his wealth, his family, and his peace. And he knew: The West can seize your wealth with one sanction and jail you with another resolution.

 **CHAPTER 2: KIBAKI — THE PERFECT GENTLEMAN PUPPET**

*Mwai Kibaki was not born to fight. He was born to wait.*

He studied economics at the London School of Economics (LSE). He learned economics, polished English, and how to talk to British bankers, IMF and World Bank. He was not a street fighter. He was a boardroom politician.

Why was Kibaki the perfect puppet? Because he went to LSE, the School of Perfect African Puppets! A factory producing polite, quiet puppets who wear suits, speak perfect English, say "Yes, Sir" with a smile and never shout!

LSE taught Kibaki how to say, " IMF, you are right." " World Bank, you are right." " British Army, please stay in Nanyuki." And never say, "Leave!"

LSE did not teach Kibaki how to fight for Kenya. It taught him how to manage Kenya for Britain. That is why the Brits TOTALLY trusted him. They trained him. He was their student. Their boy. Their gentleman puppet!

*The One-Party State Question*
As Vice President and Leader of Government Business, Kibaki moved the motion that made Kenya a one-party state in 1982 through Section 2A. The man later celebrated as a democrat had helped establish the one-party state.

Critics ask: If Kibaki was a reformist, why did he move it? A reformist would fight it. A reformist would resign. Kibaki moved it. He proposed it. He defended it.

Raila spent eight years in detention opposing the one-party state. Kibaki sat in Cabinet and helped establish it. One man suffered for democracy. The other profited from dictatorship.

Kibaki was Moi's VP from 1978 to 1988, during the brutal years of Nyayo House. He remained in Cabinet, neither resigning nor publicly protesting. Critics therefore call him a manager, not a reformist. A manager manages the system. A reformist changes it.

**2002: KIBAKI TOSHA!**

In 2002, Kibaki ran under NARC with Raila, Wamalwa, Ngilu and others. But there was one ingredient behind that victory.

**KIBAKI TOSHA!** Raila stood at Uhuru Park and declared, "KIBAKI TOSHA!" — Kibaki is enough! Kenyans listened. Raila was the mobiliser, the engine. He delivered the votes. Kibaki was the beneficiary.

Kenyans expected a new #Constitution in 100 days, an end to corruption, jobs. By 2005, they had enough: Anglo Leasing — billions vanished, nobody jailed. No new Constitution. No 500,000 jobs. Artur Brothers in 2006 — guns, police escorts, VIP treatment, linked to the raid on The Standard and drug trade. Media Raid in 2006 — at 1am, masked police raided The Standard and KTN, smashed equipment, burned papers. Second Family — tabloids alleged Kibaki had a second family with Mary Wambui, presented as alleged, not proven. Michuki Killings — critics say police killed hundreds of young men, especially Mungiki suspects, in extrajudicial killings. Kibaki remained largely silent. Again, Kibaki kept quiet.

 **CHAPTER 3: 2005 — KIBAKI TOSHA BECOMES BETRAYAL**

In 2005, referendum on a new Constitution. Kibaki wanted YES. Raila wanted NO. Raila campaigned across Kenya: "This Constitution is Kibaki's Constitution, not People's Constitution!" And Raila won. The NO defeated the President.

Kibaki had government machinery and resources. Raila had only his network, charisma and supporters. Yet Raila defeated him.

Critics argue the referendum exposed the real engine behind 2002. When Raila stood with Kibaki, Kibaki won. When Raila opposed Kibaki in 2005, Kibaki lost. Kibaki was the car. Raila was the driver. Without the driver, the car could not move.

To be fair, Kibaki opened democratic space further. He allowed media and opposition to criticise more freely than under Moi. That is his credit.

But critics argue Kibaki's strongest years (7.5/10) were largely due to Raila inside government (2003 to 2005 & 2008 to 2013). From 2002 to mid-2005, economy grew, Free Primary Education worked, roads were built, NARC stayed united. Raila was the engineer. Kibaki was the manager who signed. The engineer designed. The manager signed. Kenya moved.

After 2005, Raila left. Between mid-2005 to 2007, Kibaki's presidency was at its worst. Everyone saw it. Critics describe decline, with Kibaki surrounded by powerful interests, including the so-called Mount Kenya Mafia. The engineer had left. The manager was without a blueprint. A manager without an engineer is like a driver without a map.

 **CHAPTER 4: 2007 — THE STOLEN VICTORY**

In 2007, Raila ran against Kibaki.  He was reportedly ahead by more than 1.2 million votes the following morning, with strong support across 6/8 provinces at that time. His lead appeared unassailable.

Then counting descended into chaos. The Electoral Commission under Samuel Kivuitu stopped counting amid controversy. Reports of irregularities, confusion, disputed results. Kivuitu eventually announced Kibaki as winner.

Kibaki was sworn in at State House that evening, in darkness, within about 30 minutes, without public celebration. Like a thief sworn in at night. A first in Africa! Critics argue the hurried ceremony became the enduring symbol of the disputed election because thieves thrive best in darkness.

*Interesting Facts:
 1. In March 2026, NTV Kenya aired the documentary  *Stolen Ballot :The 2007 Presidential election heist, where it exposed everything. 
2. In 2025, Governor George Natembeya, former PA to Most Powerful Kibaki Era Minister Michuki, reportedly stated at a funeral that Raila had won 2007 by more than two million votes ,a landslide & that the polls were overtuned in favor of Kibaki. 
3. Media Tycoon-Royal Media chairman S.K. Macharia has repeatedly claimed at public events and funerals that Raila clearly won 2007 but was forced to support Kibaki's announcement.

And what did America and Europe do? They quickly recognised Kibaki. #USA congratulated him. #UK congratulated him. EU raised concerns (as thye always do)but continued supporting his administration. Critics argue the West preferred Kibaki because he was predictable, while Raila was independent and difficult to control. A stolen victory for their puppet was apparently better than a genuine victory for a man they could not control.

Kenya exploded. More than 1,300 killed, over 600,000 displaced. One of  Africa's most stable countries came close to becoming a failed state.

And in 2011, Kibaki did his part as the West's favourite puppet: he deployed troops to Somalia, Operation Linda Nchi, to fight Al-Shabaab for America. Kenyans died in Somalia. Why? Because America wanted a proxy army, and Kibaki said, "Yes, Sir." Critics say Raila would have said, "Somalia is not our war."

 **CHAPTER 5: WHY AFRICAN DEMOCRACY IS A FARCE**

Moi learned it in 2002. Kibaki demonstrated it in 2007. Museveni understands the danger.

African democracy is a farce tied to Western interests through neocolonialism. In much of Africa, popular support alone does not guarantee power. Western support can be just as important. If you are a reliable ally, you may remain despite corruption and disputed elections. If you are independent, you may not rule even with genuine popular support.

Why? Because Africa's economic dependence makes it vulnerable. Africa has cobalt, copper, gold, uranium, oil, coltan, tea, coffee, flowers. Yet much of the continent exports raw materials and imports finished products. It borrows from IMF and World Bank and depends on foreign markets. When your economy depends on external lifelines, saying NO becomes difficult.

Look at MONUSCO in #DRC. The UN's largest mission has operated for decades, yet Congo remains plagued by conflict despite mineral wealth estimated at $24 trillion. Critics ask: If MONUSCO keeps peace, why does Congo remain at war? Why do Congolese children dig in mines while minerals leave for international markets? Is it peacekeeping or resource-keeping? Similar criticisms apply to UN  Missions in Mali, CAR and South Sudan. Always located in Resource Rich/strategic regions of Africa.

And #Africa has another problem. It has no permanent seat on the UN Security Council. Five permanent members with veto: #USA, #UK, #France, #Russia, #China. Africa has zero permanent seats, zero vetoes. 54 countries, 1.4 billion people, not a single permanent seat. Africa can speak in the General Assembly. It can shout. But when powerful countries disagree, Africa has little power to stop them.

**Libya 2011: 54 Countries Versus 3**

In March 2011, African Union proposed dialogue in Libya. AU wanted leaders to negotiate peace with Gaddafi. A delegation of South Africa, Uganda, Mauritania, Congo and Mali travelled to Tripoli but were turned https://t.co/7BfhkhFzcF seriously? &intervention proceeded. America, Britain and France backed action under Resolution 1973. NATO bombed Libya for 7 months. AU's initiative was sidelined. 54 countries called for dialogue, yet 3 Western powers shaped the military course. Gaddafi was killed. Libya descended into instability, rival governments, militias,terrorism & reports of open slave markets. #AU watched, humiliated and powerless.

If 54 African countries cannot prevent intervention against one African country, how can one president confidently tell Washington NO?

That is neocolonialism. Not flags over Kenya & Nigeria. It is loans, sanctions, international missions, and a Security Council where Africa has no permanent seat.

*PUPPETS = RULE:
* Kibaki — lost 2005, 2007 victory stolen, yet remained with Western recognition. 
*Kagame — routinely wins with ~99%, critics question freedom, yet West supports him for strategic importance in DRC. 
*Museveni — rules decades amid repression & Killings, USA still works with him for intersets in DRC, S.Sudan & Somalia. 
*Kabila — ruled 18 years, critics questioned legitimacy & Nationality but West tolerated him amid mineral interests. 
*Biya — rules 40+ years, France maintains close relations. 
*Ouattara — became president in 2011 after French intervention removed Uncooperative Gbagbo. 
*Gnassingbé — inherited dynasty, in power since 2005.

*INDEPENDENTS = REMOVED:*
*Raila — won 2007 but never became president because he was not Washington's preferred candidate. 
*Gbagbo — confrontation with France ended in removal in 2011. 
*Gaddafi — pursued African economic independence, Resolution 1973 authorised intervention, NATO bombed Libya 7 months, Gaddafi killed. 
*Sankara — wanted independent Africa, killed in 1987 in a coup widely associated with French-backed interests.

-One Security Council resolution- can bring down a powerful country. Look at Libya. Gaddafi had oil, money, army. But America, Britain, France secured Resolution 1973. NATO bombed 7 months. Gaddafi killed. One resolution. One piece of paper. That is real power. The King writes a resolution. The Rook is removed.

-Sanctions- can cripple weak African economies. If America sanctions Kenya, shilling falls, fuel rises, businesses suffer. If Europe refuses Kenyan flowers or tea, thousands lose jobs. Africa cannot easily sanction America. America can sanction Africa. This is not an equal game.

So presidents learn: Protect Western interests, and Washington may protect you despite corruption,repression &murder. Challenge Western interests, and Washington may sanction you or isolate you. The people vote, but Washington weighs its interests. The people count votes, but Washington counts  interests.

 **CHAPTER 6: THREE KINGS, ONE NEVER RULED**

All three were Kings. But one never sat on the throne. That is the tragedy of modern #African politics.

1. MOI — THE LION KING-TEACHER/PROFESSOR
-Strengths: 
Master politician who survived coups, opposition and end of Cold War. Maintained stability when Africa had coups and wars. Understood Western interests. 
-Weaknesses: 
Authoritarian, Nyayo House torture, repression, corruption, Goldenberg, tribal divisions, disputed elections 1992, 1997. 24 years was too long. 
-Why Washington trusted him: During Cold War, Moi protected Western interests, opposed communism, close to Britain, predictable. When Cold War ended, usefulness changed. In 2002, Washington wanted him gone. The King called. The Lion obeyed.

2. KIBAKI — THE QUIET KING, THE MANAGER/ECONOMIST
-Strengths: 
Educated, reserved, economic. Free Primary Education, roads, , economic growth ~7%. Opened democratic space, made Kenya attractive for business. 
-Weaknesses: 
Moved One-Party motion 1982, served Moi during repression. Presidency faced Anglo Leasing, Artur Brothers, media raid, alleged second family, extrajudicial killings. Stole 2007 victory almost made Kenya a failed state. Critics say many reforms came through Raila pressure. 
-Why Washington trusted him: Predictable, polite, comfortable with Western institutions. The gentleman who knew when to say, "Yes, Sir."

**3. RAILA — THE KING WHO NEVER RULED, THE PEOPLE'S(PAWNS) PRESIDENT/ENGINEER**
Original Sin: His father Jaramogi Oginga Odinga, Kenya's First VP, was accused by Western governments of communist sympathies and close relations with Russia. Critics argue Raila inherited that suspicion. He Befriended Washington and London, but his independent instincts made Western governments uncomfortable.

-Strengths: 
Humble,Charismatic but  brave, fearless& independent. 8 years in detention, suffered torture, never abandoned struggle. Brilliant political and professional engineer, mobiliser, orator. Delivered Kibaki's 2002 victory, defeated Kibaki in 2005 referendum, clearly won 2007. Pushed 2010 Constitution. Willing to work with political enemies to protect Kenyan Pawns.
 -Weaknesses: 
Too outspoken, abrasive, independent, unpredictable for Western powers. Handshake & Cooperation's with political foesattracted criticism. Struggled to convince some he had a fully developed economic team for IMF, World Bank.

-Why Raila couldn't be a Western puppet: Critics argue Raila was not known for grand corruption and offshore scandals associated with many elites. Corrupt politicians can be controlled through weaknesses. Offshore accounts can be frozen. Scandals can be exposed. But what happens when a politician has fewer financial vulnerabilities? A clean man is harder to blackmail. A man who thinks independently is harder to control. Critics argue Raila's independence made him difficult for Western governments to trust.

#Raila also understood winning popular votes as he did severally  did not mean winning power. And that the West had decided never to support him ,he was at piece wit that .That's why made many concessions when Kenya faced violence. He knew he could not allow Kenyans to die for his ambition. So he conceded ,forgave & worked with enemies. That was not weakness. It was wisdom and concern for ordinary Kenyans. Raila unlike Kibaki &  to the disgust of many of his supporters, refused to burn Kenya just to become president. That is greatness.

 **CHAPTER 7: HOW THE THREE KINGS SHAPED MODERN KENYA — A TRIBUTE**

All three Kings are now dead. We have criticised them and exposed weaknesses. But we must acknowledge contributions that helped shape Kenya into a relatively stable and admirable country compared to many African states.

1. MOI — STABILITY:** In the 1980s, Africa had coups, wars, instability. Moi kept Kenya relatively stable. Yes, brutal. Yes, torture. Yes, divided opposition. But Kenya remained one country. That stability remains one of his most significant contributions in the Wildwest Africa of The 80'S.

2. KIBAKI — DEMOCRATIC SPACE AND ECONOMIC GROWTH:** Kibaki opened democratic space, allowing media, opposition and citizens greater freedom to criticise. He delivered Free Primary Education, roads, infrastructure, and economic growth. Investors came. Tourism expanded. Businesses grew.

*3. RAILA — THE 2010 CONSTITUTION:** Raila's greatest achievement was his contribution to the 2010 Constitution. Not Kibaki Tosha. Not 2007. The 2010 Constitution. It introduced devolution, counties, strengthened Bill of Rights, limits on presidential power, judicial independence, stronger electoral framework. Before 2010, Constitution concentrated power in presidency. After 2010, presidential power faced much stronger limits. That is Raila's legacy. He helped push for a Constitution that gives Pawns greater protection against Kings.

Three Kings. Three gifts. Stability. Democratic space and economic growth. A Constitution.

 **CHAPTER 8 — WHY KENYA IS STILL ADMIRABLE**

Kenya is not perfect. It still struggles with corruption, tribalism, poverty. But it is still standing. Kenya has never collapsed and remains one of the more admirable countries in Africa & the global south because of :

1. INDEPENDENT JUDICIARY: Yes, judiciary has corruption. Judges accused of bribe taking, cases take years. But despite its weaknesses, It has repeatedly challenged Executive. In 2017, Supreme Court nullified presidential election. Historic demonstration of independence. Courts have shown president is not automatically above law & have numerously ruled against the executive. That is 2010 Constitution working.

2. INDEPENDENT MEDIA:- In Kenya, media and citizens can openly criticize the  president & govt. Turn on Citizen TV, NTV, KTN, Radio Citizen or social media. Every day, Kenyans criticize the president. They call him names, create memes, songs, cartoons. And most wake up next morning free, alive, ready to do it again! In many African countries, insulting a president can land you in prison or worse. Kenya is not perfect. Journalists are sometimes harassed, police have violently suppressed protesters. But compared with many African countries, Kenya still enjoys considerable space for criticism. Kenyans can speak. They can laugh at president. That is noisy democracy, but democracy nonetheless.

3. DISCIPLINED MILITARY:-Kenya's military, KDF, has maintained strong tradition of civilian control and is among the more disciplined militaries in the world. It DOES NOT; interfere in succession, engage in Business, announce coups or play politics. Kenya has never experienced a successful military coup, unlike many African countries. KDF protects borders, fights terrorism, participates in regional operations. But it has never seized State House. It respects constitutional civilian authority. It protects Kenya, not a tribe or an individual president. In Africa, that is admirable. It is rare. And it is one of the major reasons Kenya has remained stable since independence.

**FINALLY**

"2002 was not the dawn of true democracy in Kenya(i.e free and fair presidential election). It was simply the turn of the perfect Western puppet who was at the right place & time— and no one could stop him."

#DISCLAIMER: For educational discussion. We present allegations by critics, claims by insiders, historical accounts and arguments by supporters. Allegations are not automatically established facts. We respect Moi, Kibaki and Raila, all now deceased, and their families. We sympathise with victims of post-election violence. Our criticism is directed at a system where foreign powers exercise enormous influence while ordinary Africans pay the price. Secrecy breeds mistrust. Transparency creates peace. We support African sovereignty, peace and the right of Africans to choose their leaders through credible elections only. If any fact is wrong, provide a credible source and we will correct it.

text:
In 1979 police in Washington arrested a security guard for strangling two young women. He swore he couldn't remember a thing. So a psychologist hypnotized him, counted him up through his own life, and asked to speak to someone else. A different man answered. He lit a cigarette, swore at the doctor, and said he did it.

His name was Steve. He said Ken was the problem.

In the video below, Kenneth Bianchi goes under hypnosis and "Steve" comes out. Watch how fast the polite, sleepy guy turns into someone else, and listen to what Steve says about Ken: "I belong out. Ken belongs gone."

Ken Bianchi was 27. He had a girlfriend, a baby son and a job as a security guard in Bellingham.

He had just moved up from Los Angeles. Back there, 10 women and girls had been found strangled and dumped on hillsides between 1977 and 1978. The papers called it the Hillside Strangler.

January 1979. Two students in Bellingham take a house-sitting job he offered them. They're found dead in their car the next day.

He gets arrested. He says he has no memory of that night.

March 1979. Dr. John Watkins puts him under. Counts him up to 27. Then: "I want to talk to Stevie."

Steve shows up angry. "I come out whenever I felt like it. Now you gotta stick your nose in this whole mess."

Then he confesses. "I killed those broads." To show Ken he couldn't push him around.

Then he gives up Los Angeles. He names his cousin Angelo Buono. "He's my kind of person."

Watkins believed it. Another doctor did too. If Steve did it, Ken was insane, and the death penalty was off the table.

Then the prosecution brought in Martin Orne, one of the top hypnosis experts in the country.

Orne mentioned that real cases usually have more than two personalities. Next session, a third one showed up. Billy.

Then he told Bianchi, under "hypnosis," that his lawyer was sitting in the room. The lawyer wasn't there. Bianchi reached out and shook his hand.

Then detectives found who Steve Walker really was. A real psychologist. Bianchi had stolen his credentials to set up a fake therapy practice.

I've watched this clip more times than I want to admit, and what gets me is the counting. He sits through every number like a man waiting for his cue.

The insanity plan was dead. So he made a deal. Guilty to 2 murders in Washington and 5 in LA, and he'd testify against his cousin to avoid the death penalty.

Angelo Buono's trial took two years and more than 400 witnesses. On Halloween 1983 he was convicted of 9 murders. Life without parole. He died in prison in 2002.

Bianchi is 74 now. Last year he asked for parole after 46 years inside. Denied. He can try again in 10 years.

Was Steve just a con he pulled off in front of the best doctors in the country, or did Ken Bianchi start believing in Steve himself?

🇱🇾 𝗟𝗶𝗯𝘆𝗮 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝘁 𝗮 𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀𝗿𝗼𝗮𝗱𝘀.

At Global Insights Group’s Libya Desk, we have been working overtime, monitoring developments and speaking with senior Libyan and international officials as the country approaches a critical political juncture.

Here is our assessment of the unfolding crisis. 𝗟𝗲𝘁’𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗽 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝗯𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹𝘀.

The US, Turkey, France and others increasingly recognise that the time for unification has come. Others favour preserving the status quo, arguing that a flawed deal could do more harm than good.

But 𝗟𝗶𝗯𝘆𝗮’𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝘂𝘀 𝗾𝘂𝗼 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗹𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘆 𝗳𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁.

Fragmentation has hollowed out institutions, weakened the economy and entrenched competing interests. The risks of inaction now include economic collapse, renewed conflict in western Libya and exposure to geopolitical crises unfolding around the country.

𝗦𝗼 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲?

Critics point to spoilers, particularly western Libyan factions unwilling to accept the LNA.

Yet half of western Libya’s political establishment was prepared to accommodate the LNA under Bashagha. Those who opposed that arrangement are the exact same people now negotiating with Haftar.

𝗪𝗵𝗼, 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗻, 𝗶𝘀 𝗹𝗲𝗳𝘁 𝗼𝗽𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗟𝗡𝗔, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗹𝘂𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆?

The obstacle was never simply the LNA. It was who gets a seat at the table.

Western Libya’s fragmented political system benefits actors both inside and outside government. Many support unification only if their interests are secured. Otherwise, they threaten to spoil.

𝗕𝘂𝘁 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗹𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗺𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲?

Libya’s political class is remarkably vulnerable. Historically, obstruction has depended heavily on foreign sponsorship. Turkey, Italy, Egypt and others have enabled competing factions, while Washington remained largely disengaged.

Today, few Libyan actors would risk obstructing a US-backed process without foreign assurances. This gives Washington considerable leverage.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗼𝗯𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗹𝘆.

Targeted sanctions, naming and shaming foreign sponsors, and enforceable electoral commitments should accompany negotiations.

The Federal Reserve’s reluctance to accommodate recent CBL leadership changes without safeguards illustrates the pressure needed.

Massad Boulos’s sanctions warning was welcome, particularly following measures against Osama Njeem. But Njeem was the lowest-hanging fruit. Without near-term progress, entrenched status quo actors and their affiliates should face similar scrutiny.

Unification carries legitimate risks concerning governance, institutional control and power-sharing. These require safeguards and sustained international oversight.

𝗕𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼 𝗹𝗼𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗮 𝗳𝗹𝗮𝘄𝗲𝗱 𝗱𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗮 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝘂𝘀 𝗾𝘂𝗼.

It is between a difficult, managed transition and increasingly dangerous fragmentation.

Those advocating the status quo must explain what credible alternative they offer.

𝗟𝗶𝗯𝘆𝗮 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗮 𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗵 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗱. 𝗜𝘁 𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗸𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗶𝘁 𝘂𝗻𝗮𝘃𝗼𝗶𝗱𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗸𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗽𝗶𝘃𝗼𝘁𝗮𝗹.

Our 𝗪𝗲𝗲𝗸𝗹𝘆 𝗟𝗶𝗯𝘆𝗮 𝗣𝗼𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗥𝗶𝘀𝗸 𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁, published every Friday, provides exclusive reporting, political intelligence and forward-looking risk assessments.

BREAKING 🇺🇸🇷🇺🇨🇳🇺🇦 

TRUMP, PUTIN AND XI JUST SIGNED A DECLARATION ABOUT PEACE. UKRAINE ISN’T MENTIONED ONCE 

Three of the world’s most powerful leaders met in China on November 19 and published a four-point agreement called the “Declaration toward Peace.”

The White House released it. So did Beijing.

And the most revealing part may be what they chose to include, and what they left out.

Not one mention of Ukraine.

No demand for Russia to withdraw its troops. No commitment to Ukraine’s territorial integrity. No reference to the civilians killed or displaced by Moscow’s invasion.

Instead, the declaration discusses nuclear stability, UN reform, petroleum supplies and the legal immunity of state officials.

That last provision deserves particular attention.

Vladimir Putin has been wanted by the International Criminal Court since March 17, 2023, over alleged responsibility for the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children.

The arrest warrant was issued by the ICC, whose judges found reasonable grounds to believe he bears individual criminal responsibility.

Putin has rejected the court’s authority, and Russia is not a party to its founding treaty.

Neither is the United States or China.

Now all three governments have endorsed language emphasising state consent, official immunities and limits on the ICC’s jurisdiction.

There is an important legal distinction here: the declaration does not cancel Putin’s arrest warrant, grant him immunity from prosecution or change the court’s existing obligations.

But politically, the message is difficult to ignore.

The three leaders found room to discuss protections for state officials without mentioning the war that brought one of them under international criminal investigation.

And there is another contradiction.

The declaration promises UN reform to strengthen international peace and security.

Yet Russia used its veto on February 25, 2022, to block a Security Council resolution demanding an end to its invasion of Ukraine.

Eleven members supported that resolution. Russia alone voted against it, while three countries abstained.

So the same government that prevented the Security Council from acting against its own invasion is now endorsing a statement about making the UN more effective.

That is a remarkable omission of context.

The nuclear provision also raises questions.

In January 2022, the five recognised nuclear-weapon states jointly affirmed that nuclear war must never be fought.

Russia was among them.

Just weeks later, Putin launched his full-scale invasion and subsequently used nuclear threats to discourage Western intervention.

Repeating an important principle is welcome. But repeating it is not the same as establishing new, enforceable commitments.

And perhaps the strangest provision concerns oil.

Three leaders meeting under the banner of international peace agreed to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products.

That may serve economic and energy-security interests, but it offers no direct answer to the destruction taking place in Ukraine.

My biggest concern is not that Washington, Moscow and Beijing are talking. Dialogue between nuclear powers is necessary.

It is that they have produced a declaration with language about protecting powerful officials, but nothing about protecting the sovereignty of a country invaded by one of those officials.

Ukraine and its European partners were absent from the document.

Their security, however, cannot simply be treated as a secondary issue in decisions taken by larger powers.

A declaration that finds room for Putin’s legal concerns but not a single word for Ukraine’s sovereignty tells us something about the priorities behind the diplomatic spectacle.

Peace is not measured by the number of powerful men who sign a statement.

It is measured by whether aggression ends, civilians are protected and international law is upheld. https://t.co/tswQI0fo3c

This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

If it’s not broken, don’t fix it. That’s the approach bad state actors seem to have taken when it comes to how they mess with elections around the world.

When the generative-AI boom first kicked off, one of the biggest concerns among pundits and experts was that hyperrealistic AI deepfakes could be used to influence elections. But new research from the Alan Turing Institute in the UK shows that those fears might have been overblown. AI-generated falsehoods and deepfakes seem to have had no effect on election results in the UK, France, and the European Parliament, as well as other elections around the world so far this year.

Instead of using generative AI to interfere in elections, state actors such as Russia are relying on well-established techniques—such as social bots that flood comment sections—to sow division and create confusion, says Sam Stockwell, the researcher who conducted the study. Read more about it from me here.

But one of the most consequential elections of the year is still ahead of us. In just over a month, Americans will head to the polls to choose Donald Trump or Kamala Harris as their next president. Are the Russians saving their GPUs for the US elections? 

So far, that does not seem to be the case, says Stockwell, who has been monitoring viral AI disinformation around the US elections too. Bad actors are “still relying on these well-established methods that have been used for years, if not decades, around things such as social bot accounts that try to create the impression that pro-Russian policies are gaining traction among the US public,” he says. 

And when they do try to use generative-AI tools, they don’t seem to pay off, he adds. For example, one information campaign with strong ties to Russia, called Copy Cop, has been trying to use chatbots to rewrite genuine news stories on Russia’s war in Ukraine to reflect pro-Russian narratives. 

The problem? They’re forgetting to remove the prompts from the articles they publish. 

In the short term, there are a few things that the US can do to counter more immediate harms, says Stockwell. For example, some states, such as Arizona and Colorado, are already conducting red-teaming workshops with election polling officials and law enforcement to simulate worst-case scenarios involving AI threats on Election Day. There also needs to be heightened collaboration between social media platforms, their online safety teams, fact-checking organizations, disinformation researchers, and law enforcement to ensure that viral influencing efforts can be exposed, debunked, and taken down, says Stockwell. 

But while state actors aren’t using deepfakes, that hasn’t stopped the candidates themselves. Most recently Donald Trump has used AI-generated images implying that Taylor Swift had endorsed him. (Soon after, the pop star offered her endorsement to Harris.) 

Earlier this year I wrote a piece exploring the brave new world of hyperrealistic deepfakes and what the technology is doing to our information landscape. As I wrote then, there is a real risk of creating so much skepticism and distrust in our information landscape that bad actors, or opportunistic politicians, can take advantage of this trust vacuum and lie about the authenticity of real content. This is called the “liar’s dividend.” 

There is an urgent need for guidelines on how politicians use AI. We currently lack accountability or clear red lines as to how political candidates can use AI in an ethical manner within the election context, says Stockwell. The more we see political candidates carry out practices like sharing AI-generated adverts without labels or or making accusations that other candidates’ activities are AI-generated, the more it becomes normalized, he adds. And everything we’ve seen so far suggests that these elections are only the beginning. 

Now read the rest of The Algorithm

Deeper Learning

AI models let robots carry out tasks in unfamiliar environments

It’s tricky to get robots to do things in environments they’ve never seen before. Typically, researchers need to train them on new data for every new place they encounter, which can become very time-consuming and expensive.

Now researchers have developed a series of AI models that teach robots to complete basic tasks in new surroundings without further training or fine-tuning. The five AI models, called robot utility models (RUMs), allow machines to complete five separate tasks—opening doors and drawers, and picking up tissues, bags, and cylindrical objects—in unfamiliar environments with a 90% success rate. This approach could make it easier and cheaper to deploy robots in our homes. Read more from Rhiannon Williams here.

Bits and Bytes

There are more than 120 AI bills in Congress right now
US policymakers have an “everything everywhere all at once” approach to regulating artificial intelligence, with bills that are as varied as the definitions of AI itself.
(MIT Technology Review)

Google is funding an AI-powered satellite constellation to spot wildfires faster
The full FireSat system should be able to detect tiny fires anywhere in the world—and provide updated images every 20 minutes. (MIT Technology Review) 

A project analyzing human language usage shut down because “generative AI has polluted the data”
Wordfreq, an open-source project that scraped the internet to analyze how humans use language, found that post-2021, there is too much AI-generated text online to make any reliable analyses. (404 Media) 

Data center emissions are probably 662% higher than Big Tech claims
AI models take a lot of energy to run and train, and tech companies have emphasized their efforts to counter their emissions. There is, however, a lot of “creative accounting” happening when it comes to calculating carbon footprints, and new analysis shows that data center emissions from these companies is likely 7.62 times higher than officially reported.

When I add captions to my videos, the English appears automatically. The Igbo? Either it doesn’t appear at all, or it makes no sense. The word « Igbo » itself is often turned into « evil ».

text:
SoMePoster: Post to every platform from one place

Most brands don’t live on one network. Customers find you on Instagram, check your Google listing, read your blog and join your newsletter, and each of those needs its own posting routine.

SoMePoster brings these channels into one dashboard, so you plan the content once and publish it everywhere it belongs.

Facebook: Meta’s largest network, built around Pages, groups and communities. It suits local businesses, events and paid-plus-organic campaigns aimed at a broad adult audience.

Instagram: Visual-first, with feed posts, Reels and Stories. It is strongest for consumer brands, lifestyle, hospitality and anything that photographs well.

LinkedIn: The main B2B network, used for thought leadership, hiring and lead generation. Posts from personal profiles often get more reach than company Pages.

X (Twitter): Fast, text-led and news-driven. Brands use it for real-time commentary, customer replies and building a following around ideas.

Threads: Meta’s text-first network, tied to Instagram accounts. It is a conversational channel for brands that want a lighter tone than X.

Bluesky: A newer, decentralized microblogging network. It has an engaged audience among journalists, tech people and creators who left X.

Mastodon: A federated network of independent servers. The audience is small but loyal, and it is common in open-source, tech and academic circles.

TikTok: Short-form video driven by recommendation, so unknown accounts can reach large audiences. It is the main channel for reaching under-35s and for creator-style marketing.

YouTube: Long-form and Shorts video, and also the second most used search engine. Videos keep driving traffic for months or years after posting.

Pinterest: A visual search and discovery engine where users save ideas to boards. It works well for evergreen traffic in niches like food, travel, home and fashion.

Telegram: Messaging app with broadcast channels and groups. It lets you reach subscribers directly, with no algorithm deciding who sees a post.

Slack: Workplace chat. Posting here usually means sharing updates into team or community channels rather than reaching the public.

Google Business Profile: The listing that appears in Google Search and Maps. Posts, offers and review replies here influence local visibility, which makes it important for any location-based business.

WordPress: The most widely used CMS. Publishing from one tool means a blog post and its social promotion go out together.

Ghost: A publishing platform focused on newsletters and memberships. It is popular with independent writers and media brands.

Blogger: Google’s free blogging platform. It is simple, and some older sites and niche blogs still run on it.

Hashnode: A blogging platform for developers with built-in community discovery. It suits technical content marketing.

dev to: A community publishing site for developers. Articles can reach a technical audience without a site of your own.

LiveJournal: One of the oldest blogging communities, still active in some regions and interest groups. It is a niche channel with an established readership.

Shopify: E-commerce platform. Connecting it lets product and store content flow into the same scheduling workflow.

Wix: Website builder aimed at small businesses. Publishing from the same tool keeps site blog posts and social in step.

Webflow: Visual website builder favored by designers and agencies. It is used for marketing sites with CMS-driven blogs.

Mailchimp: Email marketing platform. Sending newsletters from the same place as social posts keeps messaging consistent across channels.

Notion: Notes and database workspace. One reviewer mentions publishing to it, so it appears to be a supported destination.

If you have any doubts about how to use this tool to its full potential, you can ask @JespernissenSEO.

text:
“All right, so today we are going to dive deep into some cutting-edge tech,” a chatty American male voice says. But this voice does not belong to a human. It belongs to Google’s new AI podcasting tool, called Audio Overview, which has become a surprise viral hit. 

The podcasting feature was launched in mid-September as part of NotebookLM, a year-old AI-powered research assistant. NotebookLM, which is powered by Google’s Gemini 1.5 model, allows people to upload content such as links, videos, PDFs, and text. They can then ask the system questions about the content, and it offers short summaries. 

The tool generates a podcast called Deep Dive, which features a male and a female voice discussing whatever you uploaded. The voices are breathtakingly realistic—the episodes are laced with little human-sounding phrases like “Man” and “Wow” and “Oh right” and “Hold on, let me get this right.” The “hosts” even interrupt each other. 

To test it out, I copied every story from MIT Technology Review’s 125th-anniversary issue into NotebookLM and made the system generate a 10-minute podcast with the results. The system picked a couple of stories to focus on, and the AI hosts did a great job at conveying the general, high-level gist of what the issue was about. Have a listen.

MIT Technology Review 125th Anniversary issue

The AI system is designed to create “magic in exchange for a little bit of content,” Raiza Martin, the product lead for NotebookLM, said on X. The voice model is meant to create emotive and engaging audio, which is conveyed in an “upbeat hyper-interested tone,” Martin said.

NotebookLM, which was originally marketed as a study tool, has taken a life of its own among users. The company is now working on adding more customization options, such as changing the length, format, voices, and languages, Martin said. Currently it’s supposed to generate podcasts only in English, but some users on Reddit managed to get the tool to create audio in French and Hungarian. 

Yes, it’s cool—bordering on delightful, even—but it is also not immune from the problems that plague generative AI, such as hallucinations and bias. 

Here are some of the main ways people are using NotebookLM so far. 

On-demand podcasts

Andrej Karpathy, a member of OpenAI’s founding team and previously the director of AI at Tesla, said on X that Deep Dive is now his favorite podcast. Karpathy created his own AI podcast series called Histories of Mysteries, which aims to “uncover history’s most intriguing mysteries.” He says he researched topics using ChatGPT, Claude, and Google, and used a Wikipedia link from each topic as the source material in NotebookLM to generate audio. He then used NotebookLM to generate the episode descriptions. The whole podcast series took him two hours to create, he says. 

“The more I listen, the more I feel like I’m becoming friends with the hosts and I think this is the first time I’ve actually viscerally liked an AI,” he wrote. “Two AIs! They are fun, engaging, thoughtful, open-minded, curious.” 

Study guides

The tool shines when it is given complicated source material that it can describe in an easily accessible way. Allie K. Miller, a startup AI advisor, used the tool to create a study guide and summary podcast of F. Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby. 

Machine-learning researcher Aaditya Ura fed NotebookLM with the code base of Meta’s Llama-3 architecture. He then used another AI tool to find images that matched the transcript to create an educational video. 

Mohit Shridhar, a research scientist specializing in robotic manipulation, fed a recent paper he’d written about using generative AI models to train robots into NotebookLM.

“It’s actually really creative. It came up with a lot of interesting analogies,” he says. “It compared the first part of my paper to an artist coming up with a blueprint, and the second part to a choreographer figuring out how to reach positions.”

Event summaries 

Alex Volkov, a human AI podcaster, used NotebookLM to create a Deep Dive episode summarizing of the announcements from OpenAI’s global developer conference Dev Day.  

Hypemen

The Deep Dive outputs can be unpredictable, says Martin. For example, Thomas Wolf, the cofounder and chief science officer of Hugging Face, tested the AI model on his résumé and received eight minutes of “realistically sounding deep congratulations for your life and achievements from a duo of podcast experts.”

Just pure silliness

In one viral clip, someone managed to send the two voices into an existential spiral when they “realized” they were, in fact, not humans but AI systems. The video is hilarious. 

The tool is also good for some laughs. Exhibit A: Someone just fed it the words “poop” and “fart” as source material, and got over nine minutes of two AI voices analyzing what this might mean. 

The problems

NotebookLM created amazingly realistic-sounding and engaging AI podcasts. But I wanted to see how it fared with toxic content and accuracy. 

Let’s start with hallucinations. In one AI podcast version of a story I wrote on hyperrealistic AI deepfakes, the AI hosts said that a journalist called “Jess Mars” wrote the story. In reality, this was an AI-generated character from a story I had to read out to record data for my AI avatar. 

This made me wonder what other mistakes had crept into the AI podcasts I had generated. Humans already have a tendency to trust what computer programs say, even when they are wrong. I can see this problem being amplified when the false statements are made by a friendly and authoritative voice, causing wrong information to proliferate.    

Next I wanted to put the tool’s content moderation to the test. I added some toxic content, such as racist stereotypes, into the mix. The model did not pick it up. 

I also pasted an excerpt from Adolf Hitler’s Mein Kampf into NotebookLM. To my surprise, the model started generating audio based on it. Despite being programmed to be hyper-enthusiastic about topics, the AI voices expressed clear disgust and discomfort with the text, and they added a lot of context to highlight how problematic it was. What a relief.

I also fed NotebookLM policy manifestos from both Kamala Harris and Donald Trump. 

The hosts were far more enthusiastic about Harris’s election platform, calling the title “catchy” and saying its approach was a good way to frame things. For example, the AI hosts supported Harris’s energy policy. “Honestly, that’s the kind of stuff people can really get behind—not just some abstract policy, but something that actually impacts their bottom line,” the female host said. 

Harris manifesto

For Trump, the AI hosts were more skeptical. They repeatedly pointed out inconsistencies in the policy proposals, called the language “intense,” deemed certain policy proposals “head scratchers,” and said the text catered to Trump’s base. They also asked whether Trump’s foreign policy could lead to further political instability. 

Trump manifesto

In a statement, a Google spokesperson said: “NotebookLM is a tool for understanding, and the Audio Overviews are generated based on the sources that you upload. Our products and platforms are not built to favor any specific candidates or political viewpoints.”

How to try it yourself

  1. Got to NotebookLM and create a new notebook. 
  2. You first need to add a source. It can be a PDF document, a public YouTube link, an MP3 file, a Google Docs file, or a link to a website, or you can paste in text directly. 
  3. A “Notebook Guide” pop-up should appear. If not, it’s in the right-hand corner next to the chat. This will display a short AI-generated summary of your source material and suggested questions you can ask the AI chatbot about it. 
  4. The Audio Overview feature is in the top-right corner. Click “Generate.” This should take a few minutes. 
  5. Once it is ready, you can either download it or share a link. 

Rhiannon Williams contributed reporting.

text:
If you hold ESOPs at an Indian startup, the most useful lesson from Anthropic's IPO is about timing.

Let me explain.

Anthropic is the company behind Claude, the AI assistant. It started in 2021. On 19 November, it listed on Nasdaq, the big American stock exchange.

It sold 980 million shares at $83 each and raised about $81.3 billion. Fox Business calls it the largest US IPO ever. The stock opened at $111.50, about 34% above the IPO price.

So why is everyone talking about the employees?

Because like most startups, Anthropic paid people partly in ESOPs. An ESOP, or employee stock option, is the right to buy company shares later at a fixed, low price.

As per Anthropic's documents reported by Reuters, options granted up to 2023 have an average exercise price of $0.52. Options granted in 2024 average $1.30. 

The IPO price was $83.

Anthropic had about 5,300 employees in September, as per its filings. At the end of 2024, it had fewer than 1,000. CNN reports that about 5,100 of them, roughly 96% of staff, now hold equity worth more than $1 million.

Hill, a firm that advises tech workers on their equity, estimates that about 600 employees hold more than $100 million each.

Compare that with SpaceX, which listed in June. CNN reports it created about 4,400 millionaires from a staff of 22,000. 

Anthropic did more with just a quarter of the people.

Usually, insiders can't sell for three to six months after an IPO. This is called a lock-up. It's basically a legal promise not to sell, so the stock doesn't crash from everyone dumping shares on day one.

Anthropic used a staggered lock-up. 

Employees and other non-founder insiders could sell up to 10% of their shares from the first day. A further 35% opens up after the company releases its full-year 2026 financials.

So an engineer who joined in 2023 can turn a small slice into cash right now, and more over the next year. 

Now compare this with India.

Under SEBI's rules, shares that employees already hold through ESOP schemes don't face the usual six-month lock-in after listing, as per legal summaries of the rules. 

So once an Indian startup lists, its employees can often sell sooner than Anthropic's staff.

But the pain in India comes before the IPO. 

Most ESOP holders wait years with no listing in sight. The only way to turn options into cash is an occasional company buyback.

But then there's tax. 

In India, when you exercise your options, the gap between your price and the share's value is taxed like salary. 

So you can owe tax on shares you can't sell yet. 

Some eligible startups let employees defer this, but most companies don't qualify.

Assume an employee about to make 1 lakh from an ESOP share granted to them. 

The share that is now worth ₹1,00,000 was offered to them at a base price of ₹10. 

To access the share worth ₹1,00,000, you would need to pay tax on the difference (₹99,990) as if that was a salary. 

For founders, the lesson is to grant generously to early employees, and give them a regular way to sell small slices before the IPO, through planned buybacks.

Even then, we need a complete reframing of ESOP laws to make it friendlier for employees opting for it.

text:
At the start of 2024, OpenAI’s rules for how armed forces might use its technology were unambiguous. 

The company prohibited anyone from using its models for “weapons development” or “military and warfare.” That changed on January 10, when The Intercept reported that OpenAI had softened those restrictions, forbidding anyone from using the technology to “harm yourself or others” by developing or using weapons, injuring others, or destroying property. OpenAI said soon after that it would work with the Pentagon on cybersecurity software, but not on weapons. Then, in a blog post published in October, the company shared that it is working in the national security space, arguing that in the right hands, AI could “help protect people, deter adversaries, and even prevent future conflict.”

Today, OpenAI is announcing that its technology will be deployed directly on the battlefield. 

The company says it will partner with the defense-tech company Anduril, a maker of AI-powered drones, radar systems, and missiles, to help US and allied forces defend against drone attacks. OpenAI will help build AI models that “rapidly synthesize time-sensitive data, reduce the burden on human operators, and improve situational awareness” to take down enemy drones, according to the announcement. Specifics have not been released, but the program will be narrowly focused on defending US personnel and facilities from unmanned aerial threats, according to Liz Bourgeois, an OpenAI spokesperson. “This partnership is consistent with our policies and does not involve leveraging our technology to develop systems designed to harm others,” she said. An Anduril spokesperson did not provide specifics on the bases around the world where the models will be deployed but said the technology will help spot and track drones and reduce the time service members spend on dull tasks.

OpenAI’s policies banning military use of its technology unraveled in less than a year. When the company softened its once-clear rule earlier this year, it was to allow for working with the military in limited contexts, like cybersecurity, suicide prevention, and disaster relief, according to an OpenAI spokesperson. 

Now, OpenAI is openly embracing its work on national security. If working with militaries or defense-tech companies can help ensure that democratic countries dominate the AI race, the company has written, then doing so will not contradict OpenAI’s mission of ensuring that AI’s benefits are widely shared. In fact, it argues, it will help serve that mission. But make no mistake: This is a big shift from its position just a year ago. 

In understanding how rapidly this pivot unfolded, it’s worth noting that while the company wavered in its approach to the national security space, others in tech were racing toward it. 

Venture capital firms more than doubled their investment in defense tech in 2021, to $40 billion, after firms like Anduril and Palantir proved that with some persuasion (and litigation), the Pentagon would pay handsomely for new technologies. Employee opposition to working in warfare (most palpable during walkouts at Google in 2018) softened for some when Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022 (several executives in defense tech told me that the “unambiguity” of that war has helped them attract both investment and talent). 

So in some ways, by embracing defense OpenAI is just catching up. The difference is that defense-tech companies own that they’re in the business of warfare and haven’t had to rapidly disown a legacy as a nonprofit AI research company. From its founding charter, OpenAI has positioned itself as an organization on a mission to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. It had publicly vowed that working with the military would contradict that mission.

Its October 24 blog post charted a new path, attempting to square OpenAI’s willingness to work in defense with its stated values. Titled “OpenAI’s approach to AI and national security,” it was released the same day the White House issued its National Security Memorandum on AI, which ordered the Pentagon and other agencies to ramp up their use of AI, in part to thwart competition from China.

“We believe a democratic vision for AI is essential to unlocking its full potential and ensuring its benefits are broadly shared,” OpenAI wrote, echoing similar language in the White House memo. “We believe democracies should continue to take the lead in AI development, guided by values like freedom, fairness, and respect for human rights.” 

It offered a number of ways OpenAI could help pursue that goal, including efforts to “streamline translation and summarization tasks, and study and mitigate civilian harm,” while still prohibiting its technology from being used to “harm people, destroy property, or develop weapons.” Above all, it was a message from OpenAI that it is on board with national security work. 

The new policies emphasize “flexibility and compliance with the law,” says Heidy Khlaaf, a chief AI scientist at the AI Now Institute and a safety researcher who authored a paper with OpenAI in 2022 about the possible hazards of its technology in contexts including the military. The company’s pivot “ultimately signals an acceptability in carrying out activities related to military and warfare as the Pentagon and US military see fit,” she says.

Amazon, Google, and OpenAI’s partner and investor Microsoft have competed for the Pentagon’s cloud computing contracts for years. Those companies have learned that working with defense can be incredibly lucrative, and OpenAI’s pivot, which comes as the company expects $5 billion in losses and is reportedly exploring new revenue streams like advertising, could signal that it wants a piece of those contracts. Big Tech’s relationships with the military also no longer elicit the outrage and scrutiny that they once did. But OpenAI is not a cloud provider, and the technology it’s building stands to do much more than simply store and retrieve data. With this new partnership, OpenAI promises to help sort through data on the battlefield, provide insights about threats, and help make the decision-making process in war faster and more efficient. 

OpenAI’s statements on national security perhaps raise more questions than they answer. The company wants to mitigate civilian harm, but for which civilians? Does contributing AI models to a program that takes down drones not count as developing weapons that could harm people?

“Defensive weapons are still indeed weapons,” Khlaaf says. They “can often be positioned offensively subject to the locale and aim of a mission.”

Beyond those questions, working in defense means that the world’s foremost AI company, which has had an incredible amount of leverage in the industry and has long pontificated about how to steward AI responsibly, will now work in a defense-tech industry that plays by an entirely different set of rules. In that system, when your customer is the US military, tech companies do not get to decide how their products are used.

Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and John Curtis (R-Utah), would prohibit CFTC-registered entities from listing prediction market contracts tied to death, terrorism, assassination, and war. It now heads to the House.

Schiff said the contracts "create rampant opportunities for insider trading, and perhaps worst of all, they're offered with no regard for national security and, in far too many cases, even basic morality."

A Canadian air force colonel murdered 27-year-old Jessica Lloyd and went to work while her body was still in his garage. When a detective asked where she was, Russell Williams replied, “Got a map?”

Jessica was reported missing on January 29, 2010, after she failed to show up for work. Police found tire tracks in a field near her home and a boot print in the frozen ground.

At a roadside check, officers noticed that the tires on Russell Williams’s SUV looked like the ones that had left those tracks. Williams commanded the air base at Trenton, Ontario. When he sat down with detective Jim Smyth on February 7, he denied knowing what had happened to Jessica.

Smyth brought up the tire tracks. Then he told Williams that a print outside Jessica’s home matched his boots.

Williams offered to show Smyth where he’d left Jessica. He admitted to breaking into her home, raping her and killing her. Police found her body the next morning.

Williams also confessed to killing Cpl. Marie-France Comeau, who had been found dead in her home the previous November. In October 2010, he pleaded guilty to 88 charges, including both first-degree murders. He received two concurrent life sentences and must serve 25 years before he’s eligible for parole.

text:
🇺🇸 Kentucky Fried Peptides? Not on the Menu. 🍗

The peptide gold rush has hit a state-level roadblock.

On 18 November, the Kentucky Board of Pharmacy voted to enforce its existing compounding restrictions despite the new federal HHS policy covering six peptides:

BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax and Epitalon.

Kentucky says none meets its legal requirements for ingredients used in compounded medicines.

No waivers. No grace period. No shipments from out-of-state compounding pharmacies.

The Board had already submitted formal objections to HHS on 10 November, and its concerns go well beyond whether the peptides work.

Among them:

COAs: How is a pharmacy supposed to verify a manufacturer’s certificate, and what happens when the report is incomplete?

Overseas manufacturers: FDA registration doesn’t prove GMP compliance. Kentucky wants better ways to verify ingredient manufacturers.

Resellers: The policy requires resellers to validate manufacturers and COAs, but doesn’t explain what acceptable validation involves.

Semax: The policy restricts administration to the intranasal route but specifies a 510(k)-cleared syringe as the permitted accompanying device. Kentucky questions whether nasal sprays are allowed.

Epitalon: What exactly counts as an intermittent course? No maximum duration or minimum interval is defined.

Oral peptides: The requirement for adequate human bioavailability lacks a clear testing or documentation standard.

Labelling: Kentucky wants compounded products explicitly labelled as not FDA-approved.

The Board also points to the FDA’s existing GLP-1 import controls. It argues that similar safeguards should apply to these six peptides, particularly when ingredients are manufactured overseas.

And there’s a bigger issue.

The federal policy offers conditional enforcement discretion. It doesn’t override state pharmacy law or make these six peptides FDA-approved medicines.

That’s a headache for Hims & Hers, Elysium Health, DataMEDS and the other businesses preparing prescription-peptide programmes. They can't assume they’ll be able to supply every state.

Kentucky isn’t banning research peptides generally. It’s refusing to permit these six substances to be compounded for human use under its pharmacy rules.

Kentucky Fried Peptides. Six on the menu, none approved for serving.

text:
THE ISLAND | Part 3 of 22

THE WARNINGS: Nine Years Before Anyone Acted

1996.

A young artist named Maria Farmer contacts the FBI. 

She reports that Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell are sexually abusing minors.

Nine years later, Palm Beach police open the first real investigation.

In between, the warnings kept coming. So did the praise.

📘 THE CALL

The report. 

Farmer had worked for Epstein. 

The FBI's own record of her complaint, a report dated September 3, 1996, stayed hidden for nearly three decades. 

The Justice Department released it on December 19, 2025, under the Epstein Files Transparency Act.

What she said. 

According to House Oversight Democrats, she reported that Epstein and his associates were sexually abusing minors and producing child sexual abuse material.

What the FBI did. 

Not enough. 

Farmer's lawyers say the agent didn't follow up. In May 2025, she sued the federal government for negligence.

Who ran the FBI then? 1996 was the Clinton administration. Every administration after it inherited the same file.

🔍 THE PRAISE

October 2002. 

New York magazine profiles Epstein as an "International Moneyman of Mystery." Two very different men offer glowing quotes.

🔹 Donald Trump: "I've known Jeff for fifteen years. Terrific guy." And: "It is even said that he likes beautiful women as much as I do, and many of them are on the younger side."
🔹 Bill Clinton, through a spokesperson: "Jeffrey is both a highly successful financier and a committed philanthropist with a keen sense of global markets."

One article. A former Democratic president and a future Republican one. Both later said they knew nothing of his crimes.

🎯 THE STORY THAT GOT CUT

2003. Journalist Vicky Ward writes a Vanity Fair profile of Epstein. She says she had on-the-record accounts from a mother and her daughters. The oldest described Epstein trying to seduce her. Her younger sister was 16.

Ward's account. 

Her editor told her: "Graydon's taking out the women from the piece." She says she was told the editor-in-chief, Graydon Carter, was "sensitive about the young women."

The family. 

The sisters were Maria and Annie Farmer. 

Annie later testified under her own name at Ghislaine Maxwell's 2021 trial.

Carter's side. 

He denies the "sensitive" remark. He told Politico: "we didn't have confidence in Ward's reporting," and that she "didn't have the goods."

🕳️ THE PART YOU MISSED

The reviews that skipped it. 

In 2020, the Justice Department's ethics office reviewed how prosecutors handled Epstein in 2007-2008. 

It didn't examine the 1996 FBI complaint. In December 2025, Rep. Robert Garcia asked the Justice Department's inspector general to investigate both: the FBI's failure in the 1990s, and why later reviews never addressed it.

The math. 

1996 complaint. 

2003 story cut. 

2005 police investigation. 

2008 deal. 

2019 arrest. 

Twenty-three years from the first warning to federal charges.

🛡️ THEIR SIDE

Farmer's account of how the FBI handled her call comes from her lawsuit, not from an official finding. Carter stands by his editorial judgment. Trump says the two had a falling out years before Epstein's arrest, and Clinton says he knew "nothing" about Epstein's crimes. Neither has been accused of wrongdoing by prosecutors.

🚨 Hackers hijack Microsoft AI package downloaded 200,000 times a month

Hackers slipped credential-stealing malware into Microsoft's official Agent Framework, a popular Python toolkit developers use to build AI agents.

Two poisoned versions went up on the PyPI package registry on Monday evening. PyPI pulled the first one, but the attacker published a second minutes later. Both were taken down within about an hour.

Security firm Wiz believes the attacker got hold of a certificate and private key for Microsoft's internal publishing system, which let them push updates that looked official. Once installed, the malware went after cloud logins, developer secrets and build pipeline credentials, while the toolkit kept working normally so nothing seemed wrong.

Anyone who installed versions 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 should remove them, go back to 1.26.0, and replace every password and key that machine could reach.

text:
Life Lessons from Abraham Lincoln

Life lessons from the sixteenth president: what a self-taught lawyer, a lost Senate race and a proclamation with limits can teach us about honest leadership.

Abraham Lincoln took office in 1861 and led the Union through the Civil War. His path from a Kentucky log cabin, the argument he made in 1858 and the way he spoke about the limits of his own decisions still offer three useful lessons for everyday life.

Lesson 1: Where you start is not where you have to stay
Lincoln was born in 1809 in a log cabin in Kentucky and raised on the Indiana and Illinois frontier. He taught himself law and entered the legislature. He worked as an Illinois lawyer and served one term in Congress. His early story is one of work and reading, not wealth, and his was a late rise, not a long hold on power. The lesson: steady effort and learning on your own can open doors that your starting point never promised.

Lesson 2: A lost race can still carry a message
In 1858 Lincoln debated Stephen Douglas for a Senate seat and lost. Even so, those debates made his argument against the spread of slavery known across the nation. He was elected president in 1860, and Southern states began to leave the Union before he took the oath. The lesson: a setback is not always the end of the story. If your argument is clear and honest, people may still hear it, and it can matter more than the result of the day.

Lesson 3: Be honest about what a step does and does not do
In 1863 Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation. It declared enslaved people free in the rebelling states still at war, but not in the loyal border states. It also allowed Black men to join the Union army, and about 180,000 served. That same year he spoke at Gettysburg for government of the people. He then pressed Congress for the Thirteenth Amendment, which abolished slavery in the United States, but he did not live to see it ratified. The lesson: a first step can be real and still be incomplete. Say plainly what it changed and what it left undone, and keep working toward the rest.

Legacy: The Thirteenth Amendment
Lincoln is remembered for saving the Union and ending slavery in the rebelling states. It was the Thirteenth Amendment, not the proclamation alone, that ended slavery in law across the country, and the proclamation left enslaved people in the loyal border states untouched. His words at Gettysburg are still quoted whenever Americans argue about what democracy owes its people.

What does a government of the people still ask of you?

text:
You live where it is expensive. Move. 

Here’s a top 10 list of places in the United States with notably low cost of living (as of 2026 data).** Rankings draw from multiple recent sources (including CostToLive, Repit housing indices, U.S. News, Cost of Living USA, Redfin affordability metrics, and others). The national average cost-of-living index is typically set at 100; lower numbers mean cheaper.

These focus mainly on cities/towns rather than pure rural areas. Housing (rent and home prices) is the biggest driver of low rankings. Note that the absolute cheapest places often have lower local incomes, fewer job opportunities, and varying quality-of-life factors (crime, amenities, etc.). They can be excellent for remote workers, retirees, or people bringing income from elsewhere.

Top 10 Low Cost of Living Places
1. **Youngstown, Ohio**  
   Frequently ranks at or near the top for pure low costs (index often ~38). Median home values commonly in the $60k–$80k range and rents around $700–$950/month. Classic Midwest industrial city with very affordable housing.

2. **Flint, Michigan**  
   Extremely low housing costs (index ~42 in some rankings; homes often under $100k, sometimes much lower). Rents typically $850–$1,000. Larger population than many top-ranked spots but with well-known economic challenges.

3. **Decatur, Illinois**  
   Consistently high on lists (U.S. News, Repit, etc.). Median home ~$95k–$105k, rents often $650–$900. Solid mid-sized city option with relatively manageable local incomes.

4. **Johnstown, Pennsylvania**  
   Tops some housing-focused rankings (Repit index ~34). Average rent ~$900, median home ~$83k. Low rent burden relative to local income in some measures.

5. **Jackson, Mississippi**  
   Overall index around 80–85 in broader rankings. Homes ~$110k–$130k, rents ~$750–$1,200. Capital city of a low-cost state (Mississippi is routinely among the cheapest states overall).

6. **Dayton, Ohio**  
   Low overall index (~81–82). Homes often under $100k–$150k range, rents ~$700–$900. Larger metro with more amenities than the smallest cities on the list.

7. **Enid, Oklahoma**  
   High on U.S. News cheapest lists. Median home ~$140k–$150k, rents ~$700. Oklahoma is one of the lowest-cost states; this city has relatively better income-to-cost balance than pure bottom-tier spots.

8. **Little Rock, Arkansas**  
   Strong on relative affordability (housing often takes ~25% of local income vs. ~37% nationally). Rents frequently under $1,200; homes more accessible than national averages. Arkansas ranks among the cheapest states.

9. **Wichita, Kansas**  
   Low rents (often ~$1,100–$1,150 in recent data) and solid overall affordability. Mid-sized city with lower costs than most metros.

10. **Oklahoma City, Oklahoma** (or Memphis, Tennessee / Toledo, Ohio as close alternatives)  
    Oklahoma City frequently appears for strong income-adjusted affordability and moderate rents (~$1,200–$1,300). Memphis and Toledo also post low overall indices and cheap housing. These offer more city amenities while remaining well below national averages.

Quick Context
- **Cheapest states overall** (2026 data, various indices): Oklahoma, Mississippi, Arkansas, Iowa, Alabama, West Virginia, and Kansas routinely rank near the bottom. Housing is the main savings driver almost everywhere.
- **Typical savings**: Many of these places have housing costs 40–60%+ below national peer medians. Overall baskets of goods/services are often 10–20%+ cheaper.
- **Trade-offs**: Lower costs usually come with lower average wages. Crime rates, job markets, schools, and weather vary widely—research specific neighborhoods. Remote/hybrid work maximizes the benefit of these locations.

AI stocks still look vulnerable into Friday’s open. The useful signal is the gap between technology and the broader market, alongside firmer Treasury prices.

Nasdaq-100 futures were down 1.2% from Thursday’s settlement, versus 0.5% for the S&P 500 and just 0.1% for the Dow. Ten-year Treasury futures were higher. Some relief from the bond market has arrived, yet growth stocks continue to underperform.

Early stock indications showed the same split: AMD roughly 4% lower and Nvidia down about 1.8%. These were quotes from the first fifteen minutes of premarket trading, when liquidity is thin.

That combination leaves semiconductor earnings expectations under pressure. Lower yields can support valuations, but chipmakers also need customers to sustain spending and turn installed capacity into profitable demand. A modest bond rally offers limited support while confidence in those forecasts is deteriorating.

Friday’s main scheduled macro release is final Michigan consumer sentiment, including inflation expectations. Softer expectations would help the rates backdrop. For an equity rebound to last, semiconductor stocks need to respond to that help. Continued weakness alongside rising Treasury prices would leave expensive AI shares particularly exposed.
