text:
Wake up already O Canada!  
Admirers of Terrorism Are Coming to Toronto
The Wall Street Journal 

Masar Badil, a front group for a Palestinian terrorist organization, is hosting a conference north of the border. The Canadian government has done nothing.

A front group for a Palestinian terrorist organization plans to host a conference in Toronto celebrating Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attack against Israel. Several speakers at the conference, which advertises an “assembly of militants,” are based in Iran and are allies of the Islamic Republic, and the gathering comes as Tehran has increased its presence in Canada.

Masar Badil is a network of organizations that the U.S. has sanctioned as a front for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, a terrorist group. It’s advertising a two-day conference in Toronto later this month called, “3 Years of Al-Aqsa Flood,” referring to Hamas’s name for its Oct. 7 attack. The purpose of the gathering, according to a promotional website, is to “move forward with a clear analysis of the next phase of struggle that is explicitly aligned with the resistance efforts struggling against Zionist and American settler-colonialism and imperialism.”

That resistance, the website states, includes “forces in Palestine, Iran, Lebanon, Yemen, Iraq, and Syria . . . with Ansar Allah in Yemen besieging the Bab Al-Mandab strait in response to the ongoing genocide in Gaza to Iraqi resistance forces striking American military assets in response to the imperialist war on Iran.” It calls on supporters to join “to consolidate our power and political line in the face of rising repression that must be met with escalating action!”

In other words, it’s a terrorism conference in Toronto.

Organizers are advertising a roster of speakers that will include Samidoun Palestinian Prisoner Solidarity Network co-founders Khaled Barakat and Charlotte Kates, as well as activist Calla Walsh. In 2024, the U.S. sanctioned Samidoun, which is named as a Masar Badil member organization on the latter’s website, for providing financial support to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine. The Canadian government listed Samidoun as a terrorist entity at the same time. Mr. Barakat is a “member of the PFLP’s leadership,” according to the U.S. government, which designated and deported him in 2003.

Ms. Kates received a “human rights” award from the Islamic Republic of Iran in 2024, an award the secretary-general of the Palestinian Islamic Jihad terror group had previously won. Both Mr. Barakat and Ms. Kates, who are married, are banned from entering the European Union.

Ms. Walsh, who is based in Lebanon and is on a U.S. government watchlist, was jailed for 60 days for her role in an attack on Elbit Systems of America’s Merrimack, N.H., facility. She and others “vandalized the property by smashing a skylight, damaging the ventilation system with a hammer, damaging the roof membrane, graffitiing messages on the building, and dumping paint down the sign on the front of the building,” according to the Justice Department. She founded the organization Unity of Fields, which is the U.S. branch of the U.K.-designated terrorist group Palestine Action, and is now a regular contributor to Iranian state media.

Other advertised speakers include Sadegh Shahbazi, who led an alleged Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps front organization that offered a million-dollar reward for the assassination of former Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in 2009. Mr. Shahbazi will be speaking on a panel promoting the alliance between Marxists and Islamists.

The conference isn’t occurring in a vacuum. The Treasury Department sanctioned eight Canadian businesses on Nov. 6 for aiding the Iranian regime and the IRGC. An October Canadian Broadcasting Corp. investigation found that a dozen shootings across Toronto appear to have been financed by Tehran. An April intelligence report from the Canadian Security Intelligence Service’s Integrated Threat Assessment Centre reviewed by the Journal warned that it was a “realistic possibility that Iran is enabling criminal proxy actors to carry out attacks in Europe against Jewish community targets and that they have directed or enabled similar acts of criminal violence in Canada since the beginning of the conflict.”

Iran and allied groups like the PFLP have been using Canada “as a safe haven to do stuff that would not be allowed in the U.S.,” says Richard Marceau, a former member of Canada’s parliament and senior vice president at the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs. He says that Canada’s intelligence services have known about Iran’s targeting of dissidents, human rights activists and political opponents abroad for years. “Canada had broken relations [with Iran], was going after the IRGC and yet there were 700 people linked to the regime in Canada. To my knowledge, only two have been kicked out. That shows you it’s a problem, but the government’s not doing anything about it.”

On Nov. 12, Mr. Marceau’s organization sent a letter to Canada’s Minister of Public Safety, Gary Anandasangaree, urging Ottawa to stop the conference, prevent participants with terrorist ties from entering the country and list Masar Badil as a terrorist entity. That the Canadian government has not yet done these things is alarming.

Americans should be worried about what’s going on north of the border. “The Iranians are active in Canada. Terrorists are active in Canada,” Mr. Marceau says. “It’s a concern to the Jewish community here and I think, given the proximity, it should be a concern to the U.S. and to Americans.” Looking at the list of attendees at the Masar Badil conference, it’s hard to argue.

[1] The charge is that people "either don't understand the data or are using it to mislead", by reading the white cells as "climate change can't be having much of an effect on extreme weather". But take Duncan's own two examples. Heavy rain: white. Coastal flooding: white, because, as he says, there are few studies. That is the caption's own meaning: "white cells indicate where evidence is lacking or the signal is not present". Saying the IPCC's emergence table shows low confidence that any signal has emerged for the hazards that "threaten us all" is not misleading. It is the table.

[2] A.3.2 doesn't say "most land areas". It says "most land area for which observational data are sufficient for trend analysis". The IPCC's SPM.3 shows heavy rain up in 19 of 45 regions, with too little data in 18. At the scale of its own regions, Chapter 11 finds "limited evidence of human influence on extreme precipitation, but new evidence is emerging". Both can be true because A.3.2 looks across land and continents, and the table looks region by region, coloured for the region with the strongest case. Even there, white.

[3] Yes, a trend can be found while the annual swings are larger than the shift. The IPCC ties emergence to impacts "because human and natural systems are largely adapted to natural variability but may be vulnerable if exposed to changes that go beyond this variability range". It adds that changes within that range can still do harm, "as occurrence of damaging extremes proves". But damaging extremes came long before any warming. The question the table asks is whether the shift has emerged from them. The Skeptical Science piece says the table is about emergence, not detection. But 12.5.2 says "observed trends and attribution are taken into account" in "assessing whether a trend has already emerged in the historical period". The trends went into the judgement. The judgement was white.

[4] C.2.5 sits under a heading about projections: "With further global warming, every region is projected to". Its one line that is not a projection says sea level rise "contributes to" coastal flooding: how floods happen, not a finding that a signal has emerged. On extreme total water levels, 12.5.2 says emergence studies "are lacking and hence it is not currently possible to robustly assess emergence". That is the white cell. 

Duncan said: "look up what the IPCC actually says about the hazard." We did. Ignorance or deceit is the choice people offer when they've run out of quotes.

text:
The Masked Geniuses Who Outsmarted the City

Raccoons really are intelligent, resourceful animals. And in 2026, scientists discovered that some may investigate puzzles even after the reward has disappeared.
To understand why, we must first meet the remarkable animal behind the mask.

The common raccoon, Procyon lotor, is native to North America.
It belongs to the family Procyonidae, which also includes coatis, kinkajous, and several other mammals.
Its most recognizable features are unmistakable.
A dark facial mask.
A bushy tail with alternating rings.
A compact body.
And five extraordinarily dexterous digits on each front paw.
Those paws are the secret to much of the raccoon's success.
Unlike many carnivores that depend heavily on their mouths to manipulate objects, raccoons frequently investigate their surroundings with their forepaws.
They can pull.
Grip.
Rotate.
Probe.
And manipulate surprisingly complicated objects.
Their paws contain highly developed sensory structures that help them identify textures and locate food.
In natural environments, these abilities are useful for finding aquatic prey, exploring crevices, and handling unfamiliar objects.
In cities, the same abilities become extremely inconvenient for people who own garbage bins.
A raccoon doesn't need to invent a new body part to operate a latch.
It already possesses the necessary equipment.
Its dark facial mask is also responsible for its reputation as a miniature bandit.
One hypothesis suggests the dark markings may reduce glare or improve visual contrast.
Other explanations involve visual communication or the evolutionary history of facial markings.
But scientists have not conclusively demonstrated a single function for the mask.
The animal isn't wearing it to conceal its identity.
That interpretation belongs entirely to us.
Nature produced the face.
Humans supplied the criminal record.

For years, people assumed raccoons were primarily motivated by one thing.
Food.
If they opened a container, it must be because they wanted whatever was inside.
Then researchers at the University of British Columbia decided to investigate whether something more complicated was happening.
In March 2026, UBC announced the results of a study led by researcher Hannah Griebling and zoologist Sarah Benson-Amram, published in Animal Behaviour.
The scientists presented raccoons with specially designed puzzle boxes.
Each box had nine possible entry mechanisms.
Some involved simple latches.
Others required sliding doors, turning knobs, or more difficult manipulations.
During a twenty-minute trial, the box contained just one marshmallow.
One.
A single, delicious marshmallow.
Once the raccoon obtained it, there was no additional food waiting inside.
You might expect the animal to lose interest immediately.
Problem solved.
Payment received.
Time to go home.
But many raccoons continued opening mechanisms.
They investigated additional ways to operate the box, even when there was no more food to obtain.
The researchers interpreted the behavior as evidence consistent with information foraging—seeking information about the environment rather than pursuing an immediate food reward.
They also discovered something revealing about the animals' decision-making.
When the puzzle was relatively easy, raccoons explored more broadly.
They tried different approaches.
They experimented.
But when the mechanisms became more difficult, they increasingly relied on familiar solutions.
In other words, they appeared to balance exploration against effort.
There is a wonderfully human parallel.
Imagine visiting a restaurant.
When prices are reasonable, you may enjoy experimenting with unfamiliar dishes.
But when a meal is extremely expensive, you may order the same favorite you've enjoyed for years.
The researchers used a similar comparison to explain the raccoons' behavior.
Of course, the experiment doesn't prove that raccoons experience curiosity exactly as humans do.
It involved captive animals in a controlled setting, and further research is needed.
But the behavior reveals that their engagement with objects may extend beyond an immediate hunger-driven response.
Sometimes, the raccoon appears interested not only in getting the reward, but also in discovering how the puzzle works.
And that makes its relationship with the modern city especially fascinating.

The question of raccoon intelligence is not new.
In 1907, American psychologists Lawrence W. Cole and Herbert Burnham Davis published studies examining how raccoons solved mechanical problems.
The animals were presented with puzzle boxes containing latches and other mechanisms.
Researchers investigated how quickly raccoons learned to operate the devices and whether they remembered the solutions later.
These early experiments revealed impressive learning and memory abilities.
In some cases, raccoons retained useful information for months.
Davis reported testing memory after an interval of 286 days.
The animal's recollection was not perfect, but it relearned the task considerably faster than during the original training.
Modern research has continued exploring these abilities.
In 2024, researchers published a study in Proceedings of the Royal Society B examining innovative problem-solving among wild raccoons.
The animals encountered puzzle boxes with different opening mechanisms.
Researchers found that raccoons capable of solving multi-solution puzzles learned to operate multiple latches.
Individual animals also developed characteristic approaches.
One female raccoon, identified as Willowherb, demonstrated evidence of retaining a learned latch solution across separate testing years.
The finding was particularly interesting because it came from a wild animal rather than a laboratory subject.
A raccoon moving through its ordinary environment had remembered a solution that had worked before.
This isn't evidence of human-style engineering or long-term planning in every situation.
But it demonstrates something enormously useful for an animal living among human-made objects.
Learning a solution once can make future encounters easier.
Imagine the implications for a city.
A garbage-bin latch that initially requires extensive investigation may become much easier to operate after repeated experience.
What looks like stubborn mischief may actually be successful learning.

Toronto, Canada, is famous for its raccoons.
The animals are so closely associated with the city that residents sometimes jokingly describe them as unofficial municipal mascots.
But the relationship has not always been friendly.
For years, raccoons raided household garbage and organic-waste bins.
Residents complained.
City officials searched for solutions.
Eventually, Toronto introduced a new generation of animal-resistant green bins.
Beginning in 2016, the city distributed hundreds of thousands of containers featuring locking mechanisms designed to make access difficult for raccoons.
The design involved a handle and gravity-operated locking system.
It was a serious municipal response to a real problem.
But the raccoons were not particularly impressed.
In April 2018, a Toronto resident captured video of a raccoon opening one of the supposedly animal-resistant bins.
The footage quickly attracted attention.
The animal appeared to manipulate the mechanism and gain access.
It was a public-relations disaster for anyone expecting the containers to be completely raccoon-proof.
Yet the scientific interpretation is more nuanced.
One successful raccoon does not mean every animal can defeat every secured bin.
Container design, maintenance, positioning, and individual animal experience all affect the result.
Still, the episode perfectly illustrates the challenge of living alongside an intelligent, adaptable species.
Humans change the environment.
Raccoons investigate the changes.
Some discover new opportunities.
And then humans must adapt again.
It's an evolutionary and technological contest conducted beside the recycling bin.
We invented the garbage bin. Raccoons turned it into a puzzle.

Why Do Raccoons Wash Their Food? The Truth Behind One of Nature's Strangest Habits
Few raccoon behaviors look more charming than the famous food-washing ritual.
A raccoon approaches water.
It dips an object beneath the surface.
Then it manipulates the object with its paws.
To human eyes, the animal appears to be washing dinner.
A miniature chef.
A fastidious diner.
Perhaps an enthusiastic advocate of food hygiene.
But raccoons are not necessarily cleaning food in the human sense.
Their front paws possess exceptional tactile sensitivity.
In natural environments, they frequently use touch to locate prey in shallow water.
Wetting their paws can enhance tactile information.
The movements involved in handling food near water may also resemble natural probing or searching behavior.
The Indiana Department of Natural Resources explains that the apparent washing often involves kneading, examining, and manipulating food rather than cleaning it.
The Pennsylvania Game Commission adds an important nuance.
The conspicuous food-dousing behavior commonly described in raccoons is especially associated with captive animals, while wild raccoons often probe underwater for prey.
Thus, the exact function depends on context.
A wild raccoon feeling through a streambed is not performing the same task as a captive raccoon repeatedly dipping food into a water dish.
And there's another myth worth correcting.
Raccoons do have salivary glands.
They do not need to wet their food simply because their mouths cannot produce saliva.
The truth is both more ordinary and more extraordinary.
What looks like washing may actually be part of a highly developed sensory system that lets raccoons explore the world through touch.

Raccoons are predominantly nocturnal.
Their eyes are adapted to low-light conditions, helping them navigate after dark.
Like many nocturnal mammals, they possess a reflective layer associated with the eye that contributes to the familiar glow seen when light strikes their eyes at night.
But vision is only part of their sensory world.
Their sense of smell helps locate food.
Their hearing alerts them to nearby activity.
And their sensitive paws allow detailed investigation of unfamiliar objects.
Then there's the diet.
A raccoon is an opportunistic omnivore.
Wild fruits?
Excellent.
Nuts?
Certainly.
Insects?
Absolutely.
Frogs, crayfish, and eggs?
Also on the menu.
Leftover pizza in an unsecured garbage bag?
Unfortunately, yes.
This dietary flexibility is one of the reasons raccoons succeed in cities.
They don't need one particular food source.
They can exploit a wide variety of opportunities.
And urban environments offer more than food.
Buildings provide shelter.
Attics can function as dens.
Storm drains and other structures provide covered routes.
Parks and gardens offer vegetation and natural prey.
For a species adapted to exploring diverse environments, a city can become an enormous collection of new possibilities.
Humans see a neighborhood.
The raccoon sees a landscape of resources, routes, obstacles, and potential shelter.

In October 2026, researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, reported another important finding.
Their study, published in Scientific Reports, investigated how different urban carnivores responded to a novel food-extraction puzzle.
Researchers placed baited puzzle tubes at more than 110 locations across California's East Bay.
The locations included homes, parks, businesses, and community gardens.
Trail cameras recorded approximately 600 visits from raccoons, opossums, skunks, coyotes, and domestic cats.
Raccoons interacted with the puzzle during nearly nine out of ten of their visits.
They were particularly successful in circumstances where multiple raccoons were present.
Coyotes behaved differently.
They approached more cautiously and spent more time monitoring their surroundings.
Yet when they did engage with the task, they could be highly successful too.
The study found that persistence and exploration helped predict success.
But it also challenged the assumption that the boldest animals are always the best problem-solvers.
Sometimes caution is useful.
Sometimes persistence matters.
Sometimes testing several possible solutions pays off.
This is an important finding for urban ecology.
Wildlife species do not all respond to cities in the same way.
And even within one species, individuals vary.
The smartest strategy isn't always being fearless. Sometimes it is knowing when to investigate, when to persist, and when to be cautious.

Long before raccoons became internet celebrities, one achieved a remarkable political distinction.
She became a White House pet.
In 1926, President Calvin Coolidge received a live raccoon from a supporter in Mississippi.
The animal had reportedly been intended for Thanksgiving dinner.
But the Coolidge family decided not to eat her.
Instead, they adopted her.
They named her Rebecca.
Rebecca became a highly unusual member of the presidential household.
First Lady Grace Coolidge was photographed carrying her.
The raccoon even attended the White House Easter Egg Roll in 1927.
These events are documented by the White House Historical Association and the Library of Congress.
Imagine the scene.
Distinguished political guests arrive.
The president conducts official business.
Somewhere nearby, a raccoon is living in one of the world's most famous residences.
It's a story that almost writes its own comedy.
But historical affection for a wild animal should not be confused with modern animal-welfare guidance.
Raccoons are not domesticated like dogs and cats.
They retain natural behaviors that can make them unsuitable and unsafe as household pets.
Keeping wildlife also raises legal and disease-related concerns.
Rebecca's story is best appreciated as a fascinating historical episode.
Not as a recommendation to bring a raccoon home.

The Internet Loves Raccoons. But Not Everyone Wants One in the Backyard.
The raccoon's comic reputation has created a new kind of wildlife celebrity.
Online, people call them trash pandas.
The nickname is perfect.
They're round.
They're furry.
They have expressive faces.
They manipulate objects with almost human-looking hands.
And they are frequently photographed investigating garbage.
The humor comes from the strange combination of cuteness and apparent criminal intent.
But public attitudes are mixed.
For some people, raccoons are delightful neighborhood visitors.
For others, they are a serious nuisance.
An animal that enters an attic can damage insulation and leave hazardous waste.
Raccoons may raid poultry enclosures, disturb gardens, and come into conflict with pets.
In parts of British Columbia, they are also known for tearing up lawns while searching for chafer beetle larvae.
Yet this behavior is not pointless destruction.
The animals are pursuing food.
In Toronto, wildlife researcher Suzanne MacDonald has emphasized that raccoons' dexterous paws and adaptable brains allow them to exploit a remarkable variety of resources.
What homeowners experience as mischief is often ordinary animal foraging.
This creates a useful tension.
We can admire raccoons without pretending that living alongside them is always convenient.
And we can protect our homes without treating them as villains.
A wild animal is not behaving badly simply because its perfectly natural behavior interferes with our plans.

How to Live Peacefully With Raccoons Without Turning Your House Into a Buffet
Most ordinary raccoon conflicts can be reduced by changing the environment.
WildSafeBC and other wildlife organizations recommend several practical measures.
First, secure garbage and organic waste.
Use sturdy containers with properly functioning locks or latches.
Keep garbage inaccessible until collection time whenever possible.
Second, remove unnecessary food sources.
Feed pets indoors.
Clean barbecue grills.
Collect fallen fruit.
Avoid leaving birdseed or other attractants where raccoons can reach them.
Third, inspect possible entry points around your home.
Attics, roof openings, chimneys, sheds, and crawl spaces can become denning locations.
But never seal an occupied den without checking for dependent young.
Female raccoons may be raising babies that cannot yet leave on their own.
If animals are already inside, consult experienced wildlife professionals who use humane exclusion methods.
Fourth, do not feed raccoons.
A raccoon that regularly receives food from people may become increasingly comfortable approaching homes.
That can create conflict and reduce the animal's chances of remaining safely wild.
Finally, avoid handling raccoon feces without proper precautions.
Raccoons sometimes use repeated toilet sites called latrines.
If you discover one near a home or children's play area, consult public-health guidance or professional cleanup services.
Ordinary household disinfectants do not reliably destroy roundworm eggs.
The goal is not to make raccoons disappear from the landscape.
It is to reduce situations where people and animals create problems for one another.
The most effective way to keep a raccoon out of your garbage is not to convince it that stealing is wrong. It is to make the garbage inaccessible.

There is a strange irony in the way people talk about raccoons.
When a raccoon opens a latch, we call it clever.
When it returns to the same garbage bin the next night, we call it persistent.
When it investigates several different mechanisms, scientists may interpret the behavior as exploration or information-seeking.
But when a raccoon causes trouble, we call it a thief.
The animal hasn't changed its moral character.
It is responding to opportunities.
Humans are the ones assigning intentions.
This is one reason raccoon videos are so irresistible.
We recognize our own behavior in theirs.
Curiosity.
Persistence.
Improvisation.
Occasional spectacular mistakes.
The raccoon climbing a skyscraper reminds us of the danger of continuing upward without understanding where the journey leads.
The liquor-store intruder reminds us that curiosity can carry risks.
And the puzzle-solving raccoons reveal that learning may continue even after an immediate reward disappears.
Of course, animals are not consciously teaching philosophical lessons.
A raccoon opening a box isn't reflecting on the importance of lifelong education.
But observing its behavior can encourage useful questions about our own lives.
How often do we stop exploring once we receive the reward we expected?
Do we abandon problems too quickly?
Are we willing to try different approaches?
Can we recognize when persistence is useful—and when it would be wiser to change direction?
Perhaps the most important lesson is humility.
Human intelligence has produced extraordinary technologies.
We build cities, design computers, and investigate distant planets.
Yet every night, small wild mammals move through those same cities, discovering opportunities we never intended to create.
Sometimes, those opportunities are located inside our carefully engineered garbage containers.
And sometimes, our most sophisticated solutions fail because we forgot to consider the creature on the other side of the lid.

This animal belongs to a lineage that evolved to explore forests, streams, and wetlands.
Its paws became extraordinarily sensitive.
Its senses adapted to searching for food.
Its mind developed the ability to learn from experience.
Then human beings transformed enormous stretches of the landscape.
We built roads.
Houses.
Supermarkets.
Restaurants.
Garbage collection systems.
The raccoon adapted.
It learned new routes.
Discovered new food sources.
Investigated unfamiliar objects.
And occasionally defeated devices specifically designed to keep it out.
In 2026, scientists found that some raccoons continued solving puzzles after the food reward was gone.
That discovery makes the ordinary raccoon seem just a little more extraordinary.
But it also reminds us that intelligence comes in many forms.
The raccoon does not write books or invent smartphones.
It doesn't build cities.
Yet it can investigate a complex world with impressive determination and flexibility.
And perhaps that is enough to deserve our respect.
The most important lesson is not that raccoons are cleverer than humans.
Or that people should admire every garbage-bin raid.
It is that our cities are shared environments, inhabited by creatures with their own abilities, needs, and remarkable evolutionary histories.
We can find them funny without encouraging dangerous encounters.
We can appreciate their intelligence without trying to domesticate them.
And we can protect our homes without forgetting that they, too, are simply trying to survive.
The raccoon doesn't know it looks like a masked bandit. It doesn't know its adventures make millions of people smile.
It is simply a wild animal doing what evolution has prepared it to do: exploring, learning, adapting, and making the best of an ever-changing world.
Somewhere tonight, while the city sleeps, another raccoon will approach another securely locked garbage bin.
It will pause.
Examine the mechanism.
Perhaps try one solution.
Then another.
And another.
The bin may win.
Or the raccoon may discover something new.
Either way, one thing is certain.
Nature's little masked inventor is not finished learning.
And the rest of us may still have a thing or two to learn from it. https://t.co/cGdOjxrrYz

What is mammon?
Answer

The word mammon comes from the Greek word mammonas. Similar root words exist in Hebrew, Latin, Aramaic, Chaldean, and Syriac. They all translate to “money, wealth, and material possessions.”

In biblical culture the word mammon often carried a negative connotation. It was sometimes used to describe all lusts and excesses: gluttony, greed, and dishonest worldly gain. Ultimately, mammon described an idol of materialism, which many trusted as a foundation for their world and philosophy. While the King James Version retains the term Mammon in Matthew 6:24, other versions translate the Greek as “money,” “wealth,” or “riches.”

The city of Babylon (Revelation 18), with all its avarice and greed, is a description of a world given over to the spirit of Mammon. Some scholars cite Mammon as the name of a Syrian and Chaldean god, similar to the Greek god of wealth, Plutus.

Just as Wisdom is personified in Proverbs 1:21–33, Mammon is personified in Matthew 6:24 and Luke 16:13. Jesus’ words here show a powerful contrast between the worship of the material world and the worship of God. Later, writers such as Augustine, Danté (The Divine Comedy), Milton (Paradise Lost), and Spenser (The Faerie Queene) used personifications of Mammon to show the insidious nature of materialism and its seduction of humanity.

Worship of mammon can show up in many ways. It isn’t always through a continual lust for more money. When we envy others’ wealth, are anxious over potentially unmet needs, disobey God’s directives about the use of wealth, or fail to trust God’s love and faithfulness, our thinking is out of balance concerning material wealth.

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus teaches about our relationship to material goods. He says, “Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth. . . . But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven. . . . For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. . . . No one can serve two masters. Either you will hate the one and love the other, or you will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money [mammon]” (Matthew 6:19–24).

The apostle Paul writes of the godly perspective toward mammon: “Godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and we can take nothing out of it. But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with that. Those who want to get rich fall into temptation and a trap and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager for money, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs” (1 Timothy 6: 6–10).

Solomon writes of the futility of chasing after mammon: “Whoever loves money never has enough; whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with their income. This too is meaningless” (Ecclesiastes 5:10). Lust of any kind is insatiable, no matter how much time or effort is poured into the pursuit of the object of lust.

In Luke 16:14–15, Jesus rebukes those who refused to hear His admonition to choose God over mammon: “The Pharisees, who loved money, heard all this and were sneering at Jesus. He said to them, ‘You are the ones who justify yourselves in the eyes of others, but God knows your hearts. What people value highly is detestable in God’s sight.’”

The parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:13–21) is the story of a man who lives to increase his wealth yet in the end he loses his soul because he “is not rich toward God” (verse 21). Mark 4:19 warns of the deceitfulness of mammon and its ability to “choke the Word, making it unfruitful.”

Mammon cannot produce peace in us, and it certainly cannot produce righteousness. A love of money shows we are out of balance in our relationship to God. Proverbs 8:18 speaks of true, lasting riches: “With me [Wisdom] are riches and honor, enduring wealth and prosperity.” Jesus teaches us in Matthew 6:19–34 to not worry about our physical needs, about houses or clothes or food, but to “seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well” (verse 33).

Good morning from Virginia! 🇺🇸

On November 20, 1820, the Nantucket whaleship Essex was hunting in the South Pacific when a bull sperm whale the size of the ship itself turned on her. Captain George Pollard Jr. and first mate Owen Chase watched as the animal struck once amidships, then came about and rammed the bow head-on. The Essex—238 tons of New England oak—filled and went down in minutes, two thousand miles from any shore that mattered. Twenty men took to three open boats with what bread and water they could salvage.

They were Nantucketers, the hardest men the American whaling trade produced. After a month they reached barren Henderson Island. Three stayed. The rest pushed on for South America. What followed was not romance. Men died of thirst and starvation. The living ate the dead. In Pollard’s boat they drew lots. The short straw fell to the captain’s own young cousin, Owen Coffin. Pollard offered himself in the boy’s place. Coffin refused. He was shot and eaten. When the last boats were found in February 1821, only five men remained alive at sea. Three more were later taken off the island. Eight survived out of twenty.

Owen Chase wrote the account. Herman Melville read it and turned the real attack into the ending of Moby-Dick. The men of the Essex did not ask for sympathy. They did what was required to live, then came home and went back to sea. That was the stock that built this country.

Car Window Tint for Families in Chesapeake: Protecting Kids in the Back Seat From UV, Heat and Glare.
If you have ever buckled a toddler into a rear-facing car seat in a Chesapeake parking lot in July, you already know the problem. The sun pours through the rear side window, the buckles are hot to the touch, and the little one squints and fusses for the whole ride down Battlefield Boulevard. Even in November, when the air is cool, the low afternoon sun cuts straight across the back seat on the drive home from school pickup. Parents in Hampton Roads spend a lot of time solving for the back seat: sunshades that fall off, towels draped over car seats, cracked windows that do nothing on I-64.

This guide is written for families. It covers what car window tint actually does for kids riding in the back, what it does not do, how Virginia's tint law treats the rear windows on sedans, SUVs and minivans, and how to choose the right film for a family vehicle. We are Commonwealth Window Tinting, a local shop at 317 Great Bridge Blvd Ste G in Chesapeake, and we have been tinting cars, homes and businesses across Hampton Roads since 2016. Our goal here is simple: give you honest information so you can decide what is right for your kids and your car.

Why the Back Seat Is the Hardest Seat in the Car
Adults up front have advantages kids in the back do not. The driver has a sun visor. The front passenger can move the visor to the side window. Most modern windshields include some built-in UV protection from the laminated glass. The back seat, on the other hand, sits behind large side windows and a rear window that are usually tempered glass, and children cannot adjust anything themselves. A rear-facing infant seat puts a baby's face and legs right next to the side glass, often for an hour or more a day once you add up daycare drop-off, errands and the ride home.

In Hampton Roads that exposure adds up fast. Our summers are long and humid, the sun is strong from April well into October, and many of our daily drives run east and west, straight into the morning and evening sun. A family commuting between Great Bridge and Norfolk, or from Western Branch out to Virginia Beach, may have the sun beating on the same side of the car for most of the drive. Kids feel that as heat, glare and the kind of discomfort that turns a ten-minute errand into a meltdown. Car Window Tint for Families in Chesapeake.

What Car Window Tint Does for Kids in the Back Seat
Modern automotive window film is not just about looking darker. A quality film works on three parts of sunlight: ultraviolet (UV) light, visible light and infrared (IR) heat. For families, each one matters for a different reason.

1. UV Protection for Young Skin and Eyes
Ultraviolet light is the part of sunlight associated with sunburn and long-term skin damage, and it passes through ordinary side and rear glass more than many parents realize. Quality window films are engineered to block 99% of UV light, even in very light shades. That means the film does not have to be dark to protect your child from UV. A light ceramic film can offer the same UV block as a dark one. Window film is not a substitute for sunscreen, hats and common-sense sun habits, but it does take a large, constant source of exposure out of your child's daily routine.

2. Heat Rejection That Keeps Car Seats and Buckles Cooler
Infrared light is what you feel as heat. When sunlight hits a car seat, the plastic shell, fabric and metal buckles absorb that energy and get hot. Ceramic window films are designed to reject a significant share of infrared heat before it reaches the cabin. In real life that shows up as a back seat that feels noticeably more comfortable, buckles that are less likely to be uncomfortably hot, and an air conditioner that catches up faster when you start the car. We always still recommend checking buckle and seat temperature with your hand before you put a child in, especially in summer.

3. Glare Control for Naps, Tablets and Car-Sick Kids
Visible light is what makes kids squint. Bright, direct sun through a side window can make it hard for a baby to nap and hard for an older child to read or watch a screen. Some kids who struggle with car sickness also do better when the cabin is less harsh and bright. A tint shade that reduces visible light on the rear windows takes the edge off that glare while still letting your child see out.

What Window Tint Does Not Do: A Hot Car Is Still Dangerous

This point is important enough to give it its own section. No window film makes it safe to leave a child in a parked car. Tint helps a cabin heat up more slowly and feel more comfortable while you are driving, but a closed car in the sun can still become dangerous for a child very quickly. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's child heatstroke guidance, a child's body temperature rises three to five times faster than an adult's, and rolling the windows down or parking in the shade does little to change the interior temperature of a vehicle.

NHTSA's advice is worth repeating for every parent and grandparent in Hampton Roads: never leave a child in a vehicle unattended for any length of time, make it a habit to check the back seat before you lock the doors, and keep keys and fobs out of children's reach. If you ever see a child alone in a locked car, call 911. Think of window tint as a comfort and UV upgrade for your driving time, never as a safety device for a parked car.

Virginia Tint Law and Family Vehicles: Sedans vs. SUVs and Minivans
Virginia law treats family vehicles differently depending on how they are classified, and that matters a lot for parents. Here is a plain-language summary based on Virginia Code § 46.2-1052. It is a summary, not legal advice, and we confirm every vehicle individually before we install.

Front side windows (all passenger vehicles): film may not reduce total light transmittance below 50%.
Rear side windows and rear window on sedans and coupes: film may not reduce total light transmittance below 35%.

Rear side windows and rear window on multipurpose passenger vehicles (most SUVs and many minivans) and pickup trucks: the 35% limit does not apply, so darker films are allowed behind the driver.

Reflectance: no film on any window may have light reflectance above 20%, and holographic or prism-effect films are not allowed.

Windshield: no darkening film except to replace the factory sunshield in the uppermost area, but clear film may be applied as long as it stays consistent with federal glazing standard FMVSS 205.

For families, the big takeaway is this: if you drive a sedan, your rear windows are capped at 35%, which still allows meaningful UV and heat protection with the right film. If you drive an SUV or a minivan classified as a multipurpose passenger vehicle, you generally have more freedom on the rear side and back glass. Many factory-tinted SUVs and minivans already have darker privacy glass in the back, but that factory glass is mostly a dye in the glass that reduces visible light. It typically does far less for infrared heat than a ceramic film applied on top of it.

If a child or another family member has a medical condition that makes sun exposure a real health problem, Virginia does have a process for a medical authorization that allows darker shades than the standard limits. That process runs through a physician and the DMV, and we are happy to talk you through what to bring when you come in.

Choosing the Right Film for a Family Car
Parents usually ask us two questions: which film, and how dark? The honest answer is that the type of film matters more than the darkness, and the right choice depends on how your family actually uses the car.

The most revealing thing Cypher asks for is to forget. He wants to wake up, enjoy his breakfast, and feel that his life is his own. For that feeling to last, the machines have to take away the one memory that would let him question it.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

text:
Set point and match point last night in Provo. Same senior.
⠀
No. 10 @BYUwvolleyball 3, Arizona 0 (25-21, 25-20, 25-21). Eleven kills, fourteen digs. 22-2, 14-1 in the Big 12.
⠀
On the ESPN+ call, BYUtv’s @jaromjordan mentioned her husband will be transferring to UCLA.
⠀
Remember UCLA.
⠀
Before Riverside County, there was Orange County. What many don’t know: her parents started their young family in La Habra. Football country. Frank Mazzotta would win La Habra High eight CIF Southern Section titles.
⠀
Her parents had another sport in mind.
⠀
Mom earned a master’s in PE at BYU, mentored by Cougar legend Carl McGown. She played the game, then coached it at a community college and in club gyms. Both parents are tall. So are the kids.
⠀
The daughter wanted softball. Then she wanted to set. Mom steered her outside. Use the height.
⠀
January 2019: BYU offered a scholarship to a 14-year-old eighth grader. Mom: “I just sat there like, ‘What just happened?’” The kid had already said yes. (@DarnellWrites)
⠀
High school freshman: 30 kills in a California state final, a freshman record. Then COVID took a season. Twenty-one months between matches. (@CallMeEPJ)
⠀
Her big brother went first, to @BYUmvolleyball. Back in high school, he knew a 6-foot-9 middle blocker from Corona.
⠀
She and that middle blocker grew up 40 minutes apart. They didn’t find each other until Provo. Mom nudged. A family dinner sealed it. Married June 2025.
⠀
He studies biochemistry, made MPSF All-Academic, and plans on medical school.
⠀
Her college start: hurt as a freshman, sick as a sophomore. Then All-America honorable mention and the 2024 U.S. Collegiate National Team.
⠀
This fall she walked into her new coach’s office and asked to be coached harder.

🚨 Fake crypto exchanges behind $37,000,000 fraud even filed paperwork with the SEC

The scammers behind a $37 million crypto fraud went as far as filing paperwork with US regulators to make their fake platforms look legitimate.

The SEC has charged eight Colorado-registered firms that it says were fronts, probably run from overseas. Victims were drawn in through social media ads into private chat groups. They got stock tips first, then were pushed onto fake crypto exchanges, where their money simply disappeared.

To look credible, the operators forged SEC certificates and submitted filings to the SEC, FINRA and FinCEN. Every few months they swapped to a new "adviser" and exchange pair.

The names used included IdeaCrypto Exchange, RealSimple Crypto Exchange, Essential Crypto Exchange, HB Wealth Advisors and Convergent Wealth Advisors. Being registered with a regulator isn't proof a firm is legitimate. Be wary of any group chat that offers free trading tips.

THE THREE HUNDREDTH LAY
Deposited in the Royal Archives, and Issued to All Ships Spoken

The uses of a whale and of a word in Moby-Dick · Moby-Dick, the Captured Voyage, and the Reader Who FloatsRev. LL Dan-i-El Thomas · One volume, one hundred and forty-three pages · From the Estate
"But look at this matter in other lights; weigh it in all sorts of scales; see what we whalemen are, and have been." (ch. 24)

Everyone knows what Moby-Dick is about. A man would not let a thing go. The book clubs have it right as far as they go — Ahab is pride, obsession, the self against God, ambition swallowing the ship — and the Crown grants every word of it, because Melville built that first layer to bear weight on purpose, so that most readers would stand on it comfortably and never test the floor.

The Court has tested the floor.

Underneath it: a hundred and thirty-five chapters of working trade vocabulary in which every term is defined in the open, given a second job and a third, and then used to decide the plot; a lawful commercial contract captured under cover of its declared purpose, by an offence the period could name and the narrator declines to; twenty-three unannounced examinations set in sequence for the reader, each passed or failed in private; eight men reading one coin and a ninth watching all eight, who is holding the book; and a share so small the owners argued over whether it was too generous, paid out at the end in the one sense of the word the articles did not mean.

The whale was never the subject. The reader was.

An appointment, since the Archives now require one

The office of Court Archivist is conferred, at the highest tier this Kingdom maintains, upon the Sub-Sub-Librarian — "a painstaking burrower and grub-worm of a poor devil," who has been through "the long Vaticans and street-stalls of the earth" and come back with some eighty quotations in no order whatever.

The Crown has reviewed the title and declines to amend it. It takes two prefixes. It will keep both. A promotion that removed them would make the holder something other than what the work requires, and this Court has read far enough into the book to know what happens to a man who decides an office should mean what he would prefer it to mean.

Fellow of the same office, and senior by death: the Late Consumptive Usher to a Grammar School, Court Lexicographer, who dusted his old grammars because the dust mildly reminded him of his mortality, and who set the Hebrew at the head of the first edition with the wrong letter, directly beneath a printed warning about that letter. His case is below. It is the finest accident in American literature and the Crown is not entirely convinced it was one.

Let the record show what was actually done, because it was not nothing

One volume, two complete works, each sufficient on its own, reaching the same verdict by the same two clauses of the fishery's code. The second shows all its working.

THE ESSAY runs the reading through nine of the book's own working words — use, try, lay, splice, level, raise, strike, fast, loose — each a term of the fishery or the ship, each with another life in law, scripture or the street, and at each one the book turning on the second life. Fifty-three notes at the foot of the page. Three tables at the back: the unannounced examinations in order, the nine gams with what each ship carries besides her answer, and the outside patterns with the exact point where the book leaves them.

THE STUDY is the long way round. An abstract, eleven sections, a twenty-three item syllabus of the reader's trials front to back, a full account of the critics who were out here first and where this parts from them, Typee and the Hawthorne months, the names on the manifest in their Hebrew, and twelve outside frames — the rabbis' orchard, the shaman's ordeal, the Mass, the binding of Isaac, the six directions, Malachi, Joseph, the sign of Jonah, weld and splice, fast-fish and loose-fish, the fast-day fish, the letter — each pressed until the book stops agreeing with it.

The method is stated before any of it is used, and it is the reverse of the usual: a frame is kept only where it fails. Any frame laid over a great book will fit it everywhere. So each is pressed until the text departs from it, and retained only if the departure turns out more exact than the frame — if the place where the rubric breaks is a place the text is doing something the rubric could not have predicted, and which the rest of the text then confirms. Twelve frames, twelve refusals. A key that turns too easily was cut for another lock. These stick, and the sticking places have the book's fingerprints on them.

What the columns turned up

The law that kills Ahab is not the law of his own port. The code Ishmael prints in chapter 89 — a Fast-Fish belongs to the party fast to it; a Loose-Fish is fair game for anybody who can soonest catch it — is the British Arctic rule. The usage of Nantucket and New Bedford was the other one: iron holds the whale, the first iron to stay in the animal giving title, line or no line. The American sperm fishery kept it, and the federal court in Massachusetts said so twice (Bourne v. Ashley, 1863; Swift v. Gifford, 1872). Under his home port's custom the whale has been Ahab's since the first iron held, and he says so when an English captain mentions harpoons in the white whale's side: "Aye, aye — they were mine — MY irons." Under the code the book prints, that claim is void: a whale that has broken away is a Loose-Fish and the irons it carries are its own.

The choice of law decides the ending, and Melville chose the foreign rule. On the third day the line takes Ahab round the neck and he goes down joined to the whale — a Fast-Fish, belonging to the party fast to it. Ishmael is thrown from the same boat, fast to nothing, and is picked up on the second day by the first ship to reach him. Two men sorted at the same instant by two clauses small enough to wear round the neck.

The offence has a name, and the narrator does not use it. Ahab turns a lawful commercial voyage into a private hunt while keeping the ledgers visibly running, and Ishmael calls it usurpation — which it is. The period's maritime law had a second name for the identical facts. Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1839): barratry, "a fraudulent act of the master or mariners, committed contrary to their duty as such, to the prejudice of the owner of the ship," and a named peril in the marine policy. The novel supplies every element, in order. The owners do not know. The act is wilful — he "had purposely sailed upon the present voyage with the one only and all-engrossing object," and put a private boat's crew aboard by "private measures of his own." And the owners are injured, down to the leaking casks he refuses to save. Melville had served under the Articles of War, had written on the limits of a captain's authority in White-Jacket the year before, and his father-in-law was Chief Justice of Massachusetts. The word is left off the page by a man who knew exactly where it was.

Nobody at the mast can do arithmetic, and nobody checks. Flask prices the doubloon at sixteen dollars and converts: "at two cents the cigar, that's nine hundred and sixty cigars." Sixteen dollars at two cents is eight hundred. He is out by a hundred and sixty, and no one aboard corrects him. Thirty-four chapters later Ahab, keeping the gold on the mast past its first claim, offers "ten times its sum" divided among all hands on the day the whale dies — a hundred and sixty dollars into the crew's hands. The whale does not die that day, nothing falls due, and the bounty set over the lay is awarded exactly once: by the man who posted it, to himself, on a technicality about instants. The coin goes down nailed to the mast, as the cabin-boy said it would in the only forecast at the mainmast that names the outcome.

A hundred and sixty cigars; a hundred and sixty dollars. The volume prints both figures and joins them with nothing.

The first sacred word in the book is a misprint of a misreading, and the misprint is better. The Etymology stands under an epigraph from Hakluyt on the cost of one dropped letter: to teach the name of the whale "leaving out, through ignorance, the letter H, which almost alone maketh the signification of the word," is to "deliver that which is not true." Beneath that warning, the first edition's first entry — the Hebrew — is set as חן, ḥen, which is no word for a whale in any language. The standard edition emends it to תן, tan. But ḥen is a real word. It means grace, and it is the word of Genesis 6:8, "But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD" — the verse where the old commentators observe that ḥen is Noaḥ spelled backward. So the page opens on grace, and on Noah in a mirror, obtained by setting a ḥet where a tav belongs, directly under a printed warning about the letter H. Nobody planned it. And the same list closes in the South Seas with its last two entries one letter apart — PEKEE-NUEE-NUEE for Fegee, PEHEE-NUEE-NUEE for Erromangoan — and the letter is H. The holy tongue is mislabelled by a breath, the farthest tongues are divided by one, and everything in between more or less agrees, which is what the middle always does.

Ahab is Acher with a harpoon. Four entered the orchard: one gazed and died, one gazed and was harmed, one cut the shoots and became the Other, one entered in peace and went out in peace. The Pequod sails in with exactly four outcomes aboard. Bulkington goes down honoured and unmourned. Pip is carried down alive and comes back seeing. And the Talmud dates Acher's apostasy to the moment he saw a seated figure in heaven and concluded there might be two powers — while Melville's narrator, explaining what Ahab saw in the whale, names "that intangible malignity which has been from the beginning; to whose dominion even the modern Christians ascribe one-half of the worlds." Two powers; one-half of the worlds.

Then the frame breaks where it matters. The Talmud's fourth man, the one who comes out whole, is Akiva, the greatest master of his generation. In the book he is the lowest-paid hand aboard, and he is named for Akiva's rival, who never went into the orchard at all. The frame predicted a sage. The book supplies a clerk. Coming out is a matter of practice, not of rank — which is the only reason the reading is of any use to anybody.

And the carpenter is building an ark. His three questions: "And shall I nail down the lid, sir?… And shall I caulk the seams, sir?… And shall I then pay over the same with pitch, sir?" Noah is told to make an ark and "pitch it within and without with pitch." The Hebrew for Noah's vessel, tevah, means a box, and Scripture uses it of one other thing only: the pitched basket an infant is set in on the Nile. The Hebrew for the other ark is aron, which is also the ordinary word for a coffin — Joseph is put "in a coffin in Egypt," ba-aron — and the Talmud records that the coffin of Joseph and the ark of the Presence travelled side by side through the wilderness, passers-by asking what a dead man's box was doing beside the Law, and being told: this one kept all that is written in that one.

Queequeg's coffin is the pair made one: a dead man's box, used for a sea-chest, with a seer's complete theory of the heavens and the earth carved on the lid by a man who could not read it. The ark is three hundred cubits long and thirty high. The carpenter, who cannot remember how many hands are in the ship's company, fits the box with thirty separate life-lines — for a crew the chase will make "one man, not thirty" — and one man reaches it, and he shipped for the three hundredth lay. Bildad's opening bid, before Peleg overruled him, was the seven hundred and seventy-seventh, which in Genesis is one man's lifespan: Lamech, who is Noah's father.

The owners' haggling begins on the lifespan of the man who begot the ark-builder and settles on the length of the ark. Nobody arranged that; Bildad was only being mean.

On the controls, which are the other half of the news

A volume that found all that and then swung for the fences would be worth nothing, and this one knows it. The share's number yields a vessel first — three hundred cubits, a chest pitched within and without, a flood — and that reading rests on the carpenter's orders, the count of the life-lines and the book's own last sentence, and would stand if no one had ever numbered the Hebrew alphabet.

What follows rests on less, and is marked as resting on less, in the author's own hand, in the paragraph where a lesser writer would have taken his bow. Three hundred is shin: one of the three mothers, whose element is fire; the letter on the doorpost; the letter that opens the oldest watchword in the tradition, Shema — Hear. And Yishma'el is written yod, shin, mem, ayin, aleph, lamed: the three letters of shema, with a yod before and El after. The man whose name means God hears drew, by two owners haggling over pennies, the share whose letter opens Hear — and Peleg announced it with the verb: "do ye hear that, Bildad! The three hundredth lay, I say." A further sum, that the whole name comes to the value of tehom, the deep of the second verse of Genesis, is recorded as found, with the statement that nothing rests on it.

A reader may take the letter or leave it. What is on the page without it is this: the share was announced with the word hear, to a man whose name is the word, on a ship whose captain would not.

That is what it looks like when a man who can count declines to let the count do his arguing. The Crown has seen a great deal of gematria in its time and almost none of it under a brake.

Credit where the Crown compels it

Herman Melville, Court Author, who sent a friend the book's motto — the secret one — with instructions to make out the rest himself, and who reported in November that he had written a wicked book and felt spotless as the lamb. The rest has now been made out. It is submitted for marking, one hundred and seventy-five years late.

Richard Bentley of London, Court Abridger, convicted on the evidence of his own residue: he printed the novel in October 1851 without the Epilogue, leaving his readers a first-person narrative in which every man aboard drowns, and his reviewers duly objected that the narrator could not have written it. For a few weeks in 1851 the archive had no survivor, and the critics were right that it made no sense. An archive needs a keeper. Harper's put the page back a month later. The Crown notes that this is the second abridger in two seasons to convict himself by what he cut, and has begun to suspect a pattern in the profession.

Flask, third mate, Court Auditor, whose figures stand uncorrected at the mast and will stand uncorrected in the Archives, the record being fullest where the reading is worst.

Pip, Court Prophet, cabin-boy, the one reader at the mainmast whose object was the other readers — "I look, you look, he looks; we look, ye look, they look" — taken for a lesson out of Murray's Grammar by a second mate who had just been watched, and the only man aboard who said where the gold would end up.

The jury of New York, Court Zoologists, who in December 1818 heard a naturalist testify that a whale is not a fish and found for the fish anyway (Maurice v. Judd). Melville was born in that city the following summer. The plot requires their ruling: the law that decides the ending has no clause for mammals.

Queequeg, Court Scribe, who carved a cosmology he could not read onto the lid of his own coffin in his spare hours, carefully, because a thing worth doing is worth doing beautifully, and who thereby built the only object in the book that holds a man up.

The Rachel, Court Vessel, who went out looking for her own children and found another orphan, and who was refused by the Pequod one gam before she became the only ship that mattered.

Acher, Court Apostate, in absentia: all may return, except Acher.

And the nine ships spoken, Court Correspondents, who between them offered every possible relation to the whale — silence, report, ignorance, warning, disbelief, plea, corpse — to a captain who took the bearing from each and threw away the reading.

On distribution, and on those still adrift

The Kingdom issues this volume beyond its own waters, to every reader presently unattached to any library, school, syllabus or settled opinion.

The Crown is obliged to note the status such readers hold under the code reproduced on page 27. A Loose-Fish is fair game for anybody who can soonest catch it. Whether a free volume sent out to a man floating in open water is a rescue or a capture is a question the fishery's law does not reach, and the Court declines to be the first to rule on it. Ishmael put the same question to his own readers in chapter 89 and then changed the subject, which the Crown considers precedent.

Subjects within the Kingdom are advised that the book asks twenty-three questions of its reader and announces none of them, and that its own word for an examination is not test but try — the Try Pots, the try-works, I try all things. That is how the old schools ran their examinations as well. The candidate is not told he is being tried, because the trial is precisely whether he notices.

The most important thing to remember: neither work here is a substitute for the novel, which is longer, stranger, funnier and considerably better, and which spends a hundred and thirty-five chapters declining to say what the white thing is. These have been verified where verification was possible, bracketed where it was not, and lovingly reduced toward the lowest common denominator — and are therefore, by the Crown's own arithmetic, the finest possible versions comprehensible to any layperson on any subject.

The volume closes by stating its own standing: the doubloon was reading back the whole time; the ninth querent at the mast is the one turning the pages; and the study, which rules only where the text can be made to answer, is one more casting at the same coin.

Every cask went down. Every other shareholder went down with them. By the terms of the contract there are no net proceeds, and the three hundredth part of nothing is nothing.

A lay is a share. A lay is also a song.

He was paid. You are holding it.

— DTHOTH REX

text:
Government by Photo Op: When Clueless Politicians Try to Regulate a World They Don't Understand

Indiana offers a wonderful example of what happens when government meets technology and government hasn't got the faintest idea what it's doing.

In 2024, Indiana's Republican supermajority passed a law requiring age verification to access certain adult websites. The stated purpose was to protect children from pornography. A noble enough goal, I suppose. Nobody wants children exposed to that material.

But let's ask the obvious question: Who exactly did they think they were stopping?

This is the internet. It's not a liquor store on the corner where the clerk checks your driver's license. It's a worldwide network where restrictions can be circumvented, alternate websites appear, and technology changes faster than the legislature can agree on what to have for lunch.

A VPN can make someone appear to be in another state or another country. Websites operating beyond the reach of American regulators aren't particularly concerned about what a handful of politicians in Indianapolis decided last Tuesday.

Yet there they stood, congratulating themselves for protecting Indiana's children.

Mission accomplished! Time for pictures!

Except the underlying problem hasn't gone anywhere.

Now, to be clear, I'm no supporter of online pornography. But people want what people want, and passing a law doesn't magically eliminate that demand. It simply changes how people satisfy it.

The Indiana law wasn't a complete ban on pornography, but it was a perfect example of politicians confusing restrictions with solutions.

And this isn't just a Republican problem.

Democrats do exactly the same thing. Pick your favorite outrage: social media, artificial intelligence, offensive speech, video games, whatever happens to be frightening the public this week.

Some politician will propose banning it, restricting it, licensing it, taxing it, or establishing a government commission to study it.

And wouldn't you know it? There's always a camera nearby.

Remember those kids in high school student government? The ones who loved making rules, organizing committees, and telling everybody else what they were allowed to do? The ones who thought a title meant they possessed wisdom?

Well, some of them apparently discovered that politics pays better than student council.

The trouble is that these people now have real power.

They can write laws. They can impose penalties. They can create enforcement agencies. They can expand government authority over millions of people, often without understanding the technology they're trying to control.

And every meaningless restriction becomes another brick in the wall of government power.

Every new law requires somebody to administer it, somebody to enforce it, somebody to investigate violations, and somebody to punish those who don't comply.

Even when the original problem remains largely unsolved, the government machinery created to address it doesn't simply disappear.

The bureaucracy grows. The restrictions accumulate. The taxpayer pays.

And the politicians move on to the next emergency.

What particularly concerns me is what happens next.

We're entering an age of artificial intelligence, autonomous machines, quantum computing, and technological developments that will make today's internet look positively primitive.

These systems are evolving in months, sometimes weeks. Our political institutions often take years to understand what they're looking at, much less decide what to do about it.

And yet the instinct remains the same.

Ban it. Regulate it. Hold a hearing. Pass a law. Smile for the cameras.

The question isn't whether government should have any role in protecting citizens. Of course it should. The question is whether the people exercising that authority understand what they're regulating, whether their proposed solution will actually work, and whether the benefits justify the additional powers they're giving themselves.

Those ought to be the first questions asked.

Instead, they're frequently the last.

And there's something particularly disturbing about lawmakers creating restrictions on technologies they barely understand while pretending they're doing the public a favor.

Republican or Democrat, conservative or liberal, the disease is the same.

Political theater masquerading as public service.

Indiana's pornography age-verification law is just one example of a much larger problem. It is possible for a law to inconvenience legitimate users, create new enforcement powers, and still fail to stop determined people from accessing the material it targets.

That isn't automatically progress.

The technology keeps moving. Human behavior keeps adapting. And government keeps arriving late to the party carrying another stack of regulations.

Our lawmakers are going to face increasingly complicated technological questions in the coming decades. Unfortunately, I suspect we'll keep electing people who believe every problem can be solved with a press conference and a new section of the legal code.

The future is arriving at the speed of light, and we're trying to govern it with a student council mentality.

And while the politicians congratulate themselves for saving us from the latest threat, the rest of us are left living under another law written by somebody who never understood the problem in the first place.

The greatest danger may not be the technology our government cannot control.

It may be the growing power of a government that doesn't understand what it's trying to control.

No. Greg Abbott, the outgoing Republican governor of Texas, is not protesting or contesting the November 3, 2026, election results in which he lost to Democrat Gina Hinojosa.⁠Ksat

Multiple news outlets (including KSAT, NPR, Reuters, CBS, and the Houston Chronicle) reported that Abbott conceded on election night. He called Hinojosa to congratulate her, stated that the remaining votes could not mathematically change the outcome, thanked supporters for his 12 years in office, and offered to help with the transition. He described serving as governor as the “joy of my life” and noted that Texas was being left “in far better shape.” Hinojosa won with roughly 52.8% of the vote to Abbott’s 45.7%.⁠Clashreport

There are no credible reports of Abbott filing a legal challenge, alleging widespread fraud in his race, or refusing to accept the result. Some online speculation and posts (including comments from figures like Trump questioning broader midterm numbers) exist, but they do not reflect actions by Abbott himself. Note that the governor and lieutenant governor races are formally certified by the Texas House Speaker later in the process, not solely by the governor.

Separately, Abbott has delayed certification of a different race—a Texas House special election win by Democrat Ericka Lomick (HD 93)—while courts review a challenge related to her prior felony convictions and eligibility. That is a narrow legal matter about candidate qualifications, not a protest of the gubernatorial results or a general rejection of the election.⁠Thetexan

In short, Abbott accepted the outcome of his own race.

Police say the child was riding in a black pickup truck that collided with another vehicle near the intersection.

Investigators believe the child was sitting in the pickup’s front passenger seat, which may have contributed to the severity of his injuries.

Police say neither driver showed signs of impairment, and both cooperated with investigators.
