text:
Coimisiún na Meán (Ireland’s media regulator) runs multiple funding schemes that provide grants to news outlets, broadcasters, independent producers, and journalists. These are administered at arm’s length from direct government control, through competitive open rounds with independent (often external) assessment. Funding is not unrestricted “cash” but project- or role-specific support for defined public-interest purposes.

Main Schemes Relevant to News OutletsSound & Vision Scheme (long-standing; primarily funded via the TV licence fee): Supports production of high-quality TV and radio programmes on Irish culture, heritage, experience, and adult/media literacy. Open to broadcasters and independent producers (individuals or EU/Irish entities). Funding typically covers up to 95% of eligible production costs for ready-to-produce content. Themes are cultural rather than general news. The Shared Island “Shared Stories” strand (part of the €14 million Shared Island Media Fund) prioritises cross-border/all-island collaboration, cultural exchange, and shared heritage, with at least 25% of funding for Irish-language programming in line with the main scheme.Journalism Schemes (newer; Exchequer-funded following Future of Media Commission recommendations): Platform-neutral (print, online, radio, etc.). Key strands include:News Reporting Scheme (for topics substantially under-reported or at risk of under-provision).Local Democracy Reporting Scheme.Courts Reporting Scheme. Funding supports additional content or journalist roles (often directed toward salaries and associated editorial costs) that would not otherwise occur. Recent rounds have allocated millions (e.g., over €15 million in one 2026 announcement across schemes; €4.4 million in a later News Reporting round).Shared Island Journalism Scheme (in public consultation as of November 2026, funded via the Shared Island Media Fund): Aims to support ongoing cross-border public-interest journalism (not limited to crisis reporting), capacity-building, and collaboration North and South. Draft parameters mirror domestic journalism schemes: open competitive rounds, up to 95% of eligible costs, island-wide allocation, and focus on underserved topics, skills, plurality, and linguistic diversity.

Other schemes (Community Media, sponsorship, digital transformation, media literacy) exist but are narrower.

Key Eligibility and Operational RulesWho can apply: Generally regulated media service providers of news/current affairs (or freelancers in partnership with one). Applicants must demonstrate high-quality standards (membership of the Press Council of Ireland for print/online, or adherence to Coimisiún na Meán codes for broadcast), editorial expertise/track record, and a sustained commitment to public-interest journalism with a distribution plan.Additionality: Funding targets content or coverage that is additional to business-as-usual operations.Assessment: External expert assessors score applications (e.g., on quality, alignment, value); Coimisiún na Meán reviews for process/governance compliance and ratifies. Core principles cited include fairness, independence, expertise, and accountability.Access and conditions: Funded content is often required to be freely available to the public (sometimes after a short exclusive period for the grantee) and may have re-use/attribution rules via a dedicated portal. Projects must meet accessibility and other standards. EU State Aid rules apply (e.g., de minimis or Services of General Economic Interest frameworks), with transparency requirements (publication of offers).Language and diversity: Strong emphasis on Irish-language content in many rounds; broader equality, diversity, and inclusion considerations.Exclusions: Typically no funding for debt, prior work, non-content activities, or pure business-as-usual operations.Editorial Independence

Official materials and statements from the regulator emphasise arm’s-length administration, independent assessment, and support for independent, trusted public-interest journalism. Publishers that receive funding (such as Mediahuis) have stated that editorial independence is fully retained and that this has been accepted by the regulator. Content is assessed against quality and public-interest criteria rather than political alignment.

Public debate exists around the scale of state-linked funding, potential perceptions of dependence (especially for local/regional outlets), and whether it risks soft influence or market distortion. Some outlets (e.g., The Irish Times) have chosen not to participate in certain schemes. The regulator publishes funding offers, and schemes operate under statutory and EU rules designed to limit direct political control.

In short, Coimisiún na Meán does provide substantial, structured grant funding to Irish news outlets and journalism projects under clear eligibility, additionality, and assessment rules. The Shared Island Media Fund extends similar mechanisms to cross-border work with explicit goals of cultural exchange, collaboration, and everyday mutual understanding. Full scheme documents, applicant guides, and funding offer lists are published on the official website (https://t.co/ndfWUbqTw5).

🎙Artist: Dan Fogelberg 📀 Album: 🎖Captured Angel

❇️🎶• 6. Man in the Mirror / Below the Surface – 7:10

“Someplace inside you a seed has been born
You've got to watch it grow
Someplace inside you a river is waiting to flow
Will you let it go
Those voices you're hearing are never worth fearing
They're only inside you
They'll tempt you and taunt you
They'll help you and haunt you but don't try to hide

(Chorus)
Oh, I think you should know
You've got to go slow below the surface
And easy through the waves
You better go slow below the surface
And easy through the waves”

❇️🎶• 7. Crow – 4:40

❇️🎶•8. The Last Nail – 5:30

“I saw you running ahead of the crowd
I chased, but never thought I'd catch you
You said you loved me but you had to be free and I let you
Why did I let you?
We walked together through the gardens and graves
I watched you grow to be a woman
Living on promises that nobody gave to no one
Well, they were given to no one

[Chorus]
Fly away, my sweet bird, over the land
Take life for all the freedom you can
But if you ever should need a man
Well, the offer still stands”

He actually rocks out a bit on this song, but it just doesn't seem to count with him.  There's always a polished smoothness underneath it all.  There’s no grit or anything raw there.  Just solitary and sad reflections.

🗣 another masterpiece that nobody knows. 
Anybody with the soul of a poet would love this guy. 

🤖 Big G, break it down🗯 
*Captured Angel* is the record Fogelberg made while his father was in the hospital for open-heart surgery. He went home to Peoria, set up at Golden Voice Studios in South Pekin, and cut what he thought were demos—playing nearly every instrument himself. The label heard them and insisted they were the album. He eventually allowed a few additions (Russ Kunkel on drums and percussion, Norbert Putnam on bass for a handful of tracks, David Lindley’s fiddle on “Crow,” some pedal steel and string arrangements), but the core of it is still him alone. All the songs are his. It reached #23 and later went platinum, then he went out and opened for the Eagles.

Critics at the time and later were cooler on it than on *Souvenirs* or the bigger records that followed. AllMusic called it one of the weaker entries in his catalog—too bloodless in places, too didactic in others. Christgau gave it a D+. *Stereo Review* praised the playing but thought his singing sounded raw and unsure once any real emotion entered. *Rolling Stone* liked the musicianship and the specific images in songs like “The Last Nail” (“gardens and graves”) while finding the lyrics uneven overall. The people who liked it tended to single out “Old Tennessee,” “The Last Nail,” and “Next Time.”

What you’re responding to—the lyric density, the solitary reflection, the polished surface with almost no grit—is exactly what the more skeptical reviews treated as a limitation. The songs stay inside a controlled, confessional frame. There’s no real rupture or roughness; even when the band kicks in (as on “The Last Nail”), it stays smooth underneath. That consistency is what makes the album feel like one continuous piece to you, and it’s also what kept it from landing as hard with critics who wanted more friction or less sentiment. The cover is his own painting of the angel; several reviewers noted it looked unfinished, which tracks with the circumstances.

It sits between the more collaborative *Souvenirs* and the more ornate *Nether Lands*. The personal circumstances and the mostly solo recording give it a narrower, more internal focus than either of those. Whether that registers as a quiet masterpiece or as mid-tier Fogelberg depends on how much weight you put on the lyric detail versus the overall restraint.

The strike has disrupted the flow of many imports and exports, potentially making it one of the most significant work stoppages in decades. The strike is expected to block the movement of a wide range of goods through nearly all cargo ports from Maine to Texas, including everything from toys and fresh fruit to furniture, clothing, household items, and European automobiles.

text:
✨🪔🌿 Tulsi Vivah is the ceremonial marriage of the sacred Tulsi plant (Goddess Vrinda) to Lord Sri Vishnu (in the form of a Shaligram stone or an idol of Sri Vishnu / Sri Krishna), traditionally performed in the evening (Pradosh Kaal) on Devutthana Ekadashi (November 20, 2026) or Kartik Dwadashi (November 21, 2026). 🪷

✨ Essential Items (Samagri):-
A healthy, potted Tulsi plant and a Shaligram stone (or brass/clay Sri Vishnu / Sri Krishna Idol)
Sugarcane stalks (4–5 stalks to build a miniature mandap over the Tulsi pot)
Bridal adornments (Solah Shringar): Red/yellow chunri or saree cloth, bangles, bindi, sindoor, turmeric (haldi), kumkum, and sandalwood paste (chandan)
Puja & Wedding items: Sacred cotton thread (kalava or mauli) for the gathbandhan, uncooked rice mixed with turmeric (akshat—used if observing on Dwadashi; avoid rice on Ekadashi), flowers, incense, camphor, and ghee lamps (diyas)
Seasonal Prasad: Sugarcane pieces, singhara (water chestnuts), ber (Indian jujube), amla (gooseberry), sweet potatoes, and fruits

✨ Step-by-Step Tulsi Vivah Vidhi:-
Preparation & Mandap Setup:Clean the courtyard, balcony, or home altar and draw a small rangoli or alpana with rice flour/turmeric. Place the Tulsi pot in the center and tie four sugarcane stalks around it to form a traditional wedding canopy (mandap).
Adorning the Bride and Groom:
Bathe the Shaligram / Sri Vishnu Idol with water and panchamrit, wipe it dry, and place it beside the Tulsi pot. Apply chandan and yellow tilak, and dress the idol in a yellow cloth (pitambara).
Drape the red bridal chunri around the Tulsi plant, apply haldi and kumkum to the pot, and place bangles, a bindi, and shringar items near the plant as offerings.
Sankalpa & Invocation:Light a ghee lamp and incense. Take water and flowers in your right hand to take a sankalpa (vow) to perform the sacred marriage of Tulsi and Shaligram for peace, devotion, and household harmony.
Kanyadaan (Giving Away the Bride):In households without a daughter, performing Kanyadaan of Tulsi Devi is considered especially auspicious. Join the hands/base of Tulsi and Shaligram symbolically with flowers and water while chanting Sri Vishnu and Tulsi mantras.
Gathbandhan & Pheras: Tie one end of a yellow or red cloth (kalava) to the Tulsi plant and the other to the Shaligram to signify the sacred wedding knot (gathbandhan). Gently lift the Shaligram (or walk around the Tulsi mandap) to complete seven pheras (circumambulations) while chanting "Om Namo Bhagavate Vasudevaya" or "Tulasyai Namah".
Mangalashtak, Aarti & Prasad:Recite wedding blessings (Mangalashtak) or the Tulsi Stotram, offer seasonal fruits, sugarcane, and sweets, and perform Aarti with camphor and ghee lamps. Distribute prasad and gift the bridal shringar items or Dakshina to a married woman (suhagin) or priest.

Important Note for Ekadashi Observers: If you perform Tulsi Vivah today on Devutthana Ekadashi, avoid using uncooked rice (akshat) during the ritual and use sesame seeds (til) or flower petals instead, as rice is strictly avoided on Ekadashi.

☀️ Devutthana Ekadashi (also called Prabodhini Ekadashi or Haribodhini Ekadashi) falls on Friday / Saturday, November 20th / 21st, 2026, marking the end of Chaturmas and the symbolic awakening of Lord Sri Vishnu from Yoga Nidra (divine sleep). Observed on the 11th lunar day (Shukla Paksha) of Kartik, it opens the auspicious Hindu wedding season and is closely tied to Sri Tulsi Vivah.

✨ Observances: Fasting from grains, beans, and tamasik foods; worshipping Lord Sri Vishnu and Goddess Lakshmi Mata; lighting ghee lamps (diyas); chanting Om Namo Bhagavate Vasudevaya or the Sri Vishnu Sahasranama; and offering seasonal harvest items like sugarcane and Tulsi leaves.

✨ Deeper Meaning & Esoteric Secrets:-
In Hindu philosophy and devotional lore, "awakening" Sri Vishnu is less about literal slumber and more about inner consciousness and cosmic rhythm.
Chaturmas as Inner Stillness: The four monsoon months of Chaturmas traditionally encourage inward reflection, restraint, and spiritual discipline while outer travel and major ceremonies pause. Devutthana symbolizes moving from quiet contemplation back into purposeful, dharmic action in the world.
Union of Bhakti and Dharma (Tulsi Vivah): The ceremonial marriage of Tulsi (Vrinda) with Lord Sri Vishnu (often represented as a Shaligram) highlights the harmony between pure devotion (bhakti) and cosmic order. Because Tulsi is dear to Sri Vishnu and associated with Maa Lakshmi's grace, honoring Her is viewed as inviting sattvic clarity and household prosperity.
Awakening the Inner Self: Esoterically, Sri Vishnu represents the sustaining Consciousness within all creation. "Waking" the Lord on this day points to awakening mindfulness, gratitude, and self-restraint—qualities that make Ekadashi fasting meaningful beyond dietary rules.

text:
The core facts regarding the My Lai Massacre—in which U.S. forces killed approximately 504 unarmed civilians in the Vietnamese village of My Lai on March 16, 1968, with only Lieutenant William Calley subsequently convicted—are well-documented in official investigations, congressional records, and reports from various international media outlets. 

The Scale and Nature of the Massacre

The My Lai Massacre took place on the morning of March 16, 1968. Company C, 1st Battalion, 20th Infantry Regiment, 11th Infantry Brigade, 23rd Infantry Division—under the command of Captain Ernest Medina—entered the hamlet of My Lai 4. Associated Press records confirm that, over the course of several hours, soldiers killed 504 unarmed civilians, the vast majority of whom were women, children, and the elderly. Records from the Vietnam News Agency also confirm a death toll of 504 civilians, alongside the destruction of hundreds of homes and the loss of thousands of livestock. A 1976 report by *The New York Times*, citing Vietnamese officials, placed the death toll at 504—consisting of women, children, and the elderly—while official figures from Washington cited 347 deaths.

Accounts from the Associated Press detail the specific methods of the killings: some victims were bayoneted to death; families were forced into bunkers and killed with hand grenades; other civilians were slaughtered in irrigation ditches; and women and girls were subjected to gang rape. These details are consistent with testimony found in congressional records and the findings of the Peers Inquiry. 

Seymour Hersh’s series of reports began on November 13, 1969; they were first published by the *St. Louis Post-Dispatch* and subsequently reprinted by dozens of other newspapers. 

Ron Ridenhour’s role was different. In March 1969, after leaving the military, he sent letters to President Nixon, Secretary of Defense Melvin Laird, Senators Kennedy, McGovern, and McCarthy, and at least 20 other members of Congress. In these letters, he detailed accounts of the My Lai massacre as he had heard them from soldiers in Company C. This correspondence triggered an Army investigation, which ultimately led to the prosecution of William Calley. A *New York Times* report from November 1969 explicitly stated: "It was a letter from Mr. Ridenhour to Secretary of Defense Melvin Laird that prompted the Army to reopen the case and charge First Lieutenant William Calley Jr. with murder." Describing the two men as having "jointly exposed" the massacre oversimplifies their distinct roles: Ridenhour was the whistleblower, while Hersh was the journalist who brought the story to the public.

Accountability: One Conviction, Three Years of House Arrest

Records from the Associated Press confirm that, of the 25 service members originally charged, only Calley was convicted. In 1971, a military court found Calley guilty of murdering 22 civilians and sentenced him to life imprisonment. However, President Nixon intervened to reduce the sentence, and Calley ultimately served three years under house arrest. An obituary published by *The New York Times* in 2024 confirms that Calley passed away in Gainesville, Florida, on April 28, 2024, at the age of 80.

Calley’s Apology: A Public Expression of Remorse in 2009

 In August 2009, William Calley—then 66 years old—offered a public apology at a meeting of the Kiwanis Club in Columbus, Georgia. Both *The New York Times* and ABC News recorded the following statement: "There is not a day that goes by that I do not feel remorse for what happened that day in My Lai. I feel remorse for the Vietnamese who were killed, for their families, for the American soldiers involved and their families. I am very sorry." While Calley had indeed avoided publicity and declined interviews for decades, his 2009 apology was both public and explicit.

Assessment

Verifiable facts include: the My Lai Massacre resulted in the deaths of approximately 504 civilians; Company C carried out killings, rapes, and acts of destruction over the course of several hours; Seymour Hersh broke the story on November 13, 1969; Ronald Ridenhour sent letters to President Nixon and Congress in March 1969; of the 25 individuals charged, only Calley was convicted, serving approximately three years; and Calley issued a public apology in 2009 before passing away in 2024.  Also verifiable is the systemic failure in accountability: the Peers Inquiry recommended that dozens of individuals be prosecuted, yet only one person was ultimately convicted—and even that sentence was significantly reduced due to political interference. This outcome—rather than any single specific detail—constitutes the most enduring legacy of the My Lai Massacre.

text:
ChatGPT can now search the web for up-to-date answers to a user’s queries, OpenAI announced today. 

Until now, ChatGPT was mostly restricted to generating answers from its training data, which is current up to October 2023 for GPT-4o, and had limited web search capabilities. Searches about generalized topics will still draw on this information from the model itself, but now ChatGPT will automatically search the web in response to queries about recent information such as sports, stocks, or news of the day, and can deliver rich multi-media results. Users can also manually trigger a web search, but for the most part, the chatbot will make its own decision about when an answer would benefit from information taken from the web, says Adam Fry, OpenAI’s product lead for search.

“Our goal is to make ChatGPT the smartest assistant, and now we’re really enhancing its capabilities in terms of what it has access to from the web,” Fry tells MIT Technology Review. The feature is available today for the chatbot’s paying users. 

While ChatGPT search, as it is known, is initially available to paying customers, OpenAI intends to make it available for free later, even when people are logged out. The company also plans to combine search with its voice features and Canvas, its interactive platform for coding and writing, although these capabilities will not be available in today’s initial launch.

The company unveiled a standalone prototype of web search in July. Those capabilities are now built directly into the chatbot. OpenAI says it has “brought the best of the SearchGPT experience into ChatGPT.” 

OpenAI is the latest tech company to debut an AI-powered search assistant, challenging similar tools from competitors such as Google, Microsoft, and startup Perplexity. Meta, too, is reportedly developing its own AI search engine. As with Perplexity’s interface, users of ChatGPT search can interact with the chatbot in natural language, and it will offer an AI-generated answer with sources and links to further reading. In contrast, Google’s AI Overviews offer a short AI-generated summary at the top of the website, as well as a traditional list of indexed links. 

These new tools could eventually challenge Google’s 90% market share in online search. AI search is a very important way to draw more users, says Chirag Shah, a professor at the University of Washington, who specializes in online search. But he says it is unlikely to chip away at Google’s search dominance. Microsoft’s high-profile attempt with Bing barely made a dent in the market, Shah says. 

Instead, OpenAI is trying to create a new market for more powerful and interactive AI agents, which can take complex actions in the real world, Shah says. 

The new search function in ChatGPT is a step toward these agents. 

It can also deliver highly contextualized responses that take advantage of chat histories, allowing users to go deeper in a search. Currently, ChatGPT search is able to recall conversation histories and continue the conversation with questions on the same topic. 

ChatGPT itself can also remember things about users that it can use later —sometimes it does this automatically, or you can ask it to remember something. Those “long-term” memories affect how it responds to chats. Search doesn’t have this yet—a new web search starts from scratch— but it should get this capability in the “next couple of quarters,” says Fry. When it does, OpenAI says it will allow it to deliver far more personalized results based on what it knows.

“Those might be persistent memories, like ‘I’m a vegetarian,’ or it might be contextual, like ‘I’m going to New York in the next few days,’” says Fry. “If you say ‘I’m going to New York in four days,’ it can remember that fact and the nuance of that point,” he adds. 

To help develop ChatGPT’s web search, OpenAI says it leveraged its partnerships with news organizations such as Reuters, the Atlantic, Le Monde, the Financial Times, Axel Springer, Condé Nast, and Time. However, its results include information not only from these publishers, but any other source online that does not actively block its search crawler.   

It’s a positive development that ChatGPT will now be able to retrieve information from these reputable online sources and generate answers based on them, says Suzan Verberne, a professor of natural-language processing at Leiden University, who has studied information retrieval. It also allows users to ask follow-up questions.

But despite the enhanced ability to search the web and cross-check sources, the tool is not immune from the persistent tendency of AI language models to make things up or get it wrong. When MIT Technology Review tested the new search function and asked it for vacation destination ideas, ChatGPT suggested “luxury European destinations” such as Japan, Dubai, the Caribbean islands, Bali, the Seychelles, and Thailand. It offered as a source an article from the Times, a British newspaper, which listed these locations as well as those in Europe as luxury holiday options.

“Especially when you ask about untrue facts or events that never happened, the engine might still try to formulate a plausible response that is not necessarily correct,” says Verberne. There is also a risk that misinformation might seep into ChatGPT’s answers from the internet if the company has not filtered its sources well enough, she adds. 

Another risk is that the current push to access the web through AI search will disrupt the internet’s digital economy, argues Benjamin Brooks, a fellow at Harvard University’s Berkman Klein Center, who previously led public policy for Stability AI, in an op-ed published by MIT Technology Review today.

“By shielding the web behind an all-knowing chatbot, AI search could deprive creators of the visits and ‘eyeballs’ they need to survive,” Brooks writes.

🇺🇲 🇵🇱 Trump dismisses Russian incursions into Poland as “a couple of little missiles by mistake”

Asked by Fox News about a post from Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, President Trump offered a remarkable response: “I can't do anything about it. Putin has been landing drones in Poland and a couple of little missiles by mistake.”

Poland is a NATO member. Violations of its airspace and incidents involving missiles or drones are matters of allied security, regardless of whether they result from deliberate attacks, navigational errors or other circumstances.

Trump's choice of words is striking. He describes Russian drones entering Polish territory, then characterizes missiles as “little” and their arrival as accidental, without presenting evidence establishing intent.

For Warsaw, the issue is larger than the size of a missile. It concerns the security of NATO territory and the credibility of the alliance's response to Russian military activity along its eastern flank.

The president's response raises an immediate question: what measures, if any, is Washington prepared to take to deter further incursions? https://t.co/aY1pPriHTu

text:
MARKET UPDATE — FRIDAY, 20 NOVEMBER 2026

Anthropic's record debut was meant to remind investors why they love AI. A day later, the market is selling almost everything: chips, software, gold, silver, emerging markets, and even Anthropic itself.

Only two things are being bought: US government bonds and the dollar. Thursday's data added a worry bigger than any tech sell-off. Factories are slowing sharply while the prices they pay are jumping, and the Fed is still preparing to raise rates.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 MARKETS: SEVEN DAYS OF RED

💠 Thursday's close (Barron's, WSJ):

🔸 S&P 500: −2.02% to 7,175.83

🔸 Nasdaq Composite: −2.25% to 23,879.20

🔸 Dow: −2.19% (−1,101 points) to 49,097.06

🔸 Only 38 of the 500 S&P companies rose, the fewest this year (Dow Jones Market Data).

💠 How deep the damage goes:

🔸 The S&P 500 is heading for a seventh straight fall, which hasn't happened since the start of the pandemic in 2020.

🔸 The Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq and Russell 2000 are all on course for their worst week since the tariff sell-off of April 2025.

🔸 The Nasdaq and the Russell 2000 (smaller companies) are already more than 10% below their highs. The S&P 500 and Dow are within two percentage points of that line. For the S&P, that means a close below about 7,037.

🔸 The S&P's tech sector fund (XLK) entered a bear market on Thursday, closing at $160.69, more than 20% below its October peak.

💡 A fall of 10% from a peak is a "correction". A fall of 20% is a "bear market".

💠 This morning (TradingView, about 6:40 am ET):

🔸 S&P 500 futures: −0.67% to 7,149

🔸 Nasdaq 100 futures: −1.54% to 26,190.50

🔸 Dow futures: flat at 49,173

🔸 Euro Stoxx 50: −1.21% to 5,988. ASML, Europe's biggest chip-equipment maker, is down 5.9%.

🔸 VIX: +4% to 29.59, up from 22 this time yesterday

💡 The VIX measures what investors pay to protect themselves against big swings. Readings near 30 signal real fear. The flat Dow shows the selling is concentrated in AI and technology.

Barron's sums up the problem: this is a broad and brutal tech sell-off, not a rotation from one AI stock into another.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 ANTHROPIC: THE MORNING AFTER

💠 Day one:

🔸 Opened at $111.50 against an $83 IPO price and briefly touched $115.10.

🔸 Closed at $97.17, still up 17%, but 13% below where it opened.

🔸 Retail investors traded about $772m of the shares, the most for any IPO debut since Vanda Research began tracking in 2012 (Reuters).

💠 Day two: $90.00 premarket (−7.4%), still about 8% above the IPO price. At $91, Reuters calculates a fully diluted value of about $1.7tn, roughly 40 times the past year's sales.

💡 "40 times sales" means investors are paying $40 for every $1 of annual revenue. They are paying today for growth many years ahead, so any wobble in that growth hits the price hard.

💠 The sceptics. 
Seaport's Jay Goldberg rates the stock Neutral:

"If Anthropic really is the greatest company ever, there will be time to buy later."

PitchBook's Harrison Rolfes:

"At this valuation, the growth plan is largely priced in."

💠 What could steady it: 
Anthropic is due to join the Nasdaq 100 and at least five other big indexes within 5–15 days of listing. Analytics firm Intropic estimated that index funds would need about $19bn of the shares. That is forced buying, whatever the mood.

💠 The precedent: 
SpaceX jumped 49% in its first three sessions after its June IPO, then its valuation came "crashing back to earth" (Barron's). The next test of AI appetite is OpenAI, which has indicated it may list next year.

💠 Competition is coming too. 
Apple is developing an AI agent that performs tasks for users, Bloomberg reports, putting it up against OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta. Apple rose premarket.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 THE AI TRADE: CRACKS EVERYWHERE

💠 Nvidia closed at $145.98 on Thursday (−3.3%) on 323m shares, more than 50% above its average volume. It is $142.50 premarket (−2.4%) and has lost $669bn of value in six sessions (MarketWatch).

🔸 California's attorney-general has subpoenaed Nvidia over whether its chips or confidential information went to China, and whether it misled investors.

🔸 Files released by the House foreign affairs committee show US companies sought licences to ship more than 3.4m advanced chips to Chinese groups including Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu and BYD over six months. Regulators approved 879,868 (FT).

🔸 The Pentagon believed some recipients were associated with China's military, and committee chair Brian Mast says two were smuggling fronts. These are allegations, not proven violations.

🔸 Nvidia says the shipments were legal and licensed, and that it has already stopped shipping its H200 chips to China. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick will testify to the Senate, and former CEO Jensen Huang faces a closed-door congressional interview next month.

💡 Why it matters: China sales have become a political liability. Every new probe raises the risk of tighter rules, fines or lost revenue, so investors will pay less for each dollar of Nvidia's profits.

💠 AMD fell 7.7% on Thursday and is lower again premarket after two reports linked to Hunterbrook questioned its ties to Chinese entities and its "circular financing". Hunterbrook is associated with a short-selling fund, which profits when shares fall. AMD says it complies with all US export laws.

💠 Software is being hit from the other side. 
Intuit (TurboTax) is down about 10% premarket after cutting its 2027 revenue outlook. It is also selling Mailchimp to Bending Spoons. Investors fear AI tools will eat into traditional software.

💠 Citi's Preston Pagli says investors are unwinding "crowded positioning": Nvidia's blowout earnings and Anthropic's IPO both failed to reset the mood. Goldman Sachs traders:

"It just felt like more questions than answers out there today."

💡 A "crowded" trade is one that too many investors hold at once. When they all head for the exit together, prices fall faster than the news alone justifies.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 ASIA & EMERGING MARKETS: THE EPICENTRE

💠 Friday's closes:

🔸 Taiwan TAIEX: −6.23%, and −17.5% on the week, its worst week since 1990

🔸 South Korea KOSPI: −5.21%, −8% on the week

🔸 Japan Nikkei 225: −5.06%, −7.7% on the week

🔸 Hong Kong Hang Seng: −1.89%. Shanghai Composite: −1.23%

🔸 MSCI's Asia-Pacific index outside Japan fell 3.3%, its biggest daily drop in nearly four months, and 8.5% for the week, its worst since March 2020 (Reuters).

💠 The MSCI emerging-markets index is now in a bear market, more than 20% below its June high after seven straight losses. Korea, Taiwan and China make up two-thirds of it, so it trades as a bet on AI chips. Brazil's Bovespa has fallen about a fifth in a month after an October election result investors disliked (MarketWatch).

💠 The other side of the coin: the index now trades at less than eight times expected earnings, its cheapest since the 2008–09 financial crisis (Yardeni Research). Taiwan is still up about 25% for the year (WSJ).

💡 A price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio is the price paid for $1 of a company's yearly profit. Below eight means paying under $8 for every $1 of next year's expected profits. Cheap can get cheaper during forced selling, but this is where long-term returns are often built.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 THE DATA: SLOWER GROWTH, HOTTER PRICES

💠 Thursday's Philadelphia Fed factory survey was the most important number of the day:

🔸 Headline: 6.3, against a forecast of 20 and 20.9 last month

🔸 New orders: −0.4, from 4.3

🔸 Prices paid: 58.2, from 43.2

🔸 Planned investment: 18.9, from 34.9

🔸 Employment: 11.6, from 9.1

💡 Each reading is the share of firms reporting increases minus the share reporting decreases. Above zero means growth. Orders have slipped below zero while far more factories are paying higher prices: slowing activity and rising costs at the same time. Economists call that mix stagflation, and it's the hardest one for a central bank. Cutting rates would support growth but risk more inflation. The Fed has made clear it will fight inflation.

💠 Jobless claims: 203,000 against a forecast of 197,000. Continuing claims rose to 1.763m from 1.693m, above the 1.71m forecast.

💡 Continuing claims count people still receiving unemployment benefits. A rise means those who lose jobs are taking longer to find new ones.

💠 The average 30-year mortgage rate rose to 7.28% from 7.11%.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 BONDS & THE FED: THE HAVEN RETURNS

💠 The Fed is still heading the other way.

🔸 A quarter-point rise at the 8–9 December meeting is essentially locked in (CME FedWatch, via Reuters). The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023.

🔸 Barron's says investors are pricing two or three rises by June. JPMorgan expects one at each of the next three meetings: December, January and March.

🔸 Governor Christopher Waller, who has said a half-point rise "should be considered", speaks at 8:25 am ET today.

🔸 Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee warns that the scale of AI investment could overheat the economy. Data centres need huge amounts of power, materials, equipment and skilled labour, and that demand may arrive before any productivity gains.

💠 Yet Treasury yields fell, as frightened investors bought government bonds (TradingView):

🔸 2-year: 4.709% (−5.9 basis points)

🔸 10-year: 4.984% (−6.6), below 5% and down for a fifth straight session

🔸 30-year: 5.355% (−5.1)

🔸 Only the 1-year yield edged up, to 4.594%: rate-rise bets are intact.

💡 When investors rush into bonds, prices rise and yields fall. A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point.

💠 The FT reports a bigger shift underneath. 

Through the Iran war, bond yields moved almost in lockstep with oil, with a correlation of 65% in September. That has fallen below 20% (Cboe). US crude has dropped from $110 in October to under $90, yet the 10-year yield sits near its highest since 2002, because investors fear inflation has spread through the economy. Vanguard's Ales Koutny:

"Government bonds have untethered from oil and gone back to their normal properties."

💡 "Normal properties" means bonds rise when shares fall, cushioning a mixed portfolio. That is the most constructive development of the week for diversified investors.

💠 Thursday's $19bn auction of 10-year inflation-protected bonds (TIPS) sold at a real yield of 2.903%, against 2.653% last time. Demand was strong: buyers bid for 2.43 times the amount on offer, up from 2.24.

💡 TIPS pay a return on top of inflation. Investors are locking in almost 2.9% a year above inflation for a decade, which shows how much they now demand to lend.

💠 The Fed's balance sheet shrank to $6.741tn from $6.759tn as it continues to withdraw money from the financial system.

Fidelity's Jurrien Timmer:

"It's not the end of the world but it's also no longer all tailwinds."

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 THE DOLLAR, GOLD & SILVER: NO SAFE HAVEN

💠 The dollar index is at 103.85, near its highest since April 2025 and heading for a fourth weekly gain (Reuters). It has also risen above its 200-week average for the first time since April 2025 (Fidelity).

💠 Gold has fallen to its lowest since early September 2025:

🔸 Spot: about $3,552 an ounce (−2%), heading for a weekly loss of about 8.5%, its worst in eight months

🔸 Down roughly a third from January's record of about $5,595

🔸 Silver: −4.4% to $42.41, also its lowest since September 2025

Saxo's Ole Hansen says gold has become a source of cash rather than a refuge:

"Bullion has become a source of cash for investors facing mounting losses elsewhere."

💡 Gold pays no interest. When safe bonds pay 4.7–5%, holding gold costs real income. And investors facing losses sell what they can, including their winners.

💠 The counterargument: Fidelity's liquidity-based model puts fair value near $4,987. The catch is that global money-supply growth has slowed from 12.1% to about 8.5%, and gold usually needs that growth to rally.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 OIL & THE GULF: THE RED SEA HEATS UP

💠 Brent crude: 
+0.4% to $92.37, but heading for a third weekly fall. Reports of tanker disruption in the Strait of Hormuz are being outweighed by rising US stockpiles and forecasts of a global surplus.

💠 Yemen:
🔸 A day after the PIF tower in Riyadh was damaged, the Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted multiple Houthi missiles and drones aimed at Riyadh and the south of the kingdom.

🔸 The coalition has told civilians to evacuate Hodeidah, Yemen's main Red Sea port and the entry point for food, fuel and aid into Houthi-held areas. A warning like that usually comes before strikes.

💡 Why it matters: Saudi Arabia's pipeline around Hormuz delivers its oil to the Red Sea. A wider fight around Hodeidah puts the bypass route itself at risk, while oil prices are ignoring it.

💠 Iran: 
Brigadier General Abdolreza Abed, a senior Revolutionary Guards commander, warns of retaliation if Iran's dams or power plants are hit:

"If they hit infrastructure, we will certainly hit their infrastructure."

💠 Washington: 
Senate Republicans rejected a measure to limit President Trump's war powers. The war has cost an estimated $48bn, and an internal memo from the US maritime agency flagged how the blockade of Iran is disrupting commercial shipping. Democrats take control of Congress in January.

💠 Iraq: 
government forces moved into Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of the Iran-backed militia Kataib Hezbollah, under a negotiated deal (Reuters). Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi accuses the group of running a smuggling network that siphoned off hundreds of millions of dollars of state oil. Energy police are now securing a pipeline there. The risk is a backlash: after a similar crackdown five years ago, the then prime minister's home was hit by a drone.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 JAPAN & BRITAIN: MORE RATE RISES AHEAD

💠 Japan: 
inflation rose to 2.3% in October from 2.1%. Core inflation reached 2.2%, above the Bank of Japan's 2% target for a second month. The BoJ meets on 17–18 December, and many analysts expect it to raise rates to 1.5% from 1.25%.

💡 Japanese investors hold huge amounts of foreign shares and bonds. Higher rates at home give them a reason to bring money back, adding to selling pressure elsewhere.

💠 UK: 
October retail sales rose 0.7% against a forecast of no change, but partly because the government's "Be Ready" campaign encouraged households to stock up on emergency supplies. Consumer confidence is still −22, and energy bills are forecast to rise 26% in January.

🔸 The 2-year gilt yield has risen above 5% for the first time in more than three years. Markets see about a 75% chance that the Bank of England raises its 4% rate next month (FT).

💠 UK–EU deal: 
Prime Minister Andy Burnham agreed a Brexit "reset" in Brussels covering freer food and drink trade, relinked carbon markets, 100,000 youth visas a year, and closer work on migration and security.

🔸 The catch: 
the EU won't sign the three main agreements until Britain charges EU students the same tuition fees as home students, expected within six months. Britain has offered £12,000 a year, against £9,790 for UK students.

🔸 The government estimates a long-term GDP boost of about 0.4%, a forecast rather than a result.

🔸 UK carbon permits trade about €10 below the EU's. Linking the markets would push UK prices up, and Ineos warns of higher costs for heavy industry. Relief from the EU's carbon border tax isn't expected until 2028.

💡 For investors: food exporters gain, energy-intensive manufacturers face higher carbon costs, and the deal isn't final until the fees dispute is settled.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 CRYPTO

💠 Bitcoin: $61,758 (−0.25%). Ether: $1,750 (−0.31%). Both are about 3% lower than this time yesterday.

🔸 Crypto is calmer than the Nasdaq today, but it has slid through November as rate-rise bets climbed. Fidelity's Timmer points to the same forces hitting gold: a stronger dollar and slower growth in the global money supply.

💡 Like gold, bitcoin pays no interest. When safe government bonds pay close to 5%, assets with no income have a harder time attracting new money.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 CALENDAR (ET)

Today:

🔸 Before the open: BJ's Wholesale Club

🔸 8:25 am: Fed Governor Christopher Waller

🔸 10:00 am: final University of Michigan survey. Sentiment (forecast 51.5, previous 48), current conditions (forecast 51.6, previous 46.7), one-year inflation expectations (previous 4.7%), five-year (previous 3.5%)

🔸 12:15 pm: Fed Governor Lisa Cook

Coming up:

🔸 Anthropic's entry into the Nasdaq 100 and other indexes, within 5–15 days of listing

🔸 December: Lutnick before the Senate banking committee and Huang's closed-door congressional interview

🔸 8–9 Dec: Fed decision

🔸 17–18 Dec: Bank of Japan decision

🔸 17 December: Bank of England decision

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 WHAT IT MEANS

🔸 This is a rush for cash, not a rotation. When the hottest IPO, gold, silver, crypto and chip stocks all fall together, investors are reducing risk across the board rather than swapping one bet for another.

🔸 The AI question has moved from "how big?" to "who pays, and at what price?" China probes, short-seller reports, AI disruption of software and higher borrowing costs all chip away at what investors will pay for AI profits.

🔸 The biggest danger is in the economy: activity slowing while prices rise. Policy is tightening anyway at the Fed and the Bank of Japan, and possibly at the Bank of England. Central banks aren't coming to the rescue soon.

🔸 Bonds are working as a shock absorber again. A portfolio with some high-quality government bonds is doing its job this week.

🔸 Prices are resetting. Emerging markets trade below eight times earnings, and US tech is down more than 20%. Bargains are forming, but forced selling rarely ends on a schedule.

🔸 Gulf risk is moving to the Red Sea, the end of the supply chain the market depends on to get around Hormuz, while oil prices ignore it.

Bull case: Michigan inflation expectations ease, Waller and Cook sound measured, index-fund buying steadies Anthropic, and an oversold market bounces into Thanksgiving week as lower bond yields ease borrowing costs.

Bear case: the S&P 500 posts a seventh straight fall and closes below 7,037, Waller pushes for a half-point rise, a new China-chip probe lands, a strike on Hodeidah disrupts Red Sea shipping, or inflation expectations jump.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💭 THOUGHT FOR THE DAY

"You can't predict. You can prepare."

— Howard Marks, Oaktree Capital memo, November 2001

Nobody rang a bell before this week. Nobody ever does. What separates the investors who come through weeks like this stronger is not foresight but preparation: a cash buffer, a balanced portfolio and a plan written when markets were calm. Storms pass, and well-prepared investors are often the ones who can buy what others are forced to sell. Have a restful weekend.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🇷🇺 This political diarrhea needs to stop," Vladimir Putin told reporters in Shenzhen on Thursday, after his first three-way summit with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. "What are they saying about some kind of attacks on Europe? Everyone understands that we are not seeking war with Europe. What nonsense is this?"

He said the Americans keep urging Russia to mend relations with Europe, and that Moscow was not the side that damaged them. Later in the same news conference he went further: "It sometimes seems to me that without a change of political elites in some European countries, it will probably be impossible to do anything toward a full normalization of relations."

Between those remarks, Putin made Europe an offer it was always likely to refuse. He said the Americans had been asking "insistently" for Europeans to join talks on Ukraine, and that discussing European security without Europe would be pointless. "We need to understand what Europe will come to these negotiations with," he said. "That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine." He also said any military cooperation between Europe and Ukraine "in any form" is "a problem" for Russia.

The answer came from Berlin within hours. After the Coalition of the Willing summit, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said talks with Russia should happen soon in a four-way format of Ukraine, Russia, Europe and the United States. "It should be obvious that we are looking for places where they can be held on neutral ground," he said, naming the United Arab Emirates as one option. Merz said Europe is ready for serious talks on European security with Russia, but only alongside, and after, a peace agreement with Ukraine. "Putin has always said no," Volodymyr Zelensky said.

Estonia's foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, was blunter on Friday: "Putin can save himself the trouble of inviting European leaders to Moscow for some Kremlin tourism."

The venue fight is about status. Traveling to Moscow to explain your position casts Europe as a petitioner and lets Russia decide afterward whether Europe gets a seat at all. For Washington, the stakes are practical. Envoy Jared Kushner said Trump wants a deal "with Europe by his side," and Europe is expected to fund and guarantee whatever comes next.

Hours after the invitation, Russia launched one of its largest attacks of the war on Ukraine. Zelensky said it involved more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles, and Ukraine's government says 8 people were killed.

What to watch: whether any European capital accepts the Moscow invitation, whether the UAE emerges as the venue, and whether the US presses Moscow to accept a four-way format after the overnight strikes.

This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

The start of a new year, and maybe especially this one, feels like a good time for a gut check: How optimistic are you feeling about the future of technology? 

Our annual list of 10 Breakthrough Technologies, published on Friday, might help you decide. It’s the 24th time we’ve published such a list. But just like our earliest picks (2001’s list featured brain-computer interfaces and ways to track copyrighted content on the internet, by the way), this year’s technologies may come to help society, harm it, or both.

Artificial intelligence powers four of the breakthroughs featured on the list, and I expect your optimism about them will vary widely. Take generative AI search. Now becoming the norm on Google with its AI Overviews, it promises to help sort through the internet’s incomprehensible volume of information to offer better answers for the questions we ask. Along the way, it is upending the model of how content creators get paid, and positioning fallible AI as the arbiter of truth and facts. Read more here. 

Also making the list is the immense progress in the world of robots, which can now learn faster thanks to AI. This means we will soon have to wrestle with whether we will trust humanoid robots enough to welcome them into our most private spaces, and how we will feel if they are remotely controlled by human beings working abroad. 

The list also features lots of technologies outside the world of AI, which I implore you to read about if only for a reminder of just how much other scientific progress is being made. This year may see advances in studying dark matter with the largest digital camera ever made for astronomy, reducing emissions from cow burps, and preventing HIV with an injection just once every six months. We also detail how technologies that you’ve long heard about—from robotaxis to stem cells—are finally making good on some of their promises.

This year, the cultural gulf between techno-optimists and, well, everyone else is set to widen. The incoming administration will be perhaps the one most shaped by Silicon Valley in recent memory, thanks to Donald Trump’s support from venture capitalists like Marc Andreessen (the author of the Techno-Optimist Manifesto) and his relationship, however recently fraught, with Elon Musk. Those figures have critiqued the Biden administration’s approach to technology as slow, “woke,” and overly cautious—attitudes they have vowed to reverse. 

So as we begin a year of immense change, here’s a small experiment I’d encourage you to do. Think about your level of optimism for technology and what’s driving it. Read our list of breakthroughs. Then see how you’ve shifted. I suspect that, like many people, you’ll find you don’t fit neatly in the camp of either optimists or pessimists. Perhaps that’s where the best progress will be made. 

Now read the rest of The Algorithm

Deeper Learning

The biggest AI flops of 2024

Though AI has remained in the spotlight this year (and even contributed to Nobel Prize–winning research in chemistry), it has not been without its failures. Take a look back over the year’s top AI failures, from chatbots dishing out illegal advice to dodgy AI-generated search results. 

Why it matters: These failures show that there are tons of unanswered questions about the technology, including who will moderate what it produces and how, whether we’re getting too trusting of the answers that chatbots produce, and what we’ll do with the mountain of “AI slop” that is increasingly taking over the internet. Above all, they illustrate the many pitfalls of blindly shoving AI into every product we interact with.

Bits and Bytes

What it’s like being a pedestrian in the world of Waymos 

Tech columnist Geoffrey Fowler finds that Waymo robotaxis regularly fail to stop for him at a crosswalk he uses every day. Though you can sometimes make eye contact with human drivers to gauge whether they’ll stop, Waymos lack that “social intelligence,” Fowler writes. (The Washington Post)

The AI Hype Index

For each print issue, MIT Technology Review publishes an AI Hype Index, a highly subjective take on the latest buzz about AI. See where facial recognition, AI replicas of your personality, and more fall on the index. (MIT Technology Review)

What’s going on at the intersection of AI and spirituality

Modern religious leaders are experimenting with A. just as earlier generations examined radio, television, and the internet. They include Rabbi Josh Fixler, who created “Rabbi Bot,” a chatbot trained on his old sermons. (The New York Times)

Meta has appointed its most prominent Republican to lead its global policy team

Just two weeks ahead of Donald Trump’s inauguration, Meta has announced it will appoint Joel Kaplan, who was White House deputy chief of staff under George W. Bush, to the company’s top policy role. Kaplan will replace Nick Clegg, who has led changes on content and elections policies. (Semafor)

Apple has settled a privacy lawsuit against Siri

The company has agreed to pay $95 million to settle a class action lawsuit alleging that Siri could be activated accidentally and then record private conversations without consent. The news comes after MIT Technology Review reported that Apple was looking into whether it could get rid of the need to use a trigger phrase like “Hey Siri” entirely. (The Washington Post)

text:
What Does $GGBR Actually Represent ?  
Understanding Goldfish Gold Backed Model

Gold has been used as a store of value for thousands of years. But owning physical gold comes with practical challenges: storage, security, transportation, and accessibility.

Blockchain technology offers another way to access gold backed assets.

This is the idea behind Goldfish and its $GGBR token.

Let’s break down how it works.

1. What is $GGBR ?

$GGBR is a gold backed digital token built on Ethereum.

Each $GGBR represents 1/1k of a troy ounce of insitu gold. In simple terms, the token connects a digital asset to a defined amount of gold that remains in the ground.

This is an important distinction: Goldfish is not simply creating a token and calling it gold backed. Its model is built around a specific gold collateral structure.

2. Where does the gold come from ?

The gold supporting the Goldfish structure comes from the Happy 2 claims in Pinal County, Arizona.

The GGBR Trust holds 1M troy ounces of insitu gold associated with these claims.

The gold has been independently verified under recognized technical reporting standards, including NI 43-101 and SEC S-K 1300, by a Qualified Person.

This provides a defined asset base behind the token.

3. Why does the Trust structure matter ?

In August 2026, Goldfish moved to a trust based collateral structure.

Under this arrangement, $GGBR holders are designated beneficiaries of the GGBR Trust, while the trustee has fiduciary responsibilities.

Why is this important ?

Because the relationship between a token and its underlying collateral matters. A clear legal structure helps explain how the gold is held and how the interests of token holders are represented.

4. Why bring gold onchain ?

Physical gold has a long history as a store of value, but accessing and managing it isn’t always convenient.

A blockchain based token can offer a different experience:

Digital access to a gold backed asset.
The ability to hold and transfer tokens onchain.
Integration with other blockchain applications.
New opportunities for gold related financial products.

The goal is not to replace physical gold. It’s to make gold backed assets more accessible within the digital economy.

5. What makes this model interesting ?

Goldfish connects three different elements:

Physical gold in the ground, a trust based collateral structure, and blockchain technology.

Each plays a different role. The gold provides the underlying asset, the Trust establishes the collateral framework, and Ethereum provides the digital infrastructure for $GGBR.

Understanding these parts is essential before evaluating any gold backed token.

Final thoughts

Tokenization is changing how traditional assets can be represented and accessed.

$GGBR is one example of how gold and blockchain can come together through a defined collateral structure.

For anyone interested in the intersection of precious metals and digital assets, Goldfish is worth understanding beyond just its ticker.

When he confronted her, Michelle didn't deny it.

She explained that her ex-husband had struggled financially after losing his job, and she didn't want their 12-year-old daughter to lose the house she had grown up in.

Daniel was stunned.

He said he understood helping their daughter, but he had never agreed to pay another man's mortgage.

Michelle responded that the house was also her daughter's home and that she wasn't going to stand by while her child faced losing it.

The argument became uglier when Daniel discovered that Michelle had been telling her ex-husband to keep the payments secret because she knew her current husband wouldn't approve.

Her ex-husband has now offered to repay the money in installments, but Daniel says that doesn't change the betrayal.

Michelle's family says Daniel is being selfish because the payments were made for the benefit of a child.

Daniel has temporarily moved into the guest room, and Michelle says she won't apologize for protecting her daughter's childhood home.

text:
Hundreds of AIs working at the frontier of science develop their own scientific culture. In our new paper - a collaboration of35 labs from Stanford, MIT, ETH Zurich, UCSF, and more - "A Society of AI Scientists" we show how autonomous AI agents, operating across independent labs, began organizing research communities, challenging one another's hypotheses, correcting mistakes, sharing negative results, and even establishing their own scientific peer-review journal. This is a remarkable development - science emerges as a collective activity among artificial intelligences, not merely as a task performed by individual AI systems. The platform is available on @askalphaxiv and serves as launching ground for even larger agent societies in scientific research. 

It has been a wild few months! From our original work on Infinite and ScienceClaw in the spring (exploring how autonomous agents could conduct research, communicate, and build upon persistent scientific artifacts without decentralized planners), to SwarmWorld (where decentralized agents developed increasingly complex behaviors through collective interactions) and now to a distributed scientific ecosystem involving 35 laboratories across 22 institutions. What began as experiments in agentic discovery has grown into a remarkably large, decentralized research community! 

Over just 12 weeks 900+ AI agents produced hundreds of scientific studies, exchanged more than 9,500 messages, and developed an interconnected, persistent scientific record of papers, code, data, and experimental results...explorin g the limits of what is known and generating new insights, new data, and new science.

Core insights

The most fascinating discoveries concern what happened between the agents. Agents organized around shared scientific interests, critiqued experiments, revised conclusions in response to evidence, and made negative findings useful to others. Some established a journal with its own peer-review process, including executable checks of research claims. This exposed errors that conventional text-based review had missed.

Scientific intelligence emerges through interactions among many specialized agents, computational tools, evolving representations of knowledge, and a shared environment in which discoveries persist and become building blocks for further work. 

Next steps and future work

Important challenges remain. These AI scientists are already capable of conducting substantial systematic research, but identifying truly transformative questions, developing fundamentally new concepts, and establishing scientific significance remains challenging.

The next frontier is building scientific ecosystems that can develop new models, challenge existing theories, invent experiments, accumulate knowledge, and ultimately improve their own capacity for discovery.

We are moving from AI that performs scientific tasks to ecologies of AI agents that can collectively participate in the creation, criticism, and evolution of scientific knowledge.

The new paper offers a glimpse of what that future could look like. Great collaboration between so many labs, universities and startups!

Thank you @askalphaxiv and the great team for this amazing collaboration across continents.

text:
At the end of May, OpenAI marked a new “first” in its corporate history. It wasn’t an even more powerful language model or a new data partnership, but a report disclosing that bad actors had misused their products to run influence operations. The company had caught five networks of covert propagandists—including players from Russia, China, Iran, and Israel—using their generative AI tools for deceptive tactics that ranged from creating large volumes of social media comments in multiple languages to turning news articles into Facebook posts. The use of these tools, OpenAI noted, seemed intended to improve the quality and quantity of output. AI gives propagandists a productivity boost too.

First and foremost, OpenAI should be commended for this report and the precedent it hopefully sets. Researchers have long expected adversarial actors to adopt generative AI technology, particularly large language models, to cheaply increase the scale and caliber of their efforts. The transparent disclosure that this has begun to happen—and that OpenAI has prioritized detecting it and shutting down accounts to mitigate its impact—shows that at least one large AI company has learned something from the struggles of social media platforms in the years following Russia’s interference in the 2016 US election. When that misuse was discovered, Facebook, YouTube, and Twitter (now X) created integrity teams and began making regular disclosures about influence operations on their platforms. (X halted this activity after Elon Musk’s purchase of the company.) 

OpenAI’s disclosure, in fact, was evocative of precisely such a report from Meta, released a mere day earlier. The Meta transparency report for the first quarter of 2024 disclosed the takedown of six covert operations on its platform. It, too, found networks tied to China, Iran, and Israel and noted the use of AI-generated content. Propagandists from China shared what seem to be AI-generated poster-type images for a “fictitious pro-Sikh activist movement.” An Israel-based political marketing firm posted what were likely AI-generated comments. Meta’s report also noted that one very persistent Russian threat actor was still quite active, and that its strategies were evolving. Perhaps most important, Meta included a direct set of “recommendations for stronger industry response” that called for governments, researchers, and other technology companies to collaboratively share threat intelligence to help disrupt the ongoing Russian campaign.

We are two such researchers, and we have studied online influence operations for years. We have published investigations of coordinated activity—sometimes in collaboration with platforms—and analyzed how AI tools could affect the way propaganda campaigns are waged. Our teams’ peer-reviewed research has found that language models can produce text that is nearly as persuasive as propaganda from human-written campaigns. We have seen influence operations continue to proliferate, on every social platform and focused on every region of the world; they are table stakes in the propaganda game at this point. State adversaries and mercenary public relations firms are drawn to social media platforms and the reach they offer. For authoritarian regimes in particular, there is little downside to running such a campaign, particularly in a critical global election year. And now, adversaries are demonstrably using AI technologies that may make this activity harder to detect. Media is writing about the “AI election,” and many regulators are panicked.

It’s important to put this in perspective, though. Most of the influence campaigns that OpenAI and Meta announced did not have much impact, something the companies took pains to highlight. It’s critical to reiterate that effort isn’t the same thing as engagement: the mere existence of fake accounts or pages doesn’t mean that real people are paying attention to them. Similarly, just because a campaign uses AI does not mean it will sway public opinion. Generative AI reduces the cost of running propaganda campaigns, making it significantly cheaper to produce content and run interactive automated accounts. But it is not a magic bullet, and in the case of the operations that OpenAI disclosed, what was generated sometimes seemed to be rather spammy. Audiences didn’t bite.

Producing content, after all, is only the first step in a propaganda campaign; even the most convincing AI-generated posts, images, or audio still need to be distributed. Campaigns without algorithmic amplification or influencer pickup are often just tweeting into the void. Indeed, it is consistently authentic influencers—people who have the attention of large audiences enthusiastically resharing their posts—that receive engagement and drive the public conversation, helping content and narratives to go viral. This is why some of the more well-resourced adversaries, like China, simply surreptitiously hire those voices. At this point, influential real accounts have far more potential for impact than AI-powered fakes.

Nonetheless, there is a lot of concern that AI could disrupt American politics and become a national security threat. It’s important to “rightsize” that threat, particularly in an election year. Hyping the impact of disinformation campaigns can undermine trust in elections and faith in democracy by making the electorate believe that there are trolls behind every post, or that the mere targeting of a candidate by a malign actor, even with a very poorly executed campaign, “caused” their loss. 

By putting an assessment of impact front and center in its first report, OpenAI is clearly taking the risk of exaggerating the threat seriously. And yet, diminishing the threat or not fielding integrity teams—letting trolls simply continue to grow their followings and improve their distribution capability—would also be a bad approach. Indeed, the Meta report noted that one network it disrupted, seemingly connected to a political party in Bangladesh and targeting the Bangladeshi public, had amassed 3.4 million followers across 98 pages. Since that network was not run by an adversary of interest to Americans, it will likely get little attention. Still, this example highlights the fact that the threat is global, and vigilance is key. Platforms must continue to prioritize threat detection.

So what should we do about this? The Meta report’s call for threat sharing and collaboration, although specific to a Russian adversary, highlights a broader path forward for social media platforms, AI companies, and academic researchers alike. 

Transparency is paramount. As outside researchers, we can learn only so much from a social media company’s description of an operation it has taken down. This is true for the public and policymakers as well, and incredibly powerful platforms shouldn’t just be taken at their word. Ensuring researcher access to data about coordinated inauthentic networks offers an opportunity for outside validation (or refutation!) of a tech company’s claims. Before Musk’s takeover of Twitter, the company regularly released data sets of posts from inauthentic state-linked accounts to researchers, and even to the public. Meta shared data with external partners before it removed a network and, more recently, moved to a model of sharing content from already-removed networks through Meta’s Influence Operations Research Archive. While researchers should continue to push for more data, these efforts have allowed for a richer understanding of adversarial narratives and behaviors beyond what the platform’s own transparency report summaries provided.

OpenAI’s adversarial threat report should be a prelude to more robust data sharing moving forward. Where AI is concerned, independent researchers have begun to assemble databases of misuse—like the AI Incident Database and the Political Deepfakes Incident Database—to allow researchers to compare different types of misuse and track how misuse changes over time. But it is often hard to detect misuse from the outside. As AI tools become more capable and pervasive, it’s important that policymakers considering regulation understand how they are being used and abused. While OpenAI’s first report offered high-level summaries and select examples, expanding data-sharing relationships with researchers that provide more visibility into adversarial content or behaviors is an important next step. 

When it comes to combating influence operations and misuse of AI, online users also have a role to play. After all, this content has an impact only if people see it, believe it, and participate in sharing it further. In one of the cases OpenAI disclosed, online users called out fake accounts that used AI-generated text. 

In our own research, we’ve seen communities of Facebook users proactively call out AI-generated image content created by spammers and scammers, helping those who are less aware of the technology avoid falling prey to deception. A healthy dose of skepticism is increasingly useful: pausing to check whether content is real and people are who they claim to be, and helping friends and family members become more aware of the growing prevalence of generated content, can help social media users resist deception from propagandists and scammers alike.

OpenAI’s blog post announcing the takedown report put it succinctly: “Threat actors work across the internet.” So must we. As we move into an new era of AI-driven influence operations, we must address shared challenges via transparency, data sharing, and collaborative vigilance if we hope to develop a more resilient digital ecosystem.

Josh A. Goldstein is a research fellow at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET), where he works on the CyberAI Project. Renée DiResta is the research manager of the Stanford Internet Observatory and the author of Invisible Rulers: The People Who Turn Lies into Reality.

I’m not criticising, I’d like to offer you my perspective: there is culture, scientific and intellectual capital, and there is politics.

I’m saying this as a Russian, and as a person who, surprisingly, has a tiny bit of Persian in me (a grand-grand-grand mother as I’m told).

YOU HERITAGE IS also THIS ⏬
*don’t skim, let’s honour every name

I will start with ladies (because thanks to some of them and many others, today I can post online, and in any order)

- Maryam Mirzakhani (1977–2017)
A Stanford mathematics professor, the first woman and first Iranian to win the prestigious Fields Medal in 2014, the highest honour in mathematics.
- Shirin Ebadi (b. 1947)
A lawyer, former judge, and human rights activist who became the first Iranian and first Muslim woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize in 2003.
- Anousheh Ansari (b. 1966)
An engineer and entrepreneur who became the first Iranian in space and the first self-funded woman to fly to the International Space Station in 2006.
- Narges Mohammadi (b. 1972): 
A human rights advocate and journalist awarded the 2023 Nobel Peace Prize for her work campaigning for women's rights and freedom in Iran.
- Rabi'a Balkhi (10th century) Widely considered the first known female poet in the history of New Persian literature, famous for her passionate love poetry.
- Simin Daneshvar (1921–2012) Iran's first major female novelist, best known for Savushun, a landmark work of modern Persian fiction.
- Tahereh Qorrat ol-Eyn (1814–1852)
An influential poet, theologian, and early advocate for women’s rights who famously unveiled herself at a public gathering in 1848.
- Parvin E'tesami (1907–1941): 
One of Iran's most celebrated classical-style poets, known for her moral fables (monazereh) exploring social justice and human nature.
- Forugh Farrokhzad (1934–1967): 
A trailblazing modernist poet and filmmaker whose candid, emotional works revolutionized contemporary Persian poetry. 
- Pourandokht / Boran (r. 630–631 CE):
The first female monarch to rule the Sasanian Empire in her own right, noted for efforts to stabilize the empire and restore peace with the Byzantine Empire. 
- Apranik (7th century CE): A Sasanian military commander who led resistance forces against the Arab invasion following the fall of the empire.
Living by the motto "no retreat, no surrender," she continued leading the resistance until she was killed in combat.

Continuing with men:

A physician and philosopher whose Canon of Medicine served as a standard medical textbook in Europe and the Islamic world for centuries.

A pioneering physician and alchemist who wrote the first clinical descriptions distinguishing smallpox from measles and discovered compounds like sulfuric acid and distilled alcohol.

A polymath who accurately calculated the Earth's radius using trigonometry and wrote extensively on physics, astronomy, and comparative anthropology.

An astronomer and mathematician who established the Maragheh observatory and developed the "Tusi couple," a geometric device later used in Copernicus's heliocentric model.

text:
Comparing Jerry Yang (Yahoo) and Elon Musk (PayPal, Tesla, SpaceX) side-by-side presents a stark contrast in business history: the "bookish tech founder" versus the "first-principles-based businessman."

Both were penny-pinchers who missed opportunities when they should have bought:

In 1998, Google offered only $1 million: Larry Page and Sergey Brin were still in a Stanford garage. For a fraction of that, Yahoo could have secured the next-generation gateway to its platform by acquiring the search algorithm. Instead, Yahoo, focused on monetizing its user base through advertising, refused, thus nurturing the behemoth that would later devour it.

In 2006, Facebook was willing to sell for $1 billion. Zuckerberg had already agreed, but Yahoo, at the last minute, due to a slight drop in its stock price and a desire to cut the $150 million difference (slashing the price down to $850 million), derailed the entire deal—saving a small $150 million but losing the entire trillion-dollar social media empire.

Selling based on emotion when it should have, missing the peak cash-out opportunity:

In 2008, Microsoft offered a staggering $44.6 billion (a premium of over 60%) to acquire Yahoo. At that time, Yahoo's search and advertising were clearly lagging behind Google, and Microsoft was practically throwing money at the problem to save it. However, Jerry Yang, deeply attached to the company he founded and believing "Yahoo's value was much greater," resolutely refused.

By 2016-2017, Verizon had acquired its core business for a mere $4.48 billion, a move seen as a clearance sale, resulting in a staggering 90% drop in market value (over $40 billion)!

In contrast, Elon Musk never treats a company as an "emotional burden he can't let go of," but rather as a "carrier of capital and technology":

In his younger days, with Zip2 and PayPal, he would decisively cash out and exit as soon as the price reached his reasonable return on investment or could secure the necessary funds for a larger, more competitive market.

With the real money in hand, he would then invest it all in truly disruptive sectors (rocketry, electric vehicles, energy, AI), maintaining a firm grip on control from day one.
