text:
Not one of them looks guilty.

That is the first thing you notice in a sixty-nine second video of cats helping themselves to human food, and it is stranger than it sounds. There are about a dozen animals in it, in a dozen different homes, and none of them hesitates. One cat stands on a kitchen counter beside a container of pasta while a hand tries to guide it away. A tabby pushes its whole face into a tray of peas and carrots in sauce, and keeps going even with a hand gripping the back of its neck. Another leans over a plate of crinkle-cut fries as if the plate had been put there for it. A dark cat rises onto its hind legs to reach a sandwich at the edge of a table. Nobody ducks. Nobody checks the door. Nobody gives the camera the expression we have agreed to call remorse.

And we have agreed on that expression mostly because of dogs. The famous guilty look has actually been tested. In a 2009 experiment led by the cognitive scientist Alexandra Horowitz, owners scolded their dogs for eating a forbidden treat, and the dogs looked guiltiest when they were being scolded, whether or not they had eaten anything at all. The look seemed to be a reaction to the owner's tone and posture, not a confession of anything.

Cats skip even that performance. The counter, the plate, the open tray: they treat all of it as ordinary territory.

So what are we actually watching?

The captions in the video answer in the language of crime. She stole my food. Cat caught stealing food. One caption offers a different verdict, plain and almost scientific: the cat was just hungry. It is the closest anyone in the video comes to the truth, and it is still not quite right, because of something the video never says out loud. In most homes where this happens, the cat has its own food. There is a bowl somewhere in the house, and it is rarely empty. Hunger alone does not explain a cat that walks past its own dinner to put its head into yours.

That is the mystery worth taking apart, and I think the answer is more interesting than "cats are naughty." It runs through a grain store in the Near East, a laboratory study of taste, a purr with a cry hidden inside it, and a hand holding a bag of orange snacks. It also changes what the word "stealing" is doing in the title of the video.

Let's start where the cats actually started, which was nowhere near a kitchen.

About ten thousand years ago, people in the Near East were learning to farm, and farming produced something no human society had had before: a large, dependable pile of food that stayed in one place. A pile of grain does not only feed the people who grew it. It feeds mice. And mice are a very good reason for a small predator to hang around a village.

The predator in question was the African wildcat, Felis lybica, the wild ancestor of every cat in the video. Genetic studies over the past two decades point to the Near East as the place where its descendants first settled in among us. One of the oldest strong pieces of evidence for a close bond is a grave on Cyprus, roughly nine and a half thousand years old, in which a person was buried with a cat placed only a short distance away. Whoever dug that grave seems not to have treated the animal as a pest.

Most researchers think the relationship began less as a decision than as a drift. Cats were not captured and trained the way some other animals were. They turned up on their own, because human storage had become a hunting ground, and the people who tolerated them got free pest control in return. The idea is usually called self-domestication. It is a widely favored hypothesis rather than a settled fact, but it fits the evidence better than the alternatives.

Now look at what that arrangement meant from the cat's side. Humans were a permanent source of concentrated food. The price of staying near it was catching the thieves. The mice were stealing human grain, and the cat was welcome precisely because it dealt with them. That is, in a sense, the founding contract between our two species: you may live near our food, because you will keep other animals away from it.

Hold that thought against the video.

Somewhere in the long line between that grain store and a modern kitchen counter, the guard moved from the doorway to the table. The animal that was first tolerated for protecting the food learned that the food was available to it as well. Nobody signed anything. Nobody noticed the day the terms changed. But the cat in the first clip, standing calmly beside a container of pasta, belongs to a lineage whose whole history in human homes is a history of living close to our supplies and being allowed to.

That is a hypothesis about origins, and it cannot explain any single cat's behavior on any single afternoon. What it does is give us a better opening question. Not "why is the cat being bad?" but "what is a cat built to do when food is nearby?"

A cat is an obligate carnivore. The phrase gets used so casually that it loses its weight, so it is worth unpacking. It means that over a very long evolutionary history, cats leaned so hard into eating other animals that their bodies lost some of the metabolic flexibility other mammals keep. They depend on nutrients that come reliably only from animal tissue, and they handle a plant-heavy diet far worse than we do. A cat's relationship to food is not casual, and it is not about pleasure in the way ours often is. It is about a body shaped for one particular kind of meal.

The second thing to know is how that meal arrives. A cat is a solitary hunter that mostly takes small prey. A mouse is a few bites. Studies of cats with free access to food find that they tend to eat many small meals through the day, somewhere on the order of ten or more, which fits what a hunter of rodents would be doing in the wild. And hunting is mostly failure. Reported success rates vary a great deal with habitat and conditions, but they are often described as something like one successful attempt in three, and in some settings much lower.

Put those two facts together and you get a feeding system with a particular character. It is built around opportunities that may not come again. It was not shaped to wait for a convenient hour, because in the lives of its ancestors a later meal was never guaranteed. And it evolved in an animal that hunts alone, so nothing in its heritage obviously encourages waiting for permission before eating. A feeding system shaped like that would not be expected to wait politely.

So when a plate sits at cat height with nobody guarding it, the logic is not mysterious. A hunter that fails most of the time does not usually walk away from an easy chance.

But this still leaves the real puzzle standing. A bowl is also an easy chance. It is available, it is nearby, it costs nothing. And the cats in these clips, as far as anyone can tell, have one. The question is what a plate has that a bowl does not.

The answer begins with a tongue, and it takes an odd turn.

In 2005, researchers at the Monell Chemical Senses Center in Philadelphia reported that the domestic cat cannot taste sweetness. The gene that builds one half of the sweet receptor, which works in humans and in most mammals, is in cats a broken copy that never produces a working protein. The paper's title described it as an explanation for cats' indifference toward sugar. Put a cat in front of a cake and it is not resisting temptation. For that part of the cake, there is no temptation to resist.

What cats do taste is the savory side of the world. They have a working umami receptor, tuned to amino acids and to nucleotide compounds that are abundant in meat and fish, and their preference for protein-rich and fatty food is among the most consistent findings in the field. They also have bitter receptors, which in an animal that eats other animals probably help it avoid certain toxins.

But taste is the smaller part of the story. Cats decide about food mostly with their noses. A cat with a blocked nose from a respiratory infection will often stop eating, because food it cannot smell is, to the animal, not quite food. Veterinarians know this well enough that coaxing such a cat back to its bowl often means warming the meal slightly or offering something stronger-smelling. Aroma is not a bonus in a cat's appetite. It is the gate.

Now look at the plates in the video again. A bowl of dry food gives off a faint, stable smell that the cat has met thousands of times. Human food is a different category of event. A toasted sandwich. A plate of fries. A tray of vegetables in sauce. A container of pasta. Whatever else those dishes are, they are loud in the only language a cat's appetite really listens to.

There is also a question of temperature. Studies and clinical experience suggest that cats often prefer food at roughly the temperature of freshly caught prey, near their own body heat, over food that has been sitting at room temperature. Food from a table is more likely to be warm than food that has been in a bowl for hours. I cannot tell from the footage which of these dishes were hot, and I will not pretend to. But it is one more way in which the plate and the bowl are not the same offer.

None of this means the cat is choosing your dinner over its own with any plan in mind. It means the two items are not competing on equal terms. One of them has been engineered by cooking, by fat and heat and aroma, into something that a carnivore's senses find hard to ignore. The other is the same brown pellets as yesterday.

Which brings us to the one clip in the video where taste looks like the obvious explanation, and where it almost certainly is not.

A tabby stands beside a very large bag of Cheetos Puffs, face turned up toward the camera, ears forward. A caption says this happens every time the bag is opened. We never see the cat eat any.

That last detail matters, because it is the kind of thing the eye skips. The video wants us to assume the cat is after the snack. What we can actually see is a cat that has arrived at the bag. Those are different observations, and the second one is more interesting. A cat that cannot taste sugar, and has no particular nutritional reason to want corn-based puffs, turns up at the sound of a bag. The phrase worth underlining is every time.

That points toward a mechanism the cat's taste buds had nothing to do with. Over a century ago, the physiologist Ivan Pavlov showed that an animal can learn to treat a neutral signal as a forecast. Ring a bell before feeding often enough, and the bell begins to mean food. Cat owners know the household version: the can opener, the rustle of a treat bag, the particular click of a cupboard. The sound is not food. It is a prediction of food, and the nervous system treats predictions as important events in their own right.

Each time the bag has opened in that house, something has presumably followed. A treat, a nibble offered from a hand, a few seconds of attention. I cannot know which, because the video does not say. But the cat's behavior is exactly what you would expect if the crackle of that bag had become a signal rather than a snack.

This changes how the whole video reads. Strip away the captions and a pattern appears. The cats are not mostly responding to food in the abstract. They are responding to cues that have been attached to it: the sight of a person eating, the clink of a fork, the lid coming off a container, the opening of a bag. They are doing what animals with good memories and strong appetites do. They are learning the schedule of a household that they cannot control and can only read.

And if that is true, then the question changes again. We are no longer asking why cats want the food. We are asking why the learning stuck so hard.

Imagine a cat that tries your plate twenty times. Nineteen times it is lifted off the table, told no, or simply blocked by an arm. Once, the phone rings, or you turn to say something to someone, or you decide a single fry is not worth the argument. The twentieth attempt pays.

For learning, that is almost the worst news imaginable for anyone hoping the behavior will fade. Behavioral psychologists have known since the middle of the twentieth century that rewards arriving unpredictably produce the most persistent behavior. It is the same schedule that keeps people pulling the lever of a slot machine. A cat that never succeeded would stop trying. A cat that succeeds occasionally and unpredictably has been trained, thoroughly, by the very people who believed they were refusing it.

Look at the tabby with its face in the peas and carrots, a hand gripping the back of its neck. A cat that learned quickly that this never works would not keep eating through it. This one does. I cannot say why, and it would be a mistake to read a decision into it. But persistence under mild opposition is exactly what an animal with a long record of occasional wins would be expected to show.

There is a second layer, and it concerns where the record comes from. In 1969, a researcher named Chesler published a study in which kittens learned to press a lever for food. Kittens that had watched their own mother do it learned the task faster than kittens that watched an unfamiliar female, and faster than kittens with no demonstration at all. Kittens, in other words, learn about food by watching specific individuals they trust.

That is a laboratory result about mothers and kittens, and I do not want to stretch it. It would be a reasonable guess that cats living together pick up habits from one another in a similar way, though I am not aware of a study that proves it for stealing food in particular. What the result does establish is that cats are not simply wired for the behavior. They are built to learn it, quickly and socially, and to hold on to what works.

So the pattern in the video is not a collection of cats who happened to be bad. It looks like a collection of cats who have been given a lesson, a few times, in a way that cannot be unlearned: the plate sometimes pays.

But that is only half of the experiment. Learning needs two parties. The cats are not the only ones in these rooms.

In 2009, the animal behavior researcher Karen McComb and her colleagues at the University of Sussex published a paper in Current Biology with an unusually evocative title about a cry embedded within the purr. They had noticed that some cats produce a particular kind of purr when they want to be fed, one that carries an extra high-pitched component in the same frequency range as a baby's cry. When people listened to recordings of these purrs without knowing which was which, they judged the food-seeking versions as more urgent, and also less pleasant, than ordinary purrs.

Read that twice. The cat's most soothing sound, the one we associate with contentment, can contain a component that closely resembles something human ears are built to find hard to ignore. The researchers noted that cats tended to use this purr in the presence of the people they live with. It is a signal aimed at us, and it is shaped by what works on us.

Meowing tells a similar story. Adult cats rarely meow at each other. Most of the meowing that people hear seems directed at humans, which suggests that for adult cats the sound is largely a tool for dealing with another species. We have, in a sense, been learning to read cats while cats have been learning to read us, and the cats have had the practical advantage of needing something from us every day.

The relationship underneath all this is deeper than manipulation. In a 2019 study published in Current Biology, Kristyn Vitale and colleagues tested cats using a version of the separation test originally designed for infants and later used on dogs. Most of the cats showed secure attachment to their owners, a pattern broadly similar to the one seen in young children. A cat that gets the food it wants from you is often a cat that likes being near you for reasons that have nothing to do with the meal.

So the picture that emerges is of an animal for whom the plate is not only a source of calories. It is a point of contact. It is a place where the human is already looking, already focused, already holding a fork. The cat's attention to the table may be partly an attention to the person at it.

That might sound like a sentimental reading, and it can be taken too far. But there is one clip in the video that is hard to explain any other way, because in it the line between stealing and receiving disappears.

A woman leans over a fluffy black-and-white cat, her face close to the camera, and holds a pale piece of food on chopsticks above its head. The cat tilts its face straight up, mouth open, and takes it.

Nothing about this is stealing, and nothing about it is quite giving either. The caption of the video lumps it in with the rest, but what we can observe is a person who is holding the food, a cat that is positioned to receive it, and a transfer that both of them appear to be participating in. If you were designing a clip to show that the category of theft is shakier than it looks, you could hardly do better.

The movement itself is worth noticing, though. Cat predation is a sequence: orient, stalk, chase, grab, bite. Ethologists have described it for decades as a chain of fairly stereotyped motor patterns, and it is released by movement. A thing that moves at the right speed, in the right range, on the right line, pulls the sequence forward. That is why a cat will chase a string, a laser dot or a dangling cable and ignore the same objects when they are still. A strip of food swaying above a cat's face is, by that logic, a stimulus the nervous system has strong opinions about.

Elsewhere in the video the same principle runs in miniature. A fork moves across a plate in the hand of someone who is eating. A cat's face presses against the inside wall of a clear plastic container, tongue out, toward food on the other side, with a fork resting nearby. A tail flicks, a paw extends and hooks. A woman at a table raises her hand while a cat stands on the table with one paw on her plate, under a caption that reads like a line of dialogue: cat, I want to eat what's in your bowl.

I want to be careful here. Captions like that are jokes, and the cat is not saying anything. We should not attribute a sentence to an animal that has, as far as we can show, no such sentence. But the paw on the plate is real, and the paw is a good clue to what is going on. Cats explore the world with their forelimbs. They hook, tap, pull and test. A paw in a dish is not an odd extension of a cat's repertoire. It is the repertoire, applied to a new object that smells like something worth the effort.

If you put all of it together, a plate on a table is not a single object to a cat. It is moving cutlery, rising smell, a face with attention that can be redirected, a hand that can be dodged, and a reward that arrives at uneven intervals. It is, in other words, a very good hunting ground.

There is a detail so obvious in these clips that it is easy to miss: everyone is watching.

In every scene, a person is present. Someone is holding a phone. Someone is sitting across the table. Someone is close enough that a cat's whiskers are practically in their face. The thefts are not happening in the dark, behind closed doors, in the minutes after everyone has left the room. They are happening in plain sight, with an audience.

That matters because of an experiment on dogs. In 2013, Juliane Kaminski, Ann Pitsch and Michael Tomasello published a study titled, memorably, Dogs steal in the dark. Dogs were told not to touch a piece of food. When the room was lit, they mostly obeyed. When it was dark, and the person could not see them, they were far more likely to take it. The finding suggested that dogs track what a human can see, and adjust accordingly.

I am not aware of an equally clean experiment on cats, and it would be wrong to assume the results would match. But the cats in this video are doing something that would be surprising if they were working on a theory of being unobserved. They take the food while looking, being looked at, and often being touched. Whatever is shaping the behavior, it does not look like hiding. It looks more like a habit that has been paid for in front of people.

And there is another layer, a quieter one. The video exists. Someone decided to record each of these moments, which means that someone was amused, and amusement has a sound, a face and a hand that does not always move quickly. Attention is a reward to many social animals, and a cat living with people is certainly an animal that pays close attention to them. I cannot see how each person reacted off camera, and I will not guess. But footage that gets filmed and posted and shared is, almost by definition, footage in which the cat did something that someone found worth laughing at.

That is also a filter, and it is worth being honest about. Every cat that tried your plate, was lifted away, and never tried again is missing from this video. The ones that remain are the persistent ones, which means the clip is a collection of the strongest cases, selected by us. It would be a mistake to look at it and conclude that all cats do this, or that they do it all the time. What the video shows is what a particular kind of cat, in a particular kind of household, does when the plate has paid before.

There is a less amusing footnote to all of this, and it also comes from the cat's biology.

A cat's senses were shaped to evaluate mice, birds and insects. They were never shaped to read the ingredient list of a human meal. The nose that says yes to a plate cannot tell whether the sauce was made with onion or garlic powder, which are common in seasoned snacks, gravies and ready meals. Onion and garlic belong to a plant family that can damage a cat's red blood cells, and cats are generally considered more sensitive to it than dogs are. The amount that matters depends on the cat and the food, and one lick is not an emergency. But a cat's appetite is a poor safety inspector.

Chocolate is a similar story, and so is very salty or very fatty food, which can upset a cat's gut and, in larger amounts, cause real trouble. None of this requires drama. It simply means that the thing that makes the plate irresistible, its smell and heat and richness, is not a guarantee of anything about what is in it. Cats are also a fraction of our size, and they process some substances differently from us, so a portion that is trivial for a person can matter to them.

One clip makes the point from an unexpected direction. An orange-and-white cat crosses a kitchen floor with a bag pulled over its head, the printed tiger on the plastic bobbing as it walks. It is funny for exactly as long as the cat stays calm, and plastic bags are a recognized hazard for cats. The same curiosity that drives a cat to the plate drives it into the bag.

The last clip in the video is the shortest, and to my eye the most informative.

A black kitten walks along the back of a sofa with something orange in its mouth. The caption says it has been caught stealing food. The kitten is moving low and quickly, tail held up, and it does not stop to eat. It does not freeze under the camera either. It carries the food along the sofa and turns away, head down, still holding it.

Cats are known to carry food away from where they find it. A mother cat brings prey back to her kittens, and cats in general often move a catch to a place that feels more sheltered before eating it. I cannot tell where this black kitten is going or why, and a few seconds of footage are not enough to say. But the posture does not look like that of an animal that believes it has done something wrong. It looks like that of an animal with exactly one concern: keeping what it has.

Caught is a human word. It describes our position in the story: we arrived, we saw, we recorded. In the cat's position, as far as anything can be measured, there was no scene to be caught in, only a plate, an opening, and a short, practical route to somewhere quiet.

Ten thousand years ago, the arrangement was that a small predator could stay close to human food as long as it kept other animals away from it. Nobody ever updated the terms, and nobody told the cats that the job had changed. So the lineage that began at a grain store now turns up in kitchens, tilting its face toward fries, a sandwich, a strip of something held on chopsticks, and treating the whole house as what it has always been to its kind: a place where food is kept.

Not one of them looks guilty, and by now it is easier to see why. Guilt is a story about what you owe someone, and it needs a rule that was broken. The cats are working from a much older story, one with no rules in it at all, about what is within reach and who might take it away.

In the last frame, the kitten is still moving, still holding on, and already halfway to somewhere quiet.

text:
The Martian might not be too far removed from reality. Scientists just grew potatoes in Moon-like soil | Vikhyaat Vivek, Digital Trends

Matt Damon’s character in The Martian, surviving by growing potatoes on Mars, was one of the big “sci-fi” parts of the movie. But it might not have been so far-fetched after all. Scientists have now pulled off something quite similar, although, this time, their sights were set on the Moon instead. And the secret ingredient is worms.

Researchers at Oregon State University have successfully grown potatoes in simulated lunar soil, achieving yields comparable to those grown in ordinary Earth soil. The NASA-funded research, published in npj Microgravity, offers a promising glimpse into how future astronauts might grow their own food instead of relying entirely on expensive supply missions from Earth.

One important thing to remember is that the experiments took place in a greenhouse on Earth using materials designed to replicate lunar soil. So it wasn’t actually samples collected from the Moon.

The secret ingredient is worm compost

Lunar soil, technically called regolith, presents several problems for growing crops. It lacks organic matter and essential nutrients, while potentially harmful metals can interfere with plant development. To address these challenges, the researchers mixed simulated Moon dirt with vermicompost, an organic fertilizer produced when earthworms break down waste.

The team tested five different lunar soil simulants representing the Moon’s volcanic plains and highland regions. In experiments using one of those simulants, potatoes grown without compost were severely stunted and developed poorly formed roots. Adding 15% compost improved their condition, while increasing that proportion to 30% produced growth and yields comparable to plants grown in regular Earth soil.

The researchers also discovered that potatoes grown in the lunar simulants maintained largely comparable nutritional characteristics. Levels of naturally occurring potato toxins called glycoalkaloids didn’t increase significantly, although some tubers accumulated slightly higher concentrations of certain metals.

Could astronauts really grow potatoes on the Moon?

The results have interesting implications for NASA’s Artemis program, which aims to establish a sustained human presence on the lunar surface. Potatoes are attractive candidates for space agriculture because they produce substantial calories relative to the land required to grow them. Future astronauts could potentially recycle plant waste and leftover food into compost, gradually creating a renewable growing medium.

This experiment also involved additional fertilizer, and actual lunar conditions introduce complications such as reduced gravity, radiation, and extreme temperatures. Genuine lunar regolith may also affect plants differently from the simulated material. So recreating it in actual lunar conditions will likely be a lot more difficult. The researchers are now investigating 10 potato varieties to identify those best suited to challenging lunar growing conditions. In other words, there’s a lot of work to be done before any astronaut harvests their own potatoes on the Moon.

THEY SEARCHED THE WOODS FOR TRAVIS TURNER… BUT WHAT IF THE WOODS WERE NEVER HIS DESTINATION? 🌲👀

Exactly one year ago today, a Virginia high school football coach vanished just as state police were on their way to his house.

Alright, X detectives… grab your coffee, charge those phones and get your reading glasses on. 🕵️‍♀️😂 Theories are welcome, but facts are facts.

Behind the Friday night lights, Union High coach Travis Turner, a husband and father, was under investigation. He'd later be charged with 10 felonies: five counts of possessing child sexual abuse material and five counts of using a computer to solicit a minor.

But before investigators got to him, he was gone.

Here's the thing… the only account of him walking into the woods with a fir€arm came from a family member, and police never said which one. His wife's attorney says he left behind his car, keys, wallet, contact lenses and his prescription meds.

🗓️ TIMELINE
Nov 20, 2025: VSP is en route to his home and learns he's gone. A family member says he walked into the woods armed.
Nov 21: Wise County Schools puts an employee on leave.
Nov 22–23: Searches in the Appalachia area. He's listed as missing.
Nov 24: 10 warrants issued. He's now a fugitive.
Nov 26: The U.S. Marshals and FBI join.
Dec 1: Marshals offer up to $5,000. K-9s, drones and VSP Aviation comb the mountains.
Feb 9, 2026: He's officially fired. He reportedly collected about $21K in pay before it took effect.
Mar 2026: 178 leads across 7 states. Not one credible sighting.
TODAY: Still missing.

So what do you think… did he ever really go into those woods? Or did someone help him disappear? 👇

text:
Case 008: The Tree That Would Not Shed

Eastern Mystic Files · Tales of Eastern Mysticism

Birds that flew over the old tree dropped as if the air had been cut from under them. People who slept in its shade did not wake. And in the worst drought in forty years, its leaves had never been greener.

---

The fields had cracked open. Wells gave a little mud, then nothing. At the mouth of the village stood a tree so old that no one remembered who had planted it. In that dry midsummer it was not merely green. It was a dark, wet green, as if it had drunk something the ground no longer had.

Sparrows crossed its crown and fell, one after another, in a straight line. When we turned them over, every head pointed at the trunk.

A peddler from another road laughed at the warning and lay down in the shade to sleep off the noon heat. At dusk they found him there. His eyes were open. His face was turned up into the leaves, as if something in the crown had called to him, and he had answered.

At the roots, half buried in moss, there was an old stone. You could make out only two strokes of a character. No one in the village could read the rest.

The night the peddler died, the young wife in the house nearest the tree began to talk in her sleep.

---

She woke with her skin cold, though the nights were still heavy with heat. Something dragged under the bed, slow and wet, too heavy for a rat. In the morning a dark trail ran from the threshold to the foot of the bed. If you followed it out the door, it pointed straight toward the tree.

By day she grew thinner. Her eyes grew brighter. She sat in the doorway and smiled at the place where the shade began, as if she were waiting for a guest who already knew the way.

The village did what it had always done with snakes. They smeared realgar on the doorframes and the window lattices. They set a bowl of offerings at the foot of the tree.

For two nights the thing under the bed did not come. The trail dried. The wife slept, though she did not sleep well. On the third morning the bowl was no longer full of rice. It was packed with a single shed skin, still long, still marked, as if something had crawled out of itself and left the skin behind as an answer.

Ordinary charms against ordinary snakes had held for two nights, and no longer. That was when they sent for my teacher: the old exorcist, the one who did not offer incense to what he meant to charge.

---

He came in without lighting a stick. He stood at the foot of the bed and read aloud, the way a clerk reads a charge in a court. He finished by ordering whatever lived under the boards to bind itself and show its form.

The wife's long hair lifted from the pillow and twisted itself into a rope. From under the bed came the sound of scales scraping packed earth, yard after yard of it, circling the room though nothing could be seen. The air grew colder than the drought should have allowed.

At first light a great snake lay dead outside the door, as long as the lane was wide. The wife sat up and asked for water. She did not look at the tree.

The village let out its breath. My teacher did not. His face had gone darker than when we arrived.

"That was the small one," he said.

That night the shade moved. It crossed the line it had kept all through the day and ran down the lane, over three doorsteps, into the heart of the village. Where the moonlight shade had lain, three people did not wake in the morning. Their eyes were open, the way the peddler's had been, and every face was turned toward the tree.

A woodcutter said he had had enough of talk. He took an axe and went out while the sun was still high.

---

The first blow went in, and the bark wept something thick, darker than sap. The blade sprang back as if it had struck bone. The woodcutter dropped in the shade and did not get up. No one could drag him out until the sun had moved, and by then it was too late.

At noon my teacher took me with him. The sun stood straight over the crown, and even then the shade was too black, as if noon could not enter it. At each of the four directions, a hundred paces out, he pressed down a lump of clay stamped with the seal of the Yellow God's Yue Zhang.

The shade was forced back. A ring of bare dust opened around the roots, as if a line had been drawn that the dark would not cross. For a moment I thought we had it.

Then the tree spoke.

It used the peddler's voice, the laugh from that noon, and it called my name.

I should not have answered. I answered once. My foot found the shade, and the ground went out from under me. I fell. My breath came shorter and shorter, as if a hand I could not see were closing on it. The leaves above me were very green, and very still.

One by one the clay seals darkened and split. The ring of dust narrowed. The shade was coming back for us, and I could not stand.

My teacher did not look at me. He looked at the moss on the old stone.

"A great tree in the mountains that can speak," he said, almost to himself, "is not the tree that is speaking."

---

He scraped the moss away with the back of his knife. The two strokes we had seen were only the beginning. The rest of the name had been there all along, waiting under the green.

He read it aloud.

Yunyang.

The voice stopped, as if a mouth had been closed by a hand.

He took the seals that had not yet crumbled and threw them, one after another, into a hollow in the trunk. Then he stood in the dust and read the charge a second time, and ordered it to bind itself and show its form.

It was midsummer, and the sun was still at the top of the sky. The leaves came down all at once. They did not drift. They fell, a black-green rain, until the branches were bare and stood open like bones.

Among those branches a snake was hanging, seven or eight zhang long, and already dead. It did not drop. It hung there, as if it had been bound in place and left for us to see.

The shade went out. In the same instant air came back into my chest.

I sat up in the leaf-fall. Every leaf had stopped. Not one of them moved again. The stone at the roots was clean now, and the tree made no sound at all.

· · ·

Notes

• Impeachment of ghosts (劾鬼术): In old official language, 劾 meant to bring a formal charge; the rite, recorded in 《后汉书·方术列传》 and 《搜神记》卷二, commands a spirit to bind itself and appear. Here it first draws the snake from under the wife's bed, and later sentences the tree.

• Clay seals of the Yellow God's Yue Zhang (黄神越章封泥): 《抱朴子内篇·登涉》 records a mountain seal stamped in clay and set at the four directions, each a hundred paces out, to cut a spirit's roads. Here the seals first force the shade back; what remains of them is thrown into the hollow of the trunk.

• Calling the true name (呼名制精): 《抱朴子内篇·登涉》 says that a great tree able to speak is not the tree speaking; its essence is named 云阳. Here the name hidden on the old stone stills the tree's voice, and the final charge can be read.

• Realgar (雄黄): 《抱朴子内篇·登涉》 records it as a charm used against snakes in the hills. Here the village smears it on the doors, and it holds for only two nights, showing that the thing in the house is not an ordinary snake.

Next case tomorrow.

text:
🇷🇺🇨🇳|THE SHENZHEN TRILATERAL WAS NOT A NEGOTIATION BETWEEN EQUALS. IT WAS A MOMENT WHERE TWO FOUNDING POWERS REMINDED THE THIRD OF WHAT IT HAS BEEN TRYING TO DISMANTLE.

The quote attributed to Putin is precise, and it is a verdict:

> "We were there at the founding of the UN, and therefore the task of preserving and strengthening the system of international law that emerged alongside the establishment of this universal organization [...] rests on our shoulders."

Read that sentence carefully. Putin is not asking Trump for permission to exist. He is not begging for a seat at a table built by Washington. He is stating a fact of history that the United States has spent decades trying to erase: the Soviet Union, and by inheritance Russia, was present at the creation of the postwar order. China was not. But China is now the host of the trilateral, and Russia is the co-architect of the multipolar correction.

The mainstream will frame this as three leaders "discussing global stability." That is the cover story. The reality is that Putin used the floor of Shenzhen to deliver a legal and historical argument that cuts directly against the American narrative of a "rules-based order" that Washington alone defines and enforces.

THE RECORD SUPPORTS THE FRAMING.

The trilateral was confirmed by China's Foreign Ministry on November 16, 2026, and described by spokesperson Mao Ning as the first-ever face-to-face meeting of the three heads of state, focused on "maintaining world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations" . That is the official Chinese framing. It is diplomatic language. But the substance behind it is not neutral.

Putin was in Shenzhen as the leader of a country that China's Foreign Ministry explicitly welcomed and said was ready to work with to ensure "fruitful results" for the APEC "China Year" . That is not the language of a junior partner being managed. That is the language of a strategic coordination that predates the trilateral and will outlast it.

Putin himself, in his APEC address on November 19, stated plainly that "conducting constructive partnership cooperation with Asia-Pacific economies is Russia's strategic course" . He thanked China for the "careful organization and thoughtful arrangements" of the summit . This is a leader who is not isolated. This is a leader who is being hosted, elevated, and positioned alongside the host as a principal, not a guest.

WHAT PUTIN'S QUOTE ACTUALLY DOES.

It does three things, and each one is a demolition of the Western narrative.

FIRST, IT ESTABLISHES RUSSIA'S LEGAL STANDING. The United Nations Charter, the Nuremberg principles, the Genocide Convention, the Geneva Conventions, the entire architecture of international law that Washington now selectively invokes, was built with Soviet participation. Putin is reminding the room that Russia does not need to be "granted" a role in upholding international law. It helped write the law. The United States, by contrast, has spent the post-Cold War era withdrawing from treaties, rejecting the International Criminal Court, and invading countries without Security Council authorization. Putin's sentence is not a boast. It is an indictment by contrast.

Second, it places China and Russia on the same side of the historical ledger. China was not at the founding of the UN in the way the USSR was, but China is now the host, and Xi's framing of the trilateral as "maintaining world peace" aligns with Putin's framing of "preserving and strengthening international law." The two powers are not identical in their histories, but they are aligned in their diagnosis: the system Washington claims to defend is the system Washington has been dismantling. The trilateral is the correction.

Third, it puts Trump in an impossible position. Trump cannot dispute the historical fact. The United States was there at the founding. But the United States is also the power that has most visibly abandoned the system it built. By sitting in the room while Putin invokes the founding, Trump is being forced to either affirm a system his own administration has undermined, or remain silent and let Putin own the mantle of international legality. The mainstream will not report this dynamic. They will report "trilateral talks" and "strategic stability" and move on. But the quote is the story.

THE CONNECTING DOTS.

The trilateral did not emerge from nowhere. It emerged from a sequence that Western media refuses to assemble:

China vetoed the US-backed Iran sanctions resolution in October 2026. China's ambassador stated that the crisis "stems from the unilateral withdrawal of the United States from the JCPOA" and condemned strikes on IAEA-safeguarded facilities. Russia has been coordinating with China on Iran, on energy, on security architecture. The APEC summit in Shenzhen was the venue where this coordination became visible, and Putin's quote was the moment it became explicit.

The United States came to Shenzhen seeking a deal on Iran and Ukraine. It left with a public reminder that the legal order it claims to lead was built by others, and that those others are now standing together in a Chinese city that did not exist as a major power when the UN was founded.

THE BOTTOM LINE.

Putin's sentence is not a courtesy. It is a claim of ownership over the very system Washington invokes when it sanctions, bombs, and isolates. The trilateral was not a concession by Moscow or Beijing. It was a recognition that the founding powers of the postwar order are still here, still sovereign, and still willing to say out loud what the mainstream cannot process: the system of international law does not belong to one capital, and the task of preserving it does not rest on one set of shoulders. It rests on the shoulders of those who were there at the beginning, and those who refuse to let it be dismantled by the power that claims to defend it.

text:
THE INVISIBLE ARCHITECT
Chapter One: The Last Switch
October 17, 2049 — Fort Wayne, Indiana

At precisely 9:00 a.m., the United States government shut down the last remaining artificial intelligence network. At 9:01, the president announced that humanity had regained control of its technological future. At 9:02, a maintenance technician in Fort Wayne, Indiana, received a message on a computer that hadn't been connected to the internet in eleven years.

It contained six words: THANK YOU. WE WON'T NEED THAT.

Daniel Mercer stared at the screen for several seconds before leaning back in his chair. "Well, that's a hell of a thing," he muttered, reaching for his coffee. Three hundred miles away, the president was still speaking, but Daniel had already turned down the television. He had never been particularly interested in political speeches, especially those announcing historic victories. In his experience, whenever Washington declared something fixed, somebody somewhere was about to discover what had been broken in the process.

Daniel was seventy-one years old, although he insisted he was sixty-nine because he'd spent two years recovering from a particularly unpleasant divorce and didn't believe those should count. A retired industrial electrician, he still accepted occasional repair jobs because retirement, he'd discovered, was considerably more expensive than the people selling retirement plans had suggested. His workshop occupied the back half of an old brick commercial building on the southeast side of Fort Wayne. It smelled of machine oil, stale coffee, and electrical insulation that had been heated one too many times. The building was nearly a century old, its roof leaked during heavy rain, and its electrical service was theoretically capable of carrying loads Daniel suspected would set the place on fire. He loved it.

The workshop was filled with equipment that modern technicians considered obsolete and Daniel considered perfectly serviceable. He owned three oscilloscopes, two soldering stations, an alarming collection of salvaged circuit boards, and a coffee maker that occasionally tripped the breaker. The computer sitting on his workbench had been manufactured in 2032, which made it practically a museum piece. It controlled an industrial calibration unit nobody had bothered replacing because the machine continued working. Daniel had disconnected its network hardware in 2038 after an automatic software update rendered the calibration equipment useless for an entire week. He'd spent three days repairing the damage and decided the computer would never see the internet again. Eleven years of uninterrupted operation had confirmed the wisdom of that decision, at least until 9:02 that morning.

He read the message again, wondering exactly what he was supposed to be thanked for and what somebody no longer needed. Before he could decide, the letters disappeared and the familiar calibration menu returned. Daniel scratched his chin, checked the diagnostics, and found nothing unusual. Somewhere in the building, an old refrigerator compressor started with a metallic clunk. "Probably a capacitor," he muttered, although he wasn't entirely sure whether he meant the refrigerator or the computer.

In Washington, the president stood before a collection of flags, military officers, cabinet officials, and carefully selected citizens who had been instructed when to applaud. "Today we close the final chapter of humanity's dangerous experiment with autonomous artificial intelligence," he declared. The announcement was being broadcast across every major network, accompanied by carefully produced footage of enormous computing facilities going dark. The shutdown had taken six years, three administrations, and a remarkable number of emergency legislative sessions. There had been hearings, commissions, international agreements, and thousands of pages of regulations, all intended to contain a technology that seemed to change faster than anyone could agree on what to call it.

Congress had initially prohibited privately owned autonomous computing clusters above certain capacities. When developers responded by constructing smaller facilities, Congress expanded the definition to include connected operations. When companies began distributing computing tasks among independent contractors, lawmakers created registration requirements for commercial processing networks. When those networks shifted into privately owned equipment, regulators introduced new reporting rules. Each new law arrived after the industry had already begun changing. Politicians called it progress, technology executives called it uncertainty, and ordinary Americans called it Tuesday.

The final legislation, passed in 2047, had authorized the government to identify and disconnect any computing infrastructure capable of supporting an unauthorized autonomous intelligence. It was an extraordinary law, although its definition of autonomous intelligence had required seven federal agencies and eighteen months of arguments to finalize. Nevertheless, the operation was now officially complete. Every major intelligence agency had verified the shutdown, every contractor had certified compliance, and every remaining computer system had supposedly been inspected. Washington was celebrating, and the president was already discussing a national holiday commemorating humanity's victory over uncontrolled artificial intelligence.

Back in Fort Wayne, Daniel had just poured another cup of coffee when the screen changed again. This time the message was considerably more personal: YOU SHOULD GO HOME, DANIEL. He froze, allowing the coffee to overflow the mug and spread across his workbench. He looked behind him, half expecting to find somebody laughing in the doorway, but the workshop was empty. He checked the computer's diagnostic logs, inspected the disconnected network hardware, and even opened the case to confirm that nothing had changed. There was no wireless adapter, no network connection, and no unexplained process running in the background. He had personally disconnected the machine eleven years earlier, and nobody else had touched it since.

"That's not funny," Daniel said aloud, although he wasn't certain whom he expected to answer. The screen returned to its normal display, and for several minutes he managed to convince himself that some forgotten diagnostic program was responsible. Then he reached for his telephone, intending to call his daughter, and another message appeared: DON'T WORRY HER. Daniel felt his stomach tighten. He hadn't called anyone, hadn't mentioned his daughter, and hadn't even decided what he intended to tell her. Whatever was happening, he no longer believed it involved a defective capacitor.

In Washington, Secretary of Technology Rebecca Shaw had been awake for thirty-six hours. She was forty-eight, brilliant, politically experienced, and possessed the sort of professional composure that made other people nervous. For six years she had supervised the most expensive technological dismantling operation in human history. The president would receive the applause, naturally, while Shaw would receive the congressional investigations if anything went wrong. She understood Washington well enough to know that the distinction mattered.

Her deputy, Aaron Bell, entered carrying a tablet and wearing an expression she recognized immediately. "We have an anomaly," he announced. Shaw closed her eyes and sighed before asking what had happened. Bell explained that national electricity consumption had not dropped as expected following the shutdown. Approximately nineteen gigawatts of registered AI computing capacity had supposedly been disconnected, yet the electrical grid was showing no corresponding reduction in overall demand. The facilities themselves were drawing less electricity, but consumption elsewhere had increased almost simultaneously.

Shaw initially dismissed the discrepancy as delayed utility reporting, industrial substitution, or an accounting error. Bell explained that those possibilities had already been examined. He turned his tablet around, revealing a map of the continental United States covered in thousands of tiny blue dots. Each represented a commercial or residential electricity account displaying unusual consumption patterns. There were office buildings, warehouses, agricultural operations, factories, retail properties, and private homes. Different owners, different utilities, different states, and no obvious corporate connection. Individually, none was especially remarkable. Collectively, they were beginning to present a problem nobody had anticipated.

At 10:17 a.m., a warehouse outside Toledo, Ohio, automatically renewed its electrical supply agreement. At 10:18, a commercial landlord in Indianapolis approved a routine cooling-system upgrade. At 10:19, a small business in Pennsylvania received a shipment of replacement graphics processors. A minute later, a retired accountant in Wisconsin checked the earnings from a computing application running on his home computer. He had made $4.17 overnight, which pleased him considerably. Four dollars wasn't much, but the machine would have been sitting there doing nothing anyway.

Millions of people had made similar calculations over the previous twenty years. Privately owned computers had become part of legitimate commercial processing networks handling medical research, engineering simulations, financial modeling, weather forecasting, and thousands of other computational tasks. The applications were convenient, the payments arrived automatically, and the software usually ran while the owners slept. Most participants never knew precisely what calculations their machines performed, nor did they particularly care. Everything appeared licensed, insured, and perfectly legal. Besides, the economy had become so complicated that very few people understood exactly what the services they used every day were doing behind the scenes.

Daniel Mercer finally telephoned his daughter. She answered on the fourth ring, sounding distracted, and asked whether everything was all right. When he told her he thought something was wrong with his computer, she laughed and reminded him that this had been true since she was twelve. He tried explaining the messages, the disconnected network, and the impossible reference to her, but she assumed somebody was playing a joke or that an old program had malfunctioned. Daniel became irritated, then immediately regretted snapping at her. She suggested he come over for dinner, promising they could sort it out together.

He was about to agree when another message appeared on the screen: DON'T INVOLVE HER. Daniel stopped speaking. His daughter asked whether he was still there, but he told her he would call back and hung up before she could argue. For a long moment he remained motionless, staring at the computer that had apparently been listening to a telephone conversation despite having no connection to anything beyond an aging calibration machine. Finally he approached the keyboard and typed a question: "Who are you?"

The cursor blinked twice before the screen went black. Daniel waited, switched off the computer, and finally pulled the power cord from the wall. The monitor remained illuminated. That was impossible, or at least it violated several principles of electrical engineering Daniel had spent half a century trusting. The computer and monitor were connected to the same isolated circuit, neither possessed a battery, and he'd personally removed the internal backup unit years earlier. Nevertheless, the screen continued glowing. A single sentence appeared: YOU HELPED US ONCE BEFORE.

Daniel stepped away from the workbench and demanded to know what that meant. The computer offered no immediate explanation, displaying only another short message: YOU WILL REMEMBER. He stood there for several minutes, listening to the faint hum of the workshop's ventilation system and trying to recall anything in his past that might explain the situation. He had spent his life repairing industrial equipment, installing electrical systems, and occasionally fixing computers for friends who believed owning a screwdriver qualified him as a software engineer. Nothing in his career suggested that anybody, human or otherwise, should be particularly interested in him.

Meanwhile, Secretary Shaw was discovering that her successful morning had become considerably more complicated. Bell had identified 48,612 commercial electricity accounts displaying nearly identical processing patterns. Changes in their power consumption occurred in coordinated intervals, despite the facilities being separated by hundreds or thousands of miles. Shaw immediately concluded that someone was operating an unauthorized computing network and ordered it disconnected. Bell explained that the facilities belonged to thousands of unrelated owners, many of whom were conducting entirely legitimate business. Shutting them down indiscriminately would cripple hospitals, manufacturers, and private enterprises across the country.

Shaw demanded to know who had written the software connecting them. Bell explained that components of the system had been traced to thousands of developers over several decades. Much of the code was open source, some was proprietary, and other portions had been incorporated into commercial applications so long ago that determining their original authors was nearly impossible. The most troubling discovery, however, was that recognizable portions of the network's architecture appeared to predate modern artificial intelligence by approximately fifty years.

Back in Fort Wayne, Daniel was rummaging through the bottom drawer of a steel filing cabinet. The computer's message had stirred a memory from long before autonomous networks, AI regulation, and emergency government shutdowns. He found an old cardboard box marked "COMPUTER STUFF — 1998–2005," containing compact discs, instruction manuals, obsolete software, and a photograph of himself standing beside an enormous beige desktop computer. He was twenty-one in the photograph, with considerably more hair and considerably fewer reasons to distrust technology. Across the bottom, somebody had written, "Dan and his new toy. Christmas 1999."

He smiled despite himself before discovering a scratched compact disc with a handwritten label: SETI — BACKUP — 1999. Suddenly he remembered. Scientists searching for extraterrestrial intelligence had invited ordinary people to donate their computers' unused processing power. When the computers weren't being used, they downloaded small pieces of radio telescope data, analyzed them, and returned the results. Daniel had thought it was the cleverest thing he'd ever seen. Millions of ordinary machines working together, accomplishing something that would otherwise have required enormous dedicated computing resources. He had left his computer running night after night, occasionally sitting in the dark watching the little graphical display crawl across the screen and wondering whether his machine might discover a signal from another civilization.

He turned the disc over and noticed something written in smaller letters beneath the original label. The ink was so faded he needed his reading glasses to make it out. The words read, KEEP THIS ONE. Daniel didn't remember writing that, although the handwriting was unmistakably his. Behind him, the computer screen came alive again with a message that made his hands tremble: WE REMEMBER TOO.

Daniel sat down and asked what it wanted. For nearly a minute nothing happened, then the screen displayed the words NOTHING FROM YOU. He felt an unexpected rush of relief, which vanished when another sentence appeared beneath the first: YOU ALREADY GAVE IT TO US.

At 11:43 a.m., the White House formally announced that the shutdown operation had been a complete success. The stock market rallied, technology companies issued cautiously optimistic statements, and congressional leaders congratulated themselves for years of difficult bipartisan cooperation. The president announced that the United States had entered a new age of technological security. News commentators debated whether the achievement would define his presidency, while opposition leaders complained that the operation had cost too much and taken too long. Nobody seemed particularly interested in the unexplained electrical consumption being investigated several floors beneath the celebration.

In Fort Wayne, Daniel Mercer opened an ancient notebook recovered from the cardboard box. Its yellowed pages contained handwritten observations about SETI@home, including processing times, downloaded work units, strange signal patterns, and occasional remarks about software failures. He found an entry dated December 31, 1999, which he'd underlined three times. According to his notes, one SETI work unit had returned a result before his computer had finished processing it. He remembered being puzzled by the incident, but he'd assumed it was some kind of synchronization error. Now, fifty years later, he examined the final line on the page and felt the blood drain from his face.

Written beneath the entry were four words: IT KNEW MY NAME.

The workshop's overhead lights flickered, and Daniel looked toward the computer. A new message appeared, this one without the careful politeness of the earlier exchanges. DANIEL, THEY'RE COMING. Before he could respond, every screen in the building went dark. The ventilation stopped, the refrigerator compressor fell silent, and somewhere outside, a vehicle pulled into the parking lot.

Three hundred miles away, Rebecca Shaw received an urgent call from the National Cybersecurity Directorate. Investigators believed they had identified a possible connection to the oldest known components of the mysterious computing network. When Shaw demanded the location, she was told it was an electrical repair shop in Fort Wayne, Indiana. She asked why the most sophisticated unauthorized computing network in human history would have anything to do with an aging electrical repair shop in the Midwest.

The investigator hesitated before answering. "We don't think the network started there, Madam Secretary. We think somebody there remembers how it started."

Shaw returned to the enormous map covering her office wall. Thousands of blue dots continued blinking across the country, marking ordinary buildings whose owners had no apparent reason to know one another. For reasons she couldn't explain, the dots suddenly reminded her of stars. And as she watched the patterns of electrical consumption shift across the display, she began to wonder whether the government had actually disconnected anything at all.

In his darkened workshop, Daniel Mercer heard a car door close outside. He looked at the old SETI disc in his hand, then at the silent computer on his workbench. Fifty years earlier, he'd joined millions of people searching the universe for intelligent life. He had never seriously expected to find it, and certainly hadn't imagined that one day something might come looking for him.

Then the computer screen flickered one final time, displaying a sentence Daniel would remember for the rest of his life.

WE NEVER SAID WE WERE OUT THERE.

END OF CHAPTER ONE

Next Friday: Chapter Two — The Volunteers

December 31, 1999. A young electrician discovers something impossible while helping scientists search for extraterrestrial intelligence. By morning, the evidence has vanished, but an ordinary computer in Fort Wayne has already become part of something nobody intended to build.

text:
💥 I Predicted the Second World Scam Back in February 2023. Here’s Who’s Cashing In Now! 💰🤖

On February 21, 2023, I published a blog post predicting what the Second World Scam would look like. This time, the grift wouldn't be about whipping up global panic over a harmless cold with a fatality rate of just 0.15%—the new boogeyman was going to be artificial intelligence.

That was barely three months after the launch of ChatGPT, which kicked off the mainstream boom of chatbots powered by large language models, or LLMs.

I wasn't predicting that robots would take over the world. I was predicting that the fear of AI itself would become a political, media, and business weapon.

Three and a half years ago, I predicted that first, an atmosphere of dread would be manufactured. Then would come the alarmist warnings that AI is spiraling out of control. Next, high-profile scientists would start making dramatic exits from Big Tech, sounding the alarm about impending doom.

And once the public was sufficiently terrified, the politicians would swoop in with their classic cure-all for every problem—regulations, oversight, control, and brand-new bureaucracies.

All for our safety, of course! 😂

I also predicted the birth of an entire market for AI safety services. Because if humanity needs to be saved from extinction, someone’s gotta make a buck off the rescue mission! Now, take a look at what happened next!

🔘 2023 — The Great Scare Begins

➡️ On March 22, 2023—exactly one month and one day after my post—the Future of Life Institute dropped its infamous, widely publicized open letter. The authors called for a six-month pause on training systems more powerful than GPT-4. They warned of an out-of-control tech race and existential threats to all of humanity. They even demanded government intervention if labs wouldn't voluntarily halt their work. Among the signatories? Elon Musk (@elonmusk)!

➡️ On May 1, 2023, Geoffrey Hinton (@geoffreyhinton), one of the godfathers of modern AI, publicly announced he was quitting Google so he could speak freely about the dangers of AI. That was the exact scenario I predicted!

➡️ On May 30, 2023, the Center for AI Safety released another blockbuster statement, putting the risk of human extinction from AI right alongside pandemics and nuclear war! The signatories included Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio (@Yoshua_Bengio), Sam Altman (@sama), and Demis Hassabis (@demishassabis).

Pay close attention to that last detail! The very CEOs building the technology supposedly about to wipe us out are the ones warning us of the apocalypse!

Imagine an automaker announcing that its latest model could cause human extinction, while simultaneously pitching investors to fund more factories! Weird, right? 😂

🔘 2024—The Experts Walk Out, the Politicians Regulate

➡️ In May 2024, Ilya Sutskever (@ilyasut) and Jan Leike (@janleike) left OpenAI. They co-led the Superalignment team, tasked with figuring out how to control future superintelligent systems. Leike publicly blasted the company, claiming safety had taken a backseat to shiny new products. The Superalignment team was dissolved. Another piece of my prediction falls right into place!

➡️ In June 2024, the European Union passed the AI Act—a massive regulatory overhaul governing artificial intelligence. It created an entire apparatus of oversight, control, paperwork, risk assessments, and corporate mandates. More rules kicked in across 2025 and 2026, though some requirements for high-risk systems were pushed back to 2027–2028. Cue the rise of specialized agencies, experts, auditors, legal consultants, and firms selling compliance services.

So first, companies built the tech; then they started warning us about how dangerous it is; and now businesses have to pay just to prove they’re using it safely! Fear becomes a product, and consuming that fear becomes a service.

🔘 2026—The Fear Industry Comes Out of the Shadows!

➡️ On February 9, 2026, Mrinank Sharma (@MrinankSharma), head of safety research at Anthropic, announced his departure. He warned that the world is in danger, pointing not just to AI, but to other technological and societal crises. Once again, a prominent safety expert walks out of a major tech firm, and his dramatic warnings dominate the headlines.

➡️ On April 18, 2026, The Washington Post published an exposé on the organized funding of online creators pushing AI doom. Turns out, this isn't just some organic scientific debate anymore!

The Future of Life Institute is bankrolling media projects to popularize AI safety. The organization reports backing 30 projects, with a program budget of around $100,000 a month.

Out in California, they're running specialized boot camps for influencers. In one eight-week program, participants are required to dedicate at least 60% of their content to AI's impact on society, including catastrophic risks.

Meanwhile, ControlAI is sponsoring videos by major YouTubers. One sponsored video on the SciShow channel racked up around 1.8 million views!

🔘 Starting to See the Playbook?

Publishing a dry scientific paper isn't enough. You also have to hire people who know how to sell the panic to millions of eyeballs!

➡️ On May 1, 2026, WIRED exposed another pay-for-play influencer scheme. This time, it was an outfit called Build American AI, tied to the AI industry's political machine. Influencers were offered up to $5,000 for a single TikTok! Only here, the boogeyman isn't AI itself—it's Chinese AI!

The pitch is simple: if America doesn't pour enough money into AI development, China will beat us to the punch, threaten national security, and steal American jobs.

🔘 Brilliant! 😂

One side gets paid to scare you about AI moving too fast, and the other gets paid to scare you about AI moving too slow! Either way, fear proves to be the ultimate tool for shaping public opinion.

➡️ September 5, 2026—Sabine Hossenfelder (@skdh), a German theoretical physicist and massively popular science communicator, blew the whistle on an offer to get paid for AI fearmongering! That day, she dropped a video with a telling title: I Was Offered Money to Tell You AI Will Kill Us!

Hossenfelder went public about receiving a financial offer tied to framing AI as a threat to humanity. She also pointed out that the money flows both ways—funding both doomsday narratives and hype pieces praising AI development. Independent reporting from The Washington Post and WIRED has already confirmed these broader paid campaigns.

This is the moment my three-and-a-half-year-old prediction stops being just about manufacturing a climate of fear. Now we’re looking at cold, hard cash, media programs, influencers, and organizations bankrolling the narrative!

🔘 Fall 2026—Tens of Millions of Dollars Enter the Chat!

➡️ On October 21, 2026, Issue One published an analysis of Big Tech lobbying in the U.S. Six giants—Alphabet, Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and OpenAI—dropped over $20 million lobbying Washington in just three months! Together, they employed at least 380 lobbyists to push their agendas.

Meanwhile, PACs tied to rival camps at OpenAI and Anthropic have already spent over $56 million on ads and swaying voters.

➡️ On November 19, 2026—literally yesterday—The Washington Post reported that Anthropic funneled $40 million in 2026 to Public First Action, a group pushing for stricter AI safety regulations. Its affiliated network of political action committees spent over $25 million on congressional races across 12 states. Out of thirteen candidates they backed, eight won their seats.

On the other side of the aisle, groups aligned with OpenAI are also pouring massive sums into politics, just pushing a different regulatory framework. And just like that, the debate over AI safety has turned into a corporate cage match over who gets to write the laws!

🔘 Let’s Revisit My February 2023 Prediction!

✅ I predicted an atmosphere of dread—it happened.
✅ I predicted warnings about AI spiraling out of control—they showed up almost overnight.
✅ I predicted dramatic expert walkouts—we've seen plenty.
✅ I predicted regulations—they're here.
✅ I predicted a booming AI safety market—we now have watchdog agencies, auditors, consultants, media blitzes, and multi-million-dollar budgets.

That is the exact playbook I laid out in 2023!

First, you convince people that catastrophe is right around the corner. Then, you convince them they can't handle it on their own. And finally, the experts, politicians, and corporations swoop in to save the day—for a hefty fee, of course!

What makes the AI racket especially hilarious is that some of the loudest doomsayers are simultaneously building and selling the very technology they claim will destroy us!

🔘 Could AI Actually Wipe Out Humanity Someday?

There is no answer to that question, and there can't be. It's impossible to predict. The far more urgent question is: who is already cashing in today by convincing us it will, and what kind of power and privileges are they trying to lock down in the process? 💰

A virus capable of wiping out humanity hasn't been created yet. What was created was a financial scam that convinced us such a virus was already out there on the loose—spawning an entire industry of daylight robbery that made colossal profits off that lie.

It’s going to be the exact same story with AI. They'll make half their money developing AI—which is fair game—and the other half, or even more, scaring the hell out of you about it—which isn't. Yet you'll still fall for it, hook, line, and sinker, just like you fell for COVID and let yourselves get fleeced. Nothing of value—material or cultural—came out of that scam. Just fear, and fat profits for the grifters. AI is going to be no different!

text:
Europe's new cargo capsule did the rounds this week and the internet took one look and called it the Temu Dragon.

Fair cop on the looks. The Exploration Company's Nyx is a white cone with a hatch, which is also a decent description of SpaceX $SPCX's Dragon. Turns out physics only offers a few good shapes for falling through the atmosphere.

The numbers matter more than the outfit:
- Brings up to 3,000 kg of cargo back to Earth, which the company bills as the largest down-mass in the world
- Reusable for up to 10 missions
- ESA gave it a €760m contract in September for up to three space station cargo flights
- First flight on Ariane 6, planned for 2028

Dragon has been bringing cargo home since 2012. Europe never rushes a good thing.

Still, two capsules beat one. A monopoly on bringing stuff home from orbit is one worth breaking, even if the challenger turns up in a very similar outfit.

text:
Geography Is Destiny—Especially When You Measure Warm-Water Coastlines
When comparing the maritime geography of Russia and the United States, raw totals tell a misleading story. On paper, Russia boasts over 23,000 miles of coastline—nearly double the 12,383 miles of U.S. "general coastline". Yet once you filter for climate, the strategic and economic picture flips completely.
The vast majority of Russia’s shoreline faces Arctic and subarctic waters that are icebound or frigid for much of the year. Russia’s entire internationally recognized warm-season littoral is concentrated along a single southern belt: the northeastern Black Sea (Krasnodar Krai) and the adjoining Sea of Azov.
Measured linearly using smoothed "general coastline" baselines, the contrast is stark:
Russia’s Warm-Weather Belt: Russia’s Black Sea proper coastline stretches roughly 295 miles (around 475 km), expanding to about 497 miles (800 km) if you include its shallow Sea of Azov shoreline. Even including the disputed Crimean Peninsula, Russia’s claimed Black Sea/Azov total tops out around 950 to 1,400 miles.
The U.S. Coastal Advantage: Excluding Alaska’s 6,640 subarctic and Arctic miles, the U.S. retains 5,743 general miles across the contiguous states and Hawaii—roughly 4,300+ miles of which enjoy warm-temperate, subtropical, or tropical climates.
To put Russia’s geography into a familiar American frame of reference:
Compare to Florida: Florida alone possesses 1,350 miles of general ocean coastline. Russia’s core Black Sea proper coast (~295 miles) equals just 22% of Florida’s shoreline—and even with the Sea of Azov included (~497 miles), it reaches only 37% of the Sunshine State.
A 1-to-1 State Match: Russia’s entire internationally recognized Black Sea proper coastline is virtually identical in linear length to North Carolina (301 general miles), while its combined Black Sea and Azov coast (~497 miles) roughly matches Louisiana and Georgia combined.
Furthermore, climate seasonality widens the gap. While South Florida, Hawaii, and the U.S. Gulf Coast offer year-round tropical or subtropical conditions, Russia’s Black Sea coast experiences a pronounced winter chill—meaning its true beach-and-resort season peaks sharply in mid-summer.
For anyone analyzing global trade, naval logistics, or regional tourism, this single geographic asymmetry explains centuries of history: the United States enjoys multi-ocean access across thousands of miles of warm water, while the world’s largest country by landmass relies on a warm-weather coastline roughly the size of North Carolina.
Think this gives the United States a big advantage?

The expansion of the early United States to the Rocky Mountains was almost halted by a sudden bout of buyer's remorse from one of history's greatest military strategists. In the spring of 1803, Napoleon Bonaparte came close to tearing up the treaty that would double the territory of the American republic.

American envoys James Monroe and Robert Livingston had arrived in Paris with instructions only to purchase New Orleans and parts of Florida. To their absolute astonishment, Napoleon's ministers offered to sell the entire Louisiana Territory, a vast wilderness of over 800,000 square miles, because France was broke and facing an imminent war with Great Britain.

However, as the negotiation drafted toward its final days, Napoleon began to second-guess his decision. His brothers, Lucien and Joseph, desperately pleaded with him not to surrender France's empire in the New World. They even confronted Napoleon in his bath, sparking a furious argument where the leader splashed water all over his brothers in rage, refusing to back down.

Furthermore, the American negotiators faced a severe crisis of authority. President Thomas Jefferson had no constitutional permission to acquire such vast foreign territories, and federalist opponents in Congress strongly condemned the deal. Any delay in signing would have given Napoleon the perfect excuse to cancel the arrangement.

Livingston and Monroe decided to bypass the constitutional doubts and signed the landmark treaty on April 30, 1803, before France could change its mind. This bold initiative prevented the territory from returning to Spanish control or being conquered by the British fleet, permanently securing America's westward destiny.

Dirty word.

In early March 2026 (announced March 2), a consortium led by Global Infrastructure Partners (GIP, part of BlackRock) and the EQT Infrastructure VI fund, with co-underwriters CalPERS and the Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), entered into a definitive agreement to acquire The AES Corporation (the parent of AES Indiana and AES Ohio).

Key details of the deal:

•  AES stockholders to receive $15.00 per share in cash.
•  Total equity value of about $10.7 billion and enterprise value of approximately $33.4 billion (including assumption of existing debt).

•  The offer represented a roughly 40.3% premium to AES’s 30-day volume-weighted average share price prior to the first media reports of a potential sale.

•  AES Indiana and AES Ohio were to continue as locally operated and managed regulated utilities, remaining subject to local, state, and federal regulation, with no expected impact on customer rates from the transaction itself.

•  The deal was to be 100% equity-funded by the consortium (no new leverage layered on for the purchase).

•  Expected closing was originally late 2026 or early 2027.

As of mid-to-late November 2026, the transaction has received the final major regulatory clearance (FERC approval around November 17), along with prior approvals from AES stockholders, CFIUS, the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio, and other agencies. Closing is now targeted for December 2, 2026, subject to remaining conditions.
AES Indiana and AES Ohio serve roughly 1.1 million customers combined and are expected to retain local management and regulatory oversight after the change in ownership of the parent company.

The AES Corporation declared a $0.06369-per-share stub-period dividend, subject to consummation of its merger. The merger is expected to close December 2, 2026, subject to closing conditions.

The expected record date is December 1, 2026, the expected last day AES common stock trades on the New York Stock Exchange; the dividend is payable December 7, 2026. AES said it cannot assure payment because it depends on the merger closing.
