The incorporation of the Republic of Texas into the United States was far from a certainty and nearly collapsed due to deep local pride and foreign geopolitical intrigue. In 1845, the Lone Star Republic was on the verge of rejecting American annexation in favor of a sovereign empire supported by European powers.

After winning its independence from Mexico in 1836, Texas spent nearly a decade operating as an independent nation. During this era, British and French diplomats worked tirelessly to prevent Texas from joining the United States, offering to negotiate formal Mexican recognition of Texan sovereignty in exchange for Texas remaining forever independent.

Many prominent Texan leaders, including former President Sam Houston, seriously entertained this European offer. They envisioned a grand independent empire stretching to the Pacific, operating as a low-tariff agricultural nation that would rival the economic power of the northern United States.

When the annexation resolution finally came before the Texas Congress in July 1845, the debate was incredibly fierce. Anti-annexation factions argued that joining the Union would strip Texas of its hard-won freedom and entangle it in the growing American sectional conflict over slavery.

Ultimately, the desire for security against Mexico and financial stability won by a razor-thin margin. The Texas Congress accepted the annexation terms, leading to statehood in December 1845. Had the vote gone the other way, Texas would have remained a permanent geopolitical buffer state, changing the entire history of the American West.

text:
Billie Jean King signed a $1 contract, risked her place at Wimbledon and lost her first match. The next season she became the first woman in sport to earn more than $100,000 in prize money in a single year.

In the video below, King tells Amna Nawaz what was at stake for the nine women who signed. “We were willing to give up our careers.” She wanted the next girl who was good enough to have somewhere to compete, to get credit for her tennis and, in King's words, “to be able to make a living.”

In 1970, the Pacific Southwest tournament in Los Angeles offered $12,500 to the men's champion and $1,500 to the women's champion. Jack Kramer, who ran it, believed the men sold the tickets. Two players had asked spectators at the US Open which matches they liked watching. The men they spoke to slightly favoured men's matches. The women liked both equally.

Gladys Heldman, who published World Tennis magazine, found a way to test Kramer's theory. The Houston Racquet Club agreed to host a women's tournament. Local ticket sales were meant to cover $5,000 in prize money. A cigarette company put up another $2,500 for the naming rights. Heldman's contract with each player ran for one week. The fee was a dollar.

King says that about five minutes before the players posed with their dollar bills, she phoned Alastair Martin, president of the US Lawn Tennis Association. If he agreed to back a women's tour, she would go round the corner and tell the others they could put the money away. He told her the association would suspend them if they signed.

King had just had knee surgery. She only entered the Houston draw when another player pulled out. Judy Dalton beat her in straight sets, and King's doubles partner Rosie Casals won the title. By the next season the players had 21 tournaments to enter and about $336,000 in prize money between them.

I think two photographs of King's hands belong side by side. On 19 November, aged 82, she pressed them into wet cement outside the Chinese Theatre in Hollywood. In Houston, she remembers someone saving her a place in the line and handing her a dollar. She had spent the last few minutes trying to strike a deal that would make that photograph unnecessary.

If you sell one ticket for both draws, be careful who you credit for the sale, because the till records the price and never asks which match the buyer came to see.

Would you have signed for $1 alongside the other eight, or gone to Los Angeles for a shot at the $1,500?

What is mammon?
Answer

The word mammon comes from the Greek word mammonas. Similar root words exist in Hebrew, Latin, Aramaic, Chaldean, and Syriac. They all translate to “money, wealth, and material possessions.”

In biblical culture the word mammon often carried a negative connotation. It was sometimes used to describe all lusts and excesses: gluttony, greed, and dishonest worldly gain. Ultimately, mammon described an idol of materialism, which many trusted as a foundation for their world and philosophy. While the King James Version retains the term Mammon in Matthew 6:24, other versions translate the Greek as “money,” “wealth,” or “riches.”

The city of Babylon (Revelation 18), with all its avarice and greed, is a description of a world given over to the spirit of Mammon. Some scholars cite Mammon as the name of a Syrian and Chaldean god, similar to the Greek god of wealth, Plutus.

Just as Wisdom is personified in Proverbs 1:21–33, Mammon is personified in Matthew 6:24 and Luke 16:13. Jesus’ words here show a powerful contrast between the worship of the material world and the worship of God. Later, writers such as Augustine, Danté (The Divine Comedy), Milton (Paradise Lost), and Spenser (The Faerie Queene) used personifications of Mammon to show the insidious nature of materialism and its seduction of humanity.

Worship of mammon can show up in many ways. It isn’t always through a continual lust for more money. When we envy others’ wealth, are anxious over potentially unmet needs, disobey God’s directives about the use of wealth, or fail to trust God’s love and faithfulness, our thinking is out of balance concerning material wealth.

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus teaches about our relationship to material goods. He says, “Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth. . . . But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven. . . . For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. . . . No one can serve two masters. Either you will hate the one and love the other, or you will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money [mammon]” (Matthew 6:19–24).

The apostle Paul writes of the godly perspective toward mammon: “Godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and we can take nothing out of it. But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with that. Those who want to get rich fall into temptation and a trap and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager for money, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs” (1 Timothy 6: 6–10).

Solomon writes of the futility of chasing after mammon: “Whoever loves money never has enough; whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with their income. This too is meaningless” (Ecclesiastes 5:10). Lust of any kind is insatiable, no matter how much time or effort is poured into the pursuit of the object of lust.

In Luke 16:14–15, Jesus rebukes those who refused to hear His admonition to choose God over mammon: “The Pharisees, who loved money, heard all this and were sneering at Jesus. He said to them, ‘You are the ones who justify yourselves in the eyes of others, but God knows your hearts. What people value highly is detestable in God’s sight.’”

The parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:13–21) is the story of a man who lives to increase his wealth yet in the end he loses his soul because he “is not rich toward God” (verse 21). Mark 4:19 warns of the deceitfulness of mammon and its ability to “choke the Word, making it unfruitful.”

Mammon cannot produce peace in us, and it certainly cannot produce righteousness. A love of money shows we are out of balance in our relationship to God. Proverbs 8:18 speaks of true, lasting riches: “With me [Wisdom] are riches and honor, enduring wealth and prosperity.” Jesus teaches us in Matthew 6:19–34 to not worry about our physical needs, about houses or clothes or food, but to “seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well” (verse 33).

text:
My landlord evicted me for refusing to pay $3,000 in extra rent, so i bought the house next door… only to discover that he had been collecting rent from tenants in a property he didn't even own.

I was living in a three-bedroom apartment in Dallas, Texas, with my wife and our six-year-old son.

We had been tenants for almost four years, and I had never missed rent.

My landlord, Mr. Peterson, was an older man who owned several rental properties around the neighbourhood.

Everything was fine until he suddenly announced that our monthly rent would increase by $3,000.

I thought he was joking.

Our rent was already $2,100, and he wanted us to start paying $5,100.

When I asked him to explain, he simply said the neighbourhood had become expensive and I either had to accept the new price or move out.

I refused.

Two weeks later, I received an eviction notice.

My wife was devastated because our son had just started school nearby, and moving would mean disrupting his entire routine.

I tried negotiating with the landlord, but he told me something I'll never forget.

"If you cannot afford to live here, perhaps you should stop pretending you belong in this neighbourhood."

I was embarrassed, angry, and determined not to let him humiliate my family.

I eventually found another house two streets away and started moving our belongings.

But something unexpected happened during the moving process.

A real estate agent contacted me about a property that had just gone up for sale.

It was a beautiful four-bedroom house directly opposite our former apartment.

I had enough savings from selling my construction company shares, so I decided to make an offer.

Three weeks later, the house was officially mine.

On the day I moved in, I noticed Mr. Peterson standing outside my former apartment, arguing with a delivery driver.

He saw me carrying furniture into my new house and started laughing.

"Well, look who's trying to live like a millionaire!"

I ignored him.

But the following Monday, three strangers knocked on my door.

They introduced themselves as tenants from the apartment building I had just moved out of.

One of them handed me a folder.

Inside were rent receipts, bank transfers, and copies of property documents.

They explained that Mr. Peterson had been collecting rent from several tenants for years, claiming he was the owner.

However, the actual owner had died, and the property was part of an inheritance dispute.

The tenants had recently discovered that the man collecting their money wasn't legally authorised to manage the building.

I was shocked.

I contacted the attorney who handled my house purchase and asked him to investigate.

What he uncovered was unbelievable.

Mr. Peterson didn't own the apartment building at all.

He had been managing it under an arrangement that expired years earlier, but continued collecting rent without proper authority.

And the $3,000 increase he demanded from me?

Apparently, he had been telling other tenants the same story.

I thought that was the end of it.

Until one evening, I received a knock on my door.

It was Mr. Peterson.

He looked completely different from the arrogant man I knew.

He was sweating, holding a brown envelope, and asking me to let him inside.

I asked what he wanted.

He looked around, lowered his voice, and said:

"Please, I need you to help me. Those tenants have reported me, and the authorities are investigating everything."

I almost laughed.

text:
I do not know whether it is by design or coincidence, but Edwin Sifuna’s itinerary to the United States is rather interesting. Almost every state he is scheduled to visit has a history that speaks to some of the very issues he has been raising back home in Kenya.

His trip begins in New Jersey, where the Linda Mwananchi Movement plans to open an office in Hackettstown.

New Jersey has an important place in American history. It was the third state to ratify the Constitution, but even before that, it had witnessed one of the defining moments of America’s struggle for independence.

On Christmas night in 1776, George Washington led his army across the icy Delaware River from Pennsylvania into New Jersey. The following morning, his troops surprised British-allied Hessian forces at Trenton and secured a victory that revived a revolution many feared was collapsing.

From New Jersey, Sifuna heads to Pennsylvania for a town hall meeting. And this is where the itinerary becomes even more interesting.

Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, is where America’s Declaration of Independence was adopted in 1776. 11 years later, delegates gathered in the same city to draft the Constitution that would become the foundation of American government.

For a Kenyan politician who has made constitutionalism and the defence of democratic institutions central to his political message, that is quite a place to visit.

Next are Maryland and Washington, D.C.

Washington is, of course, the seat of American political power. It is where Congress makes laws, the Supreme Court interprets them, and the president exercises executive authority.

Maryland has its own story worth telling. In 1864, while America was fighting a civil war over slavery and the future of the Union, Maryland adopted a new constitution abolishing slavery within the state. It was a major political achievement, secured through a bitter struggle over who deserved freedom and the protection of the law.

On November 27, Sifuna travels to Dallas, Texas, for a Thanksgiving dinner. Two days later, he is scheduled to address a women’s caucus and town hall meeting in Houston.

Texas is another interesting stop. Before joining the United States in 1845, it had spent nearly a decade as an independent republic. Its history is full of arguments about independence, political identity and the relationship between citizens and their government.

But Houston offers another story, particularly relevant to the women’s caucus and this must have been some genius move by Sifuna’s team…

In 1966, a young Black lawyer named Barbara Jordan was elected to the Texas Senate, becoming the first Black woman to serve there. Six years later, she became the first Black woman from the American South elected to the U.S. House of Representatives.

Jordan had grown up in Houston at a time when segregation limited opportunities for Black Americans. Her political success was not handed to her. She had to build support, win elections and persuade people who had been excluded from political power that their voices mattered.

From Texas, Sifuna heads to Seattle, Washington, a city with a large Kenyan community. In fact, Washington state is increasingly mentioned alongside Texas whenever Kenyans discuss where their compatriots have settled in America.

There is another historical connection here.

In 1910, Washington became the fifth American state to grant women voting rights on equal terms with men. That was ten years before the Nineteenth Amendment prohibited denying women the vote on the basis of sex across the United States.

Think about that. Women in Washington were voting in state elections while millions of other American women were still fighting for the same right.

And finally, California.

Sifuna is expected to address a town hall meeting in San Francisco, attend a gala dinner in Oakland and, two days later, visit Silicon Valley.

California has a long history of political activism. San Francisco played an important role in the civil rights movement, while Oakland became the birthplace of the Black Panther Party in 1966. The party was founded by Huey Newton and Bobby Seale, who believed Black communities needed to organise politically and defend themselves against police brutality.

But there is something else about this California leg that caught my attention.

I do not know whether those organising Sifuna’s visit have arranged for him to stop in East Palo Alto. If they haven’t, they should consider it.

You see, in the late 1960s, when residents were discussing the future identity of East Palo Alto, one of the names proposed for the community was Nairobi.

Imagine that! Sifuna could find himself in Nairobi while thousands of miles away from the Nairobi he represents in the Kenyan Senate.

And just across the municipal boundary is Palo Alto, one of the best-known communities in Silicon Valley.

We often associate Silicon Valley with technology companies, billionaires and extraordinary wealth. But there is another side to its history that politicians understand very well. It is a place where people with money and influence have helped turn relatively unknown individuals and their ideas into national and sometimes global forces.

Which brings me to Barack Obama.

Years ago, I interviewed some Kenyans who told me about being invited to a political fundraising gathering in Silicon Valley. Among the politicians seeking support was a relatively unknown young man from Illinois named Barack Obama.

This was around 2000, long before Obama became a household name. At the time, he was a state senator trying to establish himself in American politics. He had not yet delivered the speeches that would fill stadiums, inspired millions of people or made history as America’s first Black president.

According to the Kenyans I interviewed, they did not think much of him. To them, Obama was just another politician looking for money and attention.

So they gave him a wide berth.

Four years later, that same man stood before the Democratic National Convention in Boston and delivered a speech that introduced him to millions of Americans.

By 2008, he was president-elect of the United States.

Now, I am not suggesting Edwin Sifuna is another Barack Obama, or that a visit to Silicon Valley will somehow change his political fortunes.

Sometimes the people who eventually shape a country’s political future are not the ones everyone is rushing to meet today. And sometimes those who have the opportunity to support them do not recognise what is standing right in front of them.

Isitoshe

The first six positions reproduce the commonly taught NLP model for a supposedly typical right-handed individual. Different NLP sources acknowledge reversed or individually differing patterns.
Sources: NLP eye-accessing model · NLP practitioner material NLP Center
Evidence status
These are genuine, documented claims from NLP literature.
However, they are not established neurological mappings. Experimental investigations, including Wiseman and colleagues' 2012 studies, did not support the proposed eye-direction rules for identifying lies.
An earlier experimental investigation also tested whether eye positions corresponded to visual, auditory, and kinesthetic processing. DOI
That distinction gives our project two separate questions:
Do particular mental tasks produce measurable patterns of eye movement?
Can an individual's previously measured patterns predict what type of mental processing they are performing?
The second question is testable without assuming that the traditional NLP chart must be correct.

An important correction to simplistic eye-reading theories:
Looking right does not mean the right hemisphere is exclusively active, and looking left does not mean the left hemisphere is exclusively active.
Eye movements engage distributed neural networks. Different cognitive tasks can modify those networks' activity without yielding a universal direction-to-thought mapping.
Source: Cranial Nerves III, IV, and VI: Oculomotor Function. PubMed Central (PMC)

4. Eye Direction and Memory Retrieval
This is one of the strongest scientifically supported connections to your research.
The Looking-at-Nothing phenomenon
Researchers have demonstrated that people sometimes look toward locations previously associated with information, even after that information has disappeared.
For example:
A person sees an object in the upper-right part of a room.
Later, when asked to remember the object, their eyes may return toward that location.
The object is no longer present.
Their eye movement can nevertheless be associated with retrieving the spatial memory.
Research has also investigated whether reproducing earlier eye positions can facilitate remembering spatial relationships.

Some experiments support a functional role for these movements; other studies find that the effect depends on the memory task.

Sources: Johansson and Johansson — Eye Movements and Memory Retrieval · Eye Movements Actively Reinstate Spatiotemporal Mnemonic Content. PubMed

Project implication

Rather than simply recording whether a person looks left or right, EDEN could record:

Where the original information was presented.

Where the subject looked during initial observation.

Where the subject looked during recollection.

Whether their earlier scan pattern reappeared.
How accurately they recalled the information.

This creates a measurable connection between eye movements and memory.

It does not establish whether the recalled account is truthful.

5. Lighting Direction, 
Pupil Response, and Gaze Perception
Your observation about the direction 
of incoming light is particularly relevant.

A. Pupil constriction and dilation
Pupil diameter responds to multiple influences:
InfluencePotential observable effectIncreased lightPupil constrictionDecreased lightPupil dilationIncreased cognitive effortOften pupil dilationEmotional arousalCan produce dilationSurpriseCan alter pupil sizeFatigueChanges in pupil behaviorMedicationPossible constriction or dilationEye movement angleApparent pupil-size measurement errorBlinkingTemporary disruption of visual input and pupil measurements
The size of an observed pupil is therefore not a direct measurement of one specific emotion or thought.
The same pupil diameter might arise from multiple combinations of lighting, physiology, and cognitive activity.
Research demonstrates that luminance can substantially alter the pupil response associated with emotional arousal or mental effort. PubMed Central (PMC)

B. Light direction changes apparent gaze
A study published March 13, 2026, titled Gaze Perception Under Vertical Asymmetries in Illumination, investigated how changing the elevation of a light source influences judgments of gaze direction.
The researchers found systematic changes in perceived gaze direction despite the eyes themselves maintaining the same orientation.
A separate 2026 study investigated reflections on the eye's surface, called eye glints, and their contribution to gaze perception.

Sources: 2026 Illumination Study ·
 Eye Glint as a Novel Perceptual Cue. Nature
Critical measurement variables
For our project, record:
Light source position + intensity + color temperature + head orientation + eye orientation + camera position + pupil diameter.
Also distinguish:
Direction of the light source relative to the face.
Actual gaze direction.
Direction of light entering the pupil.
Distribution of illumination across the retina.
Apparent gaze direction judged by an observer.
These quantities interact but are not interchangeable.
A person looking upward changes which parts of the environment fall on different retinal regions. That does not automatically activate a particular memory center.

6. FBI Behavioral Analysis and Deception Research
The FBI's published material includes several different approaches to behavioral assessment.
Historical investigative claims
Investigators have examined:
ObservationProposed relevanceGaze avoidanceDiscomfort, anxiety, or alleged concealmentIncreased eye contactPossible deliberate impression managementReduced blinkingConcentration or heightened attentionIncreased blinkingPhysiological arousal or stressLip compressionTension or emotional regulationFacial asymmetryPossible emotional-expression changesResponse delayCognitive processing or hesitationSelf-touchingPossible self-soothing behaviorPosture changesChanges in comfort or engagementBehavioral clustersCombined changes around a particular question
These observations have appeared in investigative interviewing literature, but interpretations vary.
An FBI Law Enforcement Bulletin article from 2001 discussed observing behavioral clusters and questioned the assumption that liars necessarily avoid eye contact.
A 2011 article explicitly stated that eye behavior and gaze aversion do not reliably establish truthfulness. FBI: Law Enforcement Bulletin
What broader experiments establish
A meta-analysis of nonverbal deception research found no evidence that people generally avoid eye contact while lying.
A scientific review published through the FBI's High-Value Detainee Interrogation Group similarly found common behavioral indicators such as gaze aversion, fidgeting, and hesitation unreliable for detecting deception. DOI
Project implication: Eye behavior should be recorded as behavioral evidence, but not converted directly into a probability of dishonesty.
A statement can instead be evaluated against verifiable facts, timelines, documents, and independently corroborated information.

We should connect the eye-movement system with our existing facial-action research.

10. Experimental Protocol: Testing Eye Direction Against Mental Activity
The most useful development would be a controlled dataset.
Tasks
TaskExampleVisual memoryRecall the color of a previously viewed objectVisual constructionImagine an unfamiliar objectAuditory memoryRecall a familiar person's voiceAuditory constructionImagine two unfamiliar sounds combinedInternal dialogueSilently rehearse a sentenceKinesthetic memoryRecall the sensation of holding somethingSpatial memoryRecall an object's locationMental arithmeticPerform calculations without speakingFree recollectionDescribe a previous eventVisual attentionFollow a moving targetNeutral baselineRest while looking at a fixed point
Experimental controls
For each participant:
Establish ordinary gaze behavior.
Measure gaze and pupil activity under controlled lighting.
Present randomized cognitive tasks.
Record the eye movements and task timing.
Repeat tasks across multiple sessions.
Test whether eye patterns predict task categories.
Compare individual models against population models.
Evaluate predictions on previously unseen trials.
Key statistical test: Does eye direction predict cognitive-task category more accurately than chance when evaluated on held-out data?
This would let us directly investigate your hypothesis that individuals possess recognizable eye-movement patterns associated with cognitive processing.
It also allows traditional NLP predictions to be tested separately from individualized patterns.

Integration With Your Existing Research
This material expands the previously recovered work on lip ratios, facial geometry, microexpressions, body language, voice, breathing, behavioral baselines, and QUALIA.

The most useful distinction for EDEN is between an observable signal, its neurological mechanism, and its proposed psychological meaning.

For example, a rightward eye movement is directly observable. Its neurological execution can be studied. Whether it indicates visual construction, attention, memory retrieval, or another activity requires additional evidence.

Your proposed individualized-baseline approach gives us a way to test those interpretations without throwing away the historical theories or assuming that they have already been demonstrated.

Research status: This is a substantial expansion covering the principal theories and scientific disciplines, not an exhaustive inventory of every publication on eye movement. The next research layer is a source-indexed experimental database organized by eye movement, cognitive task, neurological pathway, environmental condition, and observed outcome.
